Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers
Two Barracuda ESG Flaws Could Be Combined for Full Root Access; Patches Released
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: An attacker with administrator privileges could exploit it to execute operating system commands as root
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Barracuda patched two flaws that can be chained to give attackers root access to Email Security Gateway appliances.

Barracuda has patched two vulnerabilities that can be chained to gain root access to its Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances. CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score of 9.3) is an authentication bypass that lets unauthenticated attackers modify appliance configurations. CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score of 8.6) is a command injection flaw affecting six Barracuda products.

An attacker with administrator privileges could exploit it to execute operating system commands as root.

“Barracuda has identified two vulnerabilities affecting certain Barracuda products: a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability and a command injection vulnerability. The vulnerabilities have been assigned CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, respectively.” states the advisory. “Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device.”

Barracuda quickly began fixing the problem and released security patches for affected products. Customers should check the affected products and follow the remediation guidance, make sure their systems use the latest firmware, and install all security patches.

It has released patches and urges customers to update their systems, below are the affected products:

Email Security Gateway (ESG) — affected by both vulnerabilities; patch with BNSF-40425 for version 9.4.017 or later, or BNSF-40430 for versions below 9.4.017.

Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNADC-16586.

Message Archiver (BMA) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNMA-32468.

WAF Control Center (WCC) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNWF-60060.

Web Application Firewall (WAF) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNADC-16586.

Web Security Gateway (WSG) — affected by CVE-2026-111560; patch with BNYF-24789.

The vendor recommends that customers:

Restrict administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and use network access controls to reduce exposure.

Check that devices are running the latest firmware and that all security patches are installed.

If a device is several versions behind, install updates step by step; more than one update may be needed.

Contact Barracuda Support if help is required.

“If a patch has not been automatically applied, customers should manually apply the appropriate patch as soon as possible. If customers have turned off automatic patching, Barracuda recommends setting devices to automatically receive patches.” concludes the advisory.

“Guidance on how to manually apply the patch or update firmware can be found on Barracuda Campus.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Barracuda)

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Zyxel fixes zero-day exploited to hack nearly 1,000 network switches
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attacks linked to zero-day flaw On June 16, 2026, Zyxel released security updates addressing CVE-2026-7273, a pre-authentication buffer overflow vulnerability affecting the same...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that hackers exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441, is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management interface that allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to execute operating system commands using specially crafted HTTP requests.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 switch models, and Zyxel released security updates on October 22 and published a security advisory on November 3.

However, the vulnerability was initially mistaken for an older flaw that Zyxel had already patched months before the attacks began.

Attacks linked to zero-day flaw

On June 16, 2026, Zyxel released security updates addressing CVE-2026-7273, a pre-authentication buffer overflow vulnerability affecting the same GS1900 switches.

Starting around August 17, cybersecurity company GreyNoise observed a suspected Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala exploiting Zyxel switches, reporting that the attackers compromised 996 devices across 48 countries.

The threat actors exploited the flaw to execute commands remotely before downloading a script that collected device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information.

GreyNoise linked Kapibala to the Red Heron hacking campaign, which Acronis previously reported was exploiting a critical vulnerability in the self-hosted Git service Gitea.

When GreyNoise disclosed the campaign on September 21, it attributed the exploitation to CVE-2026-7273, the vulnerability Zyxel had patched in June.

That same day, CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring federal agencies to address the flaw.

However, researchers at firmware security company Binarly discovered that the exploit used in the attacks actually targeted a separate, previously unknown vulnerability that remained unpatched.

While investigating Red Heron infrastructure linked to the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT rootkit, Binarly researchers found an exposed archive containing an obfuscated Python exploit targeting Zyxel GS1900 switches.

After analyzing the exploit, the researchers found that it specifically checked for firmware versions patched for CVE-2026-7273, indicating the exploit had been developed or updated to target those versions.

Binarly confirmed on September 28 that the exploit remained effective against all ten firmware releases patched for CVE-2026-7273.

The researchers determined that the earlier security update added checks to prevent a buffer overflow, but attackers could bypass them by corrupting a parameter counter before it was validated.

This allowed the exploit to overwrite memory and execute commands without authentication, even on switches running the earlier security updates.

Binarly reported its findings to Zyxel on September 29, and the vendor confirmed the new vulnerability on October 11, assigning it CVE-2026-107441.

Zyxel classified it as a separate flaw because the exploit also abused missing validation of HTTP parameter lengths.

On October 22, Zyxel released new firmware updates that limit parameter sizes and validate the parameter count before copying data into memory, preventing the exploitation technique.

While the recovered exploit specifically targeted firmware patched for CVE-2026-7273, it remains unclear whether it was deliberately developed to bypass those updates or exploited a related vulnerability that the earlier patches failed to address.

Administrators of affected Zyxel GS1900 switches are advised to install the latest firmware updates to protect against CVE-2026-107441.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Lets MitM Attackers Swap Verified Packages and Run Code as Root
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: APT's developers, who call the flaw critical, say updates for Ubuntu and its Ubuntu Pro subscription service are being released
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A flaw in APT, the package manager for Debian and Ubuntu, allows an attacker who can modify package downloads to swap a checked package for their own.

The attacker's code then runs as root, according to advisories that Debian, Ubuntu, and APT's developers published on November 4. The attack needs APT to retry failed downloads, which it does by default from Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 onward.

Debian has released fixed versions of APT for the flaw, CVE-2026-109518. APT's developers, who call the flaw critical, say updates for Ubuntu and its Ubuntu Pro subscription service are being released. Ubuntu 14.04 users with Ubuntu Pro can already get one.

Older releases, such as Debian 11 and Ubuntu 20.04, are not exposed by default, according to Ubuntu. But many user scripts may have turned on the retry setting, Acquire::Retries, on those releases anyway, APT's developers say.

Debian's testing branch was still on the vulnerable version 3.3.5 at 14:58 UTC on November 4. For Debian 11, whose Debian long-term support ended on August 31, APT's developers have published a fixed version, 2.2.5.

Ubuntu rates the flaw as high priority, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7, and says that distributions built on Debian and Ubuntu are affected as well, without naming any.

Ubuntu published new APT builds for four of its releases to its security archive at 14:25 UTC on November 4:

Ubuntu 26.10: 3.3.3ubuntu0.1

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS: 3.2.1ubuntu0.1

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS: 2.8.4ubuntu0.1

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS: 2.4.15ubuntu0.1

At 15:46 UTC, Ubuntu still marked all eight releases it tracks for the flaw, from 14.04 LTS to 26.10, as vulnerable.

The attacker can be anyone who can change the HTTP traffic between APT and the package server, including a malicious mirror or proxy, according to Ubuntu. The attack runs when the computer installs a package. The attacker uses HTTP redirects and ordinary temporary server errors to make APT retry the download, APT's developers say.

Max Justicz reported the flaw. None of the three advisory reports describe attacks exploiting the flaw or offer a workaround for systems that cannot update yet. They describe the attack over HTTP and do not say whether package sources reached over HTTPS are exposed.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: SonicWall Won't Patch EoL GMS Flaws That Could Expose Files, Alter Database Records
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
SonicWall has warned of two vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that it said will not be patched.

Details of the security flaws, which affect SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions, are below -

CVE-2026-109593 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An unauthenticated file read vulnerability that could allow an attacker with network access to read internal GMS files, potentially exposing sensitive information.

CVE-2026-109594 (CVSS score: 6.8) - A post-authentication SQL injection vulnerability that could allow an authenticated attacker to access or modify information stored in the GMS database under specific conditions.

"The affected product has reached End-of-life (EoL)," SonicWall said in a Tuesday alert.

"As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities. Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."

The development comes less than a month after SonicWall shipped fixes for CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that could have allowed an attacker to reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

The vulnerability has since come under active exploitation in the wild, with telemetry data from Previdian recording 2,541 attack attempts from eight unique IP addresses from Singapore and the U.S. since October 9, 2026. As many as 30 exploitation attempts were registered on November 3, 2026.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Google Calendar phishing campaign hijacks sessions, bypasses MFA
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Material Security’s Threat Research team identified the campaign and has taken down hundreds of domains used by attackers in what they have dubbed Operation CloudFire
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been harvesting live Google sessions from corporate users. Every signal defenders usually rely on to judge a link returned a reassuring answer, and the operator built the chain that way on purpose.

Material Security’s Threat Research team identified the campaign and has taken down hundreds of domains used by attackers in what they have dubbed Operation CloudFire. Here’s what they learned along the way.

The lure: Google Calendar invites

The messages arrive as Google Calendar invites, sometimes delivered by BCC and often sent from an organization the recipient has already corresponded with. The pretexts are mundane: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices.

Most links point to Google itself. The typical pattern is Google’s own /url redirector with the real destination in a query parameter, though other waves used share.google and Drive file links for the same purpose. One variant used Intuit transaction notification links.

In every case, when the message is scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation displayed are legitimate and trusted.

The capture: Reverse proxy in front of a Google sign-in page

The attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the genuine Google sign-in page. The victim enters a password, receives a real prompt, and approves it, all while the operator watches the session in real time.

The server relays SMS codes, authenticator codes, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, and phone-based account recovery to Google as each one arrives, so none of the second-factor controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind this, Nyasher, has been documented publicly since February, after a hardcoded key was found in its JavaScript.

Why the controls don’t fire

Reputation systems answer a question about ownership: who registered the domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was assembled so that those answers were consistently benign, and it has three layers.

The first layer is Google’s redirector. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, which in some builds is the genuine widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third layer is the password-capture page itself, which has no static website to scan.

The Javascript constructs it in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. To Material’s knowledge, no one had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

The infrastructure is disposable by design. The initially observed campaign used many lure domains across multiple registrars, most registered only days before use. Receiving endpoints were staged one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served.

One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was registered. Blocking any single component costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon of work.

Automated Email Security for Google Workspace & Microsoft 365

Material detects and remediates phishing, BEC, and targeted attacks automatically, even after delivery.

No complex rulesets, no user quarantines, no endless manual triage.

Get a Demo

What defending it has looked like

Material has tracked the campaign since its start, following each variant as lures, gates, and receiving endpoints rotated. Since August, once the campaign was identified and detections built, Material has caught over 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%.

This has been a continuous effort as the attacker shifted their TTP’s, themes and lure text to evade static, ML and agentic detections.

The approach works because no single signal decides the outcome. Reputation alone would not have caught this, and neither would link analysis by itself, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser constructs it.

Material scores technical indicators, the apparent intent of the message, where links actually resolve, and the sending relationship behind the message. Any one of those can be enough to act on.

A detection built around one signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has spent considerable effort mapping them.

Where the analysis runs also matters. A calendar invite is a poor fit for a gateway designed to inspect mail in transit, yet much of this campaign arrives as an invite.

Material treats calendar invites as a threat surface in their own right and uses the account’s full history as context alongside the technical signals.

Where the damage lands

When the outcome is a hijacked session rather than a stolen password, the evidence appears in Workspace audit logs. A live Google session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius extends well past the inbox.

Defenders should ask two questions: who is reviewing those logs, and how quickly can they be acted on? Equally important is whether the team can revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour.

Many programs cannot, and an attacker with a live session can do a great deal in that time.

Operation CloudFire: Targeting the infrastructure

By late September, Material concluded that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents would not solve the problem alone. Detection protects customers but does nothing about the operator who is preparing the next wave.

Material’s Threat Research team therefore launched Operation CloudFire to target the infrastructure itself.

The team analyzed the gateway and backend URLs as the messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team validated the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then applied its own phishing interstitial to those destinations.

This had two effects. The attacker’s infrastructure was burned: each reported gateway and receiving endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. The broader internet also benefited.

Anyone who clicked a reported link, whether or not they were a Material customer, saw a warning rather than a credential form.

The numbers over one month

These figures come only from customers who agreed to share data with Material, so the true totals are higher. Over a month of Operation CloudFire, Material recorded:

68,676 campaign messages blocked

2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed

897 unique domains taken down

8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains

Send cadence that followed US business hours

The sender count shows how the campaign achieved its credibility. Each compromised address belonged to an account the attacker controlled before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the victim’s saved contacts, among other addresses.

Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a plausible time. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it, so every layer that scores ownership and history returned a reassuring result.

Where things stand

The phishing themes have shifted, from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Material has not seen a matching rise in other lures or TTPs, and activity from this group appears to have dispersed. The campaign looks finished.

That is a status update, not a verdict. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, the framework has been public since February, and the operator shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code.

The branch includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the brand requires dropping in a file rather than changing any code.

The operator has built the follow-on and has not activated it. Material reads the theme rotation as iteration, not retirement, and expects the next pivot to look much like this one with a different brand.

The full technical breakdown, including indicators and a timeline, is available in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: SonicWall warns of unpatched flaws in end-of-life GMS software
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: " Attackers often target SonicWall vulnerabilities in the wild and have exploited multiple ones in zero-day attacks since the start of the year
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
SonicWall warned customers of two security flaws affecting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that will not be patched.

Global Management System (GMS) helps IT admins deploy and manage thousands of SonicWall security appliances from a single interface, but SonicWall has officially replaced it with the Network Security Manager (NSM) management platform.

The two vulnerabilities were found and reported by Pentest-Tools security researchers and affect systems running SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier.

The first GMS flaw disclosed this week is tracked as CVE-2026-109593, and it enables unauthenticated attackers with network access to vulnerable instances (running GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions) to steal sensitive information by reading internal files.

SonicWall also flagged a second security issue (CVE-2026-109594) that can let threat actors with high privileges access or modify information stored in the GMS database through low-complexity SQL Injection attacks.

On Tuesday, SonicWall also urged customers to upgrade to NMS, as it will not release security patches because the vulnerable systems have now reached end of life.

"The affected product has reached End-of-Life (EOL). As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities," SonicWall warned on Tuesday.

"Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."

Attackers often target SonicWall vulnerabilities in the wild and have exploited multiple ones in zero-day attacks since the start of the year.

In February, SonicWall asked customers to patch two SMA1000 zero-days (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) and two more (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) in July. It also patched three other SMA1000 flaws exploited as zero-days in September (CVE-2026-83548 and CVE-2026-83549) and October (CVE-2026-102255).

Over the last four years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added 19 SonicWall vulnerabilities to its list of actively exploited flaws, 13 of them also abused by ransomware gangs.

SonicWall serves more than 500,000 customers (including small and medium-sized businesses, large enterprises, and government agencies) in more than 215 countries and territories through a network of over 17,000 partners.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: APT29-Linked Hackers Hijack Web Analytics Script to Deliver iOS and Android Exploits
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: 7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
The Russia-linked threat actor known as APT29 is said to be behind a large-scale watering hole campaign targeting iOS and Android users through compromised websites, fake domains, and a supply chain attack involving a Ukrainian web analytics service called Plerdy SEO Tracker.

"The injected JavaScript code collects browser and device attributes," Sekoia researchers Amaury-Jacques Garçon and Félix Aime said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "Then, the delivery infrastructure delivers a platform-specific N-day exploit chain targeting either iOS or Android."

The end goal of the attacks is to serve payloads capable of stealing browser cookies, and in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords or full mobile device data. The activity, codenamed Poisoned Source, was discovered by the French cybersecurity company in mid-October 2026.

A defining aspect of the campaign is the use of three infection vectors -

Compromise of legitimate websites to inject malicious JavaScript

Lookalike sites masquerading as high-profile websites in the U.S. ("america250[.]holiday"), Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Bulgaria

Supply chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026, by injecting malicious code into "a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js"

Some of the compromised websites include a major industry trade association representing U.S. companies operating in the chemical industry, a far-right European political party, and a Bulgarian military-related website. It's suspected that the watering hole campaign may have been designed to target specific individuals rather than a broad effort.

"It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest," Sekoia said.

"However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war. This supply chain attack spread through high-value targets, such as army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) websites."

Regardless of the method employed, all roads lead to the same payload: a JavaScript loader that profiles the visitor's device and web browser, and then serves appropriate next-stage malware. For iOS users, it leads to an exploit kit called DarkSword to harvest cookies and full device data.

On Android, the malware is equipped to exfiltrate Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence. No less than three different exploits have been identified -

Class A, which targets iOS devices running iOS 16.7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft.

Class B, which targets iOS devices running iOS 18.5 and exploits the DarkSword exploit chain comprising CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 to deliver JavaScript malware for full device data exfiltration. This includes SMS messages and iMessages; Apple Mail Envelope Index and Protected Index SQLite databases; voicemail; WhatsApp and Telegram databases; iCloud Keychain, Wi-Fi passwords; contacts; call history; Safari browser history and cookies; photos; and data from Apple Health, Calendar, Notes, and iCloud Drive.

Class C, which targets Android devices running Chrome versions from 139 through 145 (but explicitly excluding version 143 for reasons that remain presently unknown) and exploits CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 to achieve remote code execution, sandbox escape, privilege escalation, and ultimately deliver AndroSnitch to collect Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords.

In all three cases, the exfiltrated data is sent to the "ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12" endpoint. The Android attack chain incorporates a check to determine whether the targeted device is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra by examining its model identifier (i.e., SM-S938B). If the device matches, the exploitation activity is terminated.

AndroSnitch derives its name from its similarities to ANDROSNATCH, a Chrome cookie-stealing payload that Google documented in August 2024 in connection with a suspected APT29 watering hole campaign, which targeted Android users visiting a Mongolian government website by leveraging a Chrome exploit chain involving CVE-2024-5274 and CVE-2024-4671.

"This operation also confirms the continued reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendors] mobile exploit frameworks, such as DarkSword, by state-sponsored intrusion sets," Sekoia said. "The adoption of packaged N-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation."

Coruna and DarkSword Kits Evolve

The development comes weeks after iVerify and Report URI detailed the P7 variant of DarkSword being delivered via half-click attacks that leverage ad-based infrastructure. In one case, the exploit is said to have been propagated through a malicious Instagram ad themed around the World Cup and served from "ad-track[.]live."

The other pathway is part of a criminal campaign dubbed DeadTag, in which attackers acquire expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that are still loaded by thousands of websites. The idea is to serve malicious JavaScript to iPhone visitors and silently do the attacker's bidding.

"It checks who's visiting," Report URI said. "Search engines, security scanners, automated browsers and anything else that looks like a bot gets nothing."

The script then interacts with the attacker's server, which then decides the destination to which each visitor has to be redirected. The iPhone exploit paths that take advantage of DeadTag lead to the Coruna exploit kit for older iPhones running iOS version 13 to 17.2.1 and DarkSword P7 for iOS devices running 18.4 to 18.7.

"These are not phishing pages or fake app downloads, both kits attack the browser itself," Report URI's Scott Helme said. "Simply opening the page is enough for your device to be compromised. There's nothing to tap, you don't need to click any link, nothing to install and no warning. If the iPhone is running a vulnerable version of iOS, the kit breaks out of the browser and installs spyware on the device."

Other schemes lead to decoy Google redirects, betting and casino scam sign-up pages, search advertisements for car deals and dentists, and fake surveys and "you've won" prize pages. More than 660 expired and re-registered domains are part of the DeadTag network.

According to an analysis published by Zimperium zLabs, campaigns distributing Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits have continued to evolve, with 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code as of October 2026.

Although Coruna was initially developed by a nation-state actor for highly targeted operations, its subsequent leak following initial disclosure has made the toolkit widely accessible to multiple threat actors for their own campaigns.

In many cases, the lure sites have been found to explicitly instruct visitors to exit their in-app browser or alternative iOS browser and open the link in Safari so as to trigger the exploit chain depending upon the device operating system.

"Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework (exhibiting byte-identical JavaScript payloads across multiple recovered configurations)," security researcher Santiago Rodriguez said. "Conversely, devices running later iOS builds receive a DarkSword-derived execution chain."

"The analyzed distribution footprint spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and – in several instances – compromised legitimate sites serving the kit via hidden iframes."

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Barracuda ESG Authentication Bypass Flaw Opens Path to Root
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: “If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda says
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Barracuda has released patches for two vulnerabilities that can be chained to gain root access to its Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances.

The first, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score of 9.3), is an authentication bypass that affects only ESG. The second, CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score of 8.6), is a command injection issue that also impacts five other Barracuda products.

“An authentication bypass in Barracuda Email Security Gateway versions earlier than 9.4.0.030 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to invoke a configuration-import function and restore a crafted, compatible backup archive, resulting in unauthorized modification of the appliance’s global configuration,” Mandiant explains in an advisory describing CVE-2026-116606.

The command injection bug sits in the timezone configuration setting, in code shared across several Barracuda products. Mandiant says an attacker logged in with administrator privileges could abuse it to execute OS commands as root.

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda says.

In addition to ESG, the command injection flaw affects the Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall (WAF), and Web Security Gateway (WSG).

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Barracuda, attackers must be able to reach an appliance’s admin interface to exploit the flaws. The company advises organizations to keep these interfaces reachable only from trusted internal networks.

Barracuda’s advisory marks administrative access as required for both bugs, yet also calls CVE-2026-116606 a pre-authentication issue. Mandiant, which published advisories for both flaws, says the ESG bug can be exploited without authentication.

Customers are advised to update to the newest firmware and confirm that every available patch is installed. Barracuda says any patch not applied automatically should be manually installed, and that devices with automatic patching disabled should have it switched back on.

According to Mandiant, Barracuda reported the command injection on October 15 and the authentication bypass on October 22. Neither advisory says whether the flaws have been exploited in the wild.

ESG appliances were previously targeted by Chinese cyberspies who exploited a zero-day, CVE-2023-2868, starting in October 2022. That campaign led Barracuda to tell customers to replace compromised devices.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: APT29 Watering Holes Target Unpatched iPhones and Android Devices
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Sekoia said its analysis supported the idea that APT29 obtained the exploits from a third party
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A cyberespionage campaign attributed to Russia's APT29 has served exploit chains for already-patched iPhone and Android flaws to visitors of legitimate websites, with payloads built to steal cookies, device data and Wi-Fi passwords without any user interaction.

Sekoia uncovered the activity in mid-October 2026 and detailed it in research published on November 4. It assessed with moderate to high confidence that the group behind it is APT29, also tracked as Midnight Blizzard and Cozy Bear, or at least one of its subgroups. The group is widely attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).

The campaign used three delivery routes: scripts injected into legitimate websites, lookalike domains that proxied real sites while adding scripts and a week-long compromise of Plerdy, a Ukrainian website analytics tracker.

Exposed sites included a Ukrainian gas producer, Ukrainian military and military-equipment sites, a US chemical-industry trade association, a Czech far-right movement and a Bulgarian military-related site. The lookalike domains impersonated the America250 initiative and a London hotel.

Read more on Midnight Blizzard: Midnight Blizzard Targets Travelers via Captive Portals

Plerdy Compromise Expanded the Campaign's Reach

Plerdy is loaded by thousands of mostly Ukrainian websites. Sekoia said the compromise, which ran from August 27 to September 3, exposed hundreds of them and their visitors to the exploit kit.

The researchers did not say how many devices were compromised.

The campaign also cast a wider net than an earlier APT29 operation. A 2024 Google report described a campaign on Mongolian government sites that used a hardcoded filter to target specific websites, while this one had no such filter and collected any cookies in the browser.

Visitors were fingerprinted and served exploit chains matched to their devices, and the payloads did not establish persistence.

All Exploits Had Already Been Patched

One chain targeted iOS 16.7 to steal cookies. Another, based on the DarkSword exploit kit, which Sekoia described as suspected to have been developed by a commercial surveillance vendor, targeted iOS 18.5 and collected full device data. A third targeted Chrome 139 to 145 on Android, excluding version 143, for browser cookies and Wi-Fi passwords.

The chains used n-day flaws, meaning vulnerabilities already disclosed and patched: CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2024-27834, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, CVE-2025-43520, CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038.

Sekoia said its analysis supported the idea that APT29 obtained the exploits from a third party.

That also sets the limit of the threat. In Sekoia's words, "a user running an up-to-date operating system is safe from these attacks."

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: The Classics Return: Vulnerable E-Mail Scripts, (Wed, Nov 4th)
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution.

Today, I noticed a slight resurgence in scans targeting e-mail scripts on our honeypots. Today, there are numerous scripts like the old "formail" scripts, and it is hard to link a specific vulnerability to any of these scans. But my main suspect is spammers looking for webforms that allow setting arbitrary "To" headers. The URLs I am seeing:

"/sendmail.php" "/test-mail.php" "/testemail.php" "/config/mail_config.php" "/mail_config.php" "/email-test.php" "/mailtest.php"

In particular, the "Test" part of the filename suggests that the attacker is not looking for production scripts, but for test scripts left behind during development. This, along with the requests for credential/secret files that top our "Leaderboard," points to a more fundamental issue: Code hygiene. Do not leave behind development artifacts that should never have reached a live website.

For example, some excerpts from a random "mailtest.php" script that came back in a Google search [mailtest]:

<?php

/* DONT FORGET TO DELETE THIS SCRIPT WHEN FINISHED! */

$server = array( 'HTTP_HOST', 'SERVER_NAME', 'SERVER_ADDR', 'SERVER_PORT', 'SERVER_ADMIN', 'SERVER_SIGNATURE', 'SERVER_SOFTWARE', 'REMOTE_ADDR', 'DOCUMENT_ROOT', 'REQUEST_URI', 'SCRIPT_NAME', 'SCRIPT_FILENAME', ); $to = ( isset( $_GET['email'] ) ? $_GET['email'] : FALSE ); $subject = 'Mail Test Successful for ' . $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']; $message = '';

??????? foreach ( $server as $s ) { $message .= sprintf( '%s: %s', $s, $_SERVER[$s] ) . PHP_EOL; };

$success = mail( $to, $subject, $message, $headers );

The comment at the top says it all: This is not meant for production use, and even on a development site, it should likely be deployed only briefly for debugging. The script takes any "To" address from the "email" GET parameter and exfiltrates/displays part of the server configuration. It can be useful to scan your own hosts for some of these URLs as an additional control, but you really want to catch these issues during application deployment.

[CVE] https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2000-0411 [mailtest] https://gist.github.com/Porrapat/60ed7411d933122fc481

-- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter|

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux. It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google.

Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38. It will become available on Google Play over the coming days.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look.

Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

CVE-2026-121229: Memory corruption in ANGLE, which could allow a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

ANGLE is Chrome’s graphics translation layer. A buffer overflow occurs when a program puts more data into an area of memory than it can hold, overwriting data in adjoining memory. An attacker can exploit this to make the vulnerable process run malicious code.

Chrome vulnerabilities that enable remote code execution outside the browser sandbox are particularly valuable to attackers because they can turn a visit to a malicious or compromised website into direct code running on the underlying operating system, often without requiring additional exploitation steps.

CVE-2026-121035: Use-after-free in Prerender.

Chrome’s Prerender component helps pages open faster by loading and preparing a page in the background before you navigate to it. If you then visit that page, Chrome can display the prepared version almost instantly instead of loading it from scratch.

This goes beyond just downloading content: Chrome also starts rendering the page and running its JavaScript.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

CVE-2026-121156: Buffer overflow in Dawn.

Dawn powers WebGPU in Chrome, allowing websites to use a device’s graphics processor for rendering and computational tasks. It checks and translates WebGPU instructions into commands that the device’s underlying graphics system can understand.

A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to a block of memory than it can hold. This can cause a crash or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run code.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CISA flags WordPress RCE flaw as actively exploited in attacks
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers have started exploiting a recently patched high-severity WordPress...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers have started exploiting a recently patched high-severity WordPress vulnerability in the wild.

Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, this high-severity WordPress Core flaw stems from a Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition and was reported by Picus Security researcher Umut Bayram.

Successful exploitation can let remote threat actors without privileges execute code on the server in high-complexity attacks due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades.

"A weakness in the WordPress upgrade process which can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window," the WordPress security team said on October 28 when it released WordPress 7.1.4 with patches to address this security issue. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately."

CISA confirmed CVE-2026-119977 active exploitation on Tuesday and added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems by Friday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.

"This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise," the cybersecurity agency warned.

Although BOD 26-04 targets only US federal agencies, CISA urged all network defenders, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patching this vulnerability to protect their servers.

While CISA didn't provide more details on attackers exploiting CVE-2026-119977 in the wild, WordPress security firm Wordfence says in an advisory update over the weekend that it "blocked 13,095 attacks targeting this vulnerability in the past 24 hours."

In July, the WordPress security team also patched a critical vulnerability chain in WordPress Core (named wp2shell) that can be abused to deploy webshells and take over unpatched servers by exploiting a REST API batch-route confusion vulnerability (CVE-2026-63030) and an SQL injection flaw (CVE-2026-60137).

Public wp2shell exploits were released one day after the patches went live, and attackers began breaching unpatched servers a few days later to deploy persistent webshells and install malicious plugins.

A Chinese-speaking threat actor also weaponized the wp2shell exploit chain in September to steal sensitive data from more than 18,500 records stored in backend databases belonging to small businesses and government organizations.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: " Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.

Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.

XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.

Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CVE-2026-58868: Critical Android Bug Could Let Attackers Run Remote Code
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Critical Android flaw CVE-2026-58868 could allow remote code execution without user interaction on devices running Android 14 through 17.

Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17. The flaw is a critical Android vulnerability caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of FrameDecoder.cpp. The flaw can trigger an out-of-bounds write, potentially allowing a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. Exploitation requires neither user interaction nor additional execution privileges, making it a potential zero-click attack.

“cve-2026-58868 In onOutputReceived of FrameDecoder.cpp, there is a possible out-of-bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow.” reads the advisory. “This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.”

Devices receive the fix through security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, depending on manufacturers and carriers. Google is now aware of active exploitation of the flaws in its November 2026 bulletin.

Google’s November 2026 Android security bulletin addresses 216 vulnerabilities, including 23 rated Critical. Two of these flaws, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, affect the System component and could allow remote code execution without user interaction.

The bulletin also lists five other Critical flaws in the System component. Three could lead to privilege escalation, while two could cause denial-of-service conditions. Another Critical vulnerability affects the Framework component and could also allow remote code execution.

Six Critical vulnerabilities affect the Android kernel. Two involve Bluetooth code, three affect the protected Kernel-based Virtual Machine (pKVM), and one is in the Human Interface Device (HID) component. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction.

The November 5 patch level also addresses Critical vulnerabilities in MediaTek modem code and a closed-source Qualcomm component. Google’s bulletin lists eight Critical MediaTek modem flaws, while MediaTek’s own November security bulletin details six of them: CVE-2026-20499 and CVE-2026-20545 through CVE-2026-20549.

MediaTek describes these six vulnerabilities as out-of-bounds write flaws caused by missing bounds checks, integer overflow or improper input validation. The company says it is not aware of any active exploitation in the wild.

The Qualcomm issue is tracked as CVE-2026-25285 and affects a closed-source component. Google does not provide further technical details in its bulletin.

One of the critical issues fixed by Google is CVE-2026-58882 (aka SMS of Death), which could allow attackers to remotely disable a phone by sending a specially crafted SMS message. The flaw affects decodeWapPdu, a function responsible for processing WAP Push messages, a type of content delivered through the SMS infrastructure.

The vulnerability is particularly concerning because exploitation reportedly requires no user interaction. An attacker only needs the victim’s phone number to send a malicious message. The message doesn’t appear in the SMS inbox, so the victim may have no indication of what caused the problem.

The issue also raises concerns about the reliability of mobile communications during an attack. According to a technical analysis published on October 29 by security researcher Mark B, a malformed WAP Push message can crash com.android.phone, the Android system component responsible for handling telephony functions. The crash can terminate ongoing calls, including emergency calls.

Tests on several Android phone models reportedly reproduced the crash consistently. The phone can also become stuck in a crash loop because Android retries processing the malicious message whenever the device starts. As a result, the device may continue crashing until the offending message is removed.

There is an important distinction, however. Google’s security bulletin and the CVE record identify the vulnerable decodeWapPdu function, but neither explicitly confirms that CVE-2026-58882 is the same issue described in the researcher’s SMS of Death report. The technical overlap is worth investigating, but the two reports shouldn’t be treated as definitively describing the same vulnerability without further confirmation.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-58868)

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Meta Shares Top Muse Bug Bounty Findings as Payouts Reach $1.2 Million
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: A $1,000 bounty covered a Mac app flaw that let an attacker with access to the computer hijack the auto-update feature to execute code with the app’s permissions
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Meta has paid roughly $1.2 million in bug bounties for its Muse AI agent, including $300,000 for a pre-launch flaw that exposed data on internal test systems.

Muse is a personal AI agent that acts on a user’s behalf across their email, calendar, messaging and other accounts. Each user’s agent gets its own virtual machine.

The bug bounty program ran privately from April and went public at the agent’s September 8 launch, Meta’s David Singleton said in a blog post. Of the more than 630 reports received, 64 were valid.

The $300,000 reward was handed out four months before launch, while Muse was at an early internal testing stage. The researcher demonstrated access to conversations and tokens on pre-release VMs used by Meta staff to test the product.

“An authentication check treated a header added by a local HTTPS proxy as proof that a request came from a trusted source. During a system migration, the environment gained a second proxy layer. That meant requests from outside could carry the trusted header too,” Singleton explained.

Meta took the service offline, fixed the bug and stopped treating the local machine as trusted.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A $90,000 bounty was paid for a report involving a malicious web page that, when Muse was asked to summarize it, mimicked status messages from the agent’s browsing tool. “It got the agent to execute some actions which should have been caught,” Singleton noted.

Meta has since added detection signals and changed how Muse treats tool output that looks suspicious. It says that, in testing, its classifiers now catch the attack and 100 variants.

Another $90,000 went to a report showing that specific formatting could slip one-time passcodes past Muse’s email redaction filters. Meta described it as one piece of an end-to-end attack.

A $50,000 reward went to an Android app flaw that let a malicious app pass a link to a privileged web view. “The link handler recognized a shared-page path without validating its host and loaded it,” Singleton wrote, allowing an attacker’s page to grab the web view’s credentials.

A $1,000 bounty covered a Mac app flaw that let an attacker with access to the computer hijack the auto-update feature to execute code with the app’s permissions.

Meta pays up to $300,000 per valid report, which it claims is several times more than the top rewards advertised by other leading AI developers. Prompt injection attacks affecting a single user can earn up to $130,000, while a fleetwide compromise can earn as much as $250,000.

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Ashlar-Vellum Cobalt. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of XE files. The issue results from the lack of validating the existence of an object prior to performing operations on the object. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create arbitrary files on affected installations of MailEnable. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the implementation of the Save method. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied path prior to using it in file operations. Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Node-RED authentication hole being exploited in the wild
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild.

The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115, an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.”

The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live.

Patrick Garrity, the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this.

“They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview.

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild.

“The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks: equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.”

Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED.

“It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.”

Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes.

“Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway.

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed.

“They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.”

Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Critical Langflow flaws enable authentication bypass and RCE
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code.

Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August.

This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities, two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication.

Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account.

The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale.

The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image.

“Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.”

The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.
