Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: HTTP2Shell: The Brotli Vulnerability That Extends Beyond Node.js
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497) shows automated vulnerability scanning and suspicious payloads potentially associated with exploitation
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
The key point: CVE-2026-111497 now increasingly referred to as HTTP2Shell and initially reported as Node2Shell, is broader than a Node.js vulnerability. The vulnerability is associated with Brotli decompression, so defenders need to find vulnerable implementations across applications and infrastructure, confirm whether untrusted compressed data can reach them, and patch the affected component.

AT A GLANCE

· CVE: CVE-2026-111497

· Affected layer: Brotli decompression implementations used by multiple runtimes and infrastructure components

· Primary risk question: Can attacker-controlled Brotli-compressed data reach a vulnerable decoder?

· Immediate priority: Discover, assess reachability, patch, redeploy, and hunt

Context

HTTP2Shell emerged shortly after PHP2Shell, but the vulnerabilities are technically unrelated. The connection is operational: both affect widely used foundational technology that can be embedded beneath many applications. This makes dependency visibility as important as application inventory.

The issue first gained attention as Node2Shell because Node.js was an obvious exposure path. The broader concern is that vulnerable Brotli code may also appear in other runtimes, packages, proxies, service-mesh components, and container images. The name HTTP2Shell does not mean the HTTP/2 protocol itself is vulnerable.

Confirmed exploitation in the wild: On October 27, 2026, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog based on evidence of active exploitation. Organizations should prioritize remediation of reachable, affected systems. Read CISA’s announcement.

What We See

The initial Node.js-focused view is too narrow. Security teams need to search across application, cloud, container, and infrastructure environments.

The presence of vulnerable code is not enough to determine priority. Reachability matters: untrusted compressed requests, external responses, files, or other data must be able to reach the decoder.

Internet-facing services and systems that automatically decompress external Brotli data should be assessed first.

What Our Telemetry Shows

Check Point IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) telemetry associated with Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497) shows automated vulnerability scanning and suspicious payloads potentially associated with exploitation.

Scope of the percentages: All percentages below refer to the telemetry data analyzed for this assessment, not to all exploitation attempts or global activity.

Brotli-focused activity (90.5%): Requests contained Brotli-encoded HTTP payloads, consistent with vulnerability-focused testing.

Automated vulnerability scanning (33.8%): Events contained the Patrowl automation fingerprint, indicating systematic vulnerability probing.

Targeted endpoint probing (24.5%): Requests targeted upload and ingestion endpoints, suggesting focused vulnerability testing.

Exploitation indicators: Malformed binary payloads, unusual HTTP framing, and HTTP 500 server errors were observed, warranting further investigation but not confirming successful exploitation.

Overall assessment: The findings indicate widespread automated vulnerability probing alongside suspicious payload activity. Continued research and protection development are recommended. CISA’s confirmation of exploitation in the wild is separate from these telemetry findings, which do not establish successful compromise in the observed events.

What We Found

The practical exposure model has two parts:

Vulnerable component: an affected Brotli implementation exists in the application or supporting infrastructure.

Attacker reachability: attacker-controlled Brotli-compressed data can reach that implementation.

Potentially relevant environments include Node.js, Python Brotli packages, Bun, .NET, Envoy, Istio, and software that bundles or statically links affected Brotli code. Product-specific impact and fixed versions should be confirmed against the relevant vendor advisory before deployment changes are made.

How Check Point Helps Protect Organizations

Patching the affected component remains the primary remediation. Check Point controls can add visibility and risk reduction before, during, and after remediation:

IPS protection: Check Point IPS provides dedicated protection against this vulnerability with “Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497)”.

Network and application prevention: keep Check Point security protections and signatures current, and use prevention policies appropriate to the environment.

Web application and API security: inspect and restrict unnecessary compressed request paths, especially where applications do not need Brotli-encoded request bodies.

Exposure management: identify affected assets, prioritize internet-facing and reachable exposure, validate exploitability where supported, and track remediation.

Endpoint and workload detection: investigate crashes, restarts, suspicious child processes, unexpected network activity, and decompression errors on exposed systems.

Explore relevant Check Point capabilities: Check Point cyber security products | Vulnerability Response Point

What Your Security Teams Needs toDo Now

Expand discovery beyond Node.js. Inventory Brotli implementations in runtimes, packages, proxies, service meshes, containers, and statically linked software.

Test reachability. Identify where untrusted compressed requests, responses, files, or fetched content can reach a vulnerable decoder.

Patch by vendor and component. Apply the relevant vendor update, rebuild affected container images, and redeploy running workloads. Verify that production is using the patched component.

Reduce exposure if patching must wait. Disable unnecessary Brotli decompression for untrusted input, reject Brotli-encoded requests where they are not required, and restrict exposed services. Treat these as temporary measures.

Hunt while remediating. Prioritize internet-facing and unpatched systems. Review application crashes, repeated restarts, suspicious processes, anomalous outbound traffic, and Brotli decompression errors.

Keep the assessment open. Re-check software inventories and vendor advisories as affected-product guidance develops. Do not close the incident after patching Node.js alone.

Follow the Latest Guidance

For a continuously updated practitioner view of emerging vulnerabilities, affected technologies, protections, and remediation guidance, visit the Check Point Vulnerability Response Point.

For the preceding vulnerability story, read PHP2Shell: What We Know About the Leaked Critical PHP Vulnerabilities.

Check Point Research | HTTP2Shell practical follow-up

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Inexplicable Data From Italy's Threat Landscape

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Theory #1: Poor Cybersecurity Hygiene

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Nordic CISOs Handle Rising Cyber Threats Remarkably Well

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Theory #2: A Cyber Risk Network Effect

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

Theory #3: Small & Medium-Sized Businesses Shift the Data

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: ZDI-26-847: MLflow AI Gateway Server-Side Request Forgery Information Disclosure Vulnerability

Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of MLflow. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the processing of the api_base field. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a URI prior to accessing resources. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to initiate requests in the context of the service account.

Additional Details

Fixed in MLflow 3.17.0https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/25761

2026-06-30 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Node2Shell: Reproducing CVE-2026-111497 in the Node.js Brotli decoder
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation: Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Key points and observations

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder. The upstream flaw sits in the Google Brotli C library, so the blast radius reaches Python, Bun, .NET, Java brotli4j, Envoy, and Istio. Every affected runtime now has a fix available.

We reproduced the flaw on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image and verified that the patched build rejects the same bytes.

Capturing an application-level trace is difficult because the process continues running despite memory corruption.

Only patching fixes this vulnerability. The application process decodes the data, so neither the web server nor a web application firewall (WAF) ever sees the malicious content. An edge rule that rejects Brotli-compressed request bodies is a useful tripwire and nothing more.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released security updates for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The CVE record gives the flaw a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2, or Critical, while Node.js rates its severity as High. Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 contain the fix, and end-of-life release lines carry the same vulnerable decoder but have no patch.

What looked like a Node.js problem on day one turned out to be far broader. Most runtimes embed the upstream Google Brotli C library, where the bug lives. Over the following week many consumers of that decoder shipped its own advisory:

Product

Affected

First fixed release

Node.js 22, 24, and 26

Before 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1

22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1

Google Brotli

1.0.3 through 1.0.9, 1.1.0, and 1.2.0

1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1

Python Brotli and brotlicffi

1.2.0 and earlier

1.2.1 and 1.2.1.0

Bun

1.0.21 through 1.4.3

1.4.4

Java brotli4j

1.23.0 and earlier

1.24.0

.NET 8, 9, and 10

Before the October 25, 2026 out-of-band update

8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14

Envoy and Istio

All releases before the first fix in each supported branch

Envoy: 1.36.12, 1.37.8, 1.38.6, 1.39.3, 1.40.0; Istio: 1.29.9, 1.30.6, 1.31.2 (first fixed in each branch)

Two details deserve special attention. Java's brotli4j bundles its own native Brotli build inside its jars, so patching the operating system's libbrotli does not fix it. Bun executables built with bun build \--compile embed the runtime and stay vulnerable until they are rebuilt.

Before the disclosure, Imperva demonstrated code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux ARM64 image. Their exploit needed several attempts and was not released. A public proof of concept appeared on October 22, 2026. On standard builds it produces a crash and a limited memory read. As of October 29, 2026, there have been confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities catalog now lists the CVE.

How to know if you're affected

A service is exposed when it decompresses Brotli data that an attacker controls, which comes through two common paths. A few additional considerations apply to both.

Outbound requests (the quiet path)

Outbound requests are the harder path to see. Node.js's built-in fetch() decodes a Content-Encoding: br response automatically, whether or not the request asked for Brotli. The axios, got, and node-fetch clients advertise and decode Brotli by default. Any feature that fetches URLs supplied by users, such as webhooks, link previews, and feed readers, enables an attacker to force the encoding selection server side since the attacker controls the response headers, and fetch() decodes a body labeled br even when the application explicitly forces Accept-Encoding: identity.

In our testing, no exception surfaced at runtime: one crafted stream completed with an empty body and an HTTP 200, and the only visible signals were CPU usage and, under concurrency, a starved threadpool that still answered health checks.

The same holds outside Node.js: Python HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically whenever Brotli or brotlicffi is installed, even if application code never imports the package.

Inbound requests (the visible path)

Inbound attacks are easier to observe. A compressed request body is a recognizable attack surface, your reverse proxy or WAF can see the Content-Encoding: br header, and the framework parser is a known place to audit. Express 5 and body-parser 2.x accept Brotli-compressed request bodies by default in their JSON, raw, text, and URL-encoded parsers, and Koa and NestJS inherit the behavior. Express 4 rejects those bodies with an HTTP 415, and a bare Node.js HTTP server does not decompress anything. Parsers mounted before authentication expose the decoder to unauthenticated requests.

Other considerations

Both paths share a versioning trap: process.versions.brotli still reports 1.2.0 on the patched Node.js 24.22.1, because the cherry-picked fix does not bump the embedded version string. process.version is reliable only for official distributions from nodejs.org.

If you cannot patch immediately, set inflate: false on Express 5 and body-parser 2.x parsers, or reject Content-Encoding: br at the reverse proxy. These measures only mitigate the risk, as patching is the only complete solution. These mitigations could also break the functionality as they reject all compressed request bodies, do nothing for the outbound path, and break compressed bodies sent by legitimate clients.

How the vulnerability works

A Brotli stream is divided into blocks, and the decoder moves to a new block only when the current block's length budget runs out. A 23 MB stream of otherwise ordinary commands drains that budget while producing no output, and its closing commands request a block switch that the format forbids. These steps are where the attacker does the proper setup to exploit the bug.

In the next stage, we see the impact of the vulnerability. In Brotli 1.2.0, DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns a boolean, and it answers two different questions with the same "false" value: "this stream is malformed" and "I need more input". Callers cannot tell the two apart, and on the decoder's fast path the return value is dropped entirely.

The two arms then diverge. The first path is an overflow where the decoder parks the unconsumed bytes in a small internal buffer while it waits for more input. The copy has no bound check, so bytes past the end of the buffer land in adjacent decoder state. The write happens inside a single heap allocation, so the tooling built to catch memory corruption never sees it, and the process keeps running. The other path is that it keeps spinning. The decoder retries the forbidden switch in a loop, which pins a CPU core inside a single call that never returns: a one-request denial of service.

From memory corruption to code execution

In this case, memory corruption has impactful consequences. The corrupted decoder state controls where the decoder reads from and writes to next, so a crafted stream can redirect both operations. This gives an attacker two primitives:

A repeatable read of heap memory that leaves through the decompressed response.

A redirected write. In our lab, we aimed it at an unmapped page and produced a deterministic crash.

Both primitives are real. The read primitive is the most operationally interesting, because heap bytes returning over the wire are the first step of a staged attack.

Three obstacles stand between these primitives and a shell:

The addresses move. The heap layout that the corruption targets is randomized and changes between requests, so what one request leaks, the next request can’t reliably use.

The corruption bytes are also the decoder's input. The decoder consumes the bytes that steer the corruption again as it continues, so the values an attacker needs are constrained by the values the decoder will accept. This is the deepest structural obstacle we found.

A managed runtime stands in the way. Between the corrupted C state and control flow sits the machinery of a language runtime with its own allocator, its own compiled code, and its own defenses, none of which the original C library was designed around.

After measuring all three obstacles, we assess that the flaw is exploitable and that the gap between these primitives and reliable code execution is engineering effort. This matches Imperva's report of successful execution after several attempts on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image.

How the patch addresses the flaw

The patch is small and precise. The block-switch helper now returns a real error code, and both code paths treat a failed check as a hard stop instead of a request for more input. It rejects a crafted stream with a format error (-17) before anything is written to the decoder's state.

The release timeline is the troubling part. The fix was committed to the upstream Brotli repository on February 27, 2026, but the fixed library releases did not ship until October 21, 2026. For eight months, anyone who downloaded Brotli, or a runtime that embeds it, received the vulnerable version even though the corrected code sat in the public repository. The release also ships without a regression test or a changelog entry for this fix.

How to detect exploitation

This CVE involves no attacker-controlled infrastructure, so there are no conventional indicators. Detection rests on behavioral signals, and no single signal is conclusive. Correlate across three layers.

Decoder error signals

The vulnerable and patched builds respond differently to the same malicious bytes. Both responses appear in application logs and APM error spans and the error you see depends on whether the build is patched. On a vulnerable build, Node.js returns Z_BUF_ERROR with the message "unexpected end of file". On a patched build, Node.js returns ERR__ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH, and Python returns "brotli: decoder is unhealthy". The vulnerable signal also appears for benign truncated input so you have to still look a little closer and differentiate the benign truncated input vs real attacks.

Process signals

A worker that exits with signal 139 (SIGSEGV) right after a Brotli transfer is a crash attempt, and a process pinned at 100% CPU inside a decompression call is the spin arm. Correlate on workload identity (the container, pod, or service) and not the process ID, because the process that crashed is gone and a successful attempt may not crash at all. The strongest signal is behavioral: a shell or new outbound connections from the same workload.

The disclosure channel

Decompressed output that contains bytes the client never sent is the read primitive in action. Investigate any such output immediately. Because the leaked heap memory leaves through the decompressed response, start by listing the endpoints that return or reflect decompressed content back to the caller, such as echo, preview, conversion, or proxy features.

What does not work

Payload byte signatures, because the attacker-controlled parts of the stream change per target and the exploit is the decode process itself, not the decompressed content.

Content matching at the WAF, because the web server forwards compressed bytes and never decodes them.

Body-size limits, because the tested middleware counts decompressed bytes, so the 23 MB compressed trigger still reaches the decoder.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management tracks CVE-2026-111497 and the related vendor advisories as vulnerability findings on hosts and container images, so your patching status lives in one place.

Datadog Code Security reports the vulnerable services that ship dependency inventories. Its library inventory identifies which services to prioritize: those running Express 5, body-parser 2.x, or Koa parsers, and those using HTTP clients that auto-decode Brotli.

Datadog Application Performance Monitoring (APM) helps you hunt for attempts. This query requires capturing Content-Encoding, which is not set by default in Node.js spans, so make sure to check how the language tracer you are using behaves. For example in Node.js it can be enabled by including content-encoding in DD_TRACE_HEADER_TAGS. Pivot on the services that accept Content-Encoding: br request bodies using this query, and review services that fetch user-supplied URLs. Decoder failures surface as APM error spans correlated with the request and the client address. The process telemetry that the Datadog Agent collects shows a crashed attempt as a worker restart with exit code 139.

Datadog Workload Protection includes coverage through the CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell Exploit Content Pack. This pack includes a new security policy with three Agent rules that cover post-exploitation that surfaces a CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell exploitation detected signal.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation:

Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or web processes. It uses process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-111497 shows how a single unchecked return value in a widely shared C library can ripple across nearly every major runtime. Because the decoder runs inside the application's own process, the flaw sidesteps the defenses most teams rely on. The eight months between the upstream fix and its release are a reminder that a fix in a public repository protects no one until it ships.

Exploitation has been confirmed, which further proves the primitives are real and the path to code execution is a matter of effort. Patch to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 or your vendor's fixed package, rebuild container images, restart every process, and inventory the other Brotli consumers in your environment.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CVE-2026-101767: Critical Oracle EBS SQL Injection Actively Probed in the Wild
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
What is CVE-2026-101767?

A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-101767, CVSS 9.8) was disclosed affecting Oracle E-Business Suite’s Application Object Library, allowing attackers to achieve full remote code execution and system takeover via an unauthenticated SQL injection in the Thin Client Framework servlet. Due to the potential for complete compromise of financial, payroll, and HR data managed by EBS, immediate patching is required.

How the Oracle EBS SQL injection leads to remote code execution

The issue originates from the Application Object Library’s TCF servlet at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, where missing authentication on a critical function combined with improper input sanitization leads to SQL injection as the privileged APPS database user. By sending specially crafted POST requests to the servlet instantiating oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer, attackers can execute arbitrary SQL commands and chain to operating system command execution as the EBS application account, potentially achieving full takeover of the EBS instance and all data it manages. No authentication is required to exploit this issue.

CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline

The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3.ai and reported to Oracle on July 24, 2026. Oracle addressed it in the October 2026 Critical Patch Update, released October 20. Within a week of the patch release, threat intelligence firm Defused observed exploratory exploitation attempts hitting Oracle EBS honeypots on October 27. EBS has historically been a target for financially motivated threat actors, including the Cl0p group’s large-scale EBS campaign the previous year.

Which Oracle E-Business Suite versions are affected?

The following components are affected: Oracle E-Business Suite Application Object Library, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. Oracle notes that earlier unsupported versions are likely also affected. The vulnerable servlet passes through the default EBS URL firewall configuration, meaning any internet-facing EBS instance with default settings is exposed. Organizations running EBS for financial, payroll, HR, and procurement operations face elevated risk due to the sensitive data accessible through the APPS database user.

How to patch and mitigate CVE-2026-101767

Users should apply the October 2026 Critical Patch Update immediately (details in My Oracle Support Note KA923), and also patch the underlying EBS Database and Fusion Middleware components, which have separate CPU entries. As interim mitigations until patching is complete, administrators should remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict network access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks only.

Is CVE-2026-101767 being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, Horizon3.ai has published technical details of the attack chain, and active probing has been confirmed in the wild by Defused. The vulnerability is not yet listed on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments.

What attackers can do with a compromised Oracle EBS instance

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary SQL and OS commands as the APPS and EBS application accounts, exfiltrate or manipulate sensitive financial, payroll, and HR data, and potentially pivot to other systems within the network, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or full infrastructure compromise.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable Oracle EBS assets

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable versions of Oracle E-Business Suite, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the newItem view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The Cat Has Left the Bag

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: CVE-2026-111497: Node2Shell / HTTP2Shell Vulnerability May Allow RCE
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text: IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project disclosed CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. The vulnerability is also known as Node2Shell and more recently as HTTP2Shell. The CVE score, filed by Google as the numbering authority, is 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. The flaw can be triggered when a vulnerable process decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. Successful exploitation may result in process crashes, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution (RCE). Imperva reported demonstrating code execution in fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with multiple attempts required in its test environment. The vulnerable Brotli decoder may be present in a range of runtimes, libraries, and software packages, including Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli bindings, .NET, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Java brotli4j, libbrotli, curl/libcurl through Brotli dependencies, and Linux distribution packages. Applications may be exposed if they decompress attacker-controlled data using a vulnerable decoder. The vulnerability may be reachable through both inbound and outbound traffic paths. A malicious client could send a crafted request with Content-Encoding: br to a vulnerable server-side component that performs Brotli request decompression. Conversely, a malicious or compromised server could return a crafted Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable client application that automatically decodes Brotli responses. ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below. RecommendationsZscaler recommends the following measures to address CVE-2026-111497 and monitor for potentially related activity:Patch vulnerable runtimes and libraries. Upgrade vulnerable runtimes, packages, and infrastructure components to the patched versions listed in the Vulnerable Versions table. Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli data, including internet-facing applications that accept compressed request bodies and services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs. Validate each vulnerable component independently. Updating the system-wide libbrotli package may not remediate applications that statically bundle Brotli or ship their own decoder copy.Rebuild and redeploy containers. Use patched base images, runtimes, and libraries, and verify the versions in running workloads. Updating a host’s libraries does not update copies bundled within container images.Disable Brotli decoding where patching is delayed. If immediate patching is not possible, disable Brotli decompression on vulnerable paths where supported, following vendor guidance and testing for application compatibility.Monitor for exploitation and post-exploitation behavior. Investigate the following: Unexpected process crashes in Node.js, Bun, Python, .NET, Envoy Proxy, or service mesh workloads.Repeated malformed Brotli payloads.Requests containing Content-Encoding: br to endpoints that normally do not receive compressed request bodies.Abnormal memory access violations or segmentation faults.Web server or application worker crashes after compressed request handling.Unexpected child processes spawned by web application runtimes.Unexpected outbound connections following crashes or the processing of malformed compressed input. Vulnerable VersionsThe following table lists vulnerable versions and corresponding fixes for selected software that incorporates the Brotli decoder. ProductVulnerable VersionsPatched VersionsGoogle Brotli1.0.3 < 1.0.10 (semver)1.0.10Google Brotli1.1.0 < 1.1.1 (semver)1.1.1Google Brotli1.2.0 < 1.2.1 (semver)1.2.1Node.js22.0.0 - 22.23.322.23.4Node.js24.0.0 - 24.22.024.22.1Node.js26.0.0 - 26.12.026.12.1Bun< 1.4.41.4.4.NET8.0.0 - 8.0.328.0.33.NET9.0.0 - 9.0.219.0.22.NET10.0.0 - 10.0.1310.0.14.NET11.0.0-preview.1 - 11.0.0-rc.211.0.0-rc.3.26522.148Python Brotli (PyPI)1.2.01.2.1Python brotlicffi (PyPI)1.2.0.0 - 1.2.0.21.2.1.0Envoy Proxy1.39.2, 1.38.5, 1.37.7, 1.36.111.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, 1.36.12Java brotli4j< 1.24.01.24.0libbrotli (Debian)1.1.0-21.1.0-2+deb13u1libbrotliVaries by distributionApply vendor security updatesTable 1: Software versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and the corresponding patched versions. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving CVE-2026-111497 through Zscaler Deception. Within the first 24 hours following public disclosure, Zscaler Deception’s global decoy mesh observed activity from 20 source IP addresses targeting 12 customers across 402 events. Of these events, 40% involved reconnaissance and 60% involved exploitation attempts. The table below summarizes the unique payloads associated with reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497 observed through Zscaler Deception.Payload DescriptionJA4 FingerprintMalformed Brotli stream headers + valid Brotli differential check + Node.js path recont13d4312h1_c7886603b240_b26ce05bbdd6Truncated JSON Brotli + 8-byte invalid Brotli padding stream + uncompressed controlsNone22-byte & 23-byte invalid block-switch OOB-write seeds (CVE-2026-111497)t13d251100_b78ed14e2fd0_ab7e3b40a677Brotli decompression bomb / Celery stream probe + 1B controlsNoneAssetnote 1-byte malformed/valid Brotli differential checkMultiple observed3-stage Node2Shell capability, Strapi & CVE-2026-111497 JSON parser probet13d521100_b262b3658495_8e6e362c5eac14-byte Brotli {"ping":1} differential sweept13d1714h1_ab0a1bf427ad_5e078a691127Table 2: Unique payloads observed during reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497. How It WorksBrotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It is used for HTTP compression to reduce the size of web content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and API responses. Brotli-encoded HTTP content is identified by the Content-Encoding: br header.Applications may use Brotli directly or through dependencies such as runtimes, frameworks, HTTP clients, and middleware. In some configurations, these components automatically decompress Brotli-encoded content without application code explicitly calling Brotli APIs.Vulnerability detailsThe flaw occurs in Brotli’s block-decoding logic. When a stream changes block type, the decoder determines the next block type and length. In vulnerable versions, there is a macro (in the fast-path logic) that does not properly check the return value of the DecodeBlockTypeAndLength function, which can cause the decoder to continue processing an invalid state (e.g., when provided a maliciously crafted Brotli stream). This can lead to an out-of-bounds write and be used as a primitive for RCE. The upstream fix modifies the decoder so malformed block-switch conditions return a distinct error that is propagated to the caller, stopping further decoding of the malicious Brotli stream.Attack chainExploitation of CVE-2026-111497 may follow either an inbound or outbound path, depending on where Brotli decompression occurs, as shown in the figure below. Inbound attempts use crafted Brotli-compressed HTTP request bodies while outbound attempts use crafted responses returned by an attacker-controlled or compromised server. These responses may be consumed through fetch(), webhook delivery, URL previews, crawlers or scrapers, and API integrations. In either path, exploitation requires attacker-controlled Brotli data to reach a vulnerable decoder, with compressed HTTP content marked by Content-Encoding: br. Figure 1: Potential inbound and outbound exploitation paths for CVE-2026-111497. ConclusionCVE-2026-111497 affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. Exposure depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled Brotli data to a vulnerable decoder. Organizations should identify vulnerable components and apply corresponding vendor updates, including updates for applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli.Zscaler Deception has observed active reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving this vulnerability. ThreatLabz will continue monitoring for related activity and provide updates as additional findings become available. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for CVE-2026-111497 with the following signatures:Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) App ProtectionThe following ZPA App Protection signature detects attempts to exploit CVE-2026-111497 in internal applications accessed through ZPA, including activity originating from compromised endpoints or insiders:6000572: Node2Shell - Brotli Decoder Buffer Overflow (CVE-2026-111497)Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionApp.Exploit.CVE-2026-111497Zscaler Deception Organizations should deploy the following Zscaler Deception decoys to help detect reconnaissance and exploitation attempts:MLflowMetaflowBento FrontendRay ServeGitLab How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows the typical attack stages and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler.Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify internet-facing applications containing vulnerable versions using Zscaler Exposure Management.Find services running vulnerable runtimes or libraries.Reduce direct exposure by placing applications behind a Zero Trust architecture.Prevent compromiseEnable SSL/TLS inspection where appropriate. Use Advanced Threat Protection to detect exploit attempts and suspicious payload delivery. Use ZPA App Protection to inspect and block suspicious requests targeting private applications. Reduce outbound exploitation riskRoute server egress through Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to inspect outbound traffic.Restrict application egress to approved destinations. Pay special attention to webhook, crawler, URL preview, and third-party integration services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-application segmentation.Use Zscaler Deception to detect attacker movement after initial compromise. Monitor for suspicious access to internal applications following web application crashes or abnormal behavior.Detect post-exploitation activityUse Zscaler Managed Detection & Response (MDR) and Threat Hunting to investigate suspicious process behavior, command execution, unusual outbound connections, container runtime anomalies, and web application worker crashes.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP).Monitor for unusual uploads, archive transfers, credential exposure, or data movement following suspected exploitation. Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Millions of security cameras at risk: DoS vulnerability in Intelbras devices
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Background

Network-connected surveillance cameras are now widespread in both home and enterprise environments, so securing them is essential to safeguarding physical spaces and sensitive assets. As these devices continue to gain new features and network connectivity capabilities, vulnerabilities in their implementation can have significant security implications.

During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems. The flaw resides in a firmware update endpoint that is accessible without authentication and allows anyone with access to the local Wi-Fi network to knock cameras offline. A single request disrupts the camera for only about a minute, but sending periodic requests keeps the device offline indefinitely. We reported the issue to Intelbras, monitored the remediation process, validated the fix in the new firmware, and will now demonstrate the exploitation procedure step-by-step.

Following our notification, Intelbras patched the vulnerability and released updated firmware (R.260804) along with update instructions. A candidate ID of CAN-2026-2035970 has been assigned by MITRE following submission, pending the final CVE assignment. Additionally, the Intelbras team recently informed us that MITRE has classified the vulnerability as Medium, assigning it a score of 5.1 under the CVSS 4.0 framework. The issue discussed in this article is no longer present in the latest firmware version.

Firmware

Intelbras provides firmware files on its official website. While users can manually install these updates via an SD card, the cameras also natively support firmware upgrades over the local network via their web interface and mobile app. We obtained the firmware version v240927 for the iM3B-C (IM3 C) camera, which was the latest available version at the time of our research. According to Intelbras, the same firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Below, we can view the firmware version and the camera model used as an example.

To provide context, we will explain how the camera’s authentication mechanism works and why it is relevant to accessing the camera’s endpoints. The main firmware component is an ARM binary named sonia, responsible for controlling the kernel drivers used by the camera hardware, authentication, and livestream recording, among other things.

How authentication works

The global.login RPC method handles authentication at the /RPC2_Login endpoint. First, the client, such as the mobile app or a custom script, sends the username and an empty password. The camera responds with an authentication challenge (a set of values to verify the password without transmitting it). This response returns a temporary session, the encryption type in the encryption field, a random value, and a realm (authentication scope). At this stage, a false response is normal and does not indicate a failed login, as the authentication process is not yet complete.

Next, the client calculates the response password from the authentication challenge. It first generates an MD5 (username:realm:original_password) hash as the base. It then calculates a second MD5 (username:random:first_md5) hash, where first_md5 is the result of the previous step. To complete the authentication, the client sends this final result back to /RPC2_Login in a second global.login call, passing the username, calculated password, and temporary session ID.

If the login is accepted, the camera returns true and a new, authenticated session. This session must be used for all subsequent RPC calls, including the camera’s other endpoints, for example, the one that reboots the device or those that expose sensitive information.

Affected endpoint

The affected endpoint is the firmware upgrade route http://<ip_address>/firmwareUpgrade_service/Demo, which lacks authentication checks; furthermore, it fails to verify whether the firmware is actually valid before initiating the upgrade process. This creates a serious issue because the upgrade requires the camera to reboot, and that is precisely when the problem occurs: the camera enters reboot mode and eventually shuts down, appearing offline to the user and anyone who has the camera registered on their device.

PoC: vulnerability exploitation

Now that we have outlined how the vulnerability works, we will use a Python script on an iM3B-C camera to exploit it for demonstration purposes. The exploit contacts the camera’s endpoint to upload firmware. Below, we can see sonia creating the endpoint responsible for the firmware upgrade.

Next, the exploit will hit the endpoint and cause the camera to reboot. Consequently, mobile phones running the Intelbras app will lose connection with the registered device. Below, we can see the camera operating normally: the green light is on and the app is showing it is available for viewing.

The camera is online

After the exploit executes, we can see the effects: the camera goes offline and loses connection to the registered devices.

The camera is offline

The exploit is quite simple: it sends an HTTP POST request with the firmware, which causes the camera to accept the request and initiate the reboot process. It does not matter whether the firmware is original; the reboot process will start regardless.

New firmware version

After we notified Intelbras about this flaw in the endpoint implementation, the company contacted the OEM vendor. As a result, a new firmware version was released that requires authentication to initiate an update through this endpoint.

Below, we can compare the new firmware, which validates cookies and session data, with the old firmware, which performed no authentication checks and proceeded directly to the update routine.

Real risk

An attacker can remotely trigger the camera firmware upgrade and reboot process without authenticating or supplying a valid firmware image. This may cause the device to go offline, which results in a denial-of-service condition preventing legitimate users from accessing live monitoring or managing the camera.

The potential impact is significant due to the number of affected users. The Intelbras Mibo Smart app, which the company provides to connect and manage the devices mentioned in this report, has over 4,000,000 downloads. Brazil represents the largest user base, followed by Paraguay, Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Venezuela. As a result, exploitation of this issue affects a large number of users.

Takeaways

This is a medium-severity vulnerability that Intelbras is already aware of. The issue has been addressed in a newer firmware release (R.260804 along with update instructions), which mitigates this attack vector. Because the vulnerability directly affects the availability and normal operation of the affected cameras, it is highly recommended that users verify the firmware version currently installed on their devices and update to the latest available version as soon as possible. Keeping the firmware up to date is an essential security practice, especially for internet-connected surveillance devices, as outdated versions may remain exposed to known vulnerabilities.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: ZDI-26-825: (0Day) (Pwn2Own) Alpine iLX-F511 diagapp Command Injection Vulnerability
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows physically present attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Alpine iLX-F511 devices
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows physically present attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Alpine iLX-F511 devices. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the diagapp component. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to execute a system call. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of root.

Additional Details

02/05/26 - ZDI reported the vulnerability to the vendor06/07/26 - the vendor acknowledged the receipt of the report and asked for an extension07/21/26 - ZDI requested an update on the status of the fix10/15/26 - ZDI notified the vendor of the intention to publish the case as a 0-day advisory

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Disclosure Timeline

2026-02-04 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-28 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-10-28 - Advisory Updated
