Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: Broccoli2shell: Everything You Need To Know About The Critical Brotli Decoder Vulnerability
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library. The vulnerability affects multiple widely used technologies, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and more. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger memory corruption, disclose sensitive information, crash affected processes, or potentially achieve remote code execution (RCE).

Organizations using affected components to decompress untrusted Brotli-compressed data are advised to prioritize remediation.

CVE-2026-111497 was discovered and reported by Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer (OpenAI Codex Security), with fixes implemented by Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel (Node.js). Ron Masas (Imperva Red Team) demonstrated its exploitability, while OpenSourceMalware and Aikido analyzed its impact on the Python ecosystem.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

Broccoli2Shell (a.k.a Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell) originates from an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, a widely adopted compression component used to reduce the size of HTTP traffic and other data. The flaw occurs when the decoder improperly handles specially crafted compressed data during block-processing operations, potentially writing beyond allocated memory boundaries. An attacker can exploit this behavior by supplying malicious Brotli-compressed input to a vulnerable application, potentially resulting in memory disclosure, application crashes, or arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected process. Researchers have demonstrated successful exploitation against unpatched Node.js environments.

Although initially associated with Node.js, the vulnerability originates in the upstream Brotli C decoder and extends to multiple downstream technologies that incorporate the affected component. Exploitation requires an application or dependency to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data, either through incoming HTTP requests, externally fetched responses, or other untrusted compressed content. Certain HTTP clients and application frameworks may perform decompression automatically when Brotli support is enabled, potentially exposing applications even when Brotli is not explicitly referenced in application code.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

Cloud environments are particularly exposed due to the widespread use of Brotli-enabled components across containerized applications, Kubernetes clusters, API gateways, reverse proxies, serverless workloads, and cloud-hosted web services. Internet-facing applications that process attacker-controlled requests, as well as internal services that retrieve compressed responses from untrusted external sources, may provide exploitation paths. Successful exploitation could enable attackers to compromise application workloads, access sensitive information, disrupt service availability, or execute malicious code within affected containers or runtime environments.

According to Wiz data 91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497, and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances.

Which products are affected?

Additional products that bundle or link against vulnerable versions of the Brotli C decoder may also be affected. Organizations should consult vendor-specific security advisories, particularly for statically linked libraries and embedded dependencies. End-of-life runtime branches should be migrated to supported versions.

Which actions should security teams take?

Organizations should prioritize the following mitigation and remediation measures:

Apply security updates: Upgrade affected Brotli libraries, Node.js runtimes, Python packages, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and Istio deployments to their respective patched versions or later supported releases.

Identify vulnerable cloud workloads: Inventory virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, containers, serverless functions, API gateways, and application dependencies for vulnerable Brotli components. Prioritize internet-facing services and workloads processing untrusted compressed data.

Review application exposure: Identify applications that decompress Brotli-compressed HTTP requests, external HTTP responses, uploaded files, or other attacker-controlled content. Include indirect and transitive dependencies in the assessment.

Rebuild and redeploy affected workloads: Update container base images, dependency lockfiles, and bundled libraries. Rebuild and redeploy affected container images, restart running processes, and verify that patched components are loaded.

Implement temporary mitigations: Where immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling Brotli decompression or rejecting Brotli-encoded requests before they reach vulnerable components. Restrict untrusted compressed responses where feasible. These controls may reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Strengthen monitoring and detection: Review WAF, application, and network logs for suspicious Brotli-compressed traffic, unexpected application crashes, and anomalous process behavior. Monitor affected workloads for indicators of exploitation.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially...
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.

So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

Vulnerabilities & Patching.title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943)
Vulnerabilities & Patching.context: Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users
Vulnerabilities & Patching.full_text:
Executive Summary

A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111943.

The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported recovering the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates after discovering that the underlying cryptographic keys contained only a fraction of the expected entropy. Browser and OS vendors have since blocked the certificates, and eMudhra has revoked them. Security teams now face an immediate question: Where do certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates exist within my environment?

Qualys VMDR and Qualys Certificate View already collect the data needed to answer that. This post explains how to use them, with QQL queries you can run today.

What is eMudhra?

eMudhra, a digital trust and cybersecurity provider, offers solutions spanning Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, identity management, and secure digital transactions. Recent security concerns involving eight of its intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates highlight the importance of strong cryptographic key generation, rigorous validation, and continuous oversight of digital trust infrastructure. The incident reinforces a critical security lesson: trust in digital certificates depends not just on the technology, but on the operational controls protecting the keys behind them.

What Happened

A flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process produced a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step, and those weak keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw reduced the effective entropy of the affected P-384 keys to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute.

The weak keys came from a key generation ceremony held on April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. Anyone holding the private key of one of these intermediates could issue a certificate that impersonates any website or service, subject to each client’s validation controls. Some key points about the incident:

Six of the eight intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs.

Browsers: Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have blocked the TLS certificates, and Microsoft has blocked the two code-signing certificates.

Root distrust: Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from the Chrome Root Store, and Mozilla removed trust in the root that signed the intermediates.

eMudhra: has revoked the eight certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. It states that its root CA private keys and other intermediate CAs are not affected, and that the issue is limited to its global website-security business, not Indian DSC and eSign services.

Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users.

Who is at Most Risk?

Organizations should prioritize investigation if they:

Operate internet-facing websites, APIs, VPNs, or other TLS-enabled services.

Use publicly trusted certificates issued through eMudhra or emSign trust hierarchies.

Distribute signed software that relies on publicly trusted code-signing certificates.

Develop or run applications built on the Go programming language.

Maintain legacy systems, unmanaged endpoints, or custom trust stores that may not receive certificate distrust updates automatically.

How Can Qualys VMDR and Certificate View Help Identify eMudhra Certificates?

Use Certificate View, included with VMDR, to identify certificates issued by affected eMudhra authorities and use VMDR with Cloud Agent to identify hosts running vulnerable Go installations or software requiring vendor-issued updates.

Step 1: Make Sure Coverage Is Complete

Entitle Certificate View on your VMDR scan ranges. Confirm that the IP ranges you scan with VMDR are enabled in Certificate View.

Add external domains. For sites hosted by web or app providers, add the FQDNs or IP addresses in Certificate View. It runs a lightweight scan across standard ports to detect TLS services and analyze their certificates.

Use Cloud Agent where scans cannot reach. Agents report software and certificate data from endpoints, servers, and remote workers that network scans miss.

Step 2: Pinpoint the Eight Compromised Intermediates

To confirm whether any of the eight compromised intermediates appear in a chain, search for their SHA-256 fingerprints, serial numbers, or issuer names in Certificate View > Certificates.

Reference QQL Queries

By Issuer:

certificate:(issuer.name:[`EM EV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM EV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV CS CA – G3B`, `EM OV CS CA – G3C`])

By Serial Number:

certificate:(serialNumber:`c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1` or serialNumber:`6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568` or serialNumber:`a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214` or serialNumber:`8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109` or serialNumber:`296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504` or serialNumber:`588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321` or serialNumber:`7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a` or serialNumber:`544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6`)

The Information tab shows the fingerprints, serial number, and first and last found dates so that you can compare them with the SHA-256 values in the table.

Step 3: Find Software That Still Trusts the Affected Certificates

Certificates presented by your servers are only half of the exposure. Applications running older Go runtimes may continue to trust certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. VMDR/Cloud Agent can help you find them.

Find Go toolchains to update

Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block certificate chains that contain any of the eight compromised keys (CVE-2026-111943). Qualys has released QID 5019897 for SwCA scanning to detect affected Go versions. Before you scan, confirm your agents have the latest signatures that include this QID, so the new scan picks it up. Then open the Vulnerabilities tab and use the query below to list the impacted assets:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:5019897

Find Additional Vendor-Specific Updates

Qualys has also released QIDs to detect Go vulnerabilities associated with other vendor operating systems.

Enumerate Affected eMudhra Certificate Chains

In addition to software detection, Qualys is releasing QID 48395: eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration. This Information Gathered (IG) QID helps identify systems presenting or using certificate chains that contain the affected eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. Once available in your subscription, you can query for assets using:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:48395

Optional Check: Find eMudhra-Issued Certificates with QQL Queries in Certificate View

Open Certificate View > Certificates, paste the query below into the search bar, and run it. It matches any certificate whose issuer organization is one of the eMudhra entities in the affected list.

certificate:(issuer.organization:`eMudhra BV` or issuer.organization:`eMudhra Inc`)

The results list each certificate with its issuer, validity dates, and the assets and ports where it was found. Use the left-pane filters, such as Expiring Certificates and Certificate Authority, to sort the results by urgency.

The two organizations that matter most for this incident are eMudhra BV and eMudhra Inc, because they are the organizations named on the eight compromised intermediates (the G3B and G3C certificates).

Tip: save the query as a dashboard widget in Certificate View, so any new eMudhra-issued certificate that appears is flagged automatically.

Note: QQL query tokens are case-sensitive. If a query returns a syntax error, check the search token list in the Certificate View help and adjust the token name.

Response and Remediation

Replace affected certificates first. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight intermediates should be reissued by another trusted CA and redeployed with the correct chain.

Updates. Apply operating system security updates and upgrade Go runtimes to supported releases that reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates.

Confirm revocation behavior. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates, but clients that do not check revocation can still accept them. Validate that certificate revocation checks are functioning correctly and that revocation lists are up to date.

Monitor continuously. Monitor dashboards after each scan cycle until results are clean.

Conclusion

The eMudhra incident is a reminder that trust depends on both the certificates you present and the authorities you trust. Certificate View gives you the issuer search and dashboards to find eMudhra-issued certificates, and VMDR and Cloud Agent inventory show which hosts and applications still need vendor updates. Qualys enables organizations to quickly discover affected assets, validate exposure, and confidently prioritize response efforts.
