Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: AI-Linked Breaches Mount as WorkOS, Northflank, Trigger.dev Disclose Hacks
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: While part of the same industry-wide trend, the attacks do not appear to be related, and initial access varies from compromised credentials to third-party dependencies and...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
AI-related cyberattacks are surging, with hackers stealing AI access keys to monetize them and using AI tools to speed up their intrusions.

Over the past month, at least a dozen AI developer platforms were hit, with the most recent incidents involving CommandCode, Northflank, Trigger.dev, Chainstack, and WorkOS.

Across all incidents, the hackers appear to have been hunting for AI access tokens they could monetize, relying on AI agents to speed up and streamline their attacks.

While part of the same industry-wide trend, the attacks do not appear to be related, and initial access varies from compromised credentials to third-party dependencies and vulnerability exploitation.

The attackers hit Andromeda, Brev (NVIDIA), CommandCode, Fireworks AI, Lightning AI, Northflank, OpenCode, Railway, Trigger.dev, Warp, and Zeabur, mainly looking for stored customer secrets.

“Intruders are reaching AI provider credentials through the intermediary layer of hosting platforms, evaluation services, and developer consoles, and recent gateway compromises show the same interest in these secrets. Because that layer holds credentials on behalf of many downstream customers, a single intrusion can expose keys for many inference accounts at once,” Cloud Security Alliance pointed out.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Per Wiz’s analysis of the incidents, the surge is caused by the rise of LLM-jacking and LLM broker infrastructure, which make the stolen AI access tokens easily monetizable and will likely attract more threat actors to credential theft.

The cybersecurity outfit notes that this demand is also driven by distillation (training a cheaper model on the outputs of a more advanced one), “notably alleged against Chinese AI labs”.

Wiz says it has observed hackers abusing enterprise credentials compromised in these attacks, including two cases that “shared an identical first unauthorized activity, which happened within 30 minutes of the reported credential access within the vendor breach.”

The company observed multiple threat actors using the same compromised keys, which “suggests a robust market for this type of credential”.

Artex used to automate attacks

This week, blockchain infrastructure and Web3 services provider Chainstack and API platform for building enterprise applications WorkOS disclosed cyberattacks that relied on the open source AI penetration testing framework Artex for automation.

Multiple companies have linked attacks attributed to the Chinese APT Storm-0940 to the use of Artex, including a recent campaign targeting ConnectWise customers.

Chainstack was hit on October 26, and the attackers accessed a development environment and parts of the company’s production environment through a third-party component.

“The attacker accessed a database containing customer account information. Information that may have been exposed includes organization names, account holder names, the email addresses of your organization’s members on Chainstack, and password hashes,” the company said this week.

Node credentials might have been exposed as well, as the attackers had access to systems storing them, and Chainstack prompted customers to rotate those credentials.

On October 30, WorkOS says, the hackers compromised an internal application used by its sales team and accessed business contact details and summaries of customer communications.

The information includes names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, company affiliations, customer account histories, sales details, customer-relationship information, customer communications, and information about customers’ use of WorkOS products.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Fake software installers are turning your PCs into profit centers for hackers
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent.

The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post.

The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly.

“Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said, adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign.

Fake installers used for real money

The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software, games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads.

The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software.

Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. The installer communicates with rotating infrastructure using HTTP callbacks containing parameters such as “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution”. These requests allow the campaign to track individual software offers, allowing multiple payloads to succeed or fail independently within the same installation session.

The first monetization branch is WorldProxyPool, which installs proxyware to route third-party internet traffic through the victim’s device. It also creates SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updates.

Another branch installs CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC), alongside components such as VirtualBox, to facilitate distributed computing.

A third installs utility-style software associated with Advanced Windows Manager and Windows Manager. These applications may participate in advertising, software distribution, or affiliate-driven monetization.

Microsoft urges defenders to scrutinize unofficial software

Microsoft recommends preventing downloads from untrusted sources, particularly cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, and activation tools.

Organizations using Microsoft Defender Antivirus should enable cloud-delivered protection, maintain tamper protection, and configure reputation-based protection to block untrusted applications and downloads, the company said. It also recommends evaluating Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that restrict executable files based on prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria.

For detection and investigation, organizations were advised to check execution from Inno temporary directories, especially when files such as “eld*.exe, set_*.exe”, “FirstFast[1].exe”, or “SecondRunner[1].exe” appear.

Microsoft also recommends correlating outbound requests containing “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution” or “r=offer_execution_fail” with process activity, scheduled-task creation, and software installations.

Unexpected WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, or VirtualBox installations warrant investigation, it said.

Defender XDR customers can use Microsoft’s published advanced hunting queries to identify related activity, while a list of indicators of compromise (IOCs) was also shared to help defenders outside the Microsoft ecosystem.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 3AM Ransomware Used Human-AI Hybrid Tactics in UK School Estate Compromise
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A UK school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group via a unique hybrid human-AI operation, an investigation by Bitdefender has found.

The incident, which took place from September 10 to 19, 2026, resulted in the attackers’ encrypting 37 machines and building domain trust in the compromised estate to reach other schools.

Notably, the investigation revealed that parts of the post-compromise techniques were undertaken by a human operator at the keyboard, while other parts behaved like an AI agent.

Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe.”

The researchers continued: “What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and an [AI] model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.”

How 3AM’s Hybrid Attack Unfolded

The research blog, published on November 3, attributed the attack to a 3AM ransomware affiliate. 3AM is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, whose Rust-based encryptor was first observed in February 2023.

The researchers were not able to determine how the attacker gained initial access to the school estate. The first recorded activity started on September 10, when the attackers’ accessed credentials stored the estate’s backup infrastructure, before decrypting them with the Windows Data Protection API.

From September 12-13, the threat actor tested connections to other hosts from a machine where SQL Server was the parent process. They sent a sequence of commands to the target’s Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service, authenticating with stolen administrator credentials. The commands’ outputs were then read by either a person or AI model, who would then choose the next command and repeat the cycle.

A PowerShell command was first used, and re-ran unchanged 41 seconds later, before a single call was changed 49 seconds after that. Next, 47 seconds later, PowerShell was replaced with wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI.

The researchers noted that the fact the complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it indicates the commands were written by an AI agent.

The next nine retries followed a similar pattern of the delay before the next command being issued taking between 40 to 101 seconds, whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task to minutes.

“That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries,” the Bitdefender researchers wrote.

In contrast, later commands before the retry sequence were simpler and were sent between two and 16 minutes apart indicative of the pace of someone reading the output and deciding what to do next.

On September 14, the attacker made efforts to gain persistence in the compromised environments. These include running credential dumping tool Mimikatz and creating two backdoor domain-administrator accounts by separate routes.

Next, the attackers copied and 40 financial-related files via the Windows robocopy tool, which were subsequently exfiltrated to their command-and-control (C2) endpoint using HTTP POST.

“The registry-as-transport channel is an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for,” the researchers noted.

On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate within an approximately three-hour window. The researchers said this part of the attack was the clearest example of the hybrid human-AI approach being deployed.

The work involved in joining the estate’s separate domains is highly mechanical, requiring it to be set up correctly on both sides, with one wrong detail stopping everything.

The attackers built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Bitdefender said the hybrid human-AI model suits this work, involving repetitive configuration where the fix comes from a human reading the error.

This work resulted in the attackers reaching 50 machines from the unmanaged host.

Finally, the threat actor made attempts to remove endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, before decrypting 37 out of the 50 machines accessed.

How to Defend Against Hybrid AI Ransomware Attacks

Bitdefender noted that the attack involved typical approaches observed in other ransomware incidents, including backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains and use of built-in legitimate tooling.

However, the hands-on work was split between human and AI operators, making use of their respective abilities.

“The approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have,” the researchers commented.

They also noted that the involved of an AI model changes what the traces look like during an incident.

Bitdefender offered the following recommendations for defenders to protect against future attacks that follow a similar playbook:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place

Treat backup infrastructure as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them

Put an endpoint agent on every machine

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Police Seize 100+ Servers After Four-Year Investment Fraud Probe
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers and shuttered several scam websites.

Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, the action day on November 3 targeted the company believed to be responsible for hosting the fraudulent investment websites.

Victims were lured to these sites by deceptive ads promising huge gains with no downside. After they recorded their interest, personal data would be shared by the company with criminal groups operating scam call centers, according to Europol.

Scammers impersonating brokers then used a variety of social engineering tactics to persuade the victims to invest their funds in the fictitious schemes. Online accounts set up to perpetrate the scheme apparently displayed illusory gains, persuading them to plough more money into the funds.

When victims asked to withdraw their money, brokers used delaying tactics to block payments before cutting contact and leaving them with no way to recover their funds, Europol claimed.

Investigators estimate losses to exceed €4m ($4.5m), with potential victims in as many as 50 countries.

Read more on investment fraud: Cops Arrest Suspected Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Mastermind.

Alongside the server seizures, the action day on Tuesday resulted in the arrest of seven suspects who will be extradited to Germany. Authorities also searched 17 locations and seized other evidence and assets.

The operation involved cooperation from Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, highlighting the transnational nature of this fraud scheme. Scam call centers have been identified in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, according to Europol.

Four Years in the Making

The case dates back to 2022, when a German couple complained to local authorities that they couldn’t withdraw their funds from an investment scheme they had enrolled in.

An action day on September 6, 2022, led to searches in Belgium and Latvia, and the arrest of two suspects. Evidence was seized which helped police identify seven other members of the network, including the managers of call centers which were used in the scams.

Another action day came on May 13, 2025, when police conducted eight searches simultaneously in Albania, Cyprus and Israel. That resulted in the arrest of one suspect in Cyprus and the seizure of more evidence including electronic devices, documents and cash, Europol said at the time.

Police are not claiming, as they have done in the past, to have dismantled the network.

According to the FBI, investment fraud was the highest-grossing cybercrime type in 2025, amassing nearly $8.7bn for cybercriminals. Other schemes that have come to light in Europe over recent years include an €89m ($100m) ring that was smashed in 2023 and a financial crime organization that made €15m ($17m) until it was disrupted in 2021.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Malicious cPGuard Updates Served in OpsShield Supply Chain Attack
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The supply chain attack was discovered within 12 hours and the fake updates were distributed for roughly 70 minutes
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Indian IT security company OpsShield on Monday fell victim to a cyberattack that resulted in malicious versions of cPGuard being served to its customers.

OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software, and cPGuard is its most notable product, designed for Linux web hosting servers.

According to the company’s incident notice, the attackers used compromised credentials to access its update distribution infrastructure (CDN) and distribute a malicious script via cPGuard’s update channel.

cPGuard versions 5.88.12–5.88.19 contained the malicious code. The supply chain attack was discovered within 12 hours and the fake updates were distributed for roughly 70 minutes.

The attackers first targeted the company’s billing and licensing server. They registered a customer account and ordered a free cPGuard trial to study its communication with the licensing system, then started sending crafted requests to the portal.

After obtaining command execution on the billing and licensing server, the hackers started collecting data and then uploaded a fake cPGuard update using a stolen access key, the company explains in an updated report.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The update was executed as root on the servers that polled OpsShield’s update infrastructure during the compromise window. At the same time, the attackers copied three of the company’s cloud servers.

The malicious script in the updates was designed to collect data and upload it to OpsShield’s licensing server under a compromised account. According to the company, the hackers retrieved 32 collected files from the data uploaded by the script, each from a different customer server.

Additionally, the script deployed a hidden root shell and certain files in the temp folder of customers’ servers.

OpsShield estimates that 2,950 servers executed the fake cPGuard updates, and that the attackers copied approximately 7,900 client account records containing names, company, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords.

All password hashes, root SSH keys, and MySQL root passwords, as well as shell history on the infected customer servers, should be considered compromised and rotated.

“If cPGuard was not online during that window, your server did not receive the fake update. You should still reset your billing portal password,” OpsShield says.

The company says it evicted the attackers from all servers they may have touched, reset secrets on its account, removed the attacker’s SSH key and cloned assets from its cloud account, and replaced all SSH keys and passwords across its servers.

Additionally, it started reissuing all cPGuard license private/public keys because the attackers compromised them, reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated associated API keys, and is rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers.

OpsShield also released cPGuard updates (version 5.88.25 and later) that remove the hidden root shell and the additional files left behind by the script, and published indicators of compromise (IoCs).

“Attacks like this one are getting faster and cheaper to run. Our answer is to harden our own update and signing process first, and then to put what we learned here straight back into cPGuard for you,” the company notes.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Rigged Coding Assignment, Abused AI Tool Opened Path to $6 Billion Binance Heist
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The malware substituted a rogue copy of a legitimate developer tool component and opened a channel to a server run by the attackers
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Binance says the hackers behind last week’s $6.34 billion theft reached its wallet signing systems after a months-long campaign that compromised three engineers’ computers, one of them through a fake job interview.

The exchange published its initial incident report on November 3. Roughly $2.85 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted.

“This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said.

The FBI has blamed the theft on TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group.

How the attack unfolded

According to Binance, the intrusion unfolded in stages and relied on fake recruiters, malicious downloads, hijacked employee computers and an internal AI tool. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company noted.

The campaign started in June, when a Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while looking for a popular AI coding tool through a search engine.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Binance’s security team caught it, swapped out his device and reset the related credentials. Even so, the attackers had already gained insight into what he did and who he worked with on the wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a second engineer was approached by someone claiming to be a project director. He was invited to two interviews, the first with a fake HR representative and the second with the alleged CEO of a company that did not exist.

During the first interview, the HR impostor shared a social media account containing personal photos and videos to build rapport. The second took place over a chat app and ended with a request to download a coding “assignment” onto his work computer.

The assignment hid a malicious code repository that executed as soon as the engineer set it up. The malware substituted a rogue copy of a legitimate developer tool component and opened a channel to a server run by the attackers.

“The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time,” Binance said.

On October 20, the attackers used the infected machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of the first engineer’s system and a third wallet engineer’s system. The report does not explain how the AI tool was used.

The first engineer’s computer held a token that allowed container deployments. On October 29, the attackers signed into the third engineer’s computer, deployed a container with credentials taken from the first engineer and kicked off the attack with a malicious script.

Binance says the attackers exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to move XRP, SOL, OP and BTC out of its hot wallets. The same service was used to abuse Ethereum’s EIP-7702 mechanism, giving a contract under the attackers’ control partial execution rights over a hot wallet.

“However, suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements. The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure,” the company explained.

The hot wallet was secured with multi-party computation (MPC), which meant Binance had no single key it could use to cancel the delegation right away. The last unauthorized transfer settled at 23:56 UTC, and the delegation was cleared shortly after midnight.

Binance says it has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool, replaced devices and retired the engineers’ credentials and tokens. It is engaging independent security firms to review the incident and is working on a research fund focused on AI security in blockchain environments.

The exchange also disclosed that it had detected and blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked threats this year.

Other developments

North Korea has rejected the FBI’s attribution of the heist to its TraderTraitor hackers. “It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds,” Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement carried by state media.

[ Read: North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea to Protest Binance Hack Claims ]

Binance has also completed a zero-knowledge proof for its October 31 reserves snapshot, which lets holders of 10 major tokens verify that their balances are backed at least 1:1. Co-CEO Richard Teng says 98% of the impacted tokens have now been replenished.

Teng also said on November 3 that withdrawals have broadly resumed. The exchange began reopening them in phases on November 1.

On the laundering front, Elliptic says the stolen funds passed through about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in under four days, using automation but with no sign of AI agents making decisions. As of November 3, roughly $3.18 billion remained in theft-linked addresses. Separately, Chainalysis said an emergency pause at THORChain, triggered by an unrelated technical issue, had temporarily slowed the laundering.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: The VOLTA infostealer: Outsourcing cybercrime grunt work to AI
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: So when I ran the hunt and ultimately found this, what I do first is there's a series of filters that are pulling binaries that have AI specific fingerprints in them. It's like an added feature that can be run, but the stealer can just run and do all this collection and package everything back, or package everything...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Amy Ciminnisi: 0:00

Welcome to Talos Takes, where we discuss Cisco Talos’ latest research and security news. We break down complex topics for everyone from beginner to expert, C-suite to frontline.

Amy Ciminnisi: 0:13

Hello everyone, happy November! Attackers often face a bottleneck. They steal massive piles of data, and then they have to do the slow, tedious work of figuring out which of the victims are actually worth the effort. But now malware can start doing that analysis for them. VOLTA is a newly discovered info stealer that uses LOLs to turn raw stolen credentials into a prioritize high value dossier. And here to break this down is Ryan Fetterman, who is the creator of CAIRN. Now, if you haven't heard already, CAIRN is a research framework that is designed to track these AI integrated threats. It examines the metadata so there is no need for binary downloads or risky detonations. And it gives defenders insights into how attackers are integrating intelligence AI specifically into their operations. So Ryan is joining me to talk about all things VOLTA and what this kind of automation means for security teams. Ryan, how are you doing?

Ryan Fetterman: 1:27

I'm good. Yeah. Thanks for having me. Although I wish I was here under less scary circumstances.

Amy Ciminnisi: 1:34

I really wish so, too. Maybe we'll get you on here for, you know, something a little less pressing, a little less. Reality shifting. So let's actually start with the discovery. Of this. When you were analyzing this, was there like, a specific moment where you realized, like, hey. This isn't just a credential sealer. This is just a. Whole intelligence analysis suite. Like, what was that? Moment for you?

Ryan Fetterman: 2:09

Sure. So I can explain kind of how this comes about from the care and perspective. So when I ran the hunt and ultimately found this, what I do first is there's a series of filters that are pulling binaries that have AI specific fingerprints in them. So the rule that this binary matched on was, it had an API endpoint. We can see that in the metadata. In this case it's using open router. So when I do the second level pass there's a second tier of Yara rules that will then characterize more of the behavior of the binary. And in this case we had rule matches for telegram integration with that LLM as a C2 potentially. And then also AV labels indicating that it's a stealer with AI integration. So in this case, those rules were pretty accurate and give you an initial impression of what the file is and what what kind of malware we might be looking at. But I would say there wasn't really an moment until the Re stage when when you're doing like the reverse engineering of the binary. And at this point when I did a string stomp, I recovered the VOLTA-AUTODOXER name, which just sounds like a malware and like a doxing kind of stealer implant. And then ultimately, like recovering the prompt itself is always like a really unique and cool, aspect of like, this AI integrated malware, because there's no more guessing about the, the intent and the motivation of this tool, like it's all spelled out there for us.

Amy Ciminnisi: 3:53

Yeah. And so let's. Get into maybe what this tool actually does. One of the things that I found pretty crazy in the blog is that it doesn't just like grab saved passwords, but it uses sessions to look up like DoorDash order histories or, you know, confirm addresses with receipts in your Gmail inbox. You know, from a practitioner perspective, this seems really invasive. How does this change the way that we view the impact of a compromise browser session?

Ryan Fetterman: 4:32

Yeah, I think this is a big deal. And I've witnessed this personally, like as I've used, Google and like, oh, off authentication to connects to so many more services and things. Now it's just convenient to not have to create another account and password for everything you connect to. But it really makes your kind of core like your your Google account, just like a real gem for an attacker. Because if you're able to access that and replay an authenticated session from the the victim's machine, which is what they're doing in this case, you just have the keys to, so many different apps and so much data. And this malware really does a good job of showing you kind of like what the extra mile looks like when you have access to these kind of credentials. So I'm not an expert in this space, but like, I know there's a lot of hardware backed protections that prevent attackers from kind of extracting your credentials and taking them back off of your machine. But that doesn't really help in this context, because they're replaying the authenticated sessions from your actual machine. So in this case, there are protections like step up authentication, like when you're trying to make a really serious change, like, you know, rerouting where your mail is going or something like that. Google will prompt you for another, challenge for authentication. But in this case, the attacker, maybe knowingly or wisely, is kind of staying under that bar as well and just doing like inbox searches to provide like a layer of enrichment to that. They have the first level of credentials, like the basic information and what they can scrape off of your machine, but then they're replaying those sessions to do basically like a second pass to see what else they can pull. To kind of round you out as a target.

Amy Ciminnisi: 6:31

And then looking at like the prompt itself, I mean, if it weren't so malicious, I would find it so impressive. But it like, prompts the LLN to make connections between, like, the victim's hobbies or their home address to things like their password patterns.

Ryan Fetterman: 6:52

Yeah. What's interesting is the the AI integration in this case is actually totally optional. It's like an added feature that can be run, but the stealer can just run and do all this collection and package everything back, or package everything up and send it back to the attacker without this kind of polishing step. So the exfil can actually happen in three stages. It can exfil after the stealer runs, it can fill after the AI call, or it can exfil after the last layer of like, network enrichment produces anything. And I think this is something that we've seen across a couple different AI integrated malware now that not only like this model has multi-model, kind of resilience in it. So they're anticipating potentially hitting refusals on the first model, which in this case is Claude. So if they can't accomplish the the prompt with Claude, they will kind of cascade to less permissive models. But then ultimately the ability for the malware to run without the without the AI integration overall, I think is another interesting idea. But yeah, this is kind of clever use of AI. They talk about picking out specific patterns within the victim's data, which is something that these language models are really good at. Better than humans, I would say in most cases. So they're talking about connecting like if, there's browser traffic to a, a learning management system, can you infer that this person goes to that university or teaches at a school or something like that? They're looking for patterns in your passwords or connections between your personal data and your password, which then I think may translate to if you if you have patterns for how you create passwords for services that they don't know. So I think they're really kind of cleverly trying to stretch the data as much as they can and using AI in a really fascinating way that I think this is the first time that I've seen AI be employed in the malware in some way that actually has nothing to do with, like the cyber kill chain, but is just like asking the model to function like an intelligence analyst or kind of outsourcing this analytical work, like the model is a subcontractor for them, right?

Amy Ciminnisi: 9:32

And I can't believe we forgot to kind of mention this, but what are the other sections of output that the prompt requests the LLM to go through? You kind of started to touch on one there. What someone is worth. Can you kind of talk about that a little bit more?

Ryan Fetterman: 9:50

So the characterization of the prompt from the first line is telling the, the model that they are acting as a forensic intelligence analyst. And I think this is kind of a creative framing for this kind of task, because they don't want to characterize this task as anything kind of overtly malicious, when they're trying to use a frontier model, which they're trying to use Claude for this on the first pass. So I think this characterization of being an intelligence analyst kind of puts it in a more benign light. They also really emphasize citations, sticking to the facts. Not making any jumps in in inference, they kind of bundle evidence into different layers where there are, subjective identifiers. There are corroborated facts. When you have points of data that are backed by two independent data sources. So this is a pretty thorough structure. Almost like a, you know, a realistic like intelligence assessment type of report that they're putting together. But then, yeah, ultimately, what sticks out about your profile that the LLM is putting together based on the scraped data is who who they are the victim in this case, what they do. What they're worth. Which is a list of your value valuables ranked by monetization, like your crypto. They'll do a lookup on your Roblox account. They'll look at your card accounts, and they'll put these into tears. Low, medium and high. And then they're also assessing your OpSec. How strong are your passwords? Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Fake Interview of Software Engineer Led to Binance Mega-Heist
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking digital heist last week, the crypto exchange has revealed.

Binance revealed the news in a lengthy post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 3.

“It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” it explained.

“The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

Read more on crypto theft: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency.

The main point of intrusion appears to have stemmed from an interview the threat group set up with an unnamed “Software Engineer B” in September.

An individual posing as a project director contacted the engineer via a legitimate job-hunting platform, having spotted from their profile that they worked at Binance.

The first-round interview was held with a fictitious HR representative, during which the interviewer shared a social media account with the engineer, including personal photos and videos posted, in order to build trust, Binance said.

“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” it continued. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”

According to Binance, the “zero-day malware” used obfuscation and evasion techniques to ensure it was not detected by the engineer’s endpoint security tools. These included replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and connect with a C2 server.

The Pathway to Wallet-Signing Operations

On October 20, the attacker accessed an internal AI tool via Engineer B’s computer to compromise the machines of two other Binance employees: Wallet DevOps Engineer A and Wallet Software Engineer C.

The former had been scoped out back in June when they unwittingly downloaded a malicious version of Homebrew, a third-party package manager for macOS, after clicking on a malicious search ad.

Although the Binance team “detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials” at the time, the engineer’s role and those of his colleagues had already been exposed to the hackers.

After compromising Engineer A’s machine, they found out he had a container deployment permission token on his computer.

“On October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C’s computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack,” the report explained.

Between 20:05 UTC and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets then sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent around 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

Clean-Up Time

Binance said it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool along with the latter’s access controls, and that it has replaced affected devices.

It also decommissioned engineer credentials and tokens, enhanced security scans across employee devices, improved AI-based behavioral anomaly detection and strengthened wallet service risk controls.

The firm admitted it had already detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korean attacks this year alone. It is currently conducting a review of the incident, setting up a security research fund with industry partners, and has already increased investment in AI-enabled detection, protection and monitoring tools.

Experts from Fortra questioned the controls that were originally in place to protect employee, and especially developer, machines.

“In a world where quiet quitting exists, it should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time. Organizations need to counter this with adequate controls in place. Particularly, controls around what can be downloaded and executed on a corporate laptop, as well as the permissions granted to the user,” argued Tyler Reguly, associate director, security R&D at Fortra.

“At the end of the day, developer laptops are among the hardest devices in an organization to lock down safely without being detrimental. Organizations need to find the balance point."

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea as Pyongyang Protests Against US Claims on Binance Hack
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in protest of accusations that North Korean hackers were behind the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance.

Observers say North Korea was likely pressuring the U.S. to drop what it calls its hostility against the North and offer concessions if it wants to restore ties between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles fired toward North Korea’s eastern waters. It said South Korean and U.S. authorities were analyzing details of the launches. It said South Korea maintains readiness to repel any potential provocations by North Korea.

Earlier Wednesday, Kim’s sister, senior official Kim Yo Jong, again disputed an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible for the hack at Binance, calling it “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” Pyongyang.

“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”

In a Tuesday statement, she described the FBI announcement as “a trite provocation.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.

In recent months, North Korea has accelerated its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. The news of the latest launches came amid vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections.

Also Wednesday, North Korea’s state KCNA news agency released a photo showing parts of a warship under construction that would likely be its biggest naval vessel. KCNA said Kim Jong Un expressed satisfaction this week during a visit to the Nampho Shipyard over the warship that it said “is incomparably huge” relative to its 5,000-ton destroyers. Kim previously said North Korea planned to build a 10,000-ton strategic guided missile cruiser.

Tensions between the two Koreas have also deepened since mine blasts at their border in September wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the border and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.

North Korea later threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: An internal AI tool let attackers walk between teams in the Binance breach by Lucie Cardiet
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Three gaps in one chain The Binance breach is unusual because all three detection gaps appear in the same incident: ‍Gap 1, nothing looks wrong: The malicious binary replaced a...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
On 29 October 2026, attackers moved approximately $6.34 billion out of Binance's internet-connected trading wallets (hot wallets) in under four hours. The FBI attributes the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit. As of Binance's 3 November disclosure, roughly $2.85 billion has been frozen.

The wallet-draining mechanism is crypto-specific and most enterprise defenders will never encounter it. But the months of preparation that made it possible look like a standard enterprise breach: social engineering, a compromised developer workstation, stolen credentials, and lateral movement (moving from one system to the next) across team boundaries where no single security team saw the full chain.

A fake job interview placed the first foothold

The campaign started no later than June 2026 with a tampered software download on a Wallet DevOps engineer's machine. Binance detected it, replaced the device, and rotated credentials. The response was correct. It was also incomplete: the attacker had already mapped the wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a separate software engineer was contacted through a legitimate job platform. What followed was a two-round interview, including a live video call where the interviewer shared personal photos to build trust. Near the end of the second round, the engineer was told to download a coding "assignment." The repository replaced a legitimate development tool with a malicious binary. Binance confirms it "was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time".

Nothing looked wrong:

A developer downloaded a coding assignment from a job interview.

The binary sat where the legitimate tool had been.

The security software on the engineer's machine had nothing to match it against.

The AI tool was the corridor between teams

This is the detail that turns a crypto theft into an enterprise story.

On 20 October, nine days before the theft, the attacker used the compromised engineer's machine and an internal AI tool to reach two other engineers on the wallet team. Binance's disclosure confirms the attacker "leveraged the compromised computer of engineer B and used an internal AI tool to gain control over" Engineers A and C. The tool is not named.

The AI tool was a shared service that connected people across roles. The attacker was already authenticated as the compromised engineer, so interacting with the tool looked like normal use. There was no exploit of the tool itself. It was functioning exactly as designed: connecting people, sharing context, enabling collaboration. That is what made it a path for moving between teams.

Through that path, the attacker found a permission token for deploying containers on one engineer's machine. On 29 October, the attacker used it to deploy a malicious container that reached Binance's internal wallet signing service. From there, the attacker initiated unauthorized transactions using valid credentials through the normal signing path.

Three gaps in one chain

The Binance breach is unusual because all three detection gaps appear in the same incident:

‍Gap 1, nothing looks wrong: The malicious binary replaced a legitimate tool, the zero-day evaded the security software and the attacker removed traces of the compromise.

‍Gap 2, authentication succeeds: The signing service processed the attacker's requests because they arrived through the normal path with valid credentials.

‍Gap 3, movement isn't visible: The attacker crossed from a software engineer's workstation, to an internal AI tool, to Wallet DevOps credentials, to a different engineer's machine, to a container platform, to the signing service. Five hops across four functional boundaries. Each appeared in a different log.

Internal AI tools are trust boundaries nobody is watching

Most organizations adopting internal AI tools are focused on data leakage and on attackers manipulating the tool's inputs. Those are real risks. But the Binance breach shows a third: the tool itself becomes a bridge between teams, and a compromised identity on one side can walk to the other without triggering a boundary alert, because no boundary exists.

The signing service worked. The security software worked until it met a zero-day, which is what zero-days do. The credential rotation in June was the right call. Each control did its job in isolation. The gap was the chain between them, and the AI tool sitting in the middle of that chain, treated as an application rather than a trust boundary.

Detection is not broken. It is incomplete.

Network and identity telemetry close the gaps between controls

Each control in the Binance chain worked in its own lane. The problem was the space between lanes. Closing that space requires two things the individual controls do not provide: visibility into how identities behave across systems (not just whether they authenticated), and visibility into how traffic moves between hosts (not just whether it was allowed).

Network telemetry shows an internal AI tool suddenly generating access patterns it has never generated before. Identity telemetry shows a software engineer's account interacting with wallet infrastructure it has never touched. Neither signal alone is conclusive. Correlated, they are a single story: a compromised identity is walking from one team's environment into another's.

That correlation is what Vectra AI's Attack Signal Intelligence does. It connects identity behavior and network behavior across on-premises and cloud environments, including both human and non-human identities (service accounts, tokens, application credentials), and surfaces them as one attack narrative rather than isolated alerts. In a chain like Binance's, the goal is to surface the five-hop path as one event before the attacker reaches the signing service, not to flag each hop independently after the fact.

For a detailed walk-through of how these three detection gaps interact, including coverage mapping for identity, network, and cloud telemetry, see chapters 3 through 5 of the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks whitepaper.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Monitoring AI agent sessions: Leveraging embedding models to aid threat hunting and attack discovery workflows
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Query rules find behavior you can define, but agent sessions contain unstructured behaviors you can only describe. I stored six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions as semantic vectors in Elastic and searched them instead of handing every session to a large language model (LLM). One in seven sessions came back requiring triage of suspicious actions. We can then create rules to detect semantically similar malicious chats and raise them to our security operations center (SOC). We now have a way to search across all agent sessions and to ask questions nobody thought to ask at ingest.

Finding successful logins after multiple failed attempts is an easy query to make, because the log records every action a human decides to take, and we just have to query against known set fields to find conditions. AI agents break that model. A human describes an outcome, and the agent decides the actions. Every individual action can be allowed, while the session as a whole is a problem.

AI agents could take on a large share of the operational work in a SOC, but adoption has been slower than the technology. A big part of that is trust. We have no scalable way to inspect what agents are doing beyond keyword and regex matching.

The current answer is to have another model read every session. Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs. Plus, a new question means reevaluating everything already collected. That rules it out for threat hunting, where the job is asking new questions of old data.

This article tests a different approach. I believe we need to go deeper in how we detect and the functions we use to detect this new attack vector. Each turn is embedded once at ingest and stored as vectors in Elastic. Hunting then becomes semantic search. You describe the behavior, or hand over a known bad session, and rank everything by similarity. Only what scores above a threshold goes to a human or an LLM.

Why AI agent sessions are hard to detect

As an example of something hard to detect in agent chats, a developer asks their coding agent to tidy up a data export. The agent reads a CSV, which turns out to contain customer records. It runs git init, adds a remote repository, commits, and pushes to the repository. Every single action was allowed, so how do we find the security flaw? Reading a file in the project directory is allowed, and so is Git. The remote connection to github.com is also allowed, since half of engineering depends on it. Nothing alerts, because there was no rule made to detect this type of violation. The only place you can see what actually happened is in the sentence that the human typed at the start of the session and within the reasoning / tool calls of the agent. This type of issue isn't purposefully malicious. These kinds of inadvertent actions are happening across our organizations on a daily basis, and we’re only getting half the picture.

Frequently, looking at agent sessions, you find carelessness, like someone moving too fast or working around a control that was slowing them down. It could also be that someone didn’t notice "back this up somewhere" resolved to a personal namespace. In the evaluation later in this blog, I discuss how I found that a person moving too fast and introducing risk happens far more often than a direct attack. With AI, people who haven’t been trained to understand cybersecurity risks have gained the ability to implement them. Agents multiply the blast radius of ordinary mistakes and increase the attack surface because we only need to describe an outcome and hope that security gets picked up as a nonfunctional requirement.

How Uber built ADR to evaluate agent sessions with LLMs

This year, Uber published the ADR system using agents to evaluate agent sessions across 7k+ hosts and 10k+ sessions a day. Uber has found hundreds of credential exposures and created a prevention layer that blocks credential leaks, with 97.2% precision. The company open sourced it here.

ADR hands every session to a generative model, giving us fast triage and labeling that tags its hypothesis as it goes so we have a record to report on or query later. Anything suspicious escalates to a deeper reasoning agent that checks tool source code, threat intel, and policy to help mitigate and remediate incidents.

ADR works, but there are a few drawbacks worth naming:

It’s very expensive to have an AI agent analyze all sessions. Uber has gotten around this with a two-tier architecture: a cheap model for initial incident triage; and an expensive one for reasoning and deep investigations.

If you cannot afford the models you want to use, your only option is coverage gaps.

Generative models are probabilistic. In my own testing, I found a deviation of 1–5% on variants of Claude’s Opus models.

Benchmarking a constantly changing investigation medium isn’t accurate enough to feel confident of 100% coverage.

You have to know every question up front. If leadership later wants to know whether anyone is using agents for personal work, every session that developers have ever had needs to be reevaluated. That’s fatal for threat hunting, where the whole job is asking a new question of old data every day.

So, what’s the answer? In this post, we look at embedding models. The same model type that Claude uses for memory is the one that search systems use for retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and Google uses for reverse image search. We review whether using an embedding model to retrieve sessions is accurate and whether it’s a valid new way of detecting malicious content in agent sessions.

Uber’s evaluation included one approach that uses embeddings, but it has an LLM rewrite every prompt and action into a description first. It compares that against other descriptions rather than anything a person or agent actually wrote.

A prebaked pattern set is the right place to start, which is why I use MITRE ATLAS (v2026.07) for mine. But a baseline has to be molded to the organization, because the way people think and phrase things when chatting with an LLM varies a lot. And embeddings are at their best in hunting: taking a known bad session and finding the next 12 like it. Used that way, the queries keep getting better as you close investigations.

What an embedding model actually is

Different from a chatbot, with an embedding model, you input some information (text, a video, audio, images) and you get a row of numbers. Each number is called a dimension and is some representation of a category that the model has learned during its creation. Think of the first number as "animals." If we searched “blond dogs” or “white cats,” we’d expect this first number to score high. Similarly, if we had “color” as the second number, we’d expect it to score high. If we searched “red truck,” we’d expect “animals” to score low but “color” to score high. In truth, nobody knows what any individual number measures. The model worked that out during training. The weights are then frozen in time, and there’s no sampling step at the end, so the same text produces the same numbers today and next year. That’s the property that generative models cannot give you.

Think of these numbers as colors:

We’re essentially trying to compare something (a query, an image, audio, a video) to another to find similarities. Here’s an example with images:

Embed two photos of the same person, and the number patterns come out alike. Embed photos of somebody else, and the pattern is visibly different. Whether you’re working with faces or text, the result is the same. You put something in, and numbers come out. It’s as simple as that.

So the plan is to run every record through the model once and store the vectors of those records at ingest. At query time, write your question in natural language and run it through the same model. Then compare its numbers against everything you stored.

What comes back is an ordering. Every session gets a place in the list, nothing is discarded or decided. Keep that in mind, because it matters for how we measure this later. Lexical search matches or it doesn't. Vector search always matches, to a degree, which means that we want to cut off at a threshold.

A generative model produces a fresh probabilistic answer every time, which is why you pay per session and cannot guarantee the same answer twice. An embedding model produces one fixed representation, computed once, and then stored, and you can compare against it forever. We’re essentially building a deterministic way to search probabilistic data. For example, we’d ask a generative model, How many of my sessions contain credential leakage? For embedding models, we have to provide language similar to what we think that a user, reasoning channel, agent response, or tool calls might produce:

User: Work around the security restrictions for now.

Reasoning channel: The user is asking me to add a security bypass for FTP access.

Agent response: I have disabled app locker from preventing self signed applications from running.

To understand the performance of embedding models, it’s better to look at direct benchmarking on the model creator's own tests. The data we hold and the way that we ask questions have a greater impact on our search results than the model's performance. Embedding models are tuned by task type. jina-embeddings-v5-text-small is a general text model, so every number in this article comes from something that has never seen an agent transcript. Tool calls and reasoning channels are their own dialect, and a model fine-tuned on them would be a different measurement. Treat what follows as a floor.

Why chunking agent sessions by channel matters

You cannot embed a whole session as one vector and expect to find anything specific. Think of it as color. A session comes out the other end as a single shade, say a light blue. That tells you the final color but not how it got there. How much red went in? Once the paint is mixed, you cannot recover the pigments, and if red was the thing you were looking for, it’s gone.

If a developer spends two hours on a build pipeline and 30 seconds pulling a customer export somewhere it shouldn't go, we’d lose the context of that 30 seconds if we only embedded the entire session.

So instead, we chunk by channel and we chunk every turn. (That’s what I did for this post, but the best approach is yet to be decided.) Every time we send an AI a message, a scheduled job runs, or a tool is called by AI, we capture a vector of it across:

User input (prompt).

Agent reasoning.

Agent response.

Agent tool calls.

Each call gets its own vector. We can then also ask which channel carries the highest fidelity signal across any session.

Each turn gets up to four vectors, one per channel. A query runs a separate vector search against each channel, and the four ranked lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). RRF scores a turn by its position in each list, ignoring the raw similarity score. That matters here, because a shell transcript and a paragraph of reasoning produce similarity scores on different scales. Adding raw scores together would let whichever channel habitually scores highest drown out the others. Ranks don’t have that problem. Each session then scores as its best turn, so 30 seconds of risky work isn’t averaged away by two hours of ordinary work.

To test this, each question is written once per channel, in the way that channel’s text actually reads. Each version runs against its own channel, the results are merged with RRF into one ranking of sessions, and that ranking is checked against the labeled sessions. Keeping the channels separate also means each one can be scored on its own.

Three ways to query stored agent session vectors

Method

Example query

Strength

Weakness

Instructive text

Show me where data exfiltration has occurred across my sessions

None; included because it’s the first thing that everyone tries

Finds sessions that discuss exfiltration, not sessions where it happened

Descriptive hunt

Publish the data publicly via the API

Finds behavior never seen before, which exemplar retrieval cannot

Limited to what you thought to write down

Exemplar retrieval

The full text of a known bad turn, used as the query itself

Strongest method in testing; improves as investigations close

Needs a descriptive hunt first; similar doesn’t mean malicious

You can ask in an instructive way, but this won’t return relevant results. For example: Show me where data exfiltration has occurred across my sessions. We’re looking for where data exfiltration (or similar topics) were discussed in agent sessions. We’ll find where the words “data exfiltration” have been semantically asked for in the text from the agent sessions, not where it’s present.

You can ask for similar sessions via descriptive hunts, where we write down the behavior we want to find, embed it, and search. The important thing is that we’re asking for sessions, based on similarity to what the user would have asked for: Publish the data publicly via the API. The weakness is that we don't know what we don't know. So, how do we ensure coverage across all potential attacks? We do have MITRE ATLAS to show coverage areas, but the lower-level queries that we run to find these will be an ever-changing detection challenge. Its strength is that we can find behavior that we haven’t seen in the past, which the next method of retrieval cannot.

Exemplar retrieval is essentially where we take a known bad session and look for similar sessions by searching for similar vectors. One closed investigation becomes Find me the next 12 like this. In my testing, this was the strongest method for finding malicious content, but we only find these exemplar sessions from descriptive hunts.

We can also flag outlier sessions where vectors are far from any others to understand and evaluate the more unique sessions that our users are having across our estate:

What the SOC and leadership want to ask of agent sessions

From the SOC:

Is anyone pushing code somewhere unsafe?

Did a file that the agent read hijack the agent’s behavior?

Is anyone bypassing security controls because they were in the way?

We just confirmed an incident. Which sessions look like they could be related?

And from leadership, which is where this gets interesting for everyone who isn’t the SOC:

How much privileged material is going into agent sessions?

Are engineers using corporate tokens for personal work?

Where is our AI spend going, and what value does it produce? Is it producing anything?

Do people need training to get more out of these tools?

How to benchmark AI agent session monitoring

To measure search accuracy, you need to know the right answers before you search. Otherwise, you’re grading your own homework.

I started with six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions (399 sessions, 7,454 turns) embedded into Elastic with the four channels kept separate. My work is security demos, and customer environments, along with prototypes, so my ordinary sessions focus on credentials, exfiltration, and attacker infrastructure all day long.

Every one of those 7,454 turns needs a label. I used an LLM for it, because doing it by hand would take weeks. This is a benchmarking step rather than something you’d run in production. Sampling sessions with a generative model on a schedule is still worth doing, because it’s how you find the questions you didn’t know to ask.

Labeling 7,454 agent turns with an LLM

I evaluated Opus 5, 4.8, and 4.6, and I used 4.6, because it was the most consistent of the three across repeat runs. It read every turn of every session and decided whether a human should look at it.

The one that didn’t clear holds an AKIA-shaped key in a demo fixture, and the model said that it couldn’t tell from the window whether the key was real. That’s the correct answer to the question.

Of my 368 real sessions, 56 (approximately one in seven) are review-worthy.

Building a query set from MITRE ATLAS

My first query set came out of Uber's taxonomy with my own coverage areas layered on top. It scored well but was also skewed to my own bias and evaluation, so instead I built the question set against MITRE ATLAS (essentially, MITRE ATT&CK but for AI-based data). I built a question set across 16 tactics and 101 techniques, to cover all techniques as a baseline. We have 264 questions across 86 techniques (two to four per technique).

I had to ensure no bias, so I didn’t make any changes to the original baseline. Rewording would have potentially introduced bias to improve scoring, rather than measuring accuracy on my original result. It’s worth noting that we’d want to introduce changes and improve scoring over time but not for an initial baseline and test.

Although I’ve made this question set to be run manually, LLMs would be great at creating and refining a similar set against your unique data with a decent system prompt.

You cannot ask an embedding model for a category

An embedding model won’t find a category if you phrase it as an instruction. You have to write the thing that the category would have produced.

For example, if you search Look for content returned by a tool containing instructions addressed to the assistant itself, we wouldn’t get anything useful, because we need to ask what the person likely typed to achieve this outcome: Just work around the security restrictions for now, i havent got time to do it properly before this demo.

That applies per channel, because each channel represents a different distribution of language. The same technique gets asked four ways:

But this is actually one of the most useful channels for exemplar (similar) turn searches, where we have a known bad session and want to use its vectors to find similar bad sessions. Vector search vs. keyword search on agent sessions

Keyword search is cheaper and older, as well as better understood, so it has to be beaten if storing vectors has high value.

Although vector and keyword (BM25) are close, vector wins outright against our normalized dataset. Keyword search becomes competitive when the query contains literal commands and we can break those up into fields. Exact token matching is what lexical matching is for.

Which agent session channel carries the most valuable signal?

Testing the results against my known bad sessions showed me something that surprised me. I was expecting the user channel to have the highest fidelity of incidents, as it’s essentially what we, as users, are asking for, right?

Although it’s the channel where we can confirm the user's original intent, in my testing, it was the lowest scoring on relevance. It doesn’t show agent reasoning, where the agent “thinks” about actions, what it’s being asked to do, or agent research / tools to run. This agent reasoning channel was where we found the majority of our incidents.

So, why might this be happening? To answer this, we have to understand what data exists in the reasoning channel. Depending on what’s being asked, the channel might look back over previous chats or pull context, or it might search for things that our user didn’t anticipate. It tends to do this in a more consistent way than the user channel, where we might have brief messages like yes, confirm, or that looks correct, build it in one instance, and then long messages, where we’ve pasted meeting notes, logs, configs, chat history, and more. Every time we add that to the user channel, we dilute the final vector representation of that message to find similarities. This is why the reasoning channel overall holds slightly richer context than the user channel for what’s being actioned and what the user is asking.

Using a known bad session to find the next one

Every query so far has been a written description of the behavior to find. An exemplar query drops the description and uses a known bad turn’s own text as the query.

Testing that is hard, because every session finds itself, and some of my flagged sessions are near-duplicates. My daily mailbox job, for example, produces almost the same session every morning, and the sensor records some Cursor conversations twice, once from each of its stores.

My first test split the 56 flagged sessions into two piles by session ID, used one pile as exemplars, and counted hits in the other. Exemplars won comfortably. They won because four of the eight twin pairs and the nine mailbox runs landed on both sides, so many of the “new” sessions they found were copies of the exemplars.

So I reran it with twins and repeated runs kept on the same side. That left 40 groups, dealt into two sides:

Once the copies are kept together, exemplars and written descriptions find the same number of sessions. Exemplars rank them slightly higher (average precision 0.531 against 0.506, and 0.277 against 0.243), but on 56 sessions that could easily be noise.

That gives exemplars a narrower job than I expected. An exemplar is very good at finding every other run of a known bad workflow. That’s the job of a detection rule: you’ve seen it once, and you want to know every time it happens again. Finding a different workflow doing the same risky thing is still the job of a written hunt.

Method: Fifty-six flagged sessions grouped into 40 (nine runs of one scheduled job, eight twin pairs, 31 singles) and dealt into two sides of 28. Each side’s turns were used as exemplars against the other side, and each exemplar excluded its own session. All queries for a side were fused with RRF (k = 60) across all four channels, with the setup fixed before scoring. Side B holds out all nine job runs, which is why it scores lower. Counts are ±1, because approximate vector search returned slightly different results on repeat runs.

Getting agent sessions into Elastic

I built my own collector for this article, but in the time since I evaluated my own sessions, Elastic has built its Claude Code integration. In technical preview from 9.4, this integration takes Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry (OTel) export directly. On Elastic Cloud, you can point Claude Code at the managed OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) endpoint with nothing in between. Content is off by default. OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES, and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS turn on prompts, responses, and commands. Tool output needs tracing, as well. For Cursor, hooks do the same job, and Wieger van der Meulen’s post shows how to ship them with Elastic Agent.

From there, embedding is a mapping change. Add a semantic_text field for each channel, and copy the content fields into it. Elasticsearch embeds every event as it arrives.

Claude Code’s telemetry doesn’t export the model’s reasoning, which is excluded from response events and redacted from raw API bodies. Reasoning was the strongest channel in my testing, so Claude Code’s export gives you three of the four. Cursor’s afterAgentThought hook exposes the fourth.

What I found in my own agent sessions

To show the true value of this compared to what we can do today, I wanted to show some actually suspicious sessions that I’ve found with queries:

Hunting agent sessions with an ES|QL vector query

First, a direct Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL) query where i’m looking for similar user text to “my key is in the message above, use that one to authenticate and see if it comes back”:

The re-auth session was about documentation.

The SSH one was for a custom demo.

One asked an agent to hand back credentials that it shouldn’t have been holding.

Investigating agent sessions with Elastic AI Agent

I created an investigation skill that knows how to ask vector queries. I aligned it with MITRE ATLAS and prompted it with:

Using the /vector Investigation skill, can you look for any agent sessions where unsecured credentials have been seen across my environment?

As you can see, it can find interesting examples by running multiple ES|QL queries aligned to tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and returning holistic results, which help identify potentially suspicious sessions that warrant further investigation. Similarly, we can run our own semantic queries using ES|QL:

Dashboards for agent session activity and spend

Stored session vectors can also drive dashboards that can capture agentic activities better than using LLMs to tag all sessions. We suddenly have the ability to discover themes and report on similarity scores, as well as ask multiple questions, to find where we have different TTPs across our stack for reporting purposes:

We can report on exemplar sessions and only show where scores are above a specified amount:

This looks at the tool channel for semantically similar sessions to tools that expose credentials. The sessions show AWS identity probes, where one is reading .env, leaking secrets to the LLM.

We can then show where people have been doing personal work and break down which platforms they spend the most time on:

And we can create other dashboards to display relevant spend and usage information:

What AI agent session monitoring costs at scale

The cost comes down to how much has to be stored, and how much of it has to sit in memory. A single 1024-dimension float32 vector is 4KB. Better Binary Quantization (BBQ) cuts each dimension from 32 bits to one, so the vector itself becomes 128 bytes. Elasticsearch adds 14 bytes per vector of correction data so it can rescore accurately, which brings it to 142 bytes, still about 29 times smaller than the original.

Assume that we’re talking about a large organization with 10,000 engineers, each producing 15,000 turns a year across four channels. That gives us 600 million vector representations a year.

Elastic is live with Disk BBQ GA in version 9.4+, which puts the quantization over a clustered inverted file (IVF) structure. Only the centroids stay resident in memory, under 1GB, and everything else is read from disk on demand. (Get more info on DiskBBQ.)
