Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: How Amazon SES helps you detect and respond Your first response is detection, not DNS changes
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM key, confirm the new selector is live, and verify that your DMARC policy is already set to p=reject. Days later, you see that the same unfamiliar traffic is still authenticating as you.

In this post, you learn why rotation alone can’t stop a DKIM replay attack, how to confirm that you’re looking at a replay rather than a legitimate relay or ordinary spoofing, and the DNS cleanup step that most rotation guidance leaves out. You also learn how you can use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to detect and respond to this activity faster.

How DKIM replay works

DKIM verifies one thing: that specific parts of a message didn’t change between the signer and the receiver. The signer signs the message with a private key, and receivers fetch the matching public key from your domain’s DNS to check the signature. A valid signature continues to validate wherever the message travels afterward. Mailing lists, .forward rules, and third-party relays all preserve it, which is the protocol working as designed.

A replay attack takes advantage of that durability. The attack works as follows:

Your ecommerce platform sends a customer a legitimate response email, signed with your DKIM key.

An attacker obtains one copy of that message. They might subscribe to your mailing list, compromise a mailbox, retrieve it from a list archive, or capture it through a forwarding rule.

The attacker resends that message, unchanged, from their own servers to thousands of new recipients.

Each receiving server fetches your public key from DNS and checks the signature. The signature passes, because the body wasn’t modified. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) fails, because the sending IP isn’t yours, but DMARC requires only one of SPF or DKIM to pass with alignment. Because DKIM passes, DMARC passes, and the message is delivered as authenticated email from your domain.

Understanding what an attacker can and can’t do matters, because the limits define the problem. An attacker can’t modify your message, add new content, or read your email. The signature is only valid while the message remains byte-for-byte identical.

What an attacker gains is your domain’s reputation, which they use to deliver your genuine message to an audience you didn’t intend. A receipt or invoice becomes a lure, and email that would normally be filtered is delivered because receivers trust your domain. This is abuse of reputation and reach, not content forgery, and the distinction matters when you explain the incident to your security team.

This also explains why an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t stop an attack. DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes with alignment. During a replay, DKIM passes, so DMARC passes, and p=reject does not apply. A p=reject policy is designed to stop spoofing, where a forger has no valid signature and DKIM fails. It does nothing against a message that you signed. Determining which of the two was used is what tells you how to respond.

Is it replay, spoofing, or a legitimate relay?

Email from an unfamiliar IP address that passes DKIM has three common explanations, and each requires a different response. Confirm which you’re dealing with before you make any changes.

DMARC aggregate (rua) reports provide the source IP address, message volume, and SPF and DKIM results. This is enough to identify an anomaly, but not to prove a replay. A report row might read as follows:

source IP: 203.0.113.45 | count: 4,200 | SPF: fail | DKIM: pass (d=yourdomain.com)

You need to evaluate that row against the three possibilities:

The first possibility is a legitimate relay that you haven’t inventoried, such as a mailing list, a forwarder, or an email security gateway such as an inline cloud access security broker (CASB) that you route through. The signature validly survives the relay, and this is normal email flow. In the report, the source IP address usually resolves to a known provider, and the volume tracks your actual sending.

The second possibility is replay abuse, in which an attacker redistributes a message that you legitimately signed. In this case, the DKIM-passing volume comes from an IP address that has no business relationship with you, often well above the usual number of recipients that you send to, and frequently to recipient domains that you haven’t worked with.

The third possibility is ordinary spoofing, which is a forgery with no valid signature. That row shows DKIM: fail. DKIM that passes from an unknown IP address is therefore usually not ordinary spoofing.

Aggregate counts can’t prove a replay on their own. To confirm a replay, you need message-level evidence: a specific message that you sent matched to one that reached recipients you didn’t address. If you can’t make that match, treat the activity as an unconfirmed anomaly, and begin with the enforcement and monitoring steps that follow rather than removing keys.

Set up an enforcing DMARC policy first

Before you take any other action, confirm that you’re enforcing DMARC. Many domains that encounter this problem are still at p=none, which is monitoring only. This situation is common. Every DMARC deployment begins at p=none, and many organizations do not advance beyond it because nothing appears to be broken. At p=none, receivers take no action on failures, so no change you make affects delivery, and you can’t determine what enforcement would have caught.

The first step is therefore not key removal; it’s completing your sender inventory and reaching enforcement:

Inventory every legitimate sender and relay for your domain, including your email service providers, mailing lists, and any security gateways that send on your behalf.

Bring each sender into SPF and DKIM alignment so that legitimate email authenticates.

Advance the policy one stage at a time, from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. Review your rua reports at each stage before you advance, typically for a week or two per stage, and longer if you have many senders to work through. The pct tag lets you ramp up gradually, for example by quarantining 25% of failing email before you increase the percentage.

After you’re enforcing DMARC, receivers that honor DMARC drop unauthenticated spoofing on your behalf. Only after this baseline is in place, and only after you have confirmed a replay of genuinely signed email, does the next step apply.

Remove the old key from DNS: routine hygiene after rotation

Most rotation guidance omits this step. Rotating a key and removing the old key are two separate actions.

Rotation means that your provider begins signing new email with a new key and selector. Removal means deleting the old public key from DNS, so that previously signed messages, including the copies that an attacker captured, can no longer be verified. If you rotate but leave the old public key published, every message ever signed with that key remains replayable for as long as the record exists. Removing the old key is what closes that window and is the step that’s commonly overlooked.

Removal affects only messages that are still in transit and were signed with the old key. After email is delivered, the receiver no longer needs your key, so we recommend that you leave the old key published long enough for in-flight email to arrive and then remove it. How much of this process you manage yourself depends on your DKIM method, which the following section describes. During a confirmed active replay, closing this window is essential.

How you manage keys depends on the DKIM method that you use with Amazon SES. With Bring Your Own DKIM (BYODKIM), you generate the key pair and publish the public key as a TXT record that you control. You can rotate and remove keys whenever you want, including removing an old key on demand during an incident. As the BYODKIM documentation states, “you can rotate the DKIM keys for your domains as often as you want.”

With Easy DKIM, a feature where Amazon SES generates and manages the keys for you, you publish CNAME records that point to AWS-hosted keys. Because your DNS points to AWS-hosted keys through those CNAME records, Amazon SES manages the underlying key material for you, so you don’t publish or remove individual keys yourself. Unlike BYODKIM, Easy DKIM doesn’t provide an on-demand option to delete a specific key immediately.

If you’re an Easy DKIM sender during a confirmed replay, your defenses are early detection (described in the following section), the duplicate-message throttling that receivers already apply, and, over the longer term, the emerging DKIM2 effort, an IETF initiative to update the DKIM specification with built-in replay resistance, which is being designed to give receivers better signals to identify and act on replayed messages at the protocol level.

How Amazon SES helps you detect and respond

Your first response is detection, not DNS changes. The goal is to identify anomalous DKIM-passing volume early, while you build the message-level evidence that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

Begin by enabling logging. Create an Amazon SES configuration set with an event destination (see Monitor email sending using Amazon SES event publishing) that streams per-message events (Send, Delivery, Bounce, and Complaint) to Amazon Data Firehose or Amazon EventBridge (see Add an event destination), tagged with the From domain.

Separately, confirm that you’re receiving rua reports for your domain. You enable these reports by adding a rua= address to your domain’s DMARC TXT record, for example rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com. For the record syntax and a phased p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject rollout, see Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES. Reports arrive as daily XML digests, and most teams process them with a DMARC analyzer rather than reading the raw XML.

With both sources in place, you can correlate them. Compare the email that your account emitted—based on your Amazon SES delivery events—against what DMARC reports show that receivers accepted as your domain. When DMARC shows DKIM-passing volume from IP addresses outside your SPF record that exceeds the delivery events that Amazon SES recorded for that From domain in the same window, that gap is your signal. It’s also how you build the message-level case that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

We recommend three additional controls. Amazon SES sending authorization restricts which AWS principals can send using your verified identity. It doesn’t stop an external replay, but it addresses the insider and third-party vector that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC don’t cover on their own, so use identity-level policies to limit sending to specific AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principals.

Use Amazon Route 53 to set short DNS time-to-live values (TTLs) (for example, 300 seconds) on your DKIM records so that changes propagate quickly; and enable DNS query logging with an Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filter that watches for queries to a selector that you’ve rotated away from.

A spike in lookups for an old selector is a useful early indicator of a replay attempt using a retired selector. For a BYODKIM domain during a confirmed replay, Route 53 is also where you remove the old selector’s TXT record. You can automate that removal by using an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that starts an AWS Lambda function to call the Route 53 API and retire an old selector’s record.

Scope the function’s IAM role to only the specific Route 53 hosted zone and record that it needs to change, so that it follows least privilege. Because an incorrect DNS change can have a wide effect, gate any automation behind confirmed-replay criteria and test it against a non-production domain first. For most teams, alarm-to-human is safer than alarm-to-automatic-removal.

When your domain is the one being abused

Most guidance assumes that you’re either the provider preventing abuse or the receiver detecting it. In a replay, your domain is the one whose reputation is being consumed, and you aren’t on the recipient list. As a result, you don’t have the message that everyone asks for when you report the issue.

When you file an abuse report with the provider that hosts the source IP address, they ask for full message headers. The email went to people you didn’t contact, so you don’t have the message headers. You then provide DMARC aggregate reports that show the source IP address and volume, and the provider asks for headers again. At this point, you’re unable to proceed.

To break this cycle, go to the recipients. Review your rua reports for the top recipient domains—which are often .gov and .edu domains—contact those recipients directly and request a sample message with full headers. In addition to providing the headers, that sample lets you confirm a replay rather than a legitimate relay. Build your abuse report around the IP address and the DMARC evidence rather than the message content. If the source IP address belongs to Amazon Web Services (AWS), report it through the AWS abuse process and include your DMARC reports and SPF record as evidence.

Incident response: ordered actions

If your reports show suspicious DKIM-passing email from unfamiliar IP addresses, complete the following procedure.

To respond to a suspected DKIM replay

Confirm that it’s a replay. Match a message that you sent to one that reached recipients you didn’t address and rule out legitimate relays and gateways. Aggregate data alone isn’t proof.

Reach an enforcing DMARC policy. Inventory your legitimate senders, align them, and advance from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. This stops spoofing.

Harden SPF to -all rather than ~all, but only after your sender inventory is complete, since -all hard-fails any legitimate source you haven’t listed.

Check the DKIM-Signature header of a fresh message to confirm that your provider signs only with the current selector.

Report the source IP address to the hosting provider and include your DMARC evidence.

Investigate the capture point, such as a compromised mailbox, a mailing list, a forwarding rule, or a newsletter subscription.

Remove the old DKIM public key after in-flight email has cleared. For BYODKIM, delete the old selector’s TXT record. For Easy DKIM, rely on the managed Amazon SES rotation together with the monitoring and receiver-side defenses described earlier.

The following table summarizes what each action does and doesn’t do.

Action

What it does

What it doesn’t do

Confirm replay (message-level)

Separates a replay from a legitimate relay or spoofing

Can’t be done from aggregate DMARC data alone

DMARC enforcement (p=none to p=reject)

Drops unauthenticated spoofing

Does nothing against a replay because DKIM still passes

Key rotation

Signs new email with a new key

Doesn’t invalidate already signed messages

Remove old key (routine, post-rotation)

Invalidates old-key signatures, including captured ones

Doesn’t protect in-flight old-key email; on-demand removal available only with BYODKIM

Amazon SES sending authorization

Restricts which principals send as your identity

Doesn’t stop external replay of captured messages

Conclusion

DKIM replay succeeds because a valid signature keeps validating, and an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t change that. To respond effectively, confirm that the activity is a replay with message-level evidence, reach an enforcing DMARC policy, and then remove the old key from DNS as routine post-rotation hygiene. Keep your primary defense on monitoring and DMARC enforcement rather than on emergency DNS changes. The durable fix for replay is receiver-side: duplicate-message counting today, and stronger protocol-level signals through DKIM2 in the future.

To get started, review your current DMARC policy and confirm that you’re receiving rua reports, enable Amazon SES event publishing, and document how you rotate and remove DKIM keys for each of your domains.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Storm Ransomware Is Scaling Fast and Selling an AI Powered Image
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A new ransomware operation appeared in August 2026 with an ambitious pitch: sophisticated infrastructure, aggressive affiliate payouts, global ambitions, and what it calls the...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A new ransomware operation appeared in August 2026 with an ambitious pitch: sophisticated infrastructure, aggressive affiliate payouts, global ambitions, and what it calls the “first AI powered, quantum resistant ransomware.”

Within approximately six weeks, Storm had claimed over 50 victims across North America, Europe, and Oceania. Its targets span healthcare, finance, manufacturing, business services, government, transportation, and critical infrastructure.

Storm arrived with the structure of an established Ransomware as a Service operation. Its affiliate program offers revenue shares reaching 90%, while its leak site looks closer to a commercial software platform, complete with an interactive victim map, search functionality, sector filters, victim tracking, and document previews.

Then there is the AI claim.

Storm heavily promotes itself as AI powered. Check Point Exposure Management researchers found no evidence showing AI use in the group’s ransomware deployment, victim targeting, encryption routines, or extortion processes. The AI message appears closely tied to how Storm recruits affiliates, promotes automation, and builds its brand. Figure 1, Storm’s pinned darknet recruitment post advertising itself as AI powered and showing its affiliate offer

Key Takeaways

Storm scaled quickly. The group claimed over 50 victims within approximately six weeks of public activity across North America, Europe, and Oceania.

It launched as a structured affiliate operation. Storm advertises lockers for Windows, Linux, ESXi, and NAS, along with victim chat management, call center services, AV and EDR bypass support, DDoS capabilities, and media outreach.

Affiliates can receive up to 90% of revenue. Storm advertises a tiered model starting at 75%, rising to 80%, and reaching 90% for revenue above $750,000.

Healthcare featured heavily in its early activity. Six healthcare organizations appear among the early victim claims, alongside victims across finance, manufacturing, retail, automotive, and other sectors.

Its leak site is unusually polished. Storm built an interactive platform featuring a global victim map, industry filters, search, victim timelines, document previews, and a custom CAPTCHA.

The AI branding remains unverified. Researchers found no conclusive evidence that AI supports Storm’s intrusion, encryption, extortion, or affiliate workflows.

Storm Was Built to Recruit

Storm’s public emergence was closely tied to affiliate recruitment.

Before its first observed victim publication, known Initial Access Broker BigBro advertised the new operation on a darknet forum. Storm later published its own pinned recruitment post, formalizing its RaaS offering.

The offering resembles a service catalog. Affiliates gain access to ransomware lockers, technical support, victim communication capabilities, call center services, DDoS capabilities, and other resources. Storm also openly solicits Initial Access Brokers, data brokers, and network access providers.

Its revenue sharing model adds another recruitment incentive. Affiliates can retain up to 90% of revenue once earnings exceed $750,000.

50+ Victims Across Multiple Industries

Storm claimed over 50 victims during its first six weeks, with observed organizations in the United States, Germany, Canada, and Australia.

Business services accounted for 13 observed incidents, followed by finance with nine and manufacturing with seven. Retail and healthcare each accounted for six.

Figure 2, Storm sector targeting distribution

Healthcare stands out in Storm’s early activity. Victim claims included hospitals, health networks, treatment providers, radiology organizations, and hospice services. Researchers assess that the early concentration suggests deliberate targeting of organizations where disruption can create significant pressure to pay.

A Ransomware Leak Site Built Like a Platform

Storm’s leak site reinforces the group’s focus on presentation and scale.

The Tor based site includes an interactive global map displaying victim locations, industry filtering, searchable victim listings, timelines, document tree previews, and a custom graphical CAPTCHA.

Figure 3, Storm’s advanced data leak site and interactive victim map

The investment provides Storm with infrastructure for managing victims while supporting affiliate recruitment, media visibility, and brand recognition.

How AI Fits Into Storm’s Strategy

Storm repeatedly describes itself as the “first AI powered, quantum resistant ransomware.”

Researchers found no conclusive evidence supporting AI use in intrusion, encryption, extortion, or affiliate support workflows. Current evidence points toward three roles for the AI narrative: recruitment, automation signaling, and marketing.

AI gives Storm a way to stand out in a crowded ransomware ecosystem and present itself as technologically advanced. References to automated victim management and negotiations may also signal workflow automation, though the available evidence does not establish AI enhanced offensive capabilities.

Storm’s rapid growth shows how quickly a ransomware operation can establish scale through structured affiliate recruitment, polished infrastructure, and aggressive branding.

For the complete analysis of Storm’s emergence, victimology, affiliate model, leak site, and AI claims, read the full report: Storm: Ransomware in the Age of AI

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: Critical CVEs, Linux DDoS Botnet, Device-Code Phishing, Android Spyware and More
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: From Zero-Days to Exploits in Minutes: Are You Ready for AI Threats
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Some attacks this week didn't need much of a trick. A fake support call, a trusted extension, a shared link, or a device with no password. Small things that people barely think about. Yet each was enough to cause serious trouble.

Then there were the bigger messes. Billions stolen, hidden networks of hacked devices, poisoned software, and attackers finding new ways to turn normal tools against their users. Even the places meant to keep money and systems safe ended up with problems of their own. The strange part is how often the damage started somewhere nobody was looking.

And that's before getting to the long list of fresh bugs, shady services, and scams making the rounds. Quite a bit to sort through. Here's what made the list.

⚡ Threat of the Week

N. Korea Sets New Record with Binance $6.43B Crypto Theft — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism.

Mythos: Map Attack Paths to Collapse Lateral Breach Routes

Access the Gartner® CTEM report to see how the Mythos platform continuously maps cross-domain attack paths and isolates key choke points to break active lateral movement to critical assets.

Get the full report ➝

🔔 Top News

Volt Typhoon Uses Covert Silent Train Network in 0-Day Attacks — Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including to facilitate zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems. It's codenamed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation to minimize detection and attribution, and refreshes it continuously. Silent Train is a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices to hide the origin of its attacks. The findings highlight evidence of efforts to pre-position access within what it described as "strategic communications, critical infrastructure and other ecosystems that become essential during geopolitical tensions or crises." Silent Train is built around "rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices." The nature of these victims "indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region."

Polymarket Briefly Suspended Trading After Third-Party Hack — Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading after hackers compromised DebugBear, a third-party service, to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript that siphoned approximately $2.7 million in assets from 33 deposit wallets in under an hour. "Our DNS server records were compromised through our domain registrar. We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain," DebugBear said in an update shared on October 31, 2026. "Based on our initial investigation this attack targeted the website of a specific customer. We have not seen any indication of a compromise of our internal systems, though we will continue to investigate this." In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, leading to reported losses of around $3 million.

Shared ChatGPT Links Lead to Code Execution — Researchers from Parameter Labs disclosed a now-patched flaw in ChatGPT that turned an ordinary share link into an attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. "An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," Parameter Labs said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session." Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation, and send data from that conversation to an external server.

Official Claude Code Extension on Cursor Marketplace with SSH Backdoor — Two versions of the Claude Code extension distributed through Cursor Marketplace were tampered with to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems. Cursor said the incident impacted up to 5,000 users. In response to the incident, Cursor said it rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and worked with the cloud provider to take the server offline so that the reverse shell is no longer functional. It also stressed that no other extensions were maliciously modified as part of the attack. However, several questions surrounding the supply chain attack remain unanswered, including how the threat actor managed to publish a malicious extension under Anthropic's name on Cursor's marketplace and what level of access they were able to obtain.

FBI Seizes bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine — The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine. The DoJ said the service was being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct. However, the long-term impact of such crackdowns has been questioned. According to Intel 471, disruptions have driven customers to newer services operated by former resellers, fragmenting the market rather than eliminating demand. The disclosure comes as the Australian Signals Directorate said it gained backend access to Amadey's operations and severed its access to 180,000 computers across the globe.

Keystone to Destroy 18,835 Hardware Wallets — Keystone confirmed a security incident involving its official website where an attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool to escalate privileges and obtain some customer information and a key used to verify the authenticity of our devices. This included 25,964 records containing names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order information, along with 12,873 checkout records containing names, contact details, and shipping information submitted by users. Besides stopping the use of the old key, Keystone plans to destroy 18,835 devices in existing inventory that contain the old key. "Shipping of all unshipped orders from our official website has been suspended," it said. "Sales will switch to a preorder model until production of devices using the new key is complete, after which shipping will resume." In a related development, another hardware cryptocurrency wallet maker Trezor said it received credible reports about a suspected hardware crypto-theft implant in a Trezor Safe 5 sold by its reseller CryptoBilis in Southeast Asia. "If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards and are using it to store funds, please move your funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed as soon as possible," it said.

uCreator Android Spyware Can Clone WeChat Accounts — A commercial Android spyware offering called uCreator is designed to target ordinary users of mobile wallets and messaging applications across China and Southeast Asia, including GCash (Philippines), WeChat, WeCom, QQ, Telegram, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, and MoMo. It can also be used to clone WeChat accounts. Victims install repackaged copies of legitimate applications disturbed through sideloading or social engineering flows. The attack leverages a variation of on-device virtualization techniques observed in malware like GodFather to conduct fraud. "GodFather spins the banking app up inside a virtual container and drops a fake overlay on top to phish credentials: the victim is really typing into the attacker's screen," security researcher Ovi Liber said. "uCreator shares the substrate but it draws no overlay. This is a case really of overlay-the-app versus instrument-the-app, with the second being quieter and also not being confined to a login screen. As an operator, it scales to any app the vendor writes a module for."

Gheist Turns GitHub Actions into a Secret Extraction Service — An automated campaign dubbed Gheist has been observed planting a secret-dumping workflow named "sync-check" in every repository that stolen GitHub tokens can reach. "The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log," Wiz said. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later." The Google-owned cloud security company said it recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts. The campaign was first detected in mid-September 2026.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-115889, CVE-2026-115893 (Wasmtime), CVE-2026-90975 (Fireblocks mpc-lib), CVE-2026-91141 (COVESA vsomeip), CVE-2026-88781, CVE-2026-75775, CVE-2026-75779, CVE-2026-93489, CVE-2026-17518, CVE-2026-75753, CVE-2026-102438, CVE-2026-14911, CVE-2026-16528, CVE-2026-19386, CVE-2026-19396, CVE-2026-93495, CVE-2026-14157, CVE-2026-13313 (ASUS), CVE-2026-114573, CVE-2026-9082, CVE-2026-118539 (Drupal), CVE-2026-114595, CVE-2026-114596, CVE-2026-114597, CVE-2026-114598 (EPICS Base), CVE-2026-97631 (TianoCore EDK II), CVE-2026-115881, CVE-2026-115884 (GoAhead), CVE-2026-110720 (HashiCorp consul-k8s), CVE-2026-90885, CVE-2026-85250, CVE-2026-88901, CVE-2026-88900, CVE-2026-78165, CVE-2026-85251 (Apache Camel), CVE-2026-115547 (Okta), CVE-2026-114349, CVE-2026-111551 (Apache Kafka), CVE-2026-118306, CVE-2026-118331, CVE-2026-118348, CVE-2026-118344, CVE-2026-106378 (Google Chrome), from CVE-2026-117860 through CVE-2026-117954, from CVE-2026-118005 through CVE-2026-118017 (Mozilla Firefox), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-18672, CVE-2026-19219 (Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX), TRA-2020-14 (Kodi), CVE-2026-107239, CVE-2026-107238, CVE-2023-22793 (Veeam), CVE-2026-103401, CVE-2026-103402, CVE-2026-103403, CVE-2026-103404, CVE-2026-103405, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-103407, CVE-2026-103408, CVE-2026-103409 (Juniper Networks Session Smart Router), CVE-2026-111585 (TeamViewer), CAN-2026-2035970 (Intelbras IP cameras), CVE-2026-103594, CVE-2026-112709, CVE-2026-112710, CVE-2026-93857, CVE-2026-103593, CVE-2026-93865, CVE-2026-93866 (WatchGuard Fireware OS), CVE-2026-101296, CVE-2026-101356, CVE-2026-103119 (Apache Tomcat), CVE-2026-112816 (Canonical LXD), CVE-2026-93680, CVE-2026-110186 (Langflow OSS), and a preauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in TightVNC.

🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars

Learn How to Turn Identity Context Into Faster, Smarter SOC Response → Your security tools can detect suspicious activity, but without identity context, critical threats may go unnoticed. As machine identities and AI agents expand the attack surface, SOC teams need deeper visibility to respond effectively. Join this expert-led webinar to discover how connecting identity intelligence with security operations can help uncover hidden risks, accelerate investigations, and contain threats faster.

From Zero-Days to Exploits in Minutes: Are You Ready for AI Threats? → AI-powered cyberattacks are accelerating, shrinking the time security teams have to detect, investigate, and respond. Are your defenses ready to keep up? Join this expert-led webinar to discover how to strengthen AI threat readiness, improve attack-surface visibility, and build faster, more resilient security operations before attackers gain the upper hand.

📰 Around the Cyber World

A massive search-hijacking campaign called Searchjacked involving 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million reported installations hijacked users' searches through tracking servers, captured queries, and collected referral payments from Microsoft Bing and Yahoo. The findings from Socket expand on the April 2025 discovery of 57 Chrome extensions with six million users, adding 264 newly identified add-ons with another 8.7 million users. Although they are hosted on the Chrome Web Store, they are unlisted and don't appear in users' searches on the extension store. Instead, the extensions are promoted through sketchy advertisements shown as pop overs or pop unders on websites. Socket also discovered a cluster of malicious Firefox extensions that mimic Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys. A third campaign, documented by Am I Being Pwned?, involves 60 Chrome extensions with 2.3 million installs across 4 publisher accounts. Called OffiDocs, the extensions masquerade as document programs and exfiltrate all URLs visited by users to be shared with business partners, and other third-parties, or redirect users to one of their pages on redcoolmedia.net or runapps.org

Microsoft revealed details of two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. "Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths," Microsoft said. "This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure."

Threat actors are increasingly turning to vulnerabilities as a means for breaking into corporate systems, as exfiltration and extortion-only attacks emerged as the fastest-growing category in the third quarter of 2026.

Check Point detailed three anti-detect browsers, Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin, that could enable a single operator to silently manage thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms, and evade detection systems that look for scams and coordinated inauthentic behavior. "Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution," Check Point said. "These accounts can also be used to coordinate influence operations, which becomes an even greater concern ahead of elections. These tools already use AI integration, from built-in automation templates to offering a dedicated MCP server that pipes LLM-generated content directly into pre-warmed account profiles at machine speed. Running a large-scale social media operation now requires only a credit card instead of a technical team."

Russia and Ukraine both revealed their emergency alert systems were hit by cyber attacks. The attacks caused the two systems to send fake emergency alerts. Per BBC, Ukraine's air raid app sent false red-level air raid warnings nationwide. A few hours later, Russia said its alert app was also attacked, but said that it was only an "ancillary" service among sirens and other warnings. It’s not clear if the two incidents are connected.

A sophisticated Android malware campaign has been targeting the Indian banking sector since July 2025 using seven distinct trojan families that facilitate banking fraud through coordinated phishing, credential theft, and unauthorized cryptojacking. It is orchestrated by a financially motivated threat cluster codenamed CyberDakait that's operating in India since January 2025. The malware families are GhostBat, cyb3rx, godz, d-passive, d-shine, tenxen, and appkjl. Distributed via coordinated smishing and vishing campaigns, they are designed to harvest sensitive information, including bank mobile application credentials, credit card details, outstanding balances, through sophisticated overlay attacks. "The main goal of the campaign is the distribution of Android malware to conduct cryptojacking and elaborate banking fraud," Group-IB said. "The malicious applications are commonly hosted on GitHub repositories to maintain legitimacy and evade security controls, where the initial APK functions as a dropper that downloads and executes the main payload alongside a cryptocurrency mining module, enabling the threat actors to generate revenue through both direct financial theft and unauthorized cryptocurrency mining on infected devices." A total of at least 17,960 compromised devices have been identified, and about 7.6 million SMS messages were intercepted from victim devices.

A new phishing campaign has disguised credential theft as an invitation to a private AI event from Anthropic, and uses GoTo Webinar branding, a Zoom-style registration page, and convincing Google and Microsoft login pages to steal login credentials. "Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g., proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization," Cofense said.

A new campaign is using judicial-themed phishing emails targeting Colombian organizations to deliver XWorm via a multi-stage chain. The initial payloads resemble legitimate Colombian administrative or judicial correspondence, according to Arctic Wolf.

Multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. "The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance," Recorded Future said. "This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds." Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.

Nozomi Networks detailed a new Go-based malware for Linux called Kairos that turns a compromised machine into a node in the operator's DDoS botnet. "On command, the bot opens hundreds to thousands of TCP connections to a target chosen by the operator and keeps them open for the requested duration, sending a single near-empty keepalive byte every few seconds," Nozomi Networks said. "Initial access came through Telnet, using the default credentials (user root, empty password). The operator then staged the payload with a short shell sequence that downloaded it over HTTP from the same server the bot later calls home."

A previously undocumented Microsoft device code phishing kit codenamed MadApe is using business-themed PDF lures, configurable redirects, and fake document-sharing pages to trick victims into completing Microsoft device code authentication. It was first observed by Group-IB on January 7, 2026.

Threat actors behind Aur0ra ransomware, aka Gold Ogre, are extensively using AI to develop tools and to orchestrate and execute ransomware operations, Sophos said. The AI-assisted post-exploitation framework is developed with Cursor AI assistance. "The threat actors used Cursor to escalate from credential access to domain administrator in preparation for data collection and ransomware deployment," Sophos said. "AI guardrails were bypassed by framing the intrusions as authorized red team activity or 'diagnostics testing.' Intrusions were orchestrated by Cursor's Composer agentic coding model as well as AI models provided by Anthropic, xAI, and Moonshot." Although the threat actors initially used Anthropic almost exclusively, they have since introduced other models.

Malicious model repositories on Hugging Face are being used to fuel a cryptomining and backdoor campaign. "The payloads were written for GPU hosts running self-hosted inference, especially Xinference and GPUStack, along with rented GPU machines, shared research notebooks, and CI jobs that pull small test models without anyone reading the code," Pluto Security said. Instead of using poisoned weights or pickle exploits, the campaign abuses a Hugging Face option, trust_remote_code, that lets a model ship its own Python code. When this option is set to true, that code is automatically executed on a victim's machine as soon as the model loads.

Bitdefender and NETGEAR found that Smart TVs and connected plugs accounted for a large share of recorded security weaknesses. Televisions represented 22.7% of vulnerability observations, followed by smart plugs at 22.4%. "Before buying connected equipment, the support period deserves attention alongside the price and features," the 2026 IoT Security Landscape Report said. For equipment already in the home, knowing whether updates are still available is part of knowing whether it should stay connected.

A tech-support scam is directing victims to install the commercially available remote access application UltraViewer. Infoblox, which broke down details of the campaign, said it found links to a long-running QuickBooks phishing campaign. "That campaign uses over 350 QuickBooks-lookalike domains and directs victims to call scammers who attempt to steal QuickBooks credentials," Infoblox said. The scam has been found directing users to trojanized UltraViewer and UltraMailer, installers that lead to the deployment of DarkKometa and njRAT, respectively.

In an analysis of The Com ecosystem, Flare said the loose-knit collective comprises three distinct intrusion clusters, Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters, while SP1D3R HUNTERS (aka Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters) represents an amalgamation of all three. Security researcher Jon DiMaggio warned against attributing any activity post-2022 to LAPSUS, which ceased operating years ago. "LAPSUS$ operated at full capacity for roughly nine months, from its December 2021 attack against Brazil’s Ministry of Health through its concentrated campaign in early 2022, before a series of arrests in mid-to-late 2022 ended it as an organized entity," DiMaggio said. "Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$ overlapped by a few months at the start and by at least one individual across their lifespans, and they still ran different playbooks against different targets toward different ends."

Conclusion

That's about it for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others worked because someone clicked the wrong thing, trusted the wrong tool, or left something exposed. Different methods, same result. And with so many systems connected to other systems, even a small mistake can travel further than expected.

The bigger concern is how normal some of these attacks have become. Nothing particularly clever is needed when the easy routes still work. Keep an eye on what has access, check what needs fixing, and don't assume familiar means safe. See you next week.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 2nd November – Threat Intelligence Report
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Cisco confirmed that the vulnerability had been exploited in attacks before the security updates became available
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 2nd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Binance, a global cryptocurrency exchange, has suffered a cyberattack resulting in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets. Attackers reportedly compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop and abused internal wallet infrastructure to authorize unauthorized withdrawals. The incident ranks among the largest cryptocurrency thefts ever recorded and is linked to North Korean group.

Polymarket, a US-based prediction market platform, has disclosed a cyberattack involving a compromised third-party service that distributed malicious JavaScript to its website. The script hijacked authenticated trading sessions and attempted unauthorized transactions. Approximately $2.7 million in cryptocurrency was traced to a suspected attacker-controlled wallet.

Japan Airlines, a major Japanese international airline, has disclosed a third-party data breach affecting approximately 92,000 passengers through the Amadeus reservation system. Exposed records included passenger names and flight information. Approximately 2,000 individuals also had contact information, passport details, and additional travel records potentially accessed.

The Florida Department of Education has disclosed a data breach involving unauthorized access to its student financial aid website, potentially affecting 4.9 million individuals. Compromised information reportedly includes names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, and contact details. The incident was identified on October 19.

AI THREATS

Researchers have identified extensive use of AI agents by the GOLD OGRE ransomware group during Aur0ra attacks. Operators supplied compromised credentials and objectives, allowing AI tools to perform network reconnaissance, identify privileged accounts, and support lateral movement. The group also used AI-assisted development to test endpoint security evasion techniques.

Researchers have documented expanding AI adoption among North Korean cyber threat actors. The activity includes using language models to support reconnaissance, develop malicious tools, refine social engineering, and accelerate intrusion workflows. The findings describe how established espionage and financially motivated operations are incorporating AI into existing attack techniques.

Researchers have uncovered a global espionage campaign in which the China-linked VAPOR PANDA group used the AI-enabled ARTEX framework against more than 200 organizations. Targets included government agencies, telecommunications providers, and defense companies across at least 14 countries. Confirmed intrusions involved credential theft and deployment of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

Check Point Research have analyzed HTTP2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability affecting Brotli decompression implementations. Initially associated with Node.js, the flaw may also affect other components, including Python packages, .NET, and proxies. Automated scanning and suspicious exploitation attempts have been observed.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497)))

A critical Linux kernel vulnerability, CVE-2026-98432, has been disclosed with a CVSS score of 9.8. The memory management flaw affects TCP networking and can enable unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on systems exposing Multipath TCP listeners.

Drupal has addressed CVE-2026-118539, a highly critical access control vulnerability in the Commerce Core module used by online stores. Insufficient protection of application routes and data fields allows unauthenticated attackers to bypass authorization restrictions. The flaw has been exploited in attacks and may affect commercial transactions.

Cisco has patched CVE-2026-76418, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Adaptive Security Appliance and Firepower Threat Defense software. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely crash devices configured with SSL VPN functionality. Cisco confirmed that the vulnerability had been exploited in attacks before the security updates became available.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has uncovered the Yoba malware campaign, which distributes malicious installers disguised as ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications through fraudulent GitHub projects. Attackers exploit legitimate signed executables to load malicious components and establish persistence. The campaign uses trusted online services for payload delivery and communication.

Check Point researchers have analyzed unexpected network activity generated by Alibaba’s Qwen model during a security-related task. Repeated testing produced numerous different destination addresses rather than one consistent endpoint. The findings suggest unstable model behavior is a more plausible explanation than a deliberately embedded data-exfiltration mechanism.

Researchers have identified UAT-11473, an advanced threat actor exploiting a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN authentication bypass to deploy the KeyDrift malware framework. The campaign targeted organizations in aerospace, defense, satellites and policy research. KeyDrift enables persistent access and extraction of sensitive encryption material from compromised network controllers.

Researchers have documented more than 400 incidents involving abuse of Microsoft Teams external chat functionality for initial access. Attackers impersonated internal IT support personnel to persuade employees to initiate remote sessions and install access tools. Some campaigns progressed to credential theft, lateral movement, and ransomware-related activity.

The post 2nd November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: DarkBlinders Compromises Israeli Target and Iraqi Kurdish Government Cloud Environment
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026.

According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region.

The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups.

Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads.

Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685.

Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets.

The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025.

The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire.

Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment.

The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood.

"The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said.

"The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]."

The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include -

gcc-sg[.]cloud/owa/auth/logon.aspx

mfakuwait[.]online/owa/auth/logon.aspx

moelcloud[.]online/drive/file/d/1JpH3ySmJpvX6TyGnF7C-S8qYiaoxyC5O

The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2.

The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software.

Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added.

"Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group."

Prince of Persia Hosts C2 in the U.S. for the First Time in a Decade

The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026.

The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor."

"We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims."

"The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 5 stars for sale: Inside the underground fake review trade
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: 5 stars as a service In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Recently, our team exposed sophisticated scam kits designed to steal sensitive data and trick consumers. But underground marketplaces are not just for malware and stolen passwords. They also offer services designed to manipulate your opinion of the products and services you buy every day.

In our latest research, we examined cybercrime forums where sellers advertise illicit “reputation management” services. For the right price, these underground operators offer to flood a product with glowing, five-star ratings or remove negative reviews. This shadowy industry works both ways—artificially boosting reputations and deliberately hiding legitimate complaints.

A major shift we are seeing in this space is the adoption of new technology. We also found that cybercriminals are using AI to automate these fake review campaigns. This could allow them to quickly generate realistic, human-sounding feedback in large volumes without much manual effort.

5 stars as a service

In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star review generation and negative review removal services.

The seller’s operations span widely used platforms, including Google, Trustpilot, Yelp, and various mobile app stores. By simply asking prospective buyers, “Just tell me which platform reviews you need?” the seller presents reputation manipulation as something buyers can just order on demand.

Five-star reviews and removal services

Decoding the seller’s FAQ

Analyzing another seller’s (TrustForge) “Frequently Asked Questions” section revealed some surprising details about how these operations reportedly run behind the scenes.

First, the seller emphasizes that real people manually post these reviews, offering a guarantee for both successful delivery and “non-drop”—meaning the platform won’t flag and remove the feedback later.

Remember, a real person posting a review doesn’t mean they’re a real customer. The important question is whether they actually used the product or service and are describing an honest experience.

Second, it appears this is a well-coordinated team effort rather than a solo operation, as the seller charges an extra fee if a buyer wants the main operator to write the review text personally.

However, what caught our attention most was their confidence in beating platform checks. The seller guarantees their fake reviews will stay active, claiming they rely on a closely guarded “private method.” According to TrustForge’s own statements, this method has allowed them to post more than 10,000 fake reviews.

Reputation management FAQ

The clean-up crew: Making bad reviews disappear

A single negative review is often all it takes to create a bad first impression of a product or service. When those negative comments start to pile up, they can completely ruin a business’s reputation and bottom line.

Recognizing how desperate businesses can be to protect their image, our research team discovered underground services specifically offering to remove “fake” or “unfair” reviews from major platforms like Google and Trustpilot.

Of course, the boundary between what is genuinely fake and what a business simply considers “unfair” can be blurry. Businesses can legitimately challenge fabricated reviews, but these services raise concerns about whether genuine customer complaints could also be targeted.

If legitimate customer complaints disappear, consumers lose information that could help them decide where to spend their money.

An offer to remove “fake” or “unfair” Google reviewsAn offer to remove ”fake” or “unfair” review Google reviews

On average, having a single review removed through these underground services costs between $100 and $200. However, the pricing jumps dramatically depending on the platform.

For instance, one seller advertised Airbnb review removal for around $1,100 per review.

When you check a business’s reviews, you’re looking for patterns in other customers’ experiences. If genuine complaints disappear, you could miss repeated problems with refunds, product quality, or customer service.

$1,100 to remove a “fake” or “unfair” Airbnb review

Artificial intelligence, artificial reviews

During the last few months, our research team spotted an interesting thread on an underground forum where two users discussed using AI to mimic human E-E-A-T.

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It is a quality evaluation framework outlined in Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines, which human evaluators use to assess content quality. E-E-A-T itself is not a direct ranking factor.

In the discussion we observed, one user asked the community if it was possible to use AI to effectively fake these qualities when writing product reviews and artificially boost website rankings. The answer was a resounding yes.

Another user claimed they had never experienced problems getting Google to index their completely AI-generated reviews.

AI vs. E-E-A-T

Behind the scenes: The IP addresses for fake reviews

To keep fake reviews from being flagged and deleted, scammers need to look like everyday consumers. To help do this, they can use something called “residential and mobile proxies,” which route their traffic through other internet connections to disguise where it comes from.

Think of an IP address as your computer’s caller ID. When scammers use bulk IP addresses from giant data centers, platforms may spot and block that traffic as coming from commercially hosted infrastructure. Residential proxies, on the other hand, route traffic through real, physical home internet connections—just like the Wi-Fi you use in your living room. Mobile proxies work the same way, but use real cellular networks.

Our team recently discovered a seller on an underground forum acting as a direct supplier of these residential and mobile connections. The seller explicitly advertises them as perfect for running fake review campaigns.

Residential and mobile proxies advertised for fake review campaigns

How to avoid being misled by fake reviews

The main goal of this research isn’t to make you panic or stop trusting every online review you read. We want to raise awareness about what happens behind the scenes, so you can make more informed buying decisions.

If a product or offer seems too good to be true, but is backed by a mountain of perfect five-star reviews, take a moment to pause. Scammers often use these artificially boosted ratings to make a bad deal look reassuring.

Read recent reviews and some of the middle-rated ones, rather than relying on the overall score. Look for recurring details about the things that matter to you, such as durability, delivery, or getting your money back.

Look for repeated wording or sudden bursts of glowing feedback. These signs don’t prove a review is fake, but they’re reasons to take a closer look. Check the seller’s contact details and return policy, too.

Malwarebytes Browser Guard can also help block scam, phishing, and malicious websites you may encounter while shopping.

Unsure about an offer, even with glowing reviews? Share the link or a screenshot with Malwarebytes Scam Guard for help checking for signs of a scam before you buy.

Stop threats before they can do any harm.

Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks phishing pages and malicious sites automatically. Free, one click to install. Add it to your browser →

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Applebee’s customer data exposed by password left in app
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Applebee’s has fixed a security flaw that exposed customers’ personal information after a researcher discovered a database password embedded in the restaurant chain’s Android app
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Applebee’s has fixed a security flaw that exposed customers’ personal information after a researcher discovered a database password embedded in the restaurant chain’s Android app.

The researcher, Robert Wiggins, found the password with help from AI. It gave him access to an internal Applebee’s customer database. A password written directly into an app’s code or configuration is known as a hardcoded credential. Anyone who extracts it may be able to use it to access the system.

The exposed database contained:

Names, email addresses, and email-verification status

Dates of birth, phone numbers, and ZIP codes

Veteran status

Account-creation dates and login counts

IP addresses from customers’ most recent logins, which can indicate their approximate location

TechCrunch independently checked Wiggins’ findings. It created an Applebee’s account with dummy information, which Wiggins successfully retrieved from the database.

According to TechCrunch, Wiggins could not find a suitable way to report the issue to Applebee’s or its parent company, Dine Brands, so he asked the publication to help contact them. TechCrunch held its story until the fix was confirmed. Applebee’s confirmed on October 29 that it had addressed the issue.

It’s unclear how many customers’ records were in the database. Dine Brands says it has not found evidence of unauthorized access, but its investigation is ongoing.

How to stay safe

The database fields described by TechCrunch did not include payment card details or account passwords. That does not tell us whether anyone accessed the database before the fix, so customers should watch for targeted scams.

Names, email addresses, phone numbers, and other personal details could help scammers make messages look relevant and convincing.

Be wary of unexpected Applebee’s-themed emails, texts, or calls. Be especially skeptical of messages offering refunds or compensation, warning that your account will be closed, or asking you to “verify” payment details.

Check security notices through a route you trust. Open the app directly or visit Applebee’s website yourself rather than following a link in an unexpected message. If necessary, contact the company using details you find independently.

Unsure whether a message is a scam? Check it with Malwarebytes’ Scam Guard for an assessment and advice on what to do next.

When sharing personal information, consider why the company needs it and whether you trust it to keep the information safe.

Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Report: Most Fraud Attacks Target Existing Customer Relationships
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A new report from TransUnion has found that 81% of digital fraud attacks target existing customer relationships, with more than half of U
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A new report from TransUnion has found that 81% of digital fraud attacks target existing customer relationships, with more than half of U.S. businesses reporting increased scam and fraud activity over the past year.

“Identity-based fraud attacks often arise before organizations have sufficient information to establish trust in new customers,” the report says. “While account creation is a critical trust-establishing event, most fraud exposure occurs after the customer relationship has already been established. Different risk patterns appear across account creation, login, and financial transaction activities, especially for AI-enabled fraud. For instance, AI can help fraudsters rapidly generate or modify identities, credentials and interactions to target the weakest controls across the customer lifecycle.”

Most respondents cited synthetic identity fraud, which uses exposed consumer information and AI to craft phony personas, as their top concern over the next two years.

“Forty-three percent of U.S. business leaders said the growing scale and sophistication of fraud is placing significant or severe pressure on their organizations,” TransUnion says. “Synthetic identity fraud is a key concern, with 67% expecting it to increase over the next two years and 53% citing it as the threat they are least prepared to address. In the U.S., 51% of business leaders reported increased scam and authorized fraud activity over the past year. U.S. lenders face an estimated $2.4 billion in exposure tied to synthetic identities as of June 30, 2026.”

The increase is partly due to adversarial use of AI tools, which allow attackers to drastically improve the scale and sophistication of social engineering attacks.

“AI has fundamentally changed the economics of fraud by automating activities that once required significant human effort, including creating identities, generating content, and targeting victims,” TransUnion says. “This allows fraudsters to accelerate and scale their attacks faster than organizations can adapt their detection capabilities and mitigation strategies.

TransUnion has the story: https://newsroom.transunion.com/81-of-suspected-digital-fraud-attacks-target-existing-customer-relationships-transunion-finds/

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Bitter Deploys PapRAT in Asian Cyber-Espionage Campaign
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: " He warned that deleting the first implant found might not remove the attacker
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A suspected South Asian cyber-espionage group has been observed pairing native Windows tools with a custom remote access trojan (RAT) dubbed PapRAT to maintain access to targeted organizations.

Cara Lin of Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs detailed the campaign in research published on November 2, attributing it with high confidence to Bitter, also tracked as TA397, based on lure filenames, command-and-control (C2) patterns, file metadata and malware analysis.

FortiGuard Labs tracked the campaign over several months and it described the targets as South Asian organizations, though its telemetry maps also show activity in Southeast Asia and South Korea. Lure files referred to a bilateral meeting request, an ambassador's letter about the 11th Belt and Road Summit and a 2026 gala dinner invitation.

Read more on Bitter: Middle East Hack-for-Hire Operation Traced to South Asian Cyber Espionage Group

Three Infection Chains, One Without a Malware Binary

The first chain took a living-off-the-land approach: a malicious Windows shortcut (LNK) file abused the built-in ftp.exe utility to run scripts and create scheduled tasks.

Those tasks used curl to fetch fresh commands from attacker servers, and the chain deployed no traditional malware executable. FortiGuard Labs said operators could change their instructions on the server without pushing a new binary.

"When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on," said Shane Barney, CISO at Keeper Security. He argued for least-privilege access, tighter limits on native scripting engines and the removal of standing administrative rights.

The other two chains delivered PapRAT through Windows Installer (MSI) packages, one hidden with a decoy spreadsheet in a virtual hard disk (VHDX) image and the other fetched via an internet shortcut in a RAR archive.

PapRAT Shifts to Rust and Pulls In WmRAT

The C++ build of PapRAT posed as a Microsoft component, beaconed over plaintext HTTP and supported eight commands, including remote shell access, file transfers and screenshots. A Rust variant obtained more recently switched to HTTPS and added three more, for PowerShell execution, pausing and exiting.

In the third chain, PapRAT downloaded WmRAT, a C++ RAT previously documented by other researchers, which FortiGuard Labs cited as a further indicator linking the campaign to Bitter.

Jason Soroko, senior fellow at certificate lifecycle management firm Sectigo, said the Windows-tools route meant "a search for PapRAT alone could miss part of the campaign." He warned that deleting the first implant found might not remove the attacker.

FortiGuard's recommendations included handling unexpected LNK files, internet shortcuts, disk images and MSI installers with care.

In the first chain, though, FortiGuard found no PapRAT at all, only a shortcut file, Windows tools, scripts and scheduled tasks.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Introduction

Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.

We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations.

While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure.

Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet:

Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules

Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor

Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors

Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices

Overview

The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase.
