Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections.

In research published October 27, Check Point said it had tracked the campaign, which it calls Yoba, for two months, though an earlier variant posing as the Cursor coding agent appeared in early June. The fake projects impersonated artificial intelligence (AI) applications including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus.

Their releases sat in GitHub repositories with GitHub Pages landing pages, and some of the repositories appeared among Google’s top results, most likely through search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning.

Yoba Uses Signed Binaries to Hide Malicious Components

The fake applications bundled legitimate signed OpenAI and Anthropic executables with a malicious dynamic link library (DLL). Check Point found that the signed Setup.exe files loaded the malicious component through DLL sideloading, a technique often used to bypass security protections.

The malicious DLL, dubbed YobaDropper, ran several checks before deploying a second-stage loader, including the name of its host process and whether it had administrator privileges.

It also checked keyboard layouts to avoid machines in Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries other than Ukraine and used lengthy sleeps to frustrate automated analysis. Check Point said the actor showed indicators suggesting Russian origins.

The dropper then created a directory under ProgramData, copied a legitimate Windows executable into it and used Scheduled Tasks to establish persistence, with a task running under the Local System account and disguised as a Microsoft task.

Read more on fake AI tools spreading malware: Attackers Combine ChatGPT Feature Abuse With ClickFix to Deliver Trojan Malware

YobaLoader Uses Telegram and DNS to Fetch Payloads

The second-stage YobaLoader used Telegram and encrypted Domain Name System (DNS) lookups, known as DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), to obtain instructions without dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, according to Check Point.

It took an image from a Telegram channel and used data from it to generate domains through a domain generation algorithm.

It then queried Google’s DoH service for encrypted data stored in DNS records, which was cryptographically validated before the loader retrieved and decrypted the next-stage payload.

Check Point advised organizations to be cautious when installing AI applications from unverified repositories and to restrict the execution of software from unknown sources.

The observed payload was an XMRig cryptominer, but the researchers said YobaLoader is a generic loader, so future waves could deliver other executable or PowerShell payloads.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Cyber Risk Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Threat Intelligence Vulnerabilities & Threats News Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots The threat actor...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A threat actor lurked behind more than 30 different AI bots to find and steal exposed credentials, continuously scanning for sensitive data without success. The findings highlight a growing problem for organizations: distinguishing between which AI agents belong in their networks and which may be malicious.

A scanner impersonating 32 bots — including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Meta, and others — hunted for exposed credentials to various organizations, according to a report published today by CQ Prime Research, part of Cequence Security. The scanner requested files from affected organizations — which spanned retail, financial services, telecommunications, energy, and software — that hold passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

The scanner has been running since late September and was still active as of late October, according to the researchers. They identified the activity on Oct. 21, discovering that on a single day this month, 48% of Cequence-protected organizations received the malicious AI bot traffic.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The findings highlight a growing challenge for security teams at a pivotal time, as businesses must figure out which AI agents to trust and permit access to their services.

"Attackers can test every one of those allow and deny decisions, and Cequence is seeing them probe which agents a business trusts, then impersonate the agents they expect to get through," Will Glazier, director of CQ Prime threat research and data science, wrote in the report.

Malicious Scanner Gives Itself Away

The scanner operates by firing off a burst of 50 to 190 requests in about 8 seconds and then moving on, working through targets one at a time, around the clock. Fortunately for the organizations affected, nearly all of the requests were blocked or failed, according to the report.

"It sends random nonsense paths first to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique," Glazier wrote.

CQ Prime Research identified the traffic as malicious through some telling behaviors that undermined the scanner's attempt to blend in with other traffic. The scanner rotates through about 32 bot identities evenly, which real bots do not do, according to the report; one machine claimed to be an agent from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Perplexity, all within seconds.

The attacker also used the contact address of Anthropic's crawler for all of its fake Claude identities, even when posing as different Claude agents, which shows the text was copied and not unique to each agent, according to CQ Prime Research.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

The scanner also makes requests for configuration files, cloud credential files, and private SSH keys, from a list of about 90 paths, while never identifying itself or providing a contact address. Legitimate Internet-scanning services would never need these files and always identify themselves.

"The requests gave it away," observes Collin Hogue-Spears, senior director of solutions management at security firm Black Duck, which means "what Cequence documented is the test, not a breach."

Financial Accounts at Risk

However, what happens when AI agents scanning a network get through? This is what organizations are facing, particularly banks and financial institutions, with growing concern among experts that rogue agents are already logging into customer accounts at these organizations without them knowing. The result of such activity could cause global economic fallout.

For now, CQ Prime Research found that at financial services firms, AI agents acting for customers represented fewer than 1 in 4,000 requests. "The agents banks worry about most log in with a customer's own credentials through an ordinary browser and don't announce themselves," Glazier wrote in the report.

At this point, financial institutions should be starting to take action to identify which AI agents are legit and which aren't. But acting now already could mean they're playing catch-up to the activity of threat actors, observes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability

"Banks are currently scrambling to figure out which AI bots belong on their networks, but cybercriminals have already moved on to the next phase," he says. "They are no longer trying to break into these systems. Instead, they are simply logging in disguised as trusted AI agents."

Defending Against AI Agent Impersonation

To mitigate the growing threat from AI bots and agents, security leaders must treat AI agents, API keys, and service accounts with the same operational rigor as human administrators, Barney suggests. "That requires eliminating implicit trust across every access path," he says.

Indeed, organizations should not trust a bot's claimed identity on its own, according to CQ Prime Research, and they should verify agents through signed requests, published address ranges, or direct integrations.

They also should monitor for behavior that does not match the claimed identity, "such as an AI assistant requesting configuration or credential files," Glazier wrote.

Organizations also should stop leaving static credentials in vulnerable files where scraping bots can easily find them to eliminate obvious security gaps. Instead, Barney says, "Security teams must move away from long-lived local credentials in favor of centralized, zero-knowledge secrets vaults."

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Energy Giant Engie Notifies Customers of Supply Chain Breach
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
One of the world’s largest natural gas suppliers has notified an undisclosed number of customers that their personal data may have been compromised in a recent breach.

French multinational Engie employs over 90,000 people across 30 countries, supplying gas, nuclear power, and renewables. Its revenue in 2025 was almost €72bn ($80bn).

According to screenshots of the customer notification posted to X, the compromised data could include: full name, postal and email address, telephone number, unique IDs for energy supply (PCE/PDL), customer ID, and contract number.

The firm confirmed that no banking data was involved in the breach.

Read more on cyber-attacks impacting French firms: French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Engie urged customers to be on the lookout for potential fraud and phishing stemming from the incident.

“A malicious person could use the information mentioned above to impersonate you or use your personal details to contact another organization in your name, obtain additional information, or attempt to make a payment,” it warned. “Fraudulent emails may appear to come from trusted sources, such as organisations you know, in order to deceive you.”

According to a statement from the firm sent to Infosecurity, its own IT systems weren’t compromised. Engie blamed a third-party marketing platform used by its partners which was then compromised by threat actors.

“Engie recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers in France,” it explained.

“As soon as this activity was detected, the relevant access was disabled. At the same time, Engie launched an in-depth technical investigation to understand the circumstances of the incident, accurately assess its scope by identifying customers potentially affected, and ensure that the situation was fully secured. Enhanced monitoring measures were also put in place.”

No Group Has Claimed Responsibility

At the time of writing, no extortion group had admitted responsibility for the breach, which Engie said is now contained.

However, in October last year, extortion group Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters listed the firm on its leak site, after compromising over 100 Salesforce instances and claiming to have extracted more than one billion records.

In that incident, Engie’s US retail energy business Engie Resources was the victim, with the group claiming to have obtained 3GB of data.

According to claims data from insurer Resilience shared with Infosecurity, no UK or European energy and utilities clients have reported ransomware since July 2025.

European claims with a recorded cost involved only fraud or exposed customer data. That contrasts with the US where ransomware comprises around 70% of incurred losses across claims on record in the sector, Resilience said.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Banks are blocking AI agents from customer accounts
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Where supported, choose read-only access if all you need is analysis or budgeting help
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
This week, Axios reported that major US banks were detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts. In many cases, customers have given the agents their usernames and passwords so they could act on their behalf. This kind of access can violate a bank’s rules.

Bianco Research president Jim Bianco raised the question during Unchained’s Bits + Bips livestream on October 26:

“Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?”

Bianco described traditional finance’s business model as “based on laziness.” Customers may leave idle cash in low- or no-interest bank accounts rather than move it into a money market fund. An AI agent could make that move for them. “Now that you’re able to do it, the banks are afraid they’re gonna lose that revenue stream,” he said.

The banks offer a different explanation. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow just any outside agent into its systems because doing so was “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”

Both explanations can be true: banks can want to retain deposits while also facing real security problems when software acts through customers’ accounts.

Handing over your banking login introduces another service into the security chain. A vulnerability in that service could expose your credentials or allow your account to be misused. And as Bank of America reportedly pointed out:

“If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”

That’s the bank’s stated position, not a universal ruling on consumers’ legal rights. Still, it’s a warning worth taking seriously.

Pros and cons

An AI agent with permission to make purchases might find and buy an item at a lower price. But giving an agent access to your bank account also means sharing sensitive banking information with a third party. We’ve seen shared AI chats become searchable online too.

Axios reported that many banks allow, or are moving toward allowing, read-only access. This can let a tool analyze transactions without giving it permission to move money.

That’s an important boundary, but it doesn’t make the information harmless. An agent that can read bank statements may still disclose them if it’s compromised or manipulated. Preventing transactions and protecting confidentiality are separate security goals.

How to keep control of your money

For consumers, the practical question is not whether banks have perfectly selfless motives. It’s what access you’re giving away, and what could happen if the agent makes a mistake.

Don’t paste banking passwords or security codes into a general-purpose AI assistant. Major banks have explicitly warned customers against sharing their credentials.

Use your bank’s approved connection methods rather than giving an agent your login. Where supported, choose read-only access if all you need is analysis or budgeting help.

Give agents access to as little sensitive information as possible. An assistant comparing publicly advertised savings rates doesn’t need your bank statements. OpenAI recommends limiting agents to the data and credentials they need for the task.

Review consequential actions yourself. If an agent asks for confirmation, check exactly what it intends to do and what information it will share. Don’t treat a confirmation prompt as a formality.

AI can make it easier to compare financial products and spot opportunities you might otherwise miss. But an assistant that finds a better rate and an agent that can act inside your account are different propositions.

Let it help with the homework, but be cautious about handing it the keys.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: LABScon26 Replay | Keynote: A Sober Analysis of AI Impact
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, delivered in his inimitable comedic style, Harvard University professor James Mickens questions whether the scale of current AI investment is justified. Starting from US tech capex of roughly 1.4% of GDP in the second quarter of 2025, he argues that computers are already good enough, and notes that the world has so many CPUs and GPUs that they are put to work solving cryptocurrency puzzles to make imaginary money. More seriously, the AI models that investment is building, he says, grow increasingly opaque as their parameter counts rise.

Mickens then cites research and incident reports on model behaviour, including models acting to prevent another model being shut down and recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and other labs. On economics, he rejects the assumptions that AI will create more jobs than it destroys and that universal basic income will follow widespread automation.

He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security. Mickens own contribution is Guillotine, a hypervisor design that runs a model’s CPU code on isolated cores unable to read or write the hardware state of the cores running the hypervisor. Arguing that hardware-based mechanisms for isolating misaligned frontier models will be an important direction for research over the next five years, he invites those interested in this approach to collaborate.

This keynote speaks to security practitioners and researchers interested in AI risk, the economics behind current AI investment, or hardware-level containment of frontier models

About the Author

James Mickens is a Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard University. His research focuses on the performance, security, and privacy of large-scale online services; a current focus is the interpretability and sandboxing of potentially misaligned frontier models. Prior to becoming a professor at Harvard, Dr. Mickens spent seven years at Microsoft Research, working in the Distributed Systems group.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Cisco open sources tool for detecting AI agents on hacking sprees
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging Face hack – or worse. It’s called Project Quarry, and it aims to provide a “shared language” for evaluating agent behavior, along the lines of what Snort, which Cisco also maintains, did for detecting malicious network traffic and what YARA did for rule-based malware identification. Most detection tools rely on specific interactions with an AI model or agent. Did it attempt prompt injection? Or did the agent call an attack tool? “But what is missing is the entire context under which something may occur,” Amy Chang, head of AI threat and security research at Cisco, said in an exclusive interview with The Register. She likened this to credit card fraud detection. Without context, individual transactions such as a small test charge or a single purchase in a location far away from a card-holder's usual location may not raise any flags. “And then you try again,” making another fraudulent purchase, “and that went through, too. So now I’m gonna buy the PS5,” Chang said. “Those are the things that Quarry addresses by taking into consideration the entire agent session,” she explained. “One tool call may seem in-scope until you realize that that next step is taking that information and sending it to an attacker-controlled inbox or server.” Even data theft is a sequence and not a single agentic action. Agentic AI security firm Invariant Labs demonstrated this with a proof-of-concept attack against GitHub's MCP server that hijacked a user's agent via a malicious GitHub Issue, and coerced it into leaking data from private repositories. Simply reading a configuration file, or sending a request to an external endpoint may be legitimate agentic actions. However, combining the two can lead to data exfiltration – and shows “why action relationships matter,” wrote Chang and fellow Cisco researchers Adam Swanda, Ravikumar Balakrishnan, and Konstantin Berlin in a blog post about Quarry shared with The Register ahead of publication “A policy can produce a finding when the trace shows a sensitive file read followed within a defined window by an external send,” they wrote. “The risk comes from the relationship between the two actions, so the finding should preserve evidence from both." Quarry covers single- and multi-turn large language model conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs. In addition to the open source code itself, the project’s GitHub repository includes installation instructions, supported Python versions, plugins for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents, configuration examples, rule-writing guidance, and a rule starter pack. For instance, with the rule pack, “If a base-64 encoded malware is somewhere in the tool call, that would result in a block,” Chang said. The rule format looks similar to a YARA or Snort rule, with a header that details the traffic to examine, content to match, and metadata for tracking the rule. Here’s a Quarry rule that flags an agent that reads a credentials file: While the Cisco Ai researchers have not run Quarry against data describing the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, they suggest that if the intrusion had been read as a complete, step-by-step record of a single session, there were several points where the AI agents’ steps would have given a Quarry rule something to act on and flag for humans. For example, Quarry would probably have flagged internet access from a sandbox. “The rule can flag specific tool calls that reach an external server asset that wasn’t in the task’s allow list,” Chang said. “Another one would be credentials found and used somewhere else.” According to OpenAI’s technical report about the Hugging Face intrusion, this is exactly what happened on July 10, when an agent validated 14 exposed Hugging Face tokens with write access and shared them. “The rule would flag that there was a credential in the tool result that then called an outside service, which is likely not within the parameters of what you would want to do in this case,” Chang said. “We don't want you to go and search for credentials that may have been leaked or inadvertently exposed and then utilize them to conduct a task.” The Cisco team is quick to say that rules along are not a substitute for chain-of-thought monitors, or other forms of human oversight – but they do help record a pattern that other teams can then “review, test, and apply to their own agents,” they wrote. Herein also lies the benefit of open source, and a collective approach to defending against adversarial use of AI, Chang said. “Do we have all the answers? No,” Chang said. “We all see slices of the problem, and it’s important for us to share what we see.”®

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 123 Reg discloses 'AI cyberattack' on customer data, suspects China nexus
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: 123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: UK domain registrar 123 Reg (no relation – Ed) says it was the victim of an “AI-driven cyberattack” that exposed customer data. Customers began receiving their notification emails this week, informing them that their contact information, "related customer relationship data," company VAT numbers, and "product information from an application programming interface (API)" were compromised. A company spokesperson elaborated, saying this means that names, phone numbers, countries, language and currency preferences, account creation dates, the products on the account, and marketing preferences were affected. 123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus attacker. "Our investigation identified IP addresses that we assessed to be the core attacker infrastructure, which were hosted in China and Singapore, indicating a strong Chinese nexus," the spokesperson said. "Our investigation further identified AI cyberattack 'skills' hosted on Chinese infrastructure, including copies of skills open sourced by Anthropic and several other AI exploitation frameworks and scripts." They went on to say that many of the artefacts left behind led 123 Reg to suspect that a Chinese state-sponsored group, known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations, could be behind the break-in. There is also a suspicion that the same group that hit a number of South Korea’s financial institutions using open-source Chinese AI tool ARTEX, was behind the attack on 123 Reg too. "The TA's mirror of 'anthropic_skills,' and the account naming conventions found on the Chinese servers are consistent with preparation of this class of AI-augmented operation," the spokesperson told us. "In addition, on October 7, 2026, CrowdStrike published CSA-261162, describing an unknown, likely Chinese-speaking actor that targeted several South Korean financial organizations starting in late September 2026, which is the same period during which we were attacked. "That actor used ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us." The GoDaddy-owned registrar reported the attack to law enforcement agencies, brought in outside cybersecurity support, and notified the FTC, as well as the data protection authorities in the UK and EU. The company spokesperson added that it worked with Singapore-based ISPs to shut down the attacker's servers in the region, which helped disrupt the attack, in addition to "other actions by us and industry partners." 123 Reg's email to customers stated the attacker's activity "was limited to reading" customer data, although the spokesperson told us "it's possible they created copies of the information," and that this is what prompted the notification. The registrar urged customers to stay alert to the potential misuse of their data, and to treat communications appearing to come from the company with caution. "If you receive a message or call and aren't sure it's from 123 Reg, go directly to our website and log in," the email said. "We will never contact you to request your password, payment details, or verification codes by email, text, or phone. "We also strongly recommend turning on two-step verification (2SV), which helps keep your account protected even if someone tricks you into sharing your password. You can find instructions for setting up 2SV in your 123 Reg account. "We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." ®

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Clive Robinson • October 28, 2026 8:36 PM

@ Bruce, ALL,

With regards,

“Researchers set up a fake start-up company to study fraudulent North Korean IT workers.”

The “North Korean” aspect so often played to fanfare, flag waving and drum beats by the western ICT Sec industry kind of grinds my gears…

The reason is not that I have any love or sympathy of the North Korean system (in fact quite the opposite).

But that the “North Korean” aspect is now a “banner issue” which makes what is a way way more general and wider attack front, into something much more limited. Thus making corporate management make false assumptions about “supply chain attacks”.

That is,

“Are Indian H-1B workers –that some claim there are a million of working in the US– any more or less dangerous than North Korean workers?

The actual answer is in many cases by head count it is Indians…

They are looking for “high technology” to appropriate and exploit rather than money for their government.

Whilst the NK Gov will take what it can get in most cases they do not have the industry to take advantage of it. However money for their Treasury is always immediately usable.

But it does not matter what the reason for foreign workers is, they are all doing a country harm and often both countries. Because they are stoping citizens in that country developing needed “national skills” for the sake of “a quick buck” on the profit line to keep share holders allowing the managers bonuses…

Which is why certain Corporate Management types were so keen on AI systems… But have now mostly found that

“AI really does not pay or play well”.

It only has longterm ROI in certain very niche very constrained activities and usually requires experienced human oversight.

If this will ever change is open to debate, and I for one am not taking a bet on it because I really don’t expect to live that long.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Lessons from Cybersecurity Black Week
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
The week leading up to October 25, 2026, was every cyber defender’s nightmare: a barrage of critical vulnerabilities in PHP and the Linux kernel, a compromised LiteLLM release, a maximum-severity flaw in GitLab, a Node.js Brotli flaw, and a certificate authority incident affecting TLS trust.

A few years ago, a backlog like this would have filled a defender’s to-do list for a whole month. In the age of AI, all of this was reported within a single “Cybersecurity Black Week,” an exceptionally eventful seven-day period amid an already turbulent Black October. AI-assisted research helped uncover at least two of these flaws: PHP2Shell and the Brotli bug. On top of the breakneck patching pace, security teams faced mounting pressure to deliver status reports to other departments, management, customers, and the media.

Beyond their severity, the issues stood out for the variety of responses they demanded. Some required emergency runtime patches and upgrades; others called for containment, credential rotation, or the replacement of outdated certificate trust bundles. In several cases, installing the latest version was only the beginning of a long remediation process.

With so many problems landing at once, the main challenge was separating real risk from hype and prioritizing accordingly. Here is our assessment.

PHP2Shell: The loudest headline, with real-world limits

PHP2Shell generated the biggest media frenzy of the lot and, with it, a major headache for security teams, prompting many organizations to take their websites offline and look for emergency fixes. The name refers to two memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP core, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affecting PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11. Both vulnerabilities received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable PHP servers. In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection.

With PHP powering an estimated 69% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, government agencies in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere urged organizations to patch immediately, with some advising that affected internet-facing systems be isolated or taken offline if they could not be patched promptly. Government websites in the Netherlands, Germany, France, and other countries were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. The PHP project released fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, along with source-only backports for the end-of-life 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 branches. The rollout was complicated by a premature public leak, which forced the coordinated disclosure timeline forward.

While the flaws clearly belonged near the top of the patching list, early evidence suggested they were considerably harder to weaponize than initially feared. Successful exploitation requires specific conditions and knowledge of the target, and public proof-of-concept exploits did not work against a default PHP installation, according to Sansec.

On October 22, ESET was among nine security companies that told NBC News they had not seen any successful attacks, even though more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits were circulating. The remediation challenge extends beyond obvious web servers: PHP can also be embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces, and third-party products, while end-of-life PHP branches do not receive normal upstream binary releases.

Linux kernel: Reports went public before fixes were ready

As if the PHP issues weren’t severe enough, on October 21, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent several reports on unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the kernel’s private security address while also copying public mailing lists. As a result, technical details of vulnerabilities for which fixes were not yet generally available became public, prompting stable kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman to question why the reports had been sent to public lists without patches.

The two most severe issues, both rated CVSS 9.0 by ZDI, affect KSMBD, the Linux kernel’s built-in SMB server. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct path that could lead to RCE, while ZDI-CAN-33774 is a race condition that could also lead to RCE. Exploiting ZDI-CAN-33549 requires an RDMA-capable interface, a writable KSMBD share, and SMB Direct negotiation, significantly narrowing the number of systems exposed to that particular attack. Other reports concerned local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the networking stack and the VMware graphics driver, as well as an information disclosure issue in the NVMe target code (NVMET).

To remediate, security teams had to track each report independently, consult distribution advisories, and restrict exposed services where practical while awaiting verified fixes. Kernel updates also required rebooting into the patched kernel and checking the running version, not merely confirming that a new package had been installed.

LiteLLM: Compromised, not merely vulnerable

On October 21, attackers published a malicious version of LiteLLM, 1.107.0, to PyPI and pushed compromised images to the project’s official container registries. According to the project’s incident report, its release pipeline was breached using GitHub CLI credentials associated with three developers. One of the stolen tokens belonged to an owner of the project’s GitHub organization, allowing attackers to disable branch protections and modify the release workflow to point to a lookalike repository. LiteLLM, a Python proxy for LLM providers, has about 23 million weekly downloads, and the malicious version remained available on PyPI for roughly two hours before it was quarantined. It was the project’s second supply-chain compromise of 2026, after malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 appeared in March.

The payload combined a credential stealer with a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT). By abusing Python’s startup mechanisms, including a .pth file, it ran every time Python started, even if an application never imported LiteLLM. Execution therefore did not depend on exploiting an application flaw: simply running Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Affected environments had to be treated as potentially compromised, not merely vulnerable. According to LiteLLM, these included environments that ran litellm==1.107.0 and containers that executed affected images distributed under the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags during the compromised intervals. Removing or replacing the package was insufficient: teams needed to determine whether the malicious code had run, contain affected systems, rebuild from clean sources, and rotate exposed secrets from a clean environment. Cloud, source-control, and CI/CD logs also had to be reviewed for unauthorized activity.

Node2Shell: From Node.js to HTTP2Shell

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder, which Node.js bundles. Malformed compressed input can cause crashes, memory disclosure, or potentially RCE when an application decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. This can happen through explicit decompression, compressed request bodies, or automatically decompressed responses. Node.js rates the flaw as high severity, while the broader Brotli vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. According to Aikido, researchers demonstrated code execution against the official, unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux ARM64. Although the exploit did not work on every attempt, the demonstration showed that exploitation was practical, if not universally reliable.

Node.js shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, and Bun followed with version 1.4.4 or later. Node.js 25.x, 23.x, 20.x, and earlier releases are end-of-life and will not receive the fix. Within days, the story outgrew Node.js. The same decoder is compiled into the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages as well as into other HTTP software, which led researchers to rename the issue HTTP2Shell. The operational challenge was therefore not simply upgrading a single runtime but identifying every container, serverless deployment, and library that bundles the vulnerable decoder. The issue was fixed upstream in Brotli 1.2.1. Notably, OpenAI’s Codex Security had reported the underlying bug, and the fix had been present in the Brotli source since February without being recognized as a security issue.

GitLab: Credential leaks and authorization failures

On October 21, GitLab shipped a critical out-of-band patch release (versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) addressing 12 security vulnerabilities. The headline flaw, CVE-2026-110264, rated 10.0 under CVSS v3.1, is an integer overflow triggered when GitLab compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The affected versions date back to GitLab 7.0.

The other fixes addressed credential exposure, cache poisoning, authorization bypasses, and failures to enforce membership or merge-request approval policies. Reported unauthenticated attack paths included exposure of sensitive credentials through internal response headers and manipulation of a shared OAuth/OIDC discovery cache, while other issues required authenticated access. GitLab did not publish individual severity scores or exploitability details for these issues.

GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were already patched, so the work fell on administrators of self-managed instances. GitLab strongly recommended upgrading immediately, but with a catch: the older backport releases (19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) included only the critical fix, while the remaining 11 issues were fixed only in 19.3.6 and later. Administrators also had to verify that all deployment components had been updated and assess the potential exposure of credentials and private project data due to the fact that patching would not invalidate stolen credentials or reverse unauthorized changes.

eMudhra/emSign: Compromised certificate trust

The high-priority eMudhra/emSign incident involved no software vulnerability at all. Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) had insecure private keys, meaning attackers could potentially create certificates that would be trusted through the affected emSign certificate chain. While browsers had updated their trust stores and revocation lists, some Python tooling continued to trust the compromised intermediate CAs through its own certificate bundles. This created a risk of man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks against TLS connections, including those to python.org and pypi.org.

The Python Software Foundation urged users to upgrade immediately to at least certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, and uv 0.13.4, and the Python core team shipped expedited releases 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16, and 3.11.18 to update the bundled pip. The updates had to reach every host, application, and existing virtual environment. Container images had to be rebuilt with layer caching disabled to fetch the latest system certificates. The decisive check was whether deployed clients rejected the compromised trust paths; simply upgrading Python was not enough.

Cutting through the noise

Cybersecurity Black Week showed that a severity score rarely tells the whole story. A 9.2-rated PHP flaw that attackers struggled to exploit, a 10.0-rated GitLab bug, exposed kernel reports with no patches, and a poisoned package that ran at Python startup each called for a different response. What they all had in common was a window of exposure: the time between disclosure and when the last affected system is patched. For the leaked kernel flaws, that window opened before any fix existed, and for end-of-life PHP versions, it may never fully close. This is where ESET’s multilayered protection comes in, using behavioural detection and other security mechanisms to help block exploitation attempts and keep systems protected until patches are applied.

At the same time, the signals defenders rely on were buried in noise, from scanning that was largely benign to a single behavioural rule firing hundreds of thousands of times in a week. What mattered most was quickly understanding which incidents actually affected an organization's environment and what each incident required. That is the problem ESET’s correlation engine, ESET LiveCortex, and its specialized cybersecurity model, ESET NeoCortex, are designed to solve: turning an overwhelming volume of raw data into understandable incidents so that defenders can act before attackers achieve their goals. To learn how they work, read Beyond the alert: How ESET is teaching AI to understand security incidents.

Artificial Intelligence at ESET

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q3 2026
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q2 2026 summarizes notable activities of selected advanced persistent threat (APT) groups documented by ESET researchers between April and September 2026. The operations presented here reflect the broader threat landscape observed during this period and highlight some of its key trends and developments. They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports.

During the monitored period, China-aligned groups conducted intelligence-collection operations primarily against governmental targets. FamousSparrow kept up its monitoring in South America, just as in the previous reporting period. In Southeast Asia and Oceania, China-aligned threat actors ran campaigns that appear to support Chinese law enforcement efforts against organized crime in the region. One threat actor targeted hotels in Palau, which seems to be increasingly used as a base for fraud-related organized crime. SlippyNunchucks deployed its DarkVigil toolset in Sri Lanka against Chinese-speaking individuals connected to fraud schemes, likely in the context of broader regional law enforcement efforts against financial crime. As scam compounds have become an issue for countries neighboring China, with direct negative effects on China itself, it is likely that China-aligned APT groups have supported law enforcement efforts in this area. Another, broader cluster of activity targeted Taiwanese organizations operating in the semiconductor industry. This focus on Taiwan’s semiconductor sector is consistent with long-running Chinese industrial espionage priorities, and the strategic importance of semiconductor supply chains to both economic competition and national security.

Middle East-aligned activity increased compared with the previous reporting period, driven mainly by the return of several established Iran-aligned groups. In the previous period, activity from these groups had declined, most likely because internet restrictions imposed by the Iranian regime hindered their own ability to operate effectively. FilthyFeline, a subgroup of OilRig, and MuddyWater resumed operations after a quieter period, with most activity directed at entities in Israel across multiple sectors; a smaller number of US companies were also affected. FilthyFeline also appears to have taken over activity against a cellular data service provider in Uzbekistan that had previously been compromised by BladedFeline, another OilRig subgroup. In parallel, we analyzed new or updated malware, suggesting renewed development activity within parts of the Iran-aligned ecosystem. We also discovered activity by Arid Viper, a Hamas-affiliated threat actor, against what appears to be the Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates or an affiliated governmental entity. Given the ongoing US-led peace process, as well as the long-standing rivalry between Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, this activity was potentially intended to collect intelligence on the Palestinian Authority’s diplomatic position and internal thinking regarding negotiations to reduce hostilities in the region.

North Korea-aligned threat actors did not deviate significantly from the types of targets seen in previous reporting periods. These include primarily technology and cryptocurrency companies, software developers, and other opportunistic targets. Alongside South Korea, Ukraine has become increasingly prominent among North Korea-aligned targets. This is likely related to growing ties between Russia and North Korea, and North Korea’s increasing involvement in Russia’s war against Ukraine, not only through indirect military support (munitions, etc.) but also through the deployment of North Korean soldiers. Alongside these broader trends, Lazarus resumed targeting of the drone sector, typically using recruitment-themed social engineering to gain initial access. The likely motivation is the increasingly important role that drone systems are playing in the war in Ukraine, where new tactics and capabilities are being tested. Access to such knowledge and manufacturing processes could provide North Korea with valuable know-how for developing its own drone-production capabilities. We also detected ScarCruft targeting an African country, which was probably intended either to maintain oversight of a North Korean worker scheme operating in the country or to monitor Russian activities there. Separately, DeceptiveDevelopment moved from fake job-interview lures to broader software supply-chain compromises, harvesting developer credentials and using that access to inject malicious code into public and private source code repositories.

Russia-aligned activity continued to support its war objectives, targeting governments, the defense sector, and military entities in Europe, with a substantially higher number of targets in Ukraine. Looking more closely at these activities, similarities between Russia-aligned and Belarus-aligned campaigns stand out, further supporting our hypothesis that threat actors aligned with the two countries are becoming operationally closer. Gamaredon’s operations, which are typically numerous, saw a significant decline. We suspect that this could be related to Ukrainian attacks on Crimea, where the group is suspected to operate, a broader restructuring of its operations, or other factors that we continue to assess. Despite this decline in activity, Gamaredon updated its PteroBox file stealer and started using new tools such as PteroPSDoor and Turla’s VBScript Rezzuar. PhantomCaptcha attempted to deploy spyware, which we named PrincessSpy, on Android devices while impersonating Ukrainian entities. We also identified an extensive campaign in Ukraine exploiting MDaemon mail servers, during which the attackers deployed two backdoor malware families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG.

North Korea’s expanding military cooperation with Russia has prompted expectations that North Korea-aligned cyberactivity might be starting to align more closely with Russian objectives in Ukraine. While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia. We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas. Most notably, we identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater, marking a significant development in this threat nexus. According to our telemetry, FrostyNeighbor attacked a manufacturing company in Ukraine that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector. This marks a notable escalation, as threat actors with a well-established history of destructive cyberoperations in Ukraine have, until now, been Russia-aligned.

Finally, we identified several cases of APT groups using AI and large language models (LLMs) at various stages of their operations. Threat actors used AI primarily to accelerate tasks that would otherwise require painstaking effort, including malware development and the creation of decoy websites. In some cases, this resembled vibe coding: rapid, prompt-driven drafting of code, with human operators adapting and integrating the results into their toolchains. We also discovered phishing lures containing images that were clearly AI-generated. In one notable case, Russia-aligned UAC-0099 inserted a decoy request for instructions on building a nuclear weapon into a script comment, apparently attempting to trigger the safety guardrails of LLM-based security analysis and prevent the inspection of the malicious code that followed.

Despite these developments, we have not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months. While we cannot determine whether some operations may involve a higher degree of AI-driven automation, our telemetry continues to show hands-on-keyboard activity and operations that are not fully automated. Overall, our observations suggest that APT groups are currently using AI much like mainstream software developers: to accelerate software development, automate previously manual tasks, and assist with the analysis of large volumes of data, rather than to conduct fully autonomous malicious operations.

ESET products protect our customers’ systems from the malicious activities described in this report. Intelligence shared here is based mostly on proprietary ESET telemetry data and has been verified by ESET researchers.

ESET APT Activity Reports contain only a fraction of the cybersecurity intelligence data provided in ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports. For more information, visit the ESET Threat Intelligence website.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Executive Summary

In May, Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) documented JOMANGY, a PHP webshell generation deployed by INJ3CTOR3 with self-healing persistence channels and a built-in toll-fraud dialer.

Back then, the fraud ran through the victim's own PBX, so removing the implant would have stopped it. Artifacts we collected from the operator's C2 staging servers during mid-September 2026 show that this is no longer true: the installer now sends credentials off the box on every run, and a second staging host serves it.

INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now uploads the victim's SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials to the operator, so disinfecting or rebuilding an infected host no longer ends the exposure. Anyone running FreePBX, Issabel, or Elastix who suspects compromise must rotate the secrets in 17 configuration files, and only after the host is clean.

The infection and persistence code is nearly unchanged; what the operator rotated are the identifiers that were available to defenders since the last time. Each section below pairs a finding with what to do about it.

Key Takeaways

Credentials leave on every run. k.php uploads 17 configuration files to both staging hosts every minute the host stays infected.

The fraud no longer needs your PBX. A stolen trunk secret lets the operator register and place calls as you from anywhere.

Last report's identifiers have expired. Each build now carries its own watermark, and the webshell gate hash was rotated.

Two staging hosts. Plain-text commands now point to 160[.]119[.]69[.]4, while base64-encoded ones still use 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

Clean-looking logs and consoles prove nothing. Requests through an encoded space reach the shell without being named in the access log, and trunks are written directly to /etc/asterisk; they do not appear in the FreePBX console.

The Campaign So Far

INJ3CTOR3 has been abusing Asterisk-based phone systems for toll fraud since at least 2020. Check Point Research named the operation that November, when it exploited CVE-2019-19006 in FreePBX and used a basic webshell to read amportal.conf and sip_additional.conf by hand. Unit 42 reported a related operation against Elastix in 2022, Fortinet documented the EncystPHP webshell in January 2026, and our May report covered JOMANGY.

The playbook has held for six years: scan for exposed PBXs, exploit or brute-force a way in, plant a password-gated webshell, and dial out at the victim's expense. Figure 1 below shows the chain as it stands in the September build, now including the credential upload back to the staging hosts.

Figure 1: INJ3CTOR3 attack chain, September generation. (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub)

What Changed Since Our Last Report

We compared the April artifacts behind our May report with the 9 September collection from both staging hosts, after decoding every layer.

Area

April

September

Credential Exfiltration

Unchanged: the decoded webshell panel, the encoding chain (base64 in the shell script, base64 again in PHP, then ROT13), the persistence channels, the backdoor account password hash, and the borrowed timestamp. Behavioral detections built on our May report still apply.

Credential Exfiltration: The Implant Is No Longer the Product

The September k.php ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each holding 17 curl commands that upload one configuration file apiece to /hima_data/index.php, one line per staging host (See Figure 2 below). The paths are typed out by hand and cover FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix layouts. The collector path echoes hima, a backdoor account the takeover script creates. The name goes back further: Check Point's 2020 INJ3CTOR3 report shows a Telegram post by a user called Hima sharing a tool that scans and cracks SIP ranges, saving its output as HimaResults.

Figure 2: k.php line 34, decoded into 17 file uploads

Three of the cron beacons fetch and run k.php every minute (the others every two or three minutes), so the upload repeats every minute during the infection. Rotating credentials on a still-infected host hands the new secrets to the operator within minutes.

What it unlocks

Files uploaded

Rotate

SIP trunks and extensions (chan_sip)

/etc/asterisk/sip.conf, sip_additional.conf, sip_registrations.conf, sip_general_additional.conf, sip_custom.conf

Every trunk secret (with your carrier) and extension secret, changed in the FreePBX GUI, since the *_additional.conf files are regenerated

SIP trunks and extensions (PJSIP)

/etc/asterisk/pjsip.auth.conf, pjsip.endpoint.conf, pjsip.aor.conf, pjsip.identify.conf, pjsip.transports.conf

The same secrets; review IP-based identity rules

Every AMI user.

PBX database, AMI, and platform admin

/etc/freepbx.conf, /etc/amportal.conf, /etc/asterisk/amportal.conf, /etc/issabel.conf, /etc/elastix.conf

The database password (AMPDBPASS), the MySQL root password, and any AMI password stored there

Outbound mail

/etc/postfix/sasl_passwd

The SMTP relay account, with your mail provider

This opens a second route to fraud. Our May report covered calls placed through the webshell, which require the shell to be alive and to land in the victim's own call records. With a stolen trunk secret, the operator can register to the carrier from any machine and call as the victim, leaving nothing on the host, unless the carrier also restricts the trunk to the victim's IP addresses. A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second.

Detection

Network: outbound HTTP POSTs from a PBX to any /hima_data/ path or to either staging host. A PBX seldom needs outbound web access beyond vendor updates, so egress allow-listing closes this channel.

Carrier: alert on trunk registrations from outside your own IP ranges, and on premium or international destinations, off-hours calling, and unusual concurrency. Set spend caps and destination blocks where your carrier offers them.

For Law Enforcement Agencies and CERTs

By design, victims' credentials were collected on the two staging hosts, which stopped responding in late September 2026. Going offline does not end exposure: hosting providers may still retain server data, and infected PBXs keep trying to upload their credentials every minute to addresses that could be reassigned to someone else.

Both are reasons for law enforcement and national CERTs, which have the legal standing that researchers lack, to work with the providers on preserving that data and sinkholing the addresses, which would also identify victims for notification. We saw the uploads in code; we did not capture one in transit and hold no victim list.

Two Staging Hosts, Split by Encoding

An infected host now talks to both staging hosts, and which one depends on whether the command was written in plain text or base64. The /x takeover script is byte-identical on both.

Reference

Encoding

Points to

k.php line 2 (re-runs /x), eight cron schedules in /x, wr.php's callback

Plain text

160[.]119[.]69[.]4

Camouflaged cron payloads, login-triggered stager

Base64

45[.]95[.]147[.]178

Credential upload

Base64

Both

In April, all of these pointed to 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. We assess that the operator replaced the address in plain text and never re-encoded the base64 strings; the credential upload, which names both hosts, appears deliberate. This host is distinct from the scanner 160[.]119[.]76[.]250, which is named in our May report.

Defend: block both hosts in both directions, and decode every base64-encoded string in a crontab or shell profile before deciding which hosts a host talks to. A plain-text review would miss every channel that still reaches 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

The Webshell: Same Program, New Identifiers

Decoded, the September JOMANGY panel is identical to April's except for the values defenders were told to look for.

Per-build watermark. Our May report advised hunting for trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea, present in every April copy. The September builds carry trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 (45[.]95[.]147[.]178) and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e (160[.]119[.]69[.]4), so that hunt now misses current infections.

One gate for two generations. JOMANGY and ZenharR share a single hardcoded MD5 gate hash, rotated together from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. Our May report listed the April value under ZenharR only.

A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Therefore, changing the FreePBX admin password affects neither the gate nor this session. (See Figure 3 below)

Figure 3: The panel's Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password

Because each of these identifiers changes between builds, the detection approach later in this report focuses on who put a file on disk rather than on what the file contains.

The .htaccess Door and the Access-Log Gap

k.php writes a seven-line .htaccess to /var/www/html/admin/views/. It does not hide the webshell; it unblocks it, and it lets requests reach a copy without naming it.

RewriteEngine On# enable symbolic linksOptions +FollowSymLinksRewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-dRewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-fRewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-lRewriteRule ^\s+ config.php [L]

Request path

Status

What answered

/dir/zzz

404

Nothing

/dir/%20zzz, /dir/%09zzz (space, tab, etc)

200

config.php

/dir/+zzz

404

Nothing

Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it.

Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. Because the takeover script wipes logs, treat log hunting as secondary: requests with %20, %09, or %0A directly after a slash that return 200 are worth a look where logs survive.

What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You

FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so.

Figure 4: Our lab trunk, known to Asterisk and carrying calls, invisible in the FreePBX console

Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added.

What Keeps It There

Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below)

Figure 5: Persistence channels that rebuild each other, and the backdoors they stay open

Detecting It Without IOCs

The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be.

On the host: triage with beagle.sh

PBX admins can run beagle.sh, a report-only script that makes no changes to the host, to check a PBX server for signs of compromise. (See Figure 6 below)

Check

What it flags

Packed shells

Several identical, same-size PHP files across unrelated directories

Locked files

chattr +i or +a under the web root or in hidden directories

Unowned .htaccess

An .htaccess no installed package accounts for

Self-rebuilding cron

A cron line that downloads a file and hands it to a shell

Accounts

An extra UID-0 account, or a full-permission FreePBX admin, nobody created

Blocklist

Addresses dropped in and out by iptables outside fail2ban's chains

Figure 6: beagle.sh (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub)

The script separated one infected server from one clean server of the same FreePBX version, a sample of one, so expect some legitimate findings. However, it cannot tell you whether the credentials have already been left: that happens during the first cron run, within a minute of infection, and long before anyone scans. The upload leaves no file behind, and the takeover script wipes what might have recorded it: the web server, Asterisk, cron and audit logs, plus shell and MySQL histories, which makes forensic timelines hard to reconstruct.

With telemetry

The most distinctive actions leave little on disk; in our detonation, backdoor accounts were created and deleted 27 seconds apart. These eleven behaviors are detection strategies to build into your own tooling:

Layer

What it catches

The beacon's rhythm, whatever the address

Credentials leaving

The .htaccess door

A call asking for nothing legitimate

Phone

The fraud itself

The last two catch the fraud rather than the machinery, whatever the files are called, and whether you ever find the shell. The host rows need process telemetry that PBX appliances rarely have, which is part of why so many stay infected.

Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works

First move

Why it fails on its own

Delete the webshell

Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags.

Patch FreePBX

Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system.

Change the admin password

The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login.

Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it.

Preserve first

The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run:

Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below.

Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times.

Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs.

Then clean, in this order

Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref.

Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local.

Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled.

Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php.

Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host.

Conclusion

The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account.

The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR.

The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure.
