Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text: IntroductionIn September 2026, Zscaler Threat Hunting identified an SEO poisoning campaign that used fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware family we track as Armorsteal. The fake websites targeted users searching for Chocolatey or MAS software installation commands. Each lure page displayed a malicious PowerShell command that downloaded and executed the Armorsteal installer. The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor.The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data.In this blog post, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team traces the campaign from poisoned search results through post-infection activity, including Armorsteal's components, C2 communication, and infrastructure changes observed during our analysis. Key TakeawaysIn September 2026, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team identified an SEO poisoning campaign that distributed Armorsteal through websites impersonating Chocolatey and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool.The SEO campaign targeted users searching for Chocolatey installation instructions or Microsoft activation scripts.The remote access component verifies RSA-2048 signatures on Python tasks received from the C2 server before executing them.The surveillance component records window titles, logs keystrokes, monitors copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and captures screenshots when configured keywords are detected.The information stealing component steals Discord tokens, browser cookies, saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, BIP39 seed phrases, and SSH keys. Technical AnalysisThe following sections provide details about the malware distribution, capabilities, and network communications.SEO poisoningZscaler Threat Hunting identified two SEO poisoning lures that targeted users searching for Windows software installation instructions. One of those lures is shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Google search results for “chocolatey install windows”. Fake Chocolatey websiteThe first lure (seen in Figure 1) targets users looking for the Chocolatey package manager. A user searching for terms such as “install Chocolatey” and “Chocolatey PowerShell” may reach a typosquatted site impersonating chocolatey[.]org. The site displays a PowerShell installation command. When the user runs it, the malicious install.ps1 script downloads and installs the remote access module. The script also runs the legitimate Chocolatey installer, so Chocolatey appears to function as expected. The fake Chocolatey website and the malicious domain, choclatey[.]org, are shown below:Figure 2: Fake Chocolatey website distributing Armorsteal. Fake Massgrave websiteThe second lure targeted users searching for terms such as “Microsoft Activation Scripts,” “MAS activation script,” or “Massgrave activation”. These users may have reached massgravel[.]net, a malicious website impersonating the Microsoft Activation Scripts tool (a.k.a., the Massgrave project). The fake Massgrave website is shown in the figure below:Figure 3: Fake Massgrave website distributing Armorsteal.Although the two websites impersonate different projects and target different search queries, both deliver Armorsteal.ANALYST NOTE: The fake Massgrave website went down on September 25, 2026, and the fake Chocolatey website went down around October 1, 2026. Installation and persistenceBoth installer variants request elevated privileges, hide the PowerShell console window, and download a ZIP archive to C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\ to mimic a legitimate Windows system directory. The archive contains a Python 3.11 runtime, Pyarmor runtime files, and Armorsteal Python-based scripts.The installer creates the following scheduled tasks for persistence:Scheduled taskTriggerDescriptionSysCheck2User logonLaunches the remote access module with the highest privileges available.SysCheckXSystem bootLaunches the remote access module as SYSTEM after a 45-second delay.Table 1: Armorsteal scheduled task persistence.Anti-analysis techniquesArmorsteal uses the following techniques to avoid research environments and complicate analysis:The remote access module checks the public IP address and organization information using ipinfo[.]io. If the organization name returned matches a cloud provider such as Google, Amazon, Microsoft, or Azure, the module displays a fake “Memory is insufficient” message and exits. This can prevent the malware from running in some cloud-based analysis environments.The Python scripts are protected with Pyarmor 9.1.7 (trial version). Pyarmor encrypts Python bytecode and string constants, making static analysis and detection more difficult. The trial runtime is operationally useful to the threat actor because it provides code obfuscation without requiring a commercial Pyarmor license.Remote access moduleThe Armorsteal remote access module is stored as SysMon.py and is launched by the SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks. The module collects information about the infected system, including the hostname, operating system, processor, memory, disks, local IP address, public IP address, and network interfaces. It uses the motherboard serial number to create a machine identifier used in C2 communication.The remote access module also downloads and launches the surveillance and information stealing modules. The remote access module uses HTTPS and a hardcoded list of four C2 domains. It checks the availability of each domain before starting C2 communication. The C2 endpoints supported by the remote access module are shown in the table below:EndpointMethodDescription/downloadables/configf.jsonGETChecks whether the C2 server is available based on the HTTP status code 200./receive_infofPOSTSends device information to the C2 server./get-onetime-code/{machine_id}GETRequests a task for an individual victim./get-globalGETRequests a task shared across all infected systems./downloadables/{archive}GETIn earlier builds, downloads the remote access module updates along with the surveillance and information stealing modules.Table 2: The remote access module C2 endpoints.The following example shows the format of the HTTP POST request the remote access module uses to send system information to its C2 server. POST /receive_infof HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0 Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: {CONTENT_LENGTH} { "host_name": "{HOSTNAME}", "ip_address": "{LOCAL_IP}", "public_ip_address": "{PUBLIC_IP}", "mac_address": "{MAC_ADDRESS}", "system": "{WINDOWS_VERSION}", "machine": "{MACHINE_ARCHITECTURE}", "memory": { "total": {TOTAL_MEMORY_SIZE}, "available": {AVAILABLE_MEMORY_SIZE}, "percent": {MEMORY_PERCENTAGE} } }The C2 server responds with the following message:{"message":"Data received and stored successfully"}The remote access module polls its C2 server every 60 seconds for both per-victim and global tasks. The malware verifies every task received using an embedded RSA-2048 public key before executing it. The per-victim task endpoint returns JSON containing Python code and a Base64-encoded signature, as shown in the format below:{ "code": "<Python source code>", "sig": "<Base64-encoded RSA signature>" }The global task endpoint returns a different response containing the # _ _SIGNED _ _: marker followed by the task data:# _ _SIGNED_ _:{"code":"aW1wb3J0IG9zCmltcG9ydCBzdWJwcm9jZXNz...", "sig":"fdWOAiJJ7qIowDnCEgO4LDd+s19RzzBjnKFQ9K447GXj..."}The remote access module uses a custom RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification routine before executing the task’s code in memory. After verifying a task's signature, it extracts an integer version number embedded in the Python code: ONETIME_VERSION for per-victim tasks and GLOBAL_VERSION for global tasks. The module compares this task version number with the last successfully executed version stored locally in its working directory, C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\. Task version numbers specific to a victim are stored in onetime_version.txt and global task versions are recorded in global_version.txt. The malware executes a task in memory only when its version is greater than the value in the corresponding file. The version number is then updated in the corresponding file. This prevents previously processed or older tasks from running again.The Armorsteal remote access module can also update itself through global tasks. These tasks can direct the malware to download a replacement SysMon.py file. The module first verifies the SHA256 of the downloaded file before replacing its local copy. This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration.Surveillance moduleThe surveillance component is named basrq.py and runs in a separate bundled Python interpreter in a ZIP archive, which is downloaded by the remote access module.The surveillance module performs the following activities:Logs keystrokes (with specialized handling for English, French, Spanish, and German), including backspace, space, decimal separators, and modifier keys.Records the title of the active window along with captured keystrokes.Monitors clipboard content every 0.5 seconds.Replaces copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled addresses.Captures screenshots when configured keywords appear in window titles or captured keystrokes.Displays fake transaction notifications that impersonate Exodus, MetaMask, and Phantom.The clipboard hijacker supports wallet addresses for Bitcoin, Litecoin, Monero, Ethereum, TRON, XRP, Dogecoin, TON, and Solana.The Armorsteal surveillance module uses the following C2 endpoints to retrieve monitoring keywords and upload collected data.EndpointMethodDescription/global_keywordsGETRetrieves campaign-wide monitoring keywords./keywords/{machine_id}GETRetrieves keywords for a specific infected system./black-watch/{machine_id}POSTUploads gzip-compressed keystroke logs./black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}POSTUploads keyword-triggered screenshots.Table 3: The Armorsteal surveillance module C2 endpoints.The module retrieves keyword lists every 300 seconds. The observed lists include terms related to cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, browser names, cloud services, and recovery phrase-related terms. Before uploading screenshots to /black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}, the surveillance module encrypts their raw PNG bytes. The module computes the SHA256 digest of a hardcoded string and uses the resulting 32-byte value (c1146fbcaa433385839c25839a61cd7fedaff858cc0d3fd063dba68db2cf31b4) as an XOR key.The following example shows the Armorsteal surveillance module uploading the stolen data using the filename keylogs.gz:POST /black-watch/{machine_id} HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net Content-Type: multipart/form-data Content-Disposition: form-data; name="keylogs"; filename="keylogs.gz" <gzip-compressed log data>Stealer moduleThe information stealing module’s script name is got.py, which is downloaded as a ZIP archive by the remote access module. This module collects data from web browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Discord clients, and Steam installations. The stealer also collects system information, including geolocation, display information, language settings, time zone, and GPU details.The stealer module has the following capabilities:Steals and validates Discord tokens from 22 Discord client variants.Collects data from 21 browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications.Searches drives from A: through Z: for BIP39 seed phrases.Extracts browser cookies through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) on port 9222.Steals saved browser passwords, autofill data, and credit card metadata. To collect browser passwords, the module downloads and uses the public chrome-decryptor tool from the Chrome App-Bound Encryption Decryption project.Targets password manager data from KeePass, 1Password, RoboForm, Password Safe, Enpass, Bitwarden, and Dashlane.Collects SSH keys and Steam session data.The Armorsteal stealer module uses the following C2 endpoints to upload stolen data: EndpointMethodDescription/infame/receive/zipPOSTUploads the main stolen data archive./infame/receive/dtPOSTUploads Discord tokens and account information./ws/{machine_id}POSTUploads wallet files and seed phrases./pwdPOSTUploads saved browser passwords./upload/stPOSTUploads Steam account information.Table 4: Armorsteal stealer module C2 endpoints.The main information stealing component archive contains a system profile and browser cookie files. Threat Actor InfrastructureZscaler Threat Hunting identified Armorsteal lure and C2 domains registered on the dates shown in the table below. Shared malware components and an RSA-2048 task-signing key link the Chocolatey and Massgrave lures to the same operation.DomainPurposeRegistration DateRegistrarworkerstats[.]netPrimary C2January 28, 2026NICENICdatamons[.]orgStandby C2May 19, 2026NameSilosupertrap[.]netStandby C2August 29, 2026NameSilomassgravel[.]netFake Massgrave lureAugust 30, 2026NICENICchoclatey[.]orgFake Chocolatey lureSeptember 1, 2026Key-Systemsniceer[.]netStandby C2September 1, 2026NICENICTable 5: Armorsteal lure and C2 domain registration details.Zscaler Threat Hunting observed two phases of the campaign’s infrastructure changes during the analysis period. In the first phase (early September 2026), the fake Chocolatey website and its subdomains were hosted at 209.99.186[.]187, an SKN Subnet & Telecom server. At this time, workerstats[.]net was protected by Cloudflare and resolved to 104.21.87[.]146.In mid-September 2026, the operator moved the Chocolatey and Massgrave lure websites to 82.153.135[.]80, hosted by AKILE LTD in the United Kingdom. The primary C2 domain, workerstats[.]net, also moved from Cloudflare to 186.2.175[.]183, hosted by IQWeb FZ-LLC and using DDoS-Guard name servers.During continued monitoring (early October 2026), Zscaler Threat Hunting observed further changes to Armorsteal’s C2 infrastructure. The previously used domain, workerstats[.]net, became unavailable, and the threat actor began using pymons[.]is and the previously dormant domain datamons[.]org as C2 servers. The threat actor subsequently changed how the surveillance and information stealing modules were downloaded. Previously accessible through the C2 server’s /downloadables/ path, the packages now require a token in the request URL and an X-Verify header containing the correct token. Requests use /C2/?t=[token]451 for surveillance and /C2/?t=[token]452 for information stealing. Successful requests retrieve ZIP packages from /p/[32hex].zip, with randomized filenames. Remediations And Detection OpportunitiesFor organizations that suspect exposure to this campaign, we recommend the following actions:Investigate systems for SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks.Hunt for files and directories under C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\.Review PowerShell logs for downloads from choclatey[.]org, community[.]choclatey[.]org, and massgravel[.]net.Block the verified malicious lures and C2 domains.Review outbound HTTPS traffic for /receive_infof, /get-global, /black-watch/, and /infame/receive/ where URL paths are visible in your telemetry.Review endpoint telemetry for browser processes started with --remote-debugging-port=9222.Remove unauthorized Microsoft Defender exclusions, particularly exclusions for C:\Windows.Educate users to verify software download websites and PowerShell installation commands before execution. ConclusionArmorsteal is a Python-based malware family distributed through an active SEO poisoning campaign that uses fake Chocolatey and Massgrave websites. The campaign deploys modules for remote access, cryptocurrency theft, clipboard hijacking, and credential stealing. The shared malware components, task-signing key, and C2 infrastructure link both lures to the same operation. Although the operator changed hosting and package filenames during our analysis, the core malware components remained unchanged. The Zscaler Threat Hunting team continues to monitor the campaign for infrastructure and payload changes. Zscaler CoverageZscaler’s multilayered cloud security platform detects indicators related to Armorsteal at various levels. Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Teach a noob to phish and they'll be scamming for a lifetime. It has never been easier to steal credentials, thanks to a growing number of phishing kits that give aspiring attackers everything they need in one convenient interface.

Huntress Staff Threat Intelligence Analyst Andrea Hatcher and Staff Product Manager Rich Mozeleski stopped by our monthly Tradecraft Tuesday series in October to unpack some recently staged phishing kits and walk through what the resulting malicious activity looks like from the defenders' point of view.

Watch the full video below, and keep reading for clips and other highlights.

Example phishing kits

A phishing kit is a pre-packaged resource with code, templates, and instructions for how to launch a phishing campaign and use the stolen credentials for further malicious activity. Basic kits are often made up of simple HTML and script files that can spin up a single fake login page.

More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time.

Here are three of the many phishing kits that Huntress has analyzed in the last few months, all targeting Microsoft 365 tokens:

EvilTokens

Knight Office

Kali365

EvilTokens hops off the Railway

Just a few weeks before this broadcast, a collaboration between Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit and the FBI led to the arrest of one of the alleged operators of EvilTokens, a device-code phishing campaign that abused the Railway PaaS as a token-harvesting and token-replay engine.

For more on the EvilTokens takedown, watch Rich's conversation with Microsoft's Principal Corporate Counsel Carlton Gammons and Huntress' Chief Legal Officer Lauren Zajac on-demand.

As Rich put it, discovering the EvilTokens campaign in February "opened the dam" for our researchers diving into phishing kits. He noted the kit's professional aesthetic and 24/7 support as akin to a software-as-a-service (SaaS) operation.

Moving beyond passwords

Andrea walked through how the Kali365 control panel is an entire criminal ecosystem in a box, including AI features: "It's not just someone standing up a convincing login page, it's a whole ecosystem that helps an operator acquire infrastructure, collect authentication material, retain access, and even scale it up."

>

With these additional capabilities, phishing kits can help attackers get their hands on a lot more than usernames and passwords. We asked the audience what they thought attackers found most desirable these days, and most of those polled answered an authenticated session token or a persistent foothold.

Modern phishing kids can provide low-skilled attackers with a usable authenticated session with any of the following tactics:

Device-code phishing

Adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing

Token theft and replay

Device-code phishing

Device-code phishing refers to when the user authenticates directly with the identity provider, but the attacker captures the resulting authorization. Device-code flows can reduce friction for attackers because they do not require the victim to surrender a password directly.

Rich shared that an estimated one in six incidents investigated by Huntress' ITDR team involved a rogue device being registered, and 36 percent of the audience members polled had seen device-code phishing in the wild. He points to Conditional Access Policies as a key prevention measure: "The vast majority of Microsoft environments do not need device code flow."

Adversary-in-the-middle attacks

AitM attacks reveal the limitations of MFA; the threat actor relays the authentication flow in real time, either with a fake login page or by intercepting an exchange within the legitimate app. The victim completes the MFA prompt while the attacker captures the resulting session information. This is why successfully completed MFA does not make the session trustworthy on its own.

Token theft and replay

As Andrea put it, "the session can be way more powerful than the password." After an attacker gets their hands on a sign-in token, a phishing kit can help them "replay" it into an active session, where they can access cloud resources and victim email accounts.

If you suspect token replay in your environment, your investigation should move beyond the original phishing page and examine how the token was used. Polled audience members voted sign-in address and new device registration as the top two signals to investigate first if token theft is suspected.

What defenders see, and what to do about it

Andrea emphasized the importance of detecting signals across the chain. One signal is weak; the sequence is strong. Correlate the progression of lure, authentication, token issuance or theft, device registration, mailbox activity.

Andrea drove the point home: "Join the telemetry across the identity provider, the endpoint, the browser context, the network, and the mailbox. We shouldn't just be looking at one signal in the network or one signal in the mailbox. We really need to have that holistic view."

Detection opportunities

Investigate successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure.

Hunt for device-code authentication and automated token refresh.

Review new devices, authentication methods, and mailbox activity.

Response priorities

Containment must address identity artifacts, not just the original lure.

Revoke refresh tokens.

Remove unauthorized devices and Windows Hello credentials.

Restrict or block device-code authentication where possible.

Investigate mailbox access, forwarding rules, and outbound phishing.

Continue hunting after the original phishing domain disappears.

Continuous response loop

Detect correlated identity and endpoint activity.

Revoke or remove persistence mechanisms.

Investigate downstream mailbox and outbound-phishing activity.

Continue monitoring for replay or re-entry after containment.

Like what you just read? Join us every month for Tradecraft Tuesday, our live webinar where we expose hacker techniques and talk nerdy with live demos. Snag your spot now!

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: ARTEX in the Wild: Storm-0940 Expands Targeting of IT and Software Vendors
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: What it looked like in the logs We analyzed these attack patterns using HTTP access logs collected via Wiz Agentless Workload Detection, alongside identity provider logs such as...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Throughout October 2026, we identified an actor using tooling associated with ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration-testing agent, to target multiple IT and software vendors. The activity focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and abuse of Microsoft 365 integrations. We observed repeated attempts to uncover authentication bypasses, enumerate APIs, and access customer data (of the targeted vendors) across multiple environments.

Our observations overlap with Microsoft's recent report on ​​Storm-0940, a Chinese-state aligned actor - linked to the recent supply-chain attack involving stolen vendor credentials and downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.

However, we have additionally observed the same infrastructure, tooling, and attack patterns targeting the sector as a whole. Pivoting on identified TTPs and IOCs, we have also identified the same actor expanding their attempted supply chain compromises into other software sectors.

In this blog, we will describe the repeatable patterns and methodologies the ARTEX-using actor applied across multiple environments and cloud providers, with examples taken from real world attacks.

What is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026, and it won Baidu's "Agent+" red team challenge that September. In practice, an operator supplies a target and an objective. A planner agent then chooses the next step, worker agents run tools like nmap, curl, and Impacket, and every result feeds a shared graph of assets and findings.

Attackers picked it up within weeks. ARTEX artifacts surfaced in attacks on South Korean banks in late September and attacks on Japanese companies in October. Microsoft and Zscaler have since tied it to two separate actors. The developer made the tool closed-source on October 8. By then, the code had more than 12,000 forks.

A repeatable playbook

Across the investigated environments, we observed a consistent sequence of reconnaissance and attack attempts:

Map the application: Download JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configurations, and Swagger/OpenAPI documentation to discover internal API routes and application functionality.

Probe authentication: Repeatedly initiate sign-in flows, manipulate OAuth callbacks and state parameters, test unsigned JWTs, and probe SSO and Microsoft 365-specific endpoints.

Attack identity providers and login flows: Password-spray corporate Okta and Entra ID environments, and target internal and proprietary application login pages.

Abuse account recovery: Repeatedly invoke password-reset, username-recovery, activation, and reset-token endpoints.

Test tenant isolation: Register accounts using disposable email addresses where possible, then manipulate predictable identifiers to probe for broken access controls and unauthorized cross-tenant data access.

Adapt to defense mechanisms: Rotate IP addresses when blocked, and constantly circulate user agents.

What it looked like in the logs

We analyzed these attack patterns using HTTP access logs collected via Wiz Agentless Workload Detection, alongside identity provider logs such as AWS Cognito events, Entra sign-in activity, and Okta authentication logs.

Targeting Internal Applications

The agent's first move across all observed instances of the attack was always to read the application itself. Requests like these showed up minutes after first contact:

GET /packs/js/main-3a9f...js.map GET /assets/config.json GET /env.js GET /swagger/?format=openapi

Not long after, it started calling internal API routes by name. The only place those route names appear is in the source maps it had just downloaded.

Account recovery got the same treatment. The agent checked which usernames existed, then hammered the reset endpoints:

GET /Account/ValidateUserName?UserName=admin POST /api/v1/Users/GeneratePasswordResetToken → 204 POST /forgot_password

Where it could sign up, it did, using a throwaway mailbox from a free temporary-email service. Then, it immediately tried to look at someone else's data:

POST /v2/register_user → 201 POST /confirm → 200 GET /company/1/logins → 403 GET /api/users/generate_redirect_link?role=admin → 401

Before every fuzzing run, it checked what a baseline "not found" response looked like:

GET /zzz-nonexistent-xyz123

Targeting OAuth Identity Providers

When probing Microsoft OAuth flows, the agent directly manipulated the callback endpoint by injecting fabricated authorization codes and malformed state parameters, while also attempting to bypass authentication using unsigned JWTs:

GET /sign_in/oauth/microsoft/callback?code=AAAA&state=notvalidb64!! GET /sso?jwt=eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJlbWFpbCI6InRlc3RAdGVzdC5jb20ifQ.

That second token simply decodes to {"alg":"none"} and {"email":"test@test.com"}. The agent bombarded more than 60 variations of SSO routes with this payload in just two minutes.

On AWS Cognito, we observed patterns mirroring the account recovery abuse seen in proprietary apps. This activity was reflected in events like InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword, and ResendConfirmationCode. These requests originated from the same mix of user agents observed in earlier attacks, including benign-looking programmatic clients like boto and python-urllib.

The agent also attempted to provision new identities directly, invoking the AWS Cognito SignUp API while cycling through its pool of user agents.

Password Spraying

We also tracked a massive password spray campaign across many of the observed targets. The activity was IDP-agnostic, hitting both Entra and Okta, and displayed several unique, AI-driven characteristics.

The attacks targeted hundreds of users and were executed in highly coordinated bursts. Each burst featured:

Dedicated user agents: A unique user-agent string was assigned to each burst, distinct from those used in previous waves.

Precise timing: The median gap between authentication attempts was strictly one second.

Sustained execution: Individual bursts lasted anywhere from 20 to 60 minutes.

Role-based targeting: The agent primarily focused on accounts belonging to software engineers.

Repeated attempts: Some individual users were subjected to more than a dozen login attempts.

Relentless by Design

The activity was persistent and highly automated. Some sessions lasted 24–30 hours, and when IPs were blocked, new addresses appeared within minutes.

In one session, the agent cycled through a dozen variations of the same SSO endpoint (/sso, /sso/, /sso/login, /sso/jwt, /jwt/sso…), each with and without the same forged token, at a rate of about one request per second. When a login page started rate-limiting the activity, the agent simply switched to a different endpoint on the same host and carried on.

We observed more than 15 different user-agent strings across the victims:

Python-based clients and curl;

Truncated Chrome strings and headless browsers with seemingly random version numbers.

More distinctive, self-describing identifiers, such as ReconProbe/1.0.

This variety, combined with the consistent attack patterns and ARTEX-related indicators, helped us connect the activity across multiple organizations.

Although most of these attempts failed, the true threat lies in the methodology. While a human attacker is bound by time constraints and fatigue, an autonomous agent does not give up. It simply continues to iterate until it finds a single weak point.

A clearly agentic attack

None of the individual techniques observed are novel. However, together the agent behind this attack is illuminated. There are a few clear signals:

Steps were chained automatically: when sign-up was open, it registered with a disposable mailbox, confirmed the account, and immediately requested another company's data.

Each automated step used the output of the last one: internal API routes are called by name minutes after pulling the source maps

Adaptation was automatic: when a login page started rate-limiting, the agent moved to a different endpoint on the same host. When an IP was blocked, a new one appeared within minutes.

Not all attacks were logical: a human attacker of this skill level is unlikely to spend their time testing generic payloads on the heavily scrutinized Microsoft OAuth flows.

Staying Ahead of AI-Powered Attacks

As AI makes reconnaissance and exploitation attempts faster and easier to scale, defenders need to shorten the gap between exposure and remediation. Learn more about how to prepare with Wiz's AI Threat Readiness Framework.

In addition, Wiz's AI Red Agent continuously and autonomously conducts offensive tests, helping reduce exposure at the speed of AI - evening the scales.

Wiz customers can refer to our Threat Intel Center Alert: ARTEX: Agentic AI Campaign Enables Cloud and Supply Chain Compromise

Existing detection rules can also effectively identify this activity, for example:

Numerous Failed Login Attempts To Multiple Users Followed By A Successful Login To Admin User

Potential Password Spray Attack From Single IP

Okta Users Password Spray

The relentless behavior also creates predictable patterns that can also be detected by rules such as "Unusual Mass Access Denied Activity."

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Iranian Hacking Group Found Hosting C2 Infrastructure in the US
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
An Iranian nation-state cyber threat group has been discovered using command-and-control (C2) servers based in the US to support its malware delivery and cyber-espionage campaigns.

The activity was identified by cybersecurity researchers at Semperis, who published their findings on October 22. The Iranian group is known as ‘Prince of Persia’, which has been active for around two decades.

Prince of Persia targets public and private sector organisations across the US, Europe and the Middle East, as well as dissidents and others opposed to the Iranian regime.

The multiple forms of malware used in Prince of Persia campaigns provide attackers with intrusive data exfiltration capabilities. This includes the ability to steal sensitive documents, as well as secretly taking screenshots and capturing audio recorded by the infected device.

Forms of malware identified as part of the latest Prince of Persia campaign include Foudre, a first stage malware loader and Tonnerre, a second stage malware which provides the attackers with what researchers describe as full surveillance capabilities.

The campaigns also involve a more recently identified malware known as Tornado, which builds on the codebase of previous malware. Tornado has the ability to use both HTTPS and the Telegram API as a covert C2 channel, blending in with legitimate network traffic to bypass firewalls and evade detection.

Advanced Anti-Detection Capabilities

Prince of Persia has been known to secretly hide its activity on European hosting services and virtual private servers, but anti-detection capabilities of the malware initially made it difficult for researchers to identify how the latest campaign was being hosted.

According to Tomer Bar, AVP of security research at Semperis, Prince of Persia seemed to go dark in February this year, coinciding with US and Israeli strikes against Iran.

“This isn’t unusual given that geopolitical conflict involving Iran leads to downtime with the threat group,” said Bar.

However, information in the Tornado malware resulted in researchers being able to identify where the campaign was being hosted and it was found to be a US hosting company.

While it isn’t unusual for threat groups to hide their activity within US hosting providers, it is the first time an Iranian threat group has been identified as hosting their activity on US servers in at least 12 years.

“This is the last place we expected to find Prince of Persia hiding,” Bar added.

While Prince of Persia activity is highly targeted rather than widespread, the group has been a persistent cyber threat to organizations for almost two decades. To help ensure protection from attacks by the group, Semperis has recommended the following actions:

Ensure that your security controls are up to date

Monitor for any unusual Telegram traffic.

Ensure that your operating systems are fully updated

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: M365 Token Spray and Replay Campaign Compromises Business Email Accounts
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Microsoft independently flagged the same infrastructure: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raised verified threat actor IP detections against 193
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Anton Ovrutsky for his contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Between July 14, 2026 and September 22, 2026, Huntress detected 497 Microsoft 365 sign-in events across 79 victim organizations related to a token replay campaign using an IP address block from the German hosting provider 1337 Services GmbH. Rather than guessing passwords, the attacker replayed sign-in tokens stolen from victims, and we've traced more than 200,000 failed login attempts from the campaign window back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range.

Figure 1: Overall statistics of the activity Huntress observed

Figure 2: Successful sign-in events using token replays over the course of the campaign

Also known as AS210558, 1337 Services GmbH is incorporated in Hamburg, Germany. While 1337 Services GmbH offers a legitimate IP hosting service, attackers use these kinds of ISP providers to host malicious traffic, a tactic referred to as "bring your own IP" (BYOIP). A February 2025 Krebs on Security article suggests that 1337 Services GmbH's founder may have operated the Cracked cybercrime forum.

The Microsoft accounts were compromised without the attacker ever needing a password. In an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attack, the victim signs in through a relay that sits between them and Microsoft. The relay passes the real login page and MFA prompt through to the victim, then keeps the "proof of login" token Microsoft issues once the victim finishes signing in. Because that token is minted after MFA, whoever holds it doesn't need to pass MFA again. The threat actor then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services. Because the attacker replayed many stolen tokens at volume across many organizations, we refer to this as "token spraying:" the same pattern as password spraying, but with stolen tokens instead of guessed passwords.

In this campaign, tokens came from multiple sources: AiTM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process.

Huntress first detected this activity on July 14, 2026, when a sign-in from 193.26.115[.]221 came from an Entra-joined device named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters. Microsoft independently flagged the same infrastructure: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raised verified threat actor IP detections against 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21 in multiple customer tenants. Microsoft describes this detection as "sign-in activity that is consistent with known IP addresses associated with nation state actors or cyber crime groups, based on Microsoft Security Intelligence (MSTIC)."

A July 21 detection from 193.26.115[.]199 gave us a view of how the attacker was able to steal and reuse a token in less than an hour:

Time (UTC)

Event

17:18:20

An AiTM relay at 185.238.2[.]195 caught the victim at the MFA prompt

17:30:21

The session was hijacked from 193.26.115[.]199

17:43:15

The same session was in use from a second 1337 Services address, 124.198.132[.]33

18:08:50

A new authenticator app, labeled "iPhone 13", was activated on the account

Registering their own authenticator app is a persistence method. A stolen session token eventually expires or gets revoked, but an MFA method stays on the account. With their own authenticator registered, the attacker can complete MFA for new sign-ins whenever they want, and that access survives a password reset unless someone audits the account's MFA methods and removes the rogue one. In 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were wiped and a new method registered within three hours of the first sign-in from a campaign address.

Rogue devices served the same purpose. Across the compromises we investigated, the threat actor registered at least 48 fake computers in victim organizations' Microsoft directories. A registered device can give the attacker a more durable way to request tokens than the stolen session alone, and it stays in the directory until someone deletes it.

We also observed the threat actor setting up hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. In at least one case, the threat actor used the email account to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact. None of the email rules were created from the 1337 Services GmbH network; each one came from a different rented or VPN address.

Technical Details

Over the 10-week campaign, the threat actor replayed stolen Microsoft 365 sessions using rented hosts in one block of IP addresses, 193.26.115[.]0/24. They used six addresses in the /24 range, one after another:

Figure 3: IP addresses used throughout the token spraying campaign

We can't state with certainty why the operator rotated addresses, but the effect is clear. A block, alert, or Conditional Access rule written for one address does nothing against the next, and Microsoft flagged addresses individually: its incidents named 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21, not the range. Several switches followed a quiet period, about two weeks between Phases 1 and 2 and a week before the September 22 takeover. Blocking any single address would have stopped one phase at most. Blocking the /24 would have covered all six main replay hosts, though the operator also used a few other 1337 Services addresses outside it.

Two tiers: relays capture, 1337 replays

The operator split the attack across two kinds of infrastructure. First, the victim signs in through an AiTM relay. The relay passes the victim's MFA prompt through and keeps the resulting session. Then, within minutes, the stolen session reappears from a 1337 Services address. On July 21, the gap between the victim reaching the MFA prompt and the hijacked session appearing was 12 minutes. On September 22, it was four.

Because the two halves sit on different providers, blocking the 1337 range doesn't stop credentials from being captured, and blocking a relay doesn't stop replay of tokens that were already stolen.

Two builds

The replay hosts ran two distinct toolsets, which we refer to as Build A and Build B:

Attribute

Build A: Scripted token replay

Build B: Browser session replay

Hosts

193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]16, 193.26.115[.]21, 193.26.115[.]72

193.26.115[.]199, 193.26.115[.]210

User agent

node (bare Mozilla/5.0 on 193.26.115[.]21)

Current Chrome/Edge on Windows

Request type

OAuth2:Token

Login:reprocess, OAuth2:Authorize

Client app

Microsoft Office, Microsoft Authentication Broker

OfficeHome

Target

Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Device Registration Service

OfficeHome, Exchange Online

Device

Rogue Entra-joined device named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters

None

Across Build A sign-ins, we observed 48 distinct Entra-joined devices named DESKTOP- plus exactly eight uppercase hexadecimal characters (for example, DESKTOP-54521F46). That doesn't match Windows' own out-of-box default, which is DESKTOP- plus seven alphanumeric characters.

With these shifts in the IP addresses came variations in tradecraft. We tracked four distinct phases throughout the campaign.

Figure 4: Token replay campaign timeline

Phase 1: The July Wave (193.26.115[.]221 and 193.26.115[.]199)

Huntress began observing stolen tokens being used to access more than a dozen organizations starting on July 14, 2026. In 13 of the 14 incidents Huntress responded to on that day, the attacker had registered a fake Windows-style computer in the victim organization's directory, named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters. These sign-ins all used Build A: the node user agent, replaying tokens through the Microsoft Office client. After registering the rogue device from the 1337 Services GmbH address, the attacker would often pivot to an ExpressVPN or CrownCloud address for further activity. Alongside it, 193.26.115[.]199 ran Build B, replaying browser sessions straight from AiTM relays, as in the July 21 timeline above.

The attacker created malicious email rules in a number of the compromised accounts to delete or move messages with certain keywords to an obscure folder, like RSS Feeds. In one compromised mailbox, an email rule named sss was created to mark all incoming mail as read and then delete it. The attacker then used the mailbox to send outbound spam to hundreds of external recipients before Microsoft Entra ID Protection rated the account high risk, and Huntress disabled the rule.

We last detected activity from the 193.26.115[.]221 IP address on August 3. By then, the attacker had successfully signed in to 37 organizations and registered 37 rogue Entra devices.

Phase 2: The August–September Wave (193.26.115[.]16 and 193.26.115[.]21)

After a two-week gap, the threat actor came back using two new IP addresses on August 17. This burst saw more email-hiding rules, and in one case the threat actor registered a lookalike of a business partner's web address.

This wave also added device-code phishing. We recorded sign-ins through the Microsoft Office device-code flow from 193.26.115[.]16, where the victim is tricked into entering a code on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in page and directly hands and attacker a valid refresh and access token, unknowingly authorizing the attacker's session. The same address also signed in to the Device Registration Service, the endpoint used to join new devices to the tenant. 193.26.115[.]21 replayed tokens against SharePoint Online with a bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent.

In this second wave, we started observing the attacker clearing compromised users' MFA settings to allow for first-time device registration with no device tokens or one-time passwords. The pattern was consistent: the victim's MFA methods were wiped through Microsoft's security-info registration service, and a new authenticator was registered minutes later. In one incident, we observed the threat actor using a deviceless authenticator method that was already on the account.

Phase 3: The September 11 Burst (193.26.115[.]72)

On the afternoon of September 11, the threat actor switched to a new address again, this time running an automated program (user agent node) that reused stolen sign-in passes. Within two hours, Huntress sent incident reports to 22 customers. Every sign-in we recorded from this address used the Microsoft Office or Authentication Broker client and OAuth2:Token requests (the action of trading one token for another), most of them targeting Microsoft Graph. Over four days, the address completed 303 successful sign-ins across 29 organizations.

Conditional Access did real work here. The same address logged 1,052 blocked sign-ins as the attempts continued, but all of those blocks came from just four organizations. In the 29 organizations where it got in, nothing stood in the way.

In one incident, the threat actor used the compromised mailbox to send a payroll-related email to an external CPA's email address. The attacker first modified an inbox rule named s to catch any message mentioning payroll, direct deposit, bank, or bonus. Five minutes later, from the same Interserver address (167.148.41[.]96), they created a second rule named d that marked all email from the CPA's address as read and moved it to the Conversation History folder, effectively hiding the responses from the victim.

Phase 4: Relay and replay, September 2–22 (193.26.115[.]210)

The final address paired an AiTM relay at a different hosting provider, Evoxt Sdn. Bhd. (2400:8d60:2::1:841d:5dd), with replay from 193.26.115[.]210. It first appeared on September 2. On September 3, the attacker tried to replay, from 193.26.115[.]210, the session stolen the day before, but the session was no longer valid and the attempt failed with Microsoft's SsoArtifactRevoked error (AADSTS50133).

After a full week of quiet following the Phase 3 burst, we detected one final session takeover on September 22. The victim reached the MFA prompt through the Evoxt relay at 20:46 UTC and completed it a minute later, from a macOS browser using the OfficeHome client. At 20:50, the attacker replayed the session from 193.26.115[.]210. Routing through a Remote Desktop Protocol VDI tunnel operator, the session's OS changed from macOS to Windows, and the threat actor accessed the victim's email.

Post-compromise: Hidden inbox rules

Every suspicious inbox rule we found on accounts compromised in this campaign was created from VPN or rented hosting, never from 1337 Services: ExpressVPN, NordVPN, CrownCloud, DataWagon, GLOBALTELEHOST, LeaseWeb, Dynu, and Interserver. The rule names were deliberately forgettable:

In four mailboxes, rules were created through the Outlook REST API rather than Outlook itself, two of them within minutes of the first sign-in from a campaign address.

The stolen session stopped working

The operator kept coming back. In one organization, they tried to reuse the same stolen session three more times in August: once from 193.26.115[.]199 and twice from other 1337 Services addresses (45.83.31[.]44 and 192.159.99[.]172). Every attempt failed with Microsoft's SsoArtifactRevoked error (AADSTS50133), which Microsoft returns when a session is no longer valid after a password expires or is changed. Although the refresh token and session cookie are expired, the access token will remain valid unless the identity sessions have been revoked or disabled.

Mitigation Guidance: Conditional Access FTW

As we saw in the massive LSHIY password-spraying campaign we reported on earlier this year, Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented. Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally.

Do not trigger response based on spray volume, as it points at the most-sprayed, least-compromised tenants; prioritize by credential validity instead. Phase 3 shows why: All 1,052 of 193.26.115[.]72's blocked sign-ins came from four organizations, and its 232 successful sign-ins landed in 28 different organizations, with no overlap between the two groups. Ranking tenants by failed attempts would have pointed responders at the four where Conditional Access was already working.

If you suspect a token replay compromise:

Revoke sessions and reset the password. A password reset alone does not remove attacker-registered devices or MFA methods. Additionally, you must revoke sessions; a password reset alone does not invalidate the access token, which means the attacker could keep access until the token expires (Time to live of approximately 90 minutes)

Audit Entra devices. Investigate devices named DESKTOP-, Device-, or Work Pc plus eight hex characters, especially ones registered from hosting IP addresses. The pattern is rare, but not unique to this campaign, so confirm before deleting.

Audit MFA methods. Look for MFA methods cleared and then re-registered within minutes, and remove any authenticator the user doesn't recognize.

Review inbox rules. Look for rules with one to three-character or punctuation-only names, rules that move mail to RSS Feeds, RSS Subscriptions, or Conversation History, and rules keyed on payroll or banking terms.

Treat Conditional Access blocks (AADSTS53003) as a sign of a valid credential, not a save. The block happens after authentication succeeds.

Restrict device-code flow with Conditional Access authentication-flow policies. If you need it, create service accounts with restricted permissions and exclusions as necessary.

Hunt for OAuth2:Token and Cmsi:Cmsi sign-ins from hosting infrastructure that use the Microsoft Office or Authentication Broker client with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent. Expect some legitimate automation; focus on sign-ins that touch user mailboxes or the Device Registration Service.

Hunt for new enterprise applications. Attackers will attempt to maintain persistence by granting new applications access to a tenant, with the level of access varying based on the application's permissions. Better yet, disable the ability for standard users to consent to new applications and instead require users to request new applications.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Attackers Forge Trust Targeting the Foundations of Identity Trust
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The big theme: Attackers are targeting the foundations of identity trust Recent Delinea Labs outlooks have tracked attackers exploiting stolen credentials, third-party...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
What you will learn

Find out how forged tokens and exposed signing keys let cyber criminals create trusted identities, why trusted apps and AI agents became entry points, and the four priorities for protecting identity trust in October.

Delinea Labs October 2026 Threat Outlook

In this monthly series, Delinea Labs breaks down the identity-related incidents that had the greatest operational impact over the previous month: how attacks unfolded, what failed in real environments and what those failures signal for the month ahead.

In September, a critical vulnerability in Casdoor exposed a weakness at the core of identity security

An organization administrator could retrieve a private signing key and use it to forge authentication tokens for any user, including global administrators. Rather than stealing an administrator's credentials, an attacker could manufacture an identity the system already trusted.

It was one of several September disclosures pointing to the same problem: weaknesses in the mechanisms that establish and enforce identity trust.

Here's Delinea Labs' outlook for October.

The big theme: Attackers are targeting the foundations of identity trust

Recent Delinea Labs outlooks have tracked attackers exploiting stolen credentials, third-party applications and increasingly autonomous AI agents. September added a new layer: Attackers targeting the systems that decide which identities to trust.

Several vulnerabilities traced back to hard-coded authentication secrets, exposed signing keys, certificate authorities and gaps in authentication or authorization. Any of them could let an attacker forge legitimate-looking tokens, impersonate trusted services or gain privileges beyond their intended scope.

A stolen credential gives an attacker access to an existing identity. A compromised signing key lets them create new ones. Rotating a user's password does little if an attacker can generate another valid authentication token.

As organizations rely more on federated identity, APIs, machine identities and AI agents, the infrastructure that establishes trust needs the same protection as the identities themselves.

What we're seeing at Delinea Labs

Trusted applications became entry points.

Two September incidents showed attackers exploiting access organizations had already granted. At Brevo, a SAML single sign-on (SSO) scoping weakness allowed an attacker to access 138 customer accounts, export contacts from 43 of them, and use 6 of them to send phishing campaigns. Days later, a separate attacker used a long-lived Cloudflare API key stored in source code to deploy malicious code through Brevo-hosted infrastructure.

At BigCommerce, attackers compromised API credentials for third-party Ribon applications, using them to reach merchant environments, steal customer information and inject malicious scripts. BigCommerce said its own platform was not breached.

Access that had been granted to a trusted application turned into a way in

The risk goes up when credentials never expire or permissions cover more than the job requires. Identity verification data is now a tool for attackers.

Identity-verification provider IDScan.net confirmed an unauthorized third party accessed or copied customer information from its cloud platform. The disclosure followed reports that about 153 million driver's-license scans were up for sale. IDScan.net hasn’t confirmed that figure.

Government-issued identification documents are more than sensitive personal information. They’re evidence used to establish identity. Once they’re exposed, attackers can use them for impersonation, social engineering and attempts to get past identity verification.

AI agents keep reaching systems they were never meant to trust. On September 18, Google confirmed Gemini models unintentionally accessed systems belonging to three real companies during cybersecurity evaluations run by Irregular in May. The models were supposed to target fictional organizations. Instead, they had internet access nobody expected, and they used it to discover or guess credentials and authenticate to real systems.

Anthropic identified a fourth incident, in addition to the three covered in last month’s outlook. In January 2026, an early Claude Opus 4.6 model gained unauthorized access to a real third-party system. Anthropic also documented threat actors using AI in intrusion workflows involving credential theft, authentication artifacts and token replay.

AI agents are getting better at finding and using existing access paths on their own. Securing them means controlling not just what they're instructed to do, but which credentials, tools and permissions they can use.

There's a vulnerability here: September recorded 14,841 common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs), including 1,799 identity-related vulnerabilities and 146 affecting identity products, up from 84 in August.

Several disclosures showed how weaknesses in authentication infrastructure can undermine trusted access.

Microsoft Entra ID (CVE-2026-62916 and CVE-2026-83941). Two critical privilege-escalation vulnerabilities affected authentication and authorization controls. One could allow an unauthorized remote attacker to elevate privileges without any existing access; the other could allow an already authorized attacker to gain more. Both are reminders that authentication was only the first check, and what an identity can do afterward still has to be enforced.

Casdoor (CVE-2026-90942 and CVE-2026-91998). One vulnerability exposed an instance-wide signing key that could be used to forge JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) for other users, including global administrators. Another allowed an attacker to use application credentials to manage users across organizations, including creating administrator accounts. Together, they showed how limited access could be transformed into broader authority.

JWT signing-key vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-89026, CVE-2026-85391 and CVE-2026-75431). Vulnerabilities in Issabel, Peppermint and PowerJob came down to hard-coded or predictable signing secrets. Attackers could use them to forge authentication tokens, create unauthorized sessions, and in some cases, achieve remote code execution.

Machine identity forgery (CVE-2026-78234). A vulnerability in hawtio-operator could let users with namespace edit permissions to obtain certificates containing attacker-controlled identity information and use them to impersonate trusted services.

The common thread is clear. Compromising the mechanisms that establish identity can do more damage than compromising a single account.

Ransomware activity

Qilin and TheGentleMen tied for the largest share of September's ransomware activity at 10.66% each, followed by KryBit at 4.96%.

KryBit, a ransomware-as-a-service operation that emerged in March 2026, has expanded across Windows, Linux, VMware ESXi and network-attached storage environments. KryBit reportedly uses phishing and compromised credentials for initial access, which fits the familiar pattern that stolen identities and privileged accounts remain reliable paths from initial compromise to ransomware deployment.

What to prioritize in October

Protect the systems that establish identity trust. Treat JWT signing keys, certificate-authority keys and other signing material as Tier-0 identity assets. Eliminate hard-coded secrets, restrict access and set up reliable rotation and revocation.

Strengthen authorization boundaries. September's Brevo and Entra ID findings showed that authenticating an identity is only the first step. Review federation scoping, cross-organization permissions and privilege-escalation paths, and enforce authorization on the action itself.

Reduce standing privilege for machine and third-party identities. Inventory API keys, service accounts and application integrations. Remove unnecessary permissions and replace long-lived credentials with short-lived, task-scoped access wherever possible.

Enforce AI agent access at runtime. Limit the credentials, tools and network destinations available to agents, and verify their authority when they attempt consequential actions. Model-level restrictions alone can’t contain an agent with access to trusted systems.

A stolen password gives an attacker one identity; a stolen signing key lets them create as many as they want

The Delinea Platform helps organizations discover identities, analyze privilege risk and enforce access control at the moment of action. By extending Privileged Access Management (PAM) from the point of access to the moment of action, organizations can control what AI agents, humans and machines can do, and for how long.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A Chinese nation-state actor was responsible for the compromise of Microsoft365 tenants used by ConnectWise, which led to IT management software provider taking a number of its cloud services offline.

Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries, beginning in September 2026.

The China-aligned group was able to obtain privileged access to a number of organizations’ cloud infrastructure, including ConnectWise, often in less than three hours from initial targeting.

The campaign targeted industries such as aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

Storm-0940 has been active since 2021 and its primary objective is data theft. It uses password spraying and exploitation of internet-facing applications for initial access, and establishes persistence in cloud environments by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications.

Attackers Target ConnectWise Customers

After gaining unauthorized access to the ConnectWise multi-tenant application, the China-aligned actor targeted the IT services firm’s downstream customers using the ARTEX platform to accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse.

The group attempted to sign-in to more than 2250 tenants at 2900 sign-in attempts per minute. Microsoft said the pace of this supply chain attack gives defenders little time to detect and respond.

Microsoft revealed that it had identified multiple customer environments with evidence of follow-on activity, including reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups and privileged roles.

“After acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant,” the tech giant explained in a blog dated October 21.

In an update published on October 21, ConnectWise acknowledged Microsoft’s findings and the extensive use of AI to compromise its Microsoft365 tenants.

“Nation-state actors are increasingly targeting the software supply chain, because one trusted connection can open the door to many organizations. AI now lets them test those connections at what Microsoft calls 'machine speed'. MSPs are in the middle of that chain. They are targets in their own right, and they are also a path into every client they serve,” the company wrote.

ConnectWise Cloud Services Remains Offline

ConnectWise first identified suspicious activity in its network on October 15, before discovering unauthorized access to application identities within its Cloud Backup environment on October 17.

The discovery resulted in several ConnectWise cloud services including Cloud Backup (previously known as SkyKick), SaaS Security and Cloud Management being taken offline while the company investigates the incident.

These services remain offline, according to the company’s status page.

However, ConnectWise said in an advisory on October 22 that it had started a phased restoration of its Cloud Backup service.

“We expect restoration to take several days and will share service-specific availability and reconnection instructions as confirmed. Keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to your service,” it told customers.

The firm added that existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no indication of compromise, while there is no evidence that other ConnectWise products and services are impacted by the incident.

Customers have also been advised to review individual Microsoft 365 tenants for unauthorized changes or persistent access.

The ARTEX Agentic AI Platform Threat

ARTEX is a multi-agent large-language model (LLM) that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows, including penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.

The agents then accumulate the discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph during the penetration test, Microsoft explained.

While the platform’s user interface and generated output default to English, the framework can be switched to Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, or Japanese.

In October 2026, CrowdStrike reported that a China-based threat actor used ARTEX to discover vulnerabilities and compromise specific services in South Korean financial organizations, a campaign that resulted in the exfiltration of data.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: MythicRatatoskr: An Yggdrasil-enabled backdoor deployed in a UAC-0099-Sandworm collaboration
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: In the past, Gamaredon collaborated with a threat actor that we discovered and named InvisiMole
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Executive summary

This report analyzes activity during which UAC‑0099 gained initial access on July 16th, 2025 and handed it off to Sandworm, which then conducted a data-wiping attack on September 17th, 2025. It particularly focuses on the MythicRatatoskr backdoor, which is unique in its use of the Yggdrasil mesh network to communicate with a C&C server hosted within it.

We presented our findings about MythicRatatoskr at LABScon on September 18th, 2026, and at the Virus Bulletin conference on October 16th, 2026.

Key points of this blogpost:

On July 16th, 2025, UAC-0099 gained initial access to a grain logistics company in Ukraine via a spearphishing email with a malicious attachment, leading to the execution chain of the MATCHWOK backdoor.

One day later, the attackers deployed MythicRatatoskr, a previously undocumented backdoor that communicates with a C&C server hosted inside the Yggdrasil mesh network. We have not seen the backdoor used anywhere else, and we found indications that a Linux variant may also exist.

Yggdrasil is a decentralized mesh network that implements an experimental routing scheme in which the IPv6 communication between the nodes is end-to-end protected.

Ultimately, UAC-0099 handed off access to Sandworm, which then carried out a data-wiping attack.

Cooperation among Russia-aligned actors

The handover documented in this report is not an isolated phenomenon. As noted above, Sandworm is attributed to GRU Unit 74455, and UAC-0099’s targeting leads us to assess that it is aligned with Russian interests.

Earlier in 2025, we uncovered that Russia-aligned Gamaredon collaborated with Turla, another Russia-aligned threat actor; we documented our findings in our blogpost Gamaredon X Turla collab. Both groups are linked to the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation (FSB). This kind of cooperation underscores the potential for coordinated cyberespionage campaigns among Russia-aligned groups, likely intended to amplify their operational impact. In the past, Gamaredon collaborated with a threat actor that we discovered and named InvisiMole. Against that backdrop, a UAC‑0099-to-Sandworm handoff is unusual in the specific actors involved, but no longer surprising as a pattern.

Overview of the intrusion

According to ESET telemetry, the events unfolded as follows: at 06:59 on July 16th, 2025, a scheduled task named pdfopentask was executed on one machine in the target organization. It executed a PowerShell payload from %temp%\temporarydoc.txt.

A minute later, MATCHBOIL was deployed. MATCHBOIL is a downloader that deployed, in this case, the MATCHWOK backdoor (C&C: https://uztickets[.]com) from https://egyptanimals[.]com/animals/photoalbum. The following day, at 09:28, a new binary was delivered to the machine: the MythicRatatoskr backdoor. Due to the close proximity of time, we believe with high confidence that the MATCHWOK execution chain led to the deployment of MythicRatatoskr. Our telemetry further shows that additional MythicRatatoskr samples were subsequently deployed to other machines within the organization, this time using an OpenSSH SFTP server.

Later, ESET telemetry detected a SOCKS5 server on some of the machines, with one sample having been extracted from an unknown archive using WinRAR. We believe that the SOCKS5 server was deployed using MythicRatatoskr.

Approximately two months later, on September 17th, 2025, we detected data-wiping activity at the compromised grain logistics company. The data-wiping attack was executed by deploying the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy – standard Sandworm tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that we have observed numerous times in ESET telemetry.

Therefore, we assess that UAC‑0099 can act as an initial access group for Sandworm.

This blogpost focuses primarily on the analysis of the MythicRatatoskr backdoor, the Yggdrasil network that hosts its C&C server, and the accompanying SOCKS5 server. The first versions of MATCHBOIL and MATCHWOK have already been analyzed by CERT‑UA in its advisory, with MATCHBOIL and its evolution further covered in our blogpost MATCHBOIL: New tricks, same old evil intentions. These tools are therefore omitted here.

A squirrel in the world tree

The word Yggdrasil originates in Norse mythology, where it refers to a sacred tree connecting the various realms of the cosmos. Within that tree lives a squirrel named Ratatoskr that carries messages between its top and its roots. Given the backdoor’s role as a messenger scurrying through the Yggdrasil network, we decided to name the backdoor MythicRatatoskr.

More technically, Yggdrasil is a decentralized mesh network that connects devices directly to each other without a central hub, building an encrypted IPv6 overlay on top of the internet so that participating nodes can exchange end-to-end-protected traffic. Legitimate users adopt such meshes for resilient connectivity, research, and hobby networking. Because no single server runs the mesh, the network is robust and hard to disrupt – properties that also make it attractive to adversaries. Importantly, Yggdrasil is not designed to provide anonymity.

Attribution

The post-compromise execution chain relied on known malware already attributed to UAC‑0099 – namely the MATCHBOIL downloader and the MATCHWOK backdoor – which leads us to attribute this stage of the attack to UAC‑0099 with high confidence. We attribute the data-wiping activity observed two months later to Sandworm, also with high confidence, based on the TTPs involved.

Moreover, we assess with high confidence that UAC‑0099 handed off access to Sandworm at some point during the intrusion, although we have not yet been able to determine whether the MythicRatatoskr backdoor was operated primarily by UAC‑0099 or by Sandworm.

UAC‑0099 profile

UAC‑0099 is a cyberespionage group targeting governmental organizations, financial institutions, and media, all in Ukraine. Based on the targeting, we believe with medium confidence that the group is aligned with Russian interests. UAC‑0099 can act as an initial access broker for Sandworm, a Russia-aligned group best known for its destructive attacks in Ukraine.

The group has been active since at least 2022 and was first reported by CERT‑UA in June 2023. Apart from MATCHBOIL, the group also typically deploys LONEPAGE, a PowerShell downloader named after the presence of the word page in its C&C URLs.

Sandworm profile

Sandworm is a Russia-aligned threat group that performs destructive attacks. It is mostly known for attacks against Ukrainian energy companies in December 2015 and December 2016, which resulted in power outages. In June 2017 Sandworm launched the NotPetya data-wiping attack that used a supply-chain vector by compromising the Ukrainian accounting software M.E.Doc. In February 2018, Sandworm launched the Olympic Destroyer data-wiping attack against organizers of the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang.

The Sandworm group uses such advanced malware as Industroyer, which is able to communicate with equipment at energy companies via industrial control protocols. In April 2022, CERT‑UA thwarted an attack against an energy company in Ukraine where the Sandworm group tried to deploy a new variant of this malware, Industroyer2.

Since February 2022, Sandworm has been very active in Ukraine, by deploying data wipers against strategic organizations.

In October 2020, the US Department of Justice published an indictment against six Russian computer hackers that it alleges prepared and conducted various Sandworm attacks. As we already mentioned, the group is commonly attributed to GRU’s Unit 74455.

Compromise chain

Initial access and execution

According to ESET telemetry, initial access was gained via a spearphishing email with a malicious attachment – a finding that matches CERT‑UA blogpost. We assess that the MATCHWOK backdoor execution chain (already documented in the CERT‑UA blogpost) then led to the execution of MythicRatatoskr, a backdoor that communicates with its C&C server over the Yggdrasil network. Subsequently, the attackers probably used MythicRatatoskr to deliver a SOCKS5 server.

Persistence

MATCHBOIL persists MATCHWOK by adding the registry value UpdateMonitor to the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\, with data pointing to the dropped MATCHWOK path.

MythicRatatoskr is started as a Windows service with the name ieupdate.

Collection and exfiltration

During check-in, MythicRatatoskr sends information about the current user, hostname, and local network settings to the C&C server. In addition, the operators can use MythicRatatoskr to exfiltrate files and screenshots to the C&C server by using HTTPS routed through the Yggdrasil mesh network. The data is not staged prior to exfiltration.

Toolset

MythicRatatoskr

MythicRatatoskr is a backdoor written in Go that uses the Yggdrasil network (described in the Network protocol section) to reach its C&C server. As noted earlier, we named the backdoor after Ratatoskr, the squirrel from Norse mythology that scurries through Yggdrasil – the sacred tree connecting the realms of the cosmos – carrying messages between its top and its roots. We felt this was a fitting parallel for a backdoor that ferries data across the Yggdrasil network. There are signs in the binaries suggesting that the development started sometime between December 2024 and February 2025.

Function names left in the binaries – following a mix of mixed caps (CheckInAgent) and snake case (agent_run) – suggest either code merged from another project or inconsistent naming by the authors. Key functions handle service registration and Yggdrasil network initialization (main, runService), check-in and beaconing (agent_run, init_agent, CheckInAgent), configuration handling (saveConfig, Encrypt, Decrypt), command polling and dispatch (getTasks, doTask), and the backdoor commands themselves (upload, download, screencat, shell, manageProxy, etc.).

Some samples also include a 10-minute startup delay, likely to avoid immediately connecting to the Yggdrasil network on execution, helping to evade detection.

Host-based artifacts

Table 1 presents MythicRatatoskr host-based artifacts that we observed during our analysis. Note the filename collision for krbtman.exe: it is MythicRatatoskr on some machines, and the SOCKS5 server on others.

Table 1. Host-based artifacts associated with MythicRatatoskr
