Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: 5 cybersecurity assumptions AI attacks break
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: But it’s usually framed as an arms race of capability, where whoever gets AI working first wins
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
“Will frontier AI be what finally tips the scale toward attackers?”

I hear some version of that question from almost every security and identity team I talk to. After the past year, it’s a fair question. But it’s usually framed as an arms race of capability, where whoever gets AI working first wins.

That framing misses what’s actually changing. Security operations weren’t built against a specific attacker. They were built on assumptions about how human attackers work: how fast they move, what they cost, how they learn, when they quit, and what they leave behind.

AI agents break most of those assumptions. One holds, and it’s where defenders get their advantage back.

How we tested how AI attackers work

To get past speculation, a group of us across research, incident response, and product at Silverfort built an AI attack simulator. We kept it model- and tool-agnostic and ran it in a contained lab. A lab is cleaner than most production networks, so treat what follows as patterns, not benchmarks.

Assumption #1: Attacks are sequential

Human intrusions are paced by sequence and reasoning. An operator gets credentials, stops, decides what to do next, then does it: recon, then access, then escalation, then exfiltration. Most detection and response models are built around that pacing.

Agents don’t take turns. Our simulator typically ran five to 10 agents in parallel, each working a different phase toward the same objective. Once initial credentials were in hand, the phases stopped waiting on each other. One agent harvested more credentials while another moved laterally and a third escalated privilege, each acting on what the others had already found. The full chain to domain takeover completed in four to five minutes, faster than most teams can triage a single alert.

The order (or lack of order) that cyberattacks unfold in human- versus AI-led scenarios

Agents move at machine speed, limited mainly by how fast they can take in and act on information. That outpaces any human-driven response, and often automated response too, when automation depends on shipping telemetry to a central platform and processing it before it can act.

The parallelism matters just as much. Detection logic and analyst intuition are tuned to recognize a kill chain unfolding in order. When phases overlap and feed each other instead of following in sequence, the early stage defenders are trained to catch may never show up on its own.

Assumption #2: Attacks scale with headcount

The usual read on AI economics is that attacks just got cheaper, and they did. Our simulator completed a full run for the equivalent of $12, which fell to about $4 over time. A failed run that kept iterating cost $25.

But cost isn’t the shift that matters. The real constraint on attackers has rarely been exploits or tooling. It’s the skilled labor between initial access and action on objectives.

Consider a ransomware crew with candidate access to a thousand organizations and enough skilled operators to properly work ten. The other 990 aren’t failed attacks. They’re unworked inventory. Initial access can already be generated far faster than humans can turn it into compromises.

That’s the bottleneck agents remove. Booz Allen Hamilton noted in When Cyberattacks Happen at AI Speed (March 2026) that parallel activity that once required several specialists can now be done by one person. Agents don’t need to outperform a skilled operator, and they don’t even need to be cheap.

They only need to make the next unworked foothold worth pursuing.

Assumption #3: Attackers rely on what they remember

In human operations, context is hard-earned. It lives in an operator’s head, their notes, and conversations with other actors, and it moves at the speed of people. Case management, personal knowledge management, and other tools have all improved information accessibility, but its consumption and regurgitation has always been bound by human limitations.

Our agent built a plan and spawned sub-agents. Each one wrote what it found, including assets, identities, and valid credentials, into a shared memory that every other agent could read and plan against. When a human operator finds something that changes the plan, they stop and reason through it. Agents re-plan in real time from a single source of context.

Human operators leave value on the table: a credential in a deployment script, an over-permissioned group noted and never revisited, a share that looked unimportant at 2 a.m. In a human operation, findings compete for one person’s attention. In an agent operation, every finding is immediately available to every agent that can use it. The attack surface stops being what one operator noticed and becomes the sum of everything any agent found.

Assumption #4: Attackers get tired, frustrated, or scared

Defenders have quietly relied on human friction for decades. “Burden the adversary” has been a mantra for good reason. A blocked operator gets frustrated, makes mistakes, worries about getting caught, and often moves on to an easier target.

An agent doesn’t. It is a truly persistent threat. In our simulator, a blocked task didn’t end in a give-up. It ended in another attempt, and another, with no natural limit on how many. Only when enough tasks failed did the agent step back and reconsider the plan itself. A closed door meant trying the handle again, then looking for a different door. It stopped only when it ran out of paths, never out of patience. The $25 failed run wasn’t waste. It was the agent refusing to quit.

This will change the shape of cybercrime. Much of it has been opportunistic, because tenacity was expensive and reserved for high-value targets. When tenacity costs almost nothing, less sophisticated adversaries can run sustained, targeted campaigns against a specific organization.

Assumption #5: Attackers use tools defenders can recognize

Detection has long worked in layers. Some detections key on specific attack tools. Better ones key on techniques, the behavior an attack produces regardless of the tool behind it. Beneath both sit broad behavioral analytics that fire constantly. Confidence usually comes from correlating across those layers, and that takes context and time.

Agents don’t need novel malware to stress that model. Attackers have already been moving toward trusted tooling: signed admin utilities, commercial remote access, and whatever is native to the environment. Agents accelerate that shift. They’re fluent in PowerShell, WMI, LDAP queries, and built-in utilities, and they compose them on the fly for each environment rather than carrying a known kit. Tool-specific detections lose their grip, and what’s left looks a lot like administration.

That leaves defenders leaning on their lowest-fidelity layer at the moment they need certainty most, while many parallel trails flood it with noise. Teams that can’t tell which signals matter contain broadly, and broad containment becomes its own business disruption. The attacker causes damage through the defender’s response.

What the agent can’t compose its way around is authentication. Whatever tooling it uses, it still has to present a credential. It’s no coincidence that the technique detections that hold up best, like anomalous Kerberos ticket requests or directory replication from a host that isn’t a domain controller, are anchored in authentication and directory behavior. Scoping by identity, meaning which accounts authenticated where and which of those authentications were legitimate, collapses the complexity of dozens of trails into the few identities actually driving them.

What doesn’t change because of AI attacks: agents still run on access

Attack agents were built on how human attackers operate, so the overlap is as revealing as the differences.

The first overlap is identity. Like a human, an agent moves through an environment using legitimate credentials. Once it holds a valid identity, its activity looks like normal authentication, and a compromised account behaving a little oddly rarely trips EDR or network controls.

Part of the reason is how security operations treat identity. In most SOCs, identity is an artifact: a field in a log, an attribute that enriches an alert, something to pivot on after the fact. It’s rarely treated as what it is in an intrusion, both the vehicle the attacker rides and the control point where the ride can be stopped. Agents exploit that gap at machine speed.

The second overlap is the path of least resistance. Across our runs, the agent went after non-human identities first and showed a clear preference for service accounts. Service accounts often far outnumber human identities. They’re usually over-permissioned and rarely have a single point of control.

The accounts organizations monitor least are the ones agents target most.

None of this is new. Abuse of privileged and trusted identities played a central role in intrusions like SolarWinds. What’s new is that an agent can turn everything frontier models know about attacks like that into something close to instinct, applied in minutes. The identities hardest to manage are often the ones the business depends on most. Against an attacker that goes after them first, they can no longer be neglected.

Those identities are also where the agent was stopped. When we reran the same attack with two controls enforced at authentication, a service account restricted to the systems it legitimately needed and MFA required on a domain admin across all protocols, the outcome flipped from domain compromise to “could not reach objective.” The agents re-planned around each block, but every new route still ran through an identity they couldn’t use. What mattered was where the controls sat: at the access decision, the one point the agents couldn’t route around.

Access isn’t a matter of skill. It either exists to be abused or it doesn’t.

Identity Security controls are one piece of the puzzle in defending against AI attacks

Almost every intrusion has an identity component, and lateral movement and privilege escalation have to pass through authentication. That’s where the agent is most constrained and the defender has the most leverage.

But Identity Security controls aren’t a complete answer, and it’s worth being precise about where they stop. If an agent abuses access an identity already legitimately holds, no single access decision may look wrong. Data moving through permitted paths, or an exploit against an exposed service that needs no credentials, sits outside the access decision entirely. Those still need detection, data controls, and patching.

3 questions for security leaders in the AI attack era

So does AI tip the scale? Only where access is left undefended. The shift is from treating identity as an artifact to treating it as a control. Answering AI attackers with faster detection runs into the math. A team that can’t triage at the speed of the attack won’t close the gap by triaging slightly faster. The more useful question is what your decisive first line of defense will be. Three questions help answer it:

Which non-human identities can authenticate to your most critical assets, and does anyone own them?

Which of those access decisions can you deny or challenge in real time, rather than detect after the fact?

If a service account were compromised mid-incident, how long would it take to restrict it without breaking production?

If the answers are “we don’t know,” “few,” and “hours,” that’s the gap an agent will find first.

You won’t out-triage an AI agent. You can deny the access it depends on, at the moment it tries.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: European Retail Firms Confirm Cyber Incidents
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Several retail firms across Europe have confirmed cyber incidents that are causing operational disruptions.

On October 12, Netherlands-based multinational retail company Ahold Delhaize confirmed it was experiencing “a security issue” within its networks and had to take “some systems offline” to protect them.

The disruption was reported to affect three of the group’s brands, including supermarket chain Albert Heijn, operating in the Netherlands and Belgium, Dutch drugstore chain Etos and Dutch liquor store chain Gall & Gall.

The next day, Reuters reported that South African retail group The Foschini Group (TFG), owner of high-street fashion brands Hobbs and Whistles, was investigating a “cyber incident.”

The press agency said TFG became aware of an incident on October 11 affecting its UK subsidiary TFG London, with “certain IT systems” impacted.

Specifically, it was reported that the affected brands include Phase Eight and Hobbs and Whistles brands.

The South African group added there is “no reason to believe that payment information is at risk” at this stage. Other TFG high street brands, including Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected. The group’s TFG Africa and TFG Australia subsidiaries are also not experiencing any operational disruption.

TFG said it had reported the incident to the relevant UK authorities.

Commenting on this TFG incident, Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, noted, “The fact that Inside Story and White Stuff within the same group were unaffected, and that TFG’s wider Africa and Australia operations were untouched, suggests some degree of system separation was in place. That separation, which limited the blast radius, is worth noting as a positive.”

Additionally, according to The Times, H&M is also examining information circulating online about a potential incident.

However, at the time of writing, the retailer said it had found no indication that its data environment had been compromised.

There is currently no indication that these incidents are in any way related to each other.

ASOS Confirms Scope of Cyber-Attack

The incidents come days after customers of UK fashion retailer ASOS received a strange push notification indicating the company was hacked.

While the firm confirmed the unauthorized intrusion into “third-party platforms” it uses to communicate with customers and that personal information including names and contact details and some non-personal account related information “have been accessed,” it reiterated, in its latest customer update, published on October 13, that no payment-card information or account passwords were impacted.

The latest alerts also come as many supermarket chains in France are still dealing with a large-scale cyber-attack where attackers tampered with refrigeration controlling systems in the night between October 11 and 12, leading to the loss of a large amount of food products and financial losses estimated in hundreds of thousands of euros.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Weekly Update 525: AI Data Breach Hyperbole
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: I was watching it on the long-haul flight home the other day, and what I found particularly engrossing was the polar-opposite opinions from a bunch of people: "it's gonna kill...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
I remember the name of that AI doco now - The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist. I was watching it on the long-haul flight home the other day, and what I found particularly engrossing was the polar-opposite opinions from a bunch of people: "it's gonna kill us all" versus "it's gonna make us all rich", and so on. But to some extent, I can understand the gap between opinions when we're all just speculating about the future. I have much less understanding for why people infatuate with hyping AI as a data breach monster when the evidence to date is quite the opposite. In fact, I've enjoyed sharing example after example of recent breaches perpetrated by kids with a telephone (vishing), while pointing out I haven't seen a single one orchestrated by AI.

Speaking of AI, a big thanks to this week's sponsor who's doing gtreat things in the agent observability space, Origin. The machines may not be dumping data that lands in HIBP (yet), but they do go off-script and Origin will help trace back precisely what happened when it all goes wrong.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: GTA 6 leaker threatens to release full playable version of game ahead of official launch
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: The website of "CyberLeek" published the threat shortly after releasing around 25 minutes of fresh footage of the blockbuster game due to be released in November by Rockstar Games
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
The hacker behind a high-profile string of leaks involving the upcoming release of the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6 videogame has threatened to release a complete, playable build.

The website of "CyberLeek" published the threat shortly after releasing around 25 minutes of fresh footage of the blockbuster game due to be released in November by Rockstar Games.

Eurogamer, which has seen the footage, says it appears to be legitimate, and confirmed that it carries the emblem of CyberLeek.

According to CyberLeek, the full playable build of GTA 6 will be released when its own cryptocurrency coin reaches a market cap of US $30 million. In an attempt to give its claims more credence, CyberLeek says that any doubters can request specific scenes to confirm it has access to the entire game.

CyberLeek says that if the GTA 6 game is released on physical disk, and a public apology is made, it will step back from its threats.

Campaign groups like Stop Killing Games which fights games to remain playable after publishers end support, have reportedly distanced themselves from CyberLeek's actions, and in August posted on Reddit that gamers should not encourage CyberLeek:

"Do not send these people your money, no matter how much sympathy you may feel for their actions. This is illegal, and frankly, we feel for everyone at Rockstar having to go through this ordeal again, especially just over a week before Rockstar’s own official “Extended Look” premieres."

Take-Two, Rockstar’s parent company, appears to be hell bent on identifying whoever is behind the leaks, and has attempted to subpoena Microsoft and Discord in order to gather information about their possible identity.

Anyone who works in the field of cybersecurity is too familiar with the refrain of "pay up or we release it." What is unusual in this case is that the hacker in not demanding a direct ransom payment, but is instead asking their audience to pump up the value of a crypto token. The hacker's hope is that the pent-up desire of enough Grand Theft Auto fans will boost how much the crypto coins are worth.

But, of course, there is no guarantee that the hackers will release a full, playable version of the game - even if their cryptocurrency coin does reach US $30 million.

As ever, videogame fans should be very wary of believing anybody who offers a download of a supposedly leaked game. Especially when a game is as hyped-up as GTA 6, there is a real risk that unsuspecting fans will be duped into making bad decisions that could put their computer security at risk.

Besides which, the real, genuine GTA 6 is due to be released on video game platforms on 19 November. It is not worth infecting your computer, or losing money on a dodgy crypto coin, just to see it a few weeks early.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: RSVP to Disaster: How One Click Installs a RAT
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Choosing to RSVP through the attached URLs leads users to a fake event page containing malware that grants threat actors remote access to systems
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
By: Willmar Cheng, Cofense Phishing Defense Center

Imagine receiving a digital invite from a friend or relative. The message looks legitimate; the timing feels believable, and curiosity naturally takes over. This sense of curiosity and trust is exactly what cybercriminals are exploiting. The Cofense Phishing Defense Center (PDC) has recently intercepted a malicious email disguised by an online event invitation. Choosing to RSVP through the attached URLs leads users to a fake event page containing malware that grants threat actors remote access to systems.

This attack is notable because the email looks harmless, and these emails are more common as the holiday season begins. The campaign demonstrates how attackers can turn everyday social events into convincing malware lures.

Figure 1: Email Body

Phishing emails such as this sample are effective at targeting a larger scope of users as the vague wording can be applied to a variety of situations. The generic subject line, event title, and lack of organizers or details is not just an oversight – it is the strategy. Vague messages create curiosity; curiosity overrides caution, and one click later you're downloading malware or handing over your credentials.

Breaking it down piece by piece, the manipulation gets even clearer. The subject line, "You are cordially invited," and "Join Us for a Special Gathering, Let Us Celebrate a Milestone," is engineered to feel personal without saying anything too specific. It uses the language of weddings and galas to trigger a curious reaction from the user, but the invite names no one, and no specific details are present. That's not sloppy writing; it's scaled: a generic line can be blasted to thousands of inboxes while still feeling individually addressed.

Then comes the button, "Click Here to Download the Invite," where the email capitalizes on all that setup. The threat actor utilizes a forced download in this case to hide the destination of the malicious file that the user unknowingly downloads once the button is clicked.

Figure 2: CAPTCHA Verification

After clicking the download button, users are redirected to a CAPTCHA verification page. CAPTCHAs, as seen in Figure 2, are often used by threat actors to create a false sense of security for the user, making the page feel more legitimate. That illusion falls apart on closer inspection, though: the CAPTCHA is hosted on a generic, unbranded domain that's less than a month old, a strong instant indicator that the CAPTCHA and the generic URL together form a two-step confirmation that this "invite" was never legitimate to begin with.

Figure 3: Malware Download Page

After passing the CAPTCHA, the user lands on a second fake invitation page shown in Figure 3. Once again, the design is deliberately generic: there's no date, venue, time, or any of the specific details a real invitation would naturally include. The only detail that screams to the victim is to click the "eInvite" button.

Figure 4: Malware Extracted

Clicking the “eInvite” button begins the download of a zipped folder labeled “ViewDePartyyinvites”. Inside is an executable named ScreenConnect.exe, This is a legitimate ConnectWise Screen Connect installer that is being abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan,

The RAT, remote access trojan that abuses trusted remote-support software to avoid antivirus detection. Once executed, the malware grants the threat actor full remote access to the user’s device, effectively handing over control without the user realizing what they've installed.

Figure 5: Malware Executed

Finally, once the executable runs, a small icon quietly appears in the taskbar, easy to miss if you're not looking for it. Clicking it reveals a chat box along with a connection status, showing the RAT actively linking up with the host machine as seen in Figure 5. This is the moment the compromise becomes fully operational. The attacker now has a live channel into the device, and from the user’s side the only visible trace is a small, unassuming icon that gives no indication of what's happening behind it.

Campaigns like this are unique because they do not use sophisticated techniques but rather use the user's own curiosity to successfully accomplish the attack. From the vague subject, email content, webpage, all push the user to click a button. This campaign illustrates the importance of training employees to spot and report these unique attacks. Cofense is uniquely positioned to spot these attacks and also catch these types of attacks that have turned up in environments protected by SEGs. With Cofense Managed Phishing and Defense, provided through our Phishing Defense Center (PDC), enterprises benefit from our complete view of real phishing and malware threats.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: TrendAI™ Research Reinforces Japan's Urgent Cybersecurity Warning as Incidents Surge in 2026
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: " TrendAI™ Forward-Looking Threat Research data shows Japan recorded more publicly disclosed cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of 2026 than in all of 2025
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Japan-headquartered cybersecurity leader shares threat intelligence and practical guidance as AI accelerates the global threat landscape.

DALLAS, Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TrendAI™, the global AI security leader and enterprise business unit of Trend Micro Incorporated (TYO: 4704; TSE: 4704), today issued a threat advisory for organizations in Japan after Masaaki Taira, who chairs the Liberal Democratic Party's National Cybersecurity Strategy Headquarters, said that "cyberspace is in a state of emergency." TrendAI™ Forward-Looking Threat Research data shows Japan recorded more publicly disclosed cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of 2026 than in all of 2025. September alone saw 86 incidents, up about 18% from August and 37% from July.

The party's headquarters met on Oct. 9 in response to a series of cyberattacks on Japanese businesses and called on the government to strengthen public-private cooperation. Breaches at retailers, financial services firms, a car-sharing service and a rail operator have exposed data of millions of customers. The government's National Cybersecurity Office has sent guidance to ministries, local governments and private companies on keeping security protection up to date, using strong passwords and tightening security across supply chains.

The TrendAI™ Incident Response team has also seen a rise in incidents in Japan. In recent engagements, attackers exploited known vulnerabilities in public-facing applications to plant web shells on web servers, giving them a foothold from which they may attempt privilege escalation, lateral movement or access to connected databases. Japanese-language analysis of these cases from TrendAI™, along with hardening guidance, is available here.

"Cyberattacks are increasing globally, and so are the breaches and data leaks as a result. While AI might not be directly involved, its ability to help the attackers find targets and automate their operations makes cyberattacks scalable. Organizations need to shrink their cyber exposure and close the vulnerabilities in order to lower the odds of being victimized," said Ryan Flores, Co-lead, Forward-Looking Threat Research, TrendAI™.

AI is lowering the cost of attacks. TrendAI™ has not established a connection between the recent incidents in Japan and the use of AI by attackers. However, AI does let attackers accelerate reconnaissance, analyze vulnerabilities and produce convincing phishing in languages they do not speak. This weakens protections that languages, such as Japanese, once offered against foreign attackers. Automation also makes smaller organizations, including suppliers, more attractive targets given the increased return on investment for cybercriminals.

"While organizations around the world learn to work with their AI budgets, it's important to remember that AI has zero cost for cybercriminals," said Robert McArdle, Director, Forward-Looking Threat Research, TrendAI™. "There's already a robust economy for stolen accounts, APIs, and tokens, and this is driving the increasingly automated and agentic cybercrime campaigns we see today. The current surge in Japan should not be interpreted as a peak in criminal activity, it should be seen as the new baseline of attacks that will only increase in volume, speed, and relentlessness."

To harden protections, TrendAI™ recommends:

Patch internet-facing systems first. Keep an accurate inventory of public web servers, applications and cloud services, apply security updates promptly, prioritize vulnerabilities known to be actively exploited, and use virtual patching to cover the gap while fixes are tested and deployed.

Harden web servers. Restrict write access to application code, isolate file-upload directories, prevent uploaded content from running as scripts, and monitor for unauthorized changes to application files and configurations.

Watch database access. Monitor sensitive database operations and abnormal access patterns; run applications with minimum-privilege database accounts.

Check suppliers. Ask hosting and cloud providers how they would notify you of an incident, review which third parties hold customer data, and confirm critical services can recover independently of a single provider.

Strengthen identity verification. Review processes that rely solely on uploaded photographs of identity documents and adopt chip-based or other stronger verification consistent with regulatory guidance.

Bring AI usage into scope. Identify AI applications, models, and agents used across the organization, assess their provenance and reputation, review their access to sensitive data and internal systems, and apply appropriate security controls and approval processes.

TrendAI™ threat researchers and incident responders are tracking the activity behind the current wave of incidents in Japan and will publish further findings as the analysis continues. Organizations that want to discuss their exposure can contact their TrendAI™ account team.

In addition, the TrendAI Vision One™ platform is purpose-built to help organizations address their expanding AI security risks due to shadow AI, sensitive data submitted to external services, or AI agents connected to internal systems with excessive permissions. Vision One operates on a unified model of visibility, observability, actionability, and governance, spanning endpoints, cloud, identity, data, and AI, giving security practitioners the tools to anticipate and stop threats across their attack surface before they impact the business. To help organizations further identify and reduce AI risk, TrendAI is introducing new capabilities to its Vision One AI security suite in December 2026, including AI Gateway and AI Risk Insights solutions with digital asset reputation scoring. With the addition of these new controls in Vision One, organizations can holistically achieve:

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
In September 2026, Insikt Group® identified 94 high-impact vulnerabilities to prioritize for remediation, 59 of which had a Very Critical Recorded Future Risk Score. This represents a 29% increase from last month. 43 of these vulnerabilities were surfaced through the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, 37 were reported in open sources and validated by Insikt Group, and 14 were exclusively surfaced through honeypot data.

The 94 vulnerabilities identified affected products from 58 vendors, with Linux and Microsoft together accounting for approximately 13% of the vulnerabilities. The remaining exposures spanned network edge and security management appliances; operating systems (OS) and mobile devices; collaboration, content management, and enterprise platforms; artificial intelligence (AI), developer, and automation tools; and operational technology and industrial systems.

September reporting also highlighted zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (NetScaler), as well as renewed exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 (PeopleSoft) against unpatched systems.

Key trends: September 2026

September reporting linked NightEagle and UNC3569 to GhostContainer and GRAYRABBIT deployments, while Cisco FMC exploitation by three threat clusters led to credential theft, Cyclops Blink deployment, and Qilin ransomware.

A suspected Chinese-speaking actor used a SecFlow-based environment with Claude-, Qwen-, and DeepSeek-backed workers, and a suspected Russian-speaking actor used hundreds of AI agents to compromise at least 440 PaperCut NG/MF instances associated with 395 organizations.

47 of the 94 vulnerabilities enabled remote code execution (RCE). Network-edge and security-management products were the most affected product type. Apache and Google represented the largest share of vendors, with three RCE vulnerabilities each.

Insikt Group identified public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits or scanners for 75 of the 94 vulnerabilities identified in September.

The most common weakness class was CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for Critical Function), with seven vulnerabilities, followed by CWE-22 (Path Traversal), with six. CWE-78 (OS Command Injection), CWE-89 (SQL Injection), and CWE-94 (Code Injection) each affected five vulnerabilities.

Eight of the 94 vulnerabilities were at least five years old, and the oldest was approximately 12 years old.

Trend analysis

AI-assisted campaigns combine older flaws with post-compromise tooling

Insikt Group detailed a suspected Chinese-speaking actor using a SecFlow-based operations environment with Claude-, Qwen-, and DeepSeek-backed workers to support reconnaissance, exploitation, post-exploitation, and collection across Asian targets. The threat actor tested or staged workflows for CVE-2014-6271, CVE-2020-1938, CVE-2022-22965, CVE-2016-4437, CVE-2021-43798, CVE-2024-4956, CVE-2021-29441, and CVE-2021-44228. The workflow routed candidate findings to vulnerability-specific playbooks, but not every attempt produced confirmed access.

A separate September report described a suspected Russian-speaking threat actor using hundreds of AI agents in a campaign targeting PaperCut NG/MF. The campaign exploited CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, compromising at least 440 instances associated with 395 organizations.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: Malware Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) | Recorded Future
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: An IoC can provide the first concrete lead, while TTPs can help analysts search for related activity after an attacker changes a domain or recompiles malware
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
One malware hash can turn a vague alert into a concrete investigation. Analysts can search endpoints for the exact file, trace where it appeared, and determine whether related activity exists elsewhere. But if the attacker changes the file, the hash changes too. Domains and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses can also lose relevance as attackers rotate infrastructure.

This is why malware indicators of compromise work best as evidence within a larger investigation, not as isolated entries on a blocklist. Their value grows when analysts can establish where an indicator came from, how recently it was observed, what threats are connected to it, and whether those connections matter to their organization.

Malware indicators of compromise are technical artifacts or observations that suggest malicious activity. They help security teams detect, investigate, and contain threats, but an IoC is most useful when analysts can assess its source, timing, confidence, and relationship to other threat activity.

Key takeaways

Malware indicators can include file-based artifacts, network infrastructure, and other technical evidence associated with malicious activity.

IoCs do not exclusively describe past attacks. They can point to malicious activity that may be underway or has already occurred.

Indicator types have different defensive lifespans. An IP address may quickly lose relevance, while a file hash remains an exact identifier for the same sample even if attackers create a new version.

Threat intelligence can add context that helps analysts prioritize IoCs, connect related activity, and move from an isolated match toward a wider investigation.

What are malware indicators of compromise?

An indicator of compromise (IoC) is a technical artifact or observable that suggests malicious activity. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines IoCs broadly enough to include signs that an attack may be imminent, underway, or that a compromise may already have occurred.

For a security operations center (SOC) analyst or incident responder, an IoC can help answer a practical question: Have we seen evidence associated with this threat in our environment?

Analysts can use malware IoCs to validate an alert, search logs and endpoints for related activity, or scope an incident after malicious activity is confirmed. They can also use an indicator as a starting point for investigating connected infrastructure, malware, or attacker behavior.

An IoC does not automatically prove that an organization has been compromised. Context matters. Finding a malware hash executing on an endpoint carries a different meaning from finding the same hash in an intelligence feed.

IoCs and TTPs serve different purposes

Indicators of compromise identify observable evidence associated with malicious activity. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) describe how an adversary operates.

A specific command-and-control domain is an IoC. The techniques an attacker repeatedly uses to establish persistence or move through a network are TTPs.

Atomic indicators are often easier to match against security telemetry, but attackers may be able to change them quickly. TTP-based detection can be harder to evade when it focuses on established attacker behavior, but it can also demand richer telemetry and more detection engineering.

Security teams do not need to choose one or the other. An IoC can provide the first concrete lead, while TTPs can help analysts search for related activity after an attacker changes a domain or recompiles malware.

The most common types of malware indicators

Malware indicators generally appear either in files and host activity or in network communications. Each gives analysts a different view of what the malware has done.

File-based IoCs

File hashes such as SHA-256 fingerprints allow security tools to identify an exact known file. They provide a precise match, but attackers can alter a malware sample and generate a new hash.

Other file and host artifacts can reveal how malware operates after reaching a system. Analysts may examine suspicious file names and paths along with changes malware makes to the operating system, such as registry activity or mutex creation.

These artifacts can help investigators determine whether the same malware has appeared elsewhere in the environment.

Network-based IoCs

Network indicators show where malware connects or where malicious content is hosted.

These may include IP addresses associated with command-and-control infrastructure, domains used to distribute malware, or URLs connected to malicious activity. Analysts can also examine characteristics of network traffic when those characteristics are specific enough to the threat.

Network IoCs can help teams find infected systems that contacted known malicious infrastructure. Their usefulness can change over time because infrastructure may be abandoned, reassigned, or shared with legitimate services.

Why raw IoCs have limits

The main problem with raw malware indicators is not that they are useless. It is that the indicator alone often does not tell an analyst enough to make a good decision.

Indicators can lose defensive value quickly

Threat actors can move command-and-control infrastructure, register new domains, or change malware files to avoid known indicators. This makes some IoCs highly time-sensitive.

It is more accurate to think in terms of defensive lifespan than to assume every IoC simply expires. A hash continues to identify the same file, for example, but it stops detecting new versions once an attacker changes the sample.

A malicious label does not provide organizational context

An IP address listed as malicious does not tell a SOC whether its own systems communicated with it, whether the activity is current, or what defensive action is appropriate.

This is where raw feeds can create unnecessary analyst work. Teams must investigate why an indicator was flagged and decide whether that evidence applies to their environment.

Recorded Future recommends combining external indicator context with internal network data and subjecting indicators to organizational vetting before using them for detection in its guidance on indicators of compromise.

More indicators can create more noise

Threat intelligence feeds can contain overlapping, stale, or irrelevant information. Adding feeds without a way to assess their quality can increase alert volume without giving analysts better evidence.

Volume can still matter when a source provides useful threat coverage. It should not serve as the only measure of intelligence quality. Timeliness, confidence, provenance, and relevance also affect whether an indicator deserves attention.

IoCs do not provide complete threat visibility

Threat intelligence can tell analysts a great deal about an indicator that has already been observed. It cannot provide context for infrastructure or malware that its collection sources have never seen.

Better information about known IoCs can improve interpretation, but it does not guarantee complete threat visibility.

How threat intelligence makes malware indicators more useful

Security teams can get more value from IoCs by connecting individual observations to evidence that explains why they matter.

Recorded Future malware intelligence connects malware samples with associated IoCs and threat context. It also supports automated YARA rule generation for malware hunting.

Add context before taking action

Useful context can show when an indicator was observed, what malware is associated with it, and what other infrastructure or activity is connected to it.

Recorded Future uses Risk Scores to help analysts prioritize indicators. These scores can help determine what deserves attention, but they should inform security decisions rather than replace organizational context.

Automate repetitive IoC work

Large indicator volumes make manual lookup difficult. Application programming interfaces (APIs) and security integrations can automate IoC lookup, add threat context, and bring external intelligence into existing security workflows.

Recorded Future Cyber Operations supports these workflows through threat intelligence, APIs, and integrations.

Automation does not need to mean automatic blocking. Teams can automate research and prioritization while applying stronger requirements before an indicator triggers a direct enforcement action.

Turn individual indicators into threat-hunting leads

An IoC often becomes more useful when it leads analysts to related activity.

A malware sample can point investigators toward related variants, behaviors, and infrastructure. Recorded Future malware intelligence includes Auto YARA, which analyzes malware samples for distinctive patterns and generates YARA rules that analysts can use in malware hunting.

This lets teams move beyond searching only for a known hash and look for related files that share useful characteristics. Recorded Future University's guide to malware hunting provides more detail on how threat hunters approach that work.

Best practices for an IoC-driven security program

A useful IoC program should focus on the quality of security decisions rather than the size of the indicator database.

Check context before enforcement. Establish the source, confidence, and timing of an indicator before deciding whether it should trigger blocking or containment.

Match automation to the consequence. Automating lookup and prioritization carries less operational risk than automatically blocking infrastructure. Raise the confidence requirement as the action becomes harder to reverse.

Connect external intelligence with internal evidence. External threat data can show why an indicator deserves attention. Internal telemetry shows whether that threat has reached systems that matter to your organization.

Review active indicator sets over time. An indicator that no longer belongs in an active detection or blocking rule may still have value for historical investigation. Removing it from active enforcement does not mean deleting the intelligence.

Recorded Future's research into malware and vulnerability trends provides further context on changing malware activity and the threats defenders need to watch.

The future of IoC detection

Attackers can change hashes, IP addresses, and domains to evade known indicators. Security teams, therefore, need ways to connect individual IoCs to related malware activity and attacker behavior.

Automated malware analysis and detection-rule generation can help teams move from a new observation to a broader hunt with less manual work. This does not make atomic indicators obsolete. It gives teams another way to use them alongside behavioral detections and threat context.

Recorded Future combines malware analysis with threat intelligence so security teams can investigate individual IoCs in the context of related malware, infrastructure, and behavior.

Ready to spend less time chasing stale or low-value indicators? Request a demo to see how Recorded Future can help your team add context to malware IoCs and put threat intelligence into existing security workflows.

FAQs about using malware IoCs in security operations

Are YARA rules the same as malware IoCs?

No. An IoC is an observable artifact or piece of evidence associated with malicious activity. A YARA rule is detection logic that searches files or other data for defined patterns. Analysts can create YARA rules from characteristics found during malware analysis, allowing them to search for related samples rather than relying on one exact file hash.

How are malware indicators of compromise collected and shared?

IoCs can come from malware analysis, incident investigations, security telemetry, threat research, and intelligence-sharing communities. Organizations can share structured threat information using standards such as Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX), while Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information (TAXII) supports the exchange of that information between systems.

Are indicators of attack the same as indicators of compromise?

No, although the distinction is not simply that one predicts an attack and the other describes the past. Indicators of attack (IoAs) focus on behaviors or activity associated with attacker intent or an attack in progress. IoCs identify technical evidence associated with malicious activity, which may relate to activity that is ongoing or has already occurred.

Can two intelligence sources assess the same IoC differently?

Yes. Intelligence sources may rely on different observations, collection methods, scoring systems, and timeframes. Infrastructure can also change ownership or use over time. Analysts should consider the source, supporting evidence, and observation dates rather than assuming every malicious classification carries the same meaning.

Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.title: GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection has added five new indicators to surface attack sequences
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.context: Amazon GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection correlates weak GuardDuty signals into a single, critical-severity attack sequence finding when their composition crosses a threshold...
Attacks, Breaches & Threat Intel.full_text:
Amazon GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection correlates weak GuardDuty signals into a single, critical-severity attack sequence finding when their composition crosses a threshold of credibility. On May 20, 2026, the service started attaching five new indicator types to those sequences: MALICIOUS_PACKAGE, MISCONFIGURATION, REACHABILITY, SENSITIVE_DATA, and VULNERABILITY. For more information, see Document history for Amazon GuardDuty and Attack sequence finding details.

These indicators come from Amazon Inspector, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Reachability Analyzer, Amazon Macie, and posture data surfaced through AWS Security Hub. You might already run these services for other reasons, and now Extended Threat Detection folds their signals into attack sequence findings. This post is an operational guide for teams already running the prerequisite services and discusses what the new indicators look like in a finding, what the post-launch data shows, and how to fold them into your incident-response workflow. These indicators help Extended Threat Detection prioritize the highest-priority signals in your account, which provides higher confidence findings on the workload surfaces as part of an active defense strategy monitoring runtime activity on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS).

New indicators overview

In GuardDuty, a signal is any event it evaluates when looking for suspicious activity. A weak signal is one that, on its own, doesn’t clearly point to a threat which the five new indicators fall into. A single Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) finding on a host, for instance, tells you a vulnerability exists not that an attacker is exploiting it. These findings earn their value when GuardDuty correlates them with the suspicious-activity signals it already tracks, as shown in the following table:

Indicator

Source

What it tells you

VULNERABILITY

Amazon Inspector

CVE list with Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity and Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) exploit-likelihood scores.

MALICIOUS_PACKAGE

Amazon Inspector

Amazon Inspector MAL-* package indicators. For more on how Amazon Inspector scores vulnerabilities, see Amazon Inspector Security Research.

REACHABILITY

Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer

Whether the host or cluster is reachable from the internet

MISCONFIGURATION

AWS Security Hub controls (posture management)

The resource has configuration that doesn’t align with AWS or industry best practices. For example, IMDSv1 still enabled, overly permissive admin policies, or publicly accessible Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets.

SENSITIVE_DATA

Amazon Macie

Potential sensitive data has been discovered in the resource.

The five values appear on the Indicators tab of the attack-sequence finding in the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and in the GetFindings JSON file.

Figure 1: Indicators section of an attack sequence finding

A note on EPSS, because the VULNERABILITY indicator carries it. According to the FIRST EPSS overview, the score is the probability that a published CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days ranging from 0 to 1. EPSS doesn’t replace CVSS, which describes the inherent severity of a vulnerability, whereas EPSS describes how likely it is to be exploited soon making it the more useful number for incident response.

Prerequisites

To populate the indicators, you need to have the following AWS services enabled:

Amazon Inspector on Amazon EC2 and Amazon EKS to support VULNERABILITY and MALICIOUS_PACKAGE.

AWS Security Hub powers MISCONFIGURATION based on AWS Foundational Security Best Practices.

Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer on production VPCs to support REACHABILITY.

GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring on Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EKS. Every signal it produces is a potential anchor.

Amazon Macie powers SENSITIVE_DATA.

Strengthening weak runtime signals

Runtime signals such as a process invocation, a pod exec, or a syscall pattern can be noisy sometimes. A single runtime signal that doesn’t match a known offensive-tool path isn’t significant on its own, and without resource-state context it typically stays below the threshold for a Critical attack sequence.

The new indicators supply that missing context. When Extended Threat Detection sees a weak runtime signal on a host that also carries a combination of high-priority unpatched CVEs, a known malicious package, an IMDS misconfiguration, and internet reachability, it promotes the collection to a single CRITICAL attack sequence with high confidence. Customer feedback on individual GuardDuty runtime findings has consistently identified noise as a major pain point and adding this resource-state context is what turns those weak signals into actionable alerts.

In practice, this surfaces as a substantial increase in net-new attack-sequence findings on the runtime-process surface to roughly one in four prioritized runtime-process attack sequences, with little change on the network-indicator of compromise (IOC) surface. Within the first week of launch, this pattern showed up across many customer accounts where attack sequences that would previously have surfaced as a collection of weaker, unconnected findings now surface as a single CRITICAL finding.

Example: A net-new attack sequence on Amazon EKS

Now that you understand how Extended Threat Detection has improved through additional indicators, let’s walk through an example of how these indicators add value. In this example we analyze an actual scenario that was observed on an Amazon EKS cluster. The observed activity occurred over an 8-day period with eleven different GuardDuty findings.

Figure 2: Activity summary for the EKS cluster before Extended Threat Detection correlated the signals

What GuardDuty saw on the activity surface over 8 days as shown in Figure 2 was 55 EKS_AUDIT_LOGS signals across pod execs, role assumptions, and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls and 18 finding-level signals all originating from one external IP address of 198.51.100.69. This IP address authenticated as four distinct AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identities to the same EKS cluster. Runtime activity on the worker nodes was generic because there was no process that matched a known offensive-tool path and no execution-profile flag was fired. Under the pre-launch correlation, this sequence would have needed the EKS_MALICIOUS_PROCESS rule to fire, which requires either a malicious exec path or an unusual-suspicious-tool profile. Neither was present in this activity, so no correlated attack-sequence finding was raised.

What the new GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection indicators added to the EKS example:

MALICIOUS_PACKAGE on the cluster: Amazon Inspector identifier MAL-2022-4933.

VULNERABILITY (full Amazon Inspector output) on the cluster: 42 CVEs total, 33 rated CRITICAL by CVSS.

On the cluster: 12 CVEs including CVE-2022-1471 (SnakeYAML deserialization, EPSS 0.94), CVE-2024-4577 (PHP-CGI argument injection, EPSS 0.97), CVE-2024-34351 (Next.js SSRF), CVE-2025-29927 (Next.js authentication bypass), CVE-2023-44487 (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset), and CVE-2022-37434 (zlib heap overflow, EPSS 0.92).

Across the five worker nodes: 379 CVEs total, with 68 of them marked CRITICAL by Amazon Inspector.

REACHABILITY: Cluster API endpoint internet-reachable and three of five worker nodes also internet-reachable.

MISCONFIGURATION (EC2 IMDS): All five worker nodes still expose IMDSv1.

When these additional indicators are taken into consideration, this surfaces as a single AttackSequence:EKS/CompromisedCluster with a CRITICAL severity, with all four populated indicators on the Indicators tab and a MITRE ATT&CK® mapping to Initial Access (External Remote Services), Discovery, and Persistence.

Figure 3: New vulnerability indicators within an attack sequence

The finding lists more than 100 Amazon EC2 CVEs at the worker-node level, one CRITICAL CVSS, plus a long HIGH tail, but most are LOW vulnerability priority because their EPSS scores are low. Rather than sifting through more than 100 findings to decide which to address first, GuardDuty highlights the high-priority ones so you can focus your response efforts where they have the most impact.

Example: Cryptomining and a vulnerable host

In this second example we walk through an EC2 instance group where GuardDuty already had a strong network-based finding for cryptomining and the new indicators provided additional remediation context that made incident response faster.

Figure 4: Cryptomining attack on EC2 instances

A set of EC2 instances was communicating with a known cryptomining destination, which was flagged by threat intelligence as mining/misc. The network IOC evidence was strong on its own.

Observations added by the new indicators: VULNERABILITY listed CVE-2007-4559 Python tarfile with EPSS around 0.9 on two of the three involved instances.

Result: The AttackSequence:EC2/CompromisedInstanceGroup finding is now actionable beyond block the destination IP; it tells you which patch will remediate the vulnerability the cryptominer likely came in through so you can address the underlying entry point rather than only removing the outbound connection.

This attack sequence would have been generated without the vulnerability context because GuardDuty had strong evidence of cryptomining of the EC2 instance group, however, triaging is faster with more context.

Indicators of compromise observed across the first-week launch sample

The following CVEs listed, along with their EPSS scores at the time, were observed on hosts across the customer accounts that received the new Extended Threat Detection indicators during the first week after launch at the moment each indicator finding was generated. EPSS scores are point-in-time, so a CVE’s listed priority on any future finding will reflect the current EPSS rather than the values shown here.

CVE-2024-4577 – PHP-CGI argument injection on Windows. EPSS 0.97+.

CVE-2022-1471 – SnakeYAML deserialization. EPSS 0.94. Critical CVSS.

CVE-2022-37434 – zlib heap buffer overflow. EPSS 0.92.

CVE-2007-4559 – Python tarfile path-traversal. EPSS still 0.9+ in 2026.

CVE-2025-29927 – Next.js authentication bypass. Frequent on Node web tiers.

CVE-2024-34351 – Next.js SSRF.

CVE-2023-44487 – HTTP/2 Rapid Reset.

Runtime monitoring surfaced weak signals tied to malware and tooling artifacts recovered from the compromised hosts:

HackTool family Linux/frp (Fast Reverse Proxy variants were used as command-and-control tunnels), often disguised as kuboard-agent and kuboard-agent-server binaries on Amazon EKS worker nodes. Container-snapshot path matches were also observed under /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.overlayfs/snapshots/.../usr/bin/. The frp binaries are present inside the container image and on the node, which means rebuilding the node from an unpatched AMI won’t be sufficient remediation.

Burp Collaborator out-of-band callback hostnames were found under *[.]oastify[.]com, matching pattern <35-char base32>[.]oastify[.]com. These co-occurred with frp on the same EKS sequence, probably a second tool or actor on shared infrastructure.

The Amazon Inspector malicious-package indicator MAL-2022-4933 was found in both Amazon EC2 and Amazon EKS contexts.

Identity and access patterns correlated with the tooling signals above:

A single external source IP authenticated as multiple distinct human IAM identities across separate Amazon EKS, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EC2 surfaces over a short window. This was the most common identity signature on the new Amazon EKS-process net-new class.

Responding to attack sequences with these indicators

The new indicators don’t change incident-response runbooks for attack sequences that have already occurred. They matter for new findings, which are concentrated on enhancing signals related to runtime monitoring. For those:

Treat the sequence with urgency. MALICIOUS_PACKAGE and a high-priority VULNERABILITY mean the host was, and still is, at risk of being compromised. Contain the exposures and remediate the vulnerabilities. Rotate every IAM credential, instance profile, or IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)-bound role that could have been exposed.

Patch on EPSS-weighted priority, not alone on raw CVSS. The finding’s high-priority VULNERABILITY list is already filtered to high-EPSS CVEs.

Isolate public resources indicated by REACHABILITY indicators. An internet-reachable host with exploitable vulnerabilities should be isolated for remediation.

For more support, see the remediation steps in Remediating detected GuardDuty security findings and GuardDuty Investigation, an AI-powered security analysis of your GuardDuty findings and accounts.

Conclusion

GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection can deliver more high-confidence attack sequence findings on the runtime workload surfaces where your security teams often need help most: Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EKS. It does this by combining GuardDuty activity signals with resource-state context from other AWS services. Customer feedback on individual GuardDuty runtime findings has consistently identified noise as a major pain point, and correlating those weak signals with vulnerability, package-risk, reachability, misconfiguration, and sensitive-data indicators is how Extended Threat Detection turns the noise into actionable CRITICAL findings. If you’ve already enabled AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer, Macie, and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring, the new indicators automatically start showing up on your attack-sequence findings. If you aren’t using these services, we encourage you to explore enabling them to access the new GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection indicators and the value that these individual services deliver.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or contact AWS Support.

Previously, he led performance and resiliency work on Amazon OpenSearch. Including 10x cluster-manager memory reductions and enabling 1K-node clusters. Outside work, Aman enjoys traveling, adventure activities, reading and playing board games.
