Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Russian Police Arrest 3 Suspected VasyGrek Hackers, Dismantle Criminal Infrastructure
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a threat group known as VasyGrek and dismantled its criminal infrastructure.

Also known as Fluffy Wolf, the threat actor has a history of targeting Russian and international companies since 2016.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation (MVD) said members of the group are "suspected of embezzling funds from the accounts of organizations, as well as creating, distributing, and using malicious software."

In one September 2025 case highlighted by the ministry, the attackers are said to have sent a phishing email to an unnamed organization, masquerading it as business correspondence and instructing recipients to open a reconciliation report that triggered the execution of malware.

The incident resulted in losses of 660,000 rubles ($8,000) from the organization's bank account, with the attackers transferring the funds to accounts under their control.

"The attacks utilized a vast network of phishing domains imitating financial and accounting service websites, as well as virtual servers located in foreign countries," MVD said. "Tools for covert remote administration were acquired from the dark web."

The rare law enforcement action saw Russian authorities conducting searches at the suspects' residences and the office premises they used to conduct the operations. It also led to the seizure of computer equipment, communication devices, and other items of evidentiary value.

According to reports from Russian cybersecurity company BI.ZONE and F6, VasyGrek is assessed to be a financially motivated threat actor that gains initial access by sending phishing emails with attachments disguised as financial documents.

Some of the key tools in its arsenal include off-the-shelf stealers and trojans, like MetaStealer, PureCrypter, PureLogs Stealer, WarZone RAT, XMRig, BurnsRAT, PureHVNC, PureRAT, Pay2Key, and PowerLoader, as well as legitimate remote access software such as Remote Utilities.

In a report published this week, Kaspersky said it recorded over 100 attempted attacks orchestrated by VasyGrek against organizations in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan between January and September 2026. These attacks have also been observed using decoy documents to drop a Golang backdoor capable of executing arbitrary commands on the infected device.

The attacks primarily singled out entities in the metallurgical sector, along with wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial supplies and government agencies. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture sectors.

"The group expanded its attack geography: while previously its primary target was Russian organizations, this year, potential victims also included companies from Belarus and Kazakhstan," Nikita Nazarov, head of advanced threat research at Kaspersky, said.

"The attackers used multi-stage infection schemes and legitimate online services to host malicious components, which helped conceal their activity and hinder attack analysis."

The development comes as BI.ZONE it detected multiple attacks targeting Russian organizations using malware families like LxBase RAT, CoreRAT, and NightStrike RAT.

While LxBase RAT, a commercial trojan that costs $119 per month, is distributed via mass phishing campaigns, CoreRAT infection chains make use of phishing emails containing 7zSFX and Rust droppers for delivery. The activity has been attributed to Core Werewolf, which is assessed to share some level of overlap with Vortex Werewolf.

Attacks deploying NightStrike RAT have been associated with a hacktivist-turned-cyber espionage cluster dubbed Insolent Werewolf. Initial access is achieved using ClickFix-style attacks to deploy NetSupport Manager to gain remote access.

"Insolent Werewolf also utilizes Octowave Loader to deploy AdaptixC2 and Havoc post‑exploitation framework implants in compromised systems," BI.ZONE said, adding the group's malware arsenal includes other remote access trojans like CapDoor and NightWire.

"A RAT written in C++, NightStrike has presumably been created by the developer of NightWire, based on similarities in coding style. Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection."

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Google: LLMjacking attacks rack up $1 million in cloud AI charges
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: The researchers have also observed threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-40217, a vulnerability in LiteLLM that allows running arbitrary code on the server by leveraging the custom-...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Large language model hijacking attacks, also known as LLMjacking, are generating large fraudulent cloud charges, with some organizations losing more than $100,000 per day.

Companies can record costs as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant in analyzed incidents.

Based on their observations, there are "two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure."

The researchers identified two categories of threat actors: those who scan for publicly exposed LLM endpoints and those who steal valid API keys from unprotected machines.

After gaining initial access, the attackers sell it to services known as LLM mixers, which provide their subscribers with unauthorized access to LLMs.

Once access is resold, request volumes can spike suddenly, sometimes exceeding 1,000 requests per second. The service provider records the requests as legitimate consumption and charges the victim organization for the tokens.

GTIG and Mandiant observed an increase in this type of activity this year, with fraudulent charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, and cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1,000,000.

LLM mixers offer access to AI resources at very low prices, using their proxy infrastructure to relay customers' prompts to hijacked services through stolen API keys.

The researchers found several examples of such relaying infrastructure, including Jet Night, which sells “unlimited access plans” for $60/month, and the newapi[.]pro service.

“Another threat actor that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours leveraged stolen third-party API keys to power the token routing service jet-night.com,” Google says.

“Jet Night passed nearly one million dollars in token costs to the victim organization.”

Google also identified the threat cluster UNC6993, which appears to use gateway tools to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests, and likely sells access via underground forums.

The attackers gain access via exposed or compromised cloud credentials, service account keys, GitHub tokens, active session tokens, and LLM API keys.

Attackers search the compromised environment for credentials, logs, databases, and secret managers, and try to create backdoor accounts or inject SSH keys to maintain persistent access.

The researchers have also observed threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-40217, a vulnerability in LiteLLM that allows running arbitrary code on the server by leveraging the custom-code guardrail testing endpoint.

In some cases, Google says that attackers used the victim's cloud infrastructure to host unauthorized proxy endpoints and agentic workloads.

"For example, one threat actor enabled agents, deployed publicly accessible reverse proxies, and used custom Node.js proxy bundles to expose endpoints compatible with multiple frontier LLMs rebranded under a persona known as D1337-KAIROS," the researchers say.

Google recommends several actions to protect against LLMjacking attacks, which start with prioritizing Identity and Access Management (IAM) and securing the supply chain.

Companies should use centralized secrets platforms to enable the rotation and management of sensitive keys and secrets. Users should not have extended privileges unless required by their role and tasks.

"Deny all permissions that are not explicitly required, including access to Cloud LLM services," Google recommends.

Enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), ensuring monitoring tools provide comprehensive visibility across the environment to identify unauthorized LLM and AI services (shadow AI), and setting API usage and spending limits can help organizations detect LLMjacking attacks early, limit their impact, or prevent them altogether.

Furthermore, cloud audit and inference logs should be enabled and monitored for unauthorized service activation, suspicious credential checks, unusual usage, and attempts to disable logging.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Smashing the botnet

Google worked with several other organizations to disrupt the x.cpe network, including Japan’s National Police Agency, Synthient, and Trend Micro. Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware. It also went after command-and-control servers operated by Videostrong that were connected to other malware campaigns. Google estimates Videostrong has been cut off from about 10 million compromised devices.

This action should make the affected devices safe to use, but probably not as safe as they should be. Play Protect is still disabled, and the inert malware modules are still installed. Since they are loaded as system apps, users cannot easily remove them.

Synthient has published a list of 182 device model names known to be included in the botnet. Anyone who has purchased a MECOOL or white label Android TV box of unknown origin should check it. Trend Micro counted a total of 1,472,554 infected devices, somewhat higher than Google’s estimate. The overwhelming majority were in Brazil, Malaysia, Iraq, Mexico, and Taiwan, but tens of thousands were also online in the US, Germany, the UK, Australia, and Canada.

Google determined the operation was not the work of a rogue actor, so it has ended its relationship with Videostrong. The company, as well as any subsidiaries, will not be permitted to use Google’s Android apps and services.

Google also notes that it is updating its certification process to close the loophole that allowed Videostrong to operate its botnet on certified devices. Android is open source, though, and there are countless uncertified Android-based TV boxes out there. Videostrong could continue to sell malicious hardware under other brands without Google apps. But it would still have to rebuild its malware operation from scratch.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: FedRAMP Authorization Is the Easy Part: How to Stay Authorized with Qualys Policy Audit
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Key Takeaways

FedRAMP authorization isn’t the finish line. Providers are expected to keep monitoring their security posture and give federal agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions.

CISA’s BOD 26-04, issued on June 10, 2026, moves federal vulnerability management toward risk-based prioritization instead of a single fixed deadline for every finding.

FedRAMP has said the legacy monthly scan is no longer sufficient. Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026.

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey, 85% of executives said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years.

Qualys Policy Audit supports a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate, and report workflow. Audit Fix automates remediation, and control mapping lets one validated control count across multiple frameworks.

Ask anyone who has taken a cloud service through the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) what the process feels like, and you’ll hear roughly the same story. Months of control documentation, a System Security Plan running hundreds of pages, a Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) assessment that turns up gaps nobody saw coming, and finally an Authority to Operate (ATO) letter. What that story usually leaves out is that the letter isn’t the finish line. It’s where the real work starts.

Once a Cloud Service Offering is authorized, FedRAMP expects the provider to continue monitoring its security posture and keep feeding federal agencies the information they need to make ongoing, risk-based decisions. On June 10, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) raised that bar again with Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, and FedRAMP moved fast to bring its own rules with it.

The takeaway is fairly simple. Getting authorized was never the hard part. Proving, day after day, that your controls are still doing what they’re supposed to do is the hard part, and it’s the problem policy audit automation exists to solve.

Getting FedRAMP authorized is step one. Learn how to stay authorized.

Watch on Demand

Why Point-in-Time Compliance Stopped Working

FedRAMP used to run on a predictable cadence. Assess, authorize, submit monthly scans, repeat. That model has been cracking for a while now, and three things are driving it.

Vulnerability doesn’t just mean a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry anymore. Misconfigurations and control drift are squarely in scope now, so a clean scan can still be hiding a compliance failure.

Environments move faster than assessment cycles do. Cloud-native infrastructure can drift a dozen times a week, while monitoring reports still tend to go out monthly or quarterly.

Regulators have stopped accepting “we’ll catch it at the next audit.” Federal risk management is moving away from calendar-based reviews and toward real-time, exposure-based decisions.

CISA BOD 26-04, in Plain Terms

BOD 26-04, issued by CISA in June 2026, moved federal vulnerability expectations toward continuous, risk-based validation instead of a single fixed deadline applied to every finding. FedRAMP responded within days, confirming that the legacy monthly scan most Rev5 Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) still lean on for their compliance evidence isn’t going to hold up anymore, and setting December 7, 2026, as the date its new Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules become mandatory for certification. For compliance and audit teams, the practical read is simple. The evidence you hand to an assessor has to reflect what’s true right now, not what was true at the last scan.

The Pain Points Teams Keep Naming

Talk to FedRAMP compliance teams, and the same challenges come up again and again:

Finding control gaps before an assessor does, instead of during the assessment window

Keeping configurations from drifting after they were compliant on day one

Prioritizing remediation when continuous assessment produces a continuous stream of findings

Providing continuous visibility instead of handing over a report generated the week before an audit

Producing audit-ready evidence on demand instead of assembling it after the fact

Cutting duplicate effort across overlapping frameworks, since most FedRAMP teams are also carrying National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC), Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and increasingly the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) on the same infrastructure

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey of 1,802 executives across 63 territories, 85% said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years, and nearly 90% said the breadth of their compliance responsibilities has expanded over that same period. That pressure adds cost and strains the teams that have to prove compliance. Misconfigurations make it worse: Qualys analysis of more than 1 billion misconfiguration findings shows access control failures account for 38% of exposures, and organizations take an average of 14 months to fix these basic gaps.

None of this is a documentation problem. It’s an automation problem that’s been wearing a documentation costume.

How Policy Audit Solves the Problem

This is where a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate report workflow stops being a slide in a deck and starts being how the work actually gets done.

On the assessment side, instead of a monthly scan, Qualys Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline, mapping each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result across every system in scope. That’s the difference between documenting a control on paper and being able to prove it’s still operating the way it was the day you got your ATO.

Qualys lays this out as five practical steps rather than a single feature:

Connect findings to the control context. Connect raw findings to the control and framework context instead of handing teams a pile of technical output to interpret on their own.

Prioritize what impacts audit outcomes. This is where the volume problem gets solved. Research behind the approach found that fewer than 1% of vulnerabilities in a typical environment pose the highest risk or genuinely need immediate action to move audit outcomes, so results get filtered by control criticality, asset scope, internet-facing devices, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, and risk signals like MITRE ATT&CK mappings, not just counted.

Automate remediation. Remediation is where the old workflow falls apart. Flag a finding, file a ticket, wait, hope someone remembers to re-scan. That process was never fast, and BOD 26-04’s tighter windows make it untenable. Audit Fix closes the loop instead, automating the fix itself and applying it consistently across assets rather than leaving it to a ticket queue.

Map controls across frameworks. A control validated once, whether that’s for FedRAMP, System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2, ISO 27001, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), or something else, counts toward every other framework it maps to as well, so teams stop re-proving the same control for every audit that comes around.

Shift to continuous audit readiness. Audit outcomes should reflect the current state of the environment, not a snapshot from whenever someone last pulled a report. That’s the same point CISA and FedRAMP are making. For a closer look at each step, read 5 Steps to Turn Compliance Checks into Audit Outcomes.

Qualys Policy Audit doesn’t replace governance, training, or personnel security. Those stay organizational, and a configuration scanner can’t assess them. On the technical side, it assesses your systems against NIST 800-53 controls in families such as:

Configuration management (CM): settings checked against baselines, with drift flagged

System and information integrity (SI): integrity protections and file changes

Audit and accountability (AU): logging and audit settings

Risk assessment (RA): gaps ranked by risk, not just counted

Assessment, authorization, and monitoring (CA): continuous monitoring of control status

That’s not a coincidence. It’s the reason this category of tooling exists in the first place.

The Takeaway

FedRAMP compliance isn’t a project with an end date anymore. It’s an ongoing discipline, and the rules keep tightening. Teams that still treat authorization as the finish line keep getting caught off guard at reassessment. The teams staying ahead of directives like BOD 26-04, rather than scrambling to react to them, are the ones who’ve built assessing, prioritizing, remediating, and reporting into how they run compliance day-to-day, not just how they prepare for an audit.

If you want to see what that looks like, watch our on-demand webinar, “FedRAMP Authorization and What It Now Takes to Keep It.” It features Kaleb Knobel, Senior Security Analyst and Information System Security Officer (ISSO), and Anu Kapil, Director of Product Management. They share how Policy Audit helps organizations continuously assess, prioritize, remediate, and report on FedRAMP readiness, plus what FedRAMP Moderate and High teams should be doing right now.

See what FedRAMP Moderate and High teams should be doing right now.

Watch on Demand

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Why isn’t FedRAMP authorization the finish line?

After authorization, FedRAMP expects providers to keep monitoring their security posture and give agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions. Proving that controls still work, day after day, is the harder part.

What is CISA BOD 26-04?

It’s a Binding Operational Directive that CISA issued on June 10, 2026. It prioritizes vulnerability remediation by risk factors such as public exposure, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) status, automatability, and technical impact, instead of applying one fixed deadline to every finding.

How did FedRAMP respond to BOD 26-04?

Within days, FedRAMP said the legacy monthly scanning that most Rev5 services rely on is insufficient. It set December 7, 2026, as the date its new VDR and VER rules become mandatory for certification. Under these rules, providers must evaluate whether each vulnerability is reachable from the internet and likely to be exploited, fix KEVs within BOD 26-04 timelines, and keep responding to vulnerabilities on an ongoing basis.

How does Qualys Policy Audit support FedRAMP compliance?

Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline. It maps each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result so that teams can prioritize, remediate, and report on gaps between audits.

Does Policy Audit replace governance or training?

No. Governance, training, and personnel security remain organizational responsibilities. Policy Audit focuses on technical controls.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: AI Outside Your Pipelines: Orca Extends AI AppGen Security to Base44’s Compliance API
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Base44 just launched its Compliance API, and Orca is ready on day one
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
For years, software reached production through checkpoints security controlled: a ticket, a code review, a CI gate and a security sign-off.

AI app builders skip all of them. An HR coordinator describes an app in plain English and can publish it within the hour. 52% of organizations already build custom applications with AI. The opportunity is huge, and so is the need to secure it without slowing anyone down.

Base44 is where much of that building happens, no coding required. Base44 passed $100M in annual recurring revenue by early March 2026 and $200M ARR in August. JH Kelly builds department apps in about a week with a 4-person data team, and teams can go from an idea to a live app in a single day.

Every AI-generated app has the same parts: the builder, the site it runs on, the database, the login and, more and more often, an AI agent. Most stacks spread those parts across 4 or 5 vendors. Base44 puts all of them in one workspace. With its new Compliance API, it also gives enterprise admins one place to govern them: who can open an app, who can read its data and who its agents can talk to.

Base44 just launched its Compliance API, and Orca is ready on day one. Today, Orca is extending AI AppGen Security to Base44. It joins Vercel and Claude in the same risk model and alert queue you already use for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

You can’t block your way out of AI outside your pipelines. You secure it through the platform’s control plane, then rank its risk against everything else you run.

Base44 built the controls. Orca keeps drift in check.

A single Base44 app now leaves a trail in three places: its settings live in Base44, its code can sync to GitHub, and the data it touches sits in your cloud. Each place has its own security view, and none of them shows the whole app. Security teams end up asking three tools one question: can this app put us at risk?

Base44’s enterprise controls are the foundation: SSO enforcement, SCIM, audit logs, IP allowlists, a Security Center that scans app code, and now a Compliance API that opens workspace settings to the rest of the security stack. The next question for security teams is whether those controls stay on as builders publish new apps.

Across AI app builders as a whole, drift is common for security controls. Escape’s passive scan of 5,600+ public vibe-coded apps found 2,000+ vulnerabilities, 400+ exposed secrets and 175 instances of exposed PII.

Take two apps from the same well-governed workspace:

App A is a sales deal-tracking dashboard. It’s restricted to the workspace, each rep sees only their own records, and every admin uses MFA.

App B is an HR onboarding portal published last week. Its builder switched it to public for a vendor demo and never switched it back, so its Employees table is now readable without login.

From the outside, both are just URLs. Only the workspace configuration, now readable through Base44’s Compliance API, shows that App B drifted from policy.

The question isn’t “is anything misconfigured?”

It’s “which of these apps can actually create risk?”

Introducing the Orca Base44 connector

Orca’s connector is built on Base44’s new Compliance API, which gives enterprise admins a read-only view of how a workspace is set up. There’s nothing to install, and nothing to add to the builder’s workflow. The Compliance API is available to Base44 Enterprise customers. A workspace admin creates an API key with the Compliance API permissions and adds it to Orca’s Base44 connector.

Discover. Orca inventories apps, data schemas, backend functions, secret names, API keys, integrations, custom domains and AI agents, plus members if the admin allows it. It ties each app to the person who built it.

Inventory of Base44 apps and assets in the Orca Platform.

Govern. Orca checks the workspace against more than 30 out-of-the-box posture rules:

Data exposure: Public apps without login, data entity permissions that don’t match app visibility, public apps holding secrets, and backend functions with no login wall.

Identity: Admins without MFA, SSO that is configured but not enforced, guest SSO exemptions, and risky or stale API keys.

AI agents: Superagent and embedded-agent access settings, checked against each app’s visibility.

Workspace guardrails: Public default visibility, non-admins who can publish to the internet, a disabled IP allowlist, unrestricted iframe embedding, and domains that point at deleted apps.

Findings map to SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, GDPR, PCI DSS and HIPAA, so GRC teams get evidence without chasing app owners.

Security alerts for a Base44 app in the Orca Platform.

Context that tells you which app to fix first

In Orca, Base44 findings join the same Unified Data Model as the rest of your environment.

Exposure, ranked. Orca adds every live, published Base44 app to its exposure graph as internet-reachable. It then precisely prioritizes apps that combine public access with open data, secrets, outside connectors or anonymous agents. App B rises to the top, and App A stays quiet.

One queue for every AI builder. Base44 findings sit next to Vercel and Claude findings, with the same workflow, ticketing and compliance reports, and a named business owner on every finding.

Code and workspace, side by side. Base44 builders usually never see a pull request, yet their apps still produce code, and with Base44’s GitHub sync (Builder plan and up) that code lands in your repos. Orca already scans the repos you connect to. Now it also sees the workspace that published them: who has access, what is exposed, and what agents and connectors can reach. Base44’s Security Center also checks code inside the builder.

Builders keep their platform and their speed. Security gets enough context to approve apps instead of blocking them. That’s how AI AppGen Security turns “no” into “go.”

Want to see how Orca keeps your Base44 workspace enterprise ready? Book a demo and we’ll walk through a live workspace.

About the Orca Platform

Orca Security delivers security for the companies that build. As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. Trusted by hundreds of organizations, including SAP, Autodesk, Gannett, Lemonade, and Digital Turbine, Orca is backed by leading investors including Temasek, CapitalG, ICONIQ Capital, and Redpoint Ventures.

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: NIS2 Makes Board Members Personally Liable for Access Control Decisions
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Approval is only part of the job Article 20 requires management bodies to both approve cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
NIS2 Article 20 makes management bodies answerable for the access controls they approve, and boards are starting to ask for proof that those controls work.

NIS2 board accountability gives directors a more direct role in cybersecurity. Under Article 20, the management bodies of essential and important entities must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures required by the directive, oversee their implementation, and can be held liable for infringements, subject to national law.

That obligation is live across most of the EU, with four member states going to the Court of Justice in July for failing to notify full transposition.

Access control is one of the required measures. Directors are not expected to decide who gets administrator rights or review individual user accounts. They do, however, need to know that access is being controlled, that someone has responsibility for managing the risk, and that problems are being addressed.

An estimated 160,000 entities fall within the scope of NIS2 across the EU.

Approval is only part of the job

Article 20 requires management bodies to both approve cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation. It also requires the members of those bodies to undergo cybersecurity training, and to offer comparable training to employees on a regular basis.

The measures themselves are set out in Article 21. They include access control policies and asset management, along with the use of multi-factor authentication or continuous authentication solutions where appropriate.

Many organizations have traditionally left these decisions to security and IT teams. Under NIS2, the board still needs to know whether the measures it approved are being implemented.

Day-to-day responsibility can remain with the CISO and IT teams. The difficulty comes when the person responsible for a risk does not control the budget, systems, or people needed to address it.

Greece’s implementation goes further in defining who carries that responsibility. Its NIS2 law requires essential and important entities to appoint a suitably qualified member of their organization as an Information and Communication Systems Security Officer. The officer coordinates compliance, must have the resources needed to do the job, and operates independently of the company’s data protection officer.

Access problems also need to reach the board in terms that it can act on. If an MFA rollout has failed or administrators have more access than they need, the board needs to understand the risk of leaving it unresolved. The CISO may be responsible for the risk without controlling the budget or teams needed to fix it.

The board needs evidence

Board reports often show what the access control policy requires, rather than whether it is being followed.

For example, a company policy will likely require MFA and the removal of accounts when employees leave.

However, the board also needs to know about the exceptions, including old accounts that remain active, excessive privileges, MFA exemptions that have never been reviewed, and suppliers whose access has outlasted their contracts.

The board needs information about how the controls are working in practice.

In a NIS2 access management report from European password and secrets manager Passwork, regulators from two national cybersecurity authorities and independent security leaders describe boards that have absorbed the liability change and now ask for proof that controls work, where they once accepted a summary of the policy.

Organizations should be able to show who can access critical systems, why that access was granted, who approved it, how long it is valid, and when it was changed or revoked. The board needs to know whether that evidence exists and what it says about material access risk.

Personal liability raises the stakes

Implementation is still catching up in parts of Europe. In July 2026, the European Commission referred Ireland, Spain, France, and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice of the European Union for failing to notify full transposition of NIS2 into national law. The Commission also asked the Court to impose financial sanctions.

For organizations in countries where NIS2 has been transposed, regulators have significant enforcement powers.

For essential entities, member states must set a maximum fine of at least €10,000,000 or 2% of the global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Important entities are subject to a lower maximum threshold, of at least €7,000,000 or 1.4% of their global annual turnover, in a similar capacity.

Article 32 also allows competent authorities, in specific circumstances, to seek the temporary prohibition of someone at CEO or legal representative level from exercising managerial functions in an essential entity. This can happen where enforcement action has failed to produce the required response. It is not an automatic consequence of a cyber incident.

Article 20 separately requires member states to ensure that management bodies can be held liable for infringements of Article 21, subject to the applicable rules under national law.

Approving the policy is not the end of the board’s involvement. It also needs information on whether the policy is being followed and what is happening with known problems.

Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found credential abuse somewhere in the chain of 39% of breaches, more than any other vector. Stolen credentials also circulate at scale, as the exposed database of 24 billion credential records reported in June showed. Directors should expect an answer on which accounts and credentials reach critical systems, who is responsible for them, and whether that access is being controlled.

Give access risk an owner with authority

CISOs briefing their boards should be able to say who owns access-control risk and whether that person has the authority to address it. The board also needs evidence of what is happening.

When an access problem is identified, someone needs to be responsible for getting it fixed. That might mean removing unnecessary privileges or dealing with an MFA exception that has remained in place. If the fix depends on another team’s budget or resources, the board needs to know.

Board reporting should show whether the controls it approved are working, flag significant exceptions that remain unresolved, and who is accountable for closing them.

Her focus areas include cybersecurity, cloud, channel, enterprise IT, and data centre operations. She works across many formats: news, features, white papers, eBooks, and thought leadership. Kirsten has many years of experience in journalism and editing for both print and digital media, and has supported plenty of go-to-market and PR programmes with technically grounded writing that holds up to scrutiny. Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register. “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking, and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Telegram channel, which the Google threat hunters note is “likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises.” Specialized LLMjacking roles As more criminals join the LLMJacking ecosystem, Google says it has documented a division of labor between the criminals that establish initial access to compromised cloud and AI services, and those that manage downstream monetization infrastructure, called “LLM Mixers.” In one case that Mandiant responded to in mid-2026, UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to a model API. The crooks also spun up a session hijacking page purporting to be an application portal to join a group of LLM users. “This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls,” the report says. Google predicts miscreants will “increasingly prioritize LLMJacking” compared to other types of resource theft like cryptojacking. And to prevent cloud LLM service abuse, the security firm says defenders should prioritize identity and access management plus supply chain security, and use a centralized secrets management platform to rotate keys and secrets. Also apply least-access privileges to users and service accounts, ensuring that they only have permissions necessary to complete their roles and tasks. And automate secrets scanning within codebases to identify and then remove any API keys and secrets added to source code. ®

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday, the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange, the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals, which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024. The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday, crypto exchange Bitget has now confirmed that the cyberattack where hackers drained $387.5 million worth of digital assets from the exchange’s wallets also has all the hallmarks of a North Korean operation. Its CEO did not go into too much detail, but did say that “IP behavioral patterns and on-chain signatures” suggest it was Kim’s cronies at work. This isn’t Binance's first expensive encounter with hackers, either. Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens. Four years later, the sums have grown considerably. Binance may have the reserves to make its customers whole, but the attackers responsible for the latest raid still have billions of dollars to launder. ®

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: GM cracks the petty cash box for multistate driver tracking settlement
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: The settlement comes more than two years after a 2024 New York Times investigation found that GM had been selling the data collected from vehicle owners through its Smart Driver...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text: General Motors is taking what looks like a light slap on the wrist from a coalition of 35 states and the District of Columbia after agreeing to settle allegations that it collected drivers' data without proper consent and sold it to data brokers that supplied insurance companies. The Washington state AG's office said on Thursday that GM had reached a $220 million settlement with 36 attorneys general over the automaker's collection and sharing of driving data, including precise location information, speed, seatbelt use, and other metrics. According to investigators, GM sold that data to brokers, which in turn supplied it to insurance companies that could use it to set customers' premiums, without drivers' informed consent. For reference, the $220 million settlement, which will be distributed among the participating jurisdictions, equates to less than 7 percent of GM's $3.3 billion in net income attributable to stockholders for its third quarter, which ended on September 30, 2026. Don't spend it all in one place, y'all. The settlement comes more than two years after a 2024 New York Times investigation found that GM had been selling the data collected from vehicle owners through its Smart Driver program. That program, part of GM subsidiary OnStar’s offering, collected the aforementioned data and handed it back to vehicle owners in reports designed to inform better driving habits. Unbeknownst to Smart Driver subscribers, their data was also being forked over to data brokers despite GM telling customers it wouldn't share that information with insurers without their express consent. The insurers ultimately obtained the data by purchasing it from brokers with which GM had struck deals. To make matters worse, the Washington AG's office said GM incentivized dealerships to enroll customers in Smart Driver, with employees in some cases accepting terms and conditions on customers' behalf without their knowledge or consent. GM also failed to notify many drivers that their information was being collected and shared. Its OnStar app incorrectly told more than 370,000 drivers they were not enrolled in Smart Driver, even as GM continued collecting and selling their data, according to investigators. “The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific,” the AG’s office said. GM canned the Smart Driver program in April 2024, just over a month after the New York Times exposed its data-sharing practices, citing customer feedback. In addition to the monetary pittance it’s handing over to the states, GM also agreed with the 36 AGs to limit the driving data it collects, better protect customer PII, and establish a "comprehensive data privacy program.” The Washington AG’s office described its settlement as “significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct.” Speaking of those other terms, GM finalized its settlement of the same allegations with the Federal Trade Commission in January 2026. The FTC order required GM to obtain drivers' express consent before collecting, using, or sharing covered driving data, subject to certain exceptions. It also required the company to offer a simple way for drivers to request a copy of their data, request its deletion, and disable precise geolocation data collection where their vehicles support it. The state of California separately reached a $12.75 million settlement with GM in the matter in May; a separate case in Texas is ongoing. “This agreement … reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices,” a GM spokesperson told The Register, though the company noted that it still stands by driver data collection as a best practice. “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” the spokesperson added. ®

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: ICO Reprimands Staffordshire Police After Domestic Abuse Breach
Policy, Legal & Compliance.context: Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to...
Policy, Legal & Compliance.full_text:
A UK police force committed a serious breach of data protection law after sharing the home address of a domestic abuse victim with their abuser, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has revealed.

The privacy regulator issued a reprimand to Staffordshire Police on October 28, following the incident in March 2024.

The force had served the abuser, “P,” a Domestic Violence Protection Notice (DVPN) on their release from prison in order to protect the abuse victim, or “data subject.”

However, it erroneously included that person’s home address, which was not previously known to P.

“As a consequence of the investigation into the relevant incident the commission has become aware of allegations that P subjected the data subject to both physical and emotional abuse over a period of several years, resulting in the data subject having to relocate their home address on numerous occasions in order to escape the alleged abuse,” the reprimand noted.

“In this context, the data subject’s current address was highly sensitive information and should have been handled as such.”

Read more on police privacy breaches: Police Scotland Fined After Sharing Victim’s Phone Data.

Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to prevent the disclosure, “including poor completion rates for mandatory training in both data protection and issuing DVPNs.”

It argued that Staffordshire Police had since made improvements to reduce the risk of a similar event taking place in the future. These included increased training completion rates, new leadership roles for domestic abuse cases, new internal procedures and new technology to improve services for victims.

ICO head of investigations, Sally-Anne Poole, said the case is a reminder of the importance of getting the basics right.

“Every organization must be doing everything necessary to protect the personal information in their care, especially where there is a known risk to someone's safety,” she added. “Whether in policing, health or local government, we urge organizations to take responsibility for training their staff and putting appropriate systems in place to avoid these incidents and the harm they can cause.”

Advice for Handling Sensitive Information

The ICO warned back in 2023 that organizations handling the personally identifiable information (PII) of domestic abuse victims could put lives at risk if breaches occur.

It said at the time that it had issued reprimands to seven organizations in the previous 14 months after sensitive PII was breached, including one police force.

The latest revelations will do little to allay concerns that the regulator’s public sector approach – which favors warnings, reprimands and enforcement notices over fines – is not having the desired effect.

After this latest incident the ICO advised organizations handling sensitive PII to:

Ensure staff know how to handle the PII of people experiencing domestic abuse with extra care

Review default templates and processes to ensure PII is only included where legally necessary

Regularly check contact information to avoid disclosing information to an old address, email or phone number

Always double check before any PII is transferred, altered or disclosed

Ensure training is thorough, relevant and tailored to the tasks staff actually carry out

Policy, Legal & Compliance.title: NIST Publishes Guidance to Meet Federal Post-Quantum Deadlines
