Product & Roadmap.title: Wait, Did We Just Invent Classifiers Again? Introducing Jev, a new way to do AI.
Product & Roadmap.context: This week TypeSafe AI launched a new kind of model, called Jev, and it’s very interesting
Product & Roadmap.full_text:
For the last few years, when somebody says “AI,” what they are usually referring to is a Large Language Model, or LLM for short. You chuck some text in, it has a think, and it gives you some more text back. This is brilliant if you want code written, documents summarised, or quantum physics explained to you in a limerick, but while this is great for humans, most software doesn’t actually want a beautifully written paragraph. Software just wants an answer so it can make a decision. Is this event suspicious? Should I escalate it? Is this high risk? Which workflow should deal with it? For this, LLMs aren’t really the ideal tool of choice. This is all about to change.

This week TypeSafe AI launched a new kind of model, called Jev, and it’s very interesting. This AI model doesn’t want to have a conversation with you – you cannot use it conversationally. Jev is just trying to do one thing, and it wants to do that one thing well: It’s trying to decide.

So, what is Jev exactly?

Jev is what TypeSafe calls a “System One” model. Rather than primarily generating a sequence of tokens like a traditional LLM, you give Jev some state (think datapoints), define questions about that state (what you want to know), and tell it what valid answers look like (to format the output). Jev then interprets all your inputs, does some smart things, and returns probabilistic decisions. So rather than asking an LLM, “Can you analyse this security event and tell me what you think?,” you can ask Jev for substantially more specific things like: Is this likely malicious? Does this warrant investigation? Is credential compromise likely? How severe is it? What is great is that you can define those outputs beforehand. You’re asking for a decision, rather than hoping the model eventually buries one somewhere inside three paragraphs of text.

Now before anybody says anything, I know what you’re thinking: “Hang on, haven’t we just invented classifiers again?” I had the same reaction. If you’ve never head of a classifier, this is what we used to use before everybody decided their product desperately needed a chatbot glued to the side of it. Machine learning was full of classifiers: Spam or not spam? Fraud or legitimate? Malware or benign? Cat or, tragically, not cat? Classifiers were incredibly useful, but normally quite narrow. You needed training data, labels, pipelines, and usually a model built specifically for that problem. Generative AI gave us something far more flexible because we could suddenly describe what we wanted in natural language. Jev feels a bit like taking that semantic understanding and putting it back inside the old classifier model, but with significantly more accessibility.

The real-world approach: Jev in action with Cato

Let’s use Jev for something a little more interesting than asking whether an ice cream sandwich is technically a sandwich, using the the TypeSafe Playground. Let’s use Jev to interpret data taken from the Cato Management Application via the EventsFeed API.

We will start with a deliberately boring question: a finance employee in the UK, using their normal managed laptop, was successfully authenticating with MFA and downloading four files from SharePoint during the working day. All this extracted information from our API will populate the ‘State’ field – this is the current state of the query, and it should represent what we want to interpret. We then can add a few “Questions” to the field below, as we want to specify a formatted output:

The questions asked were not difficult for a human, but very difficult for a traditional LLM to give a succinct answer due to generative analysis:

Does this require investigation?

Is it likely malicious?

Is credential compromise likely?

What should the security response be?

How severe is the risk?

Instead of producing a 300-page AI slop security report, Jev instead evaluates those individual decisions and responds with probabilities of likelihood. After clicking the “Run” button to process the query, Jev outputted the following:

So far, lovely. This event doesn’t need investigation, and Jev believes that there should be a 100% probability that this incident should be closed. There is a 5% chance that this could be likely malicious, but the correlated signals overall indicate that the current state of the event is benign. Fantastic – but what if we did something a little more interesting, like changing the state of the event? After all, the state of your users (and network) is always changing.

We will now use the same user, application, and questions. Except now the device state has changed. The device is now unknown and unmanaged, the connection is coming from Russia (22 minutes after a UK session), it’s 3:17 in the morning, there are impossible-travel indicators, and instead of downloading four files from SharePoint, our finance user has just hoovered up 1,847 documents from Finance and M&A folders. In technical security terminology: that looks a bit dodgy, but these are all parameters we can extract via the Cato API to help Jev make a judgement call.

After hitting Run again, Jev reprocessed the input and a different decision was output based on the evidence provided. This model was able process the data feed and reclassify this not as a benign event that should be instantly closed, but instead the user should be “Contained” as there’s enough evidence to imply a device compromise with 99% certainty.

This capability is incredibly awesome. We have given it the same questions and same output structure, but with a different state of the world and different decisions. I haven’t overcomplicated the process by asking the model to become my SOC analyst 0; instead it’s just used the power of AI to help me accelerate my business decisions. ChatGPT would attempt write an incident report, create a ticket, isolate the device, burn $40k in tokens, and notify somebody on Slack, but this isn’t what most companies want. I’ve asked Jev to perform the fuzzy bit: make a semantic judgement. This output can then actually drive business decisions.

Normal software can then do the boring bit, and boring is rather lovely (and desired) when it comes to security. Imagine a world where a Jev decision greater than 90% confidence automatically creates an investigation. Perhaps 60–90% confidence rate automatically triggers a human review. Perhaps a combination of credential compromise and high severity triggers another workflow; the model provides the judgement and deterministic controls decide what that judgement is actually allowed to do.

Models like Jev are the next logical evolution in business process automation – where we start to leverage AI not to just provide a fuzzy output, but instead provide an actionable decision and output to accelerate your business. The probability percentage could drive accountability, while also retaining control. This is very important when we consider the current “rogue” nature of AI we hear in the news.

Secure, Contain, Protect.

If you’re still reading, I believe that what we are seeing here goes beyond Jev itself, but Jev is the starting point of re-taking control from the chaos of our current software landscape. AI is starting to disappear inside applications, with embedded AI being the bane of most organisations. It won’t always announce itself with a giant “Ask AI” button. Models today increasingly make tiny decisions inside APIs, workflows, agents, and applications, often without the end user even realising an AI model was involved. For security teams, that should set a few alarm bells ringing, as you are no longer in the driving seat when it comes to your applications and their output.

Today if organisations only monitor visits to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, they’re going to miss a huge part of what AI adoption is becoming. You need to understand where AI is being used, which models and services your organisation is communicating with, what data is being sent to them, and what those AI-driven decisions can cause downstream.

The classifier might be back. But this time it could be buried absolutely everywhere. Your job now is to make sure you can see it, govern it, and apply controls without impacting your user experience. For this, Cato Networks can help.

The post Wait, Did We Just Invent Classifiers Again? Introducing Jev, a new way to do AI. appeared first on Cato Networks.

Product & Roadmap.title: Introducing AlertZero: Inbox zero for your alert queue
Product & Roadmap.context: Hunt Uses threat research to look for evidence of attacks in the available telemetry
Product & Roadmap.full_text:
For the last several months, we’ve been busy talking to security teams and building answers to the AI-accelerated challenges that you’ve told us you’re facing. Among these are the overwhelming volume and velocity of alerts, exacerbated by attackers equipped with AI. The Hugging Face incident demonstrated another core challenge in the security operations center (SOC). Even if all of the signals are detected, that’s not enough, unless something connects them as part of a single attack. Combined, these problems force most teams to ration coverage by headcount, so the contents of the alert queue decide what gets attention, and the rest ages out unexamined. Spending time on proactive defenses then feels even more challenging.

Today, we’re giving you a peek at AlertZero, the new agentic layer of Elastic Security. AlertZero has a straightforward premise: put SOC teams on the path to the equivalent of inbox zero for alerts, with every alert answered. It does this by reducing the existing queue and the false positives that contribute to it, through high-volume correlation and enrichment, proposing actions, and then helping to create and tune detections.

AlertZero has agents, called Watches, each with one named job: Triage, Hunt, Detection, or Forensics. The Watches run on triggers and schedules to propose evidence-backed conclusions, called Proposed Actions, for approval, modification, escalation, or dismissal. Each Watch surfaces decisions to the analyst based on its autonomy level: manual, assisted, or supervised. Regardless of level, every consequential action is proposed to the analyst for approval.

AlertZero retains the same ″open by design″ philosophy as Elastic Security. You can use the model that works best for your team, including proprietary and open source models, with the same product and features, across Elastic Cloud, self-managed, or fully air-gapped.

We didn’t think of this overnight. AlertZero builds on three years of generative AI (GenAI) innovation in Elastic Security. Elastic AI Assistant started with conversational help in 2023. Attack Discovery extended that into a dedicated investigation task in 2024, connecting related alerts into an attack narrative. Elastic Agent Builder and security skills added agents that use tools and apply domain expertise, while Elastic Workflows supplies repeatable execution. AlertZero brings these capabilities together, tailored to the responsibilities of a SOC.

AlertZero Watches stay in their lane (and they handle it well)

Every Watch in AlertZero is directly aligned with the key responsibilities in the SOC, and their levels of autonomy are customizable. Within each Watch, Workers carry out specific tasks. For example, a Triage Worker runs Attack Discovery, which connects related alerts into attack narratives, while a Forensics Worker examines endpoint activity. Your team controls how much each Worker can do without human review, so you can tailor Watches to help your team in the places you most need it.

The upcoming technical preview introduces four Watches:

Watch name

What it helps your team do

Triage

Assesses alerts, connects related activity, and identifies findings that need attention.

Hunt

Uses threat research to look for evidence of attacks in the available telemetry.

Detection

Investigates noisy rules and coverage gaps and then prepares detection changes for review.

Forensics

Examines endpoint activity to establish what happened and to identify supported response actions.

A hunt can start from new threat research, and detection analysis can start from recurring false positives. Endpoint analysis can start from a finding that needs a closer look, and all of the Watches can run on triggers or a schedule. Watches don’t form a mandatory pipeline.

How AlertZero handles suspicious login sessions

The following example shows how the Triage and Forensics Hunts work together. We’re starting on the Proposed Actions page, where Watches awaiting human approval show their work before carrying out an action.

Proposed Actions are grouped by the type of action they’re waiting for. In this specific scenario, under Respond, an impossible-travel finding for an executive account, cfo@corp, has an endpoint-isolation action waiting for review. Before we even open this screen, the Triage Watch and Forensics Watch have already gathered the findings behind that recommendation.

Opening the item reveals the associated Investigation and its supporting evidence.

In this example, the account was active in Boston and then, 39 minutes later, it was active from a distant hosting network, using the same session identifier without a fresh multifactor authentication (MFA) event.

The endpoint findings add more context: an unsigned process accessing browser session material. If needed, we can examine how that process started and what it contacted, along with the time period covered. To see the full scope of the incident, there are the related alerts and affected entities, in addition to endpoint findings, in the same flyout. In this case, the pattern warrants investigating session replay. Virtual private network (VPN) use and proxies also need consideration, as does inaccurate geolocation.

From the Investigation’s conversation, we can ask these follow-up questions before deciding how to proceed: What did the account access after the suspicious sign-in? What would isolating the endpoint interrupt? These questions also prompt further analysis, and the existing findings are available as context.

In this scenario, the endpoint response is set to manual review. So, after checking the target, rationale, and likely impact, we can approve or decline the Proposed Action. An approval would trigger host isolation through Elastic Defend. The Investigation records the decision and the execution outcome separately for auditability.

When an Investigation (or set of Investigations) needs a coordinated and constrained response, an analyst can open an Escalation and link the relevant Investigations.

Teammates can discuss the evidence and, in the same conversation, ask an agent follow-up questions. They can also opt to never invoke an agent in particularly sensitive situations.

Beyond alert triage: What else does AlertZero do?

Reducing the alert queue by handling the correlation and enrichment at scale is one part of the solution. On the other side of things, we’re helping with the work that happens when nothing is on fire.

A head start on your hunt

For threat hunting, the Hunt Watch:

Continuously observes your environment.

Maps observed technologies and exposures to relevant threats.

Proposes hunts, findings, coverage improvements, or escalations.

Its core purpose is to answer the question Is there evidence of this threat in my environment?, without requiring you to provoke the hunt or feed the intel.

The Hunt Watch gets you started with threat research, even when no detection alert has been fired. It relates that research to the environment and available telemetry and searches for relevant indicators. It also examines supporting behavior. The findings identify what was searched and what was found.

Turning false positives and coverage gaps into rule changes

To improve your environment-specific defenses, hunt findings can inform the Detection Watch by looking at whether existing rules would detect the behavior.

Suppose a legitimate administrative tool repeatedly triggers a rule. The closure itself is useful feedback, but someone still has to connect several decisions to a common cause in the rule. This is how false-positive closures provide another input for the Detection Watch to contextualize. The Watch reviews the alert examples and existing logic and then prepares a proposed change, like an exception, with the supporting diagnosis. From there, a detection engineer can assess whether a narrow exception fits the benign activity while preserving detection of malicious use of the same tool.

As an example, the Watch would run an Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL) query like this:

Once the Watch reviews the rules’ rankings based on their recently closed false positives, it identifies those with high counts to investigate further. A high count doesn’t necessarily prove that the rule is defective, but the analysis needs to inspect the examples and their closure rationale, because an incorrect false-positive label can otherwise become an incorrect exclusion.

In this example, the Detection Watch’s Rule Tuning Worker is set to manual. After the analyst authorizes the analysis, the resulting Proposed Action brings together the diagnosis, the motivating alerts, the existing logic, the proposed logic, and backtest results. That gives a detection engineer an actual change to assess and the evidence used to construct it.

With the proposal, we can see that the five sample false positives no longer match the revised query.

We can open the Proposed Action to review the change and ask follow-up questions in the linked Investigation, such as What other activity would this exclusion suppress? Because this backtest only covers benign samples, the analyst still needs to validate detection of known malicious activity through the team’s existing testing process before approving. If it’s approved, the change is applied; if it’s declined, the rule is unchanged.

You can decide how much to delegate

You choose which Watches run and how far each goes, with autonomy configurable per Worker. We’ve built this into AlertZero because no two security teams are organized the same way. Some run tiers, some run pods, many have no detection engineer, and most cannot staff nights. Regardless of team structure, autonomy also is configurable because different jobs carry different risks, like assessing an alert versus responding on an endpoint. You can delegate routine analysis while choosing more cautiously when a host may be affected. As an example, the Triage Watch Worker runs Attack Discovery, while a Forensics Watch Worker performs endpoint analysis. Each runs as an Elastic Workflow, calling Agent Builder agents and skills for analysis.

For true-positive or inconclusive Attack Discovery assessments, manual review lets the analyst decide whether to close an Investigation or request endpoint analysis. In supervised operation, a true-positive assessment can continue into endpoint analysis automatically. An inconclusive assessment still needs a person's decision.

Endpoint analysis has its own control. Manual operation presents supported response actions for review. Supervised operation is designed to permit host isolation, process termination, and process suspension without an additional approval for each action. Detection changes continue to require approval. Teams can therefore automate one part of the sequence while retaining review of another.

Every alert is answered, and every decision is yours

As AI that helps move an investigation forward, AlertZero connects work that too often stops at a handoff. The evidence gathered during triage can guide endpoint analysis and support a response decision. It can also give teammates a place to continue the investigation. Teams choose what to delegate and where their judgment is needed.

To know when future AlertZero news is published, sign up for updates. AlertZero will be available soon to all users of Elastic Security.

Glossary

AlertZero: The agentic layer of Elastic Security, connecting alert triage, threat hunting, detection engineering, and endpoint forensics.

Watch: A grouping of automated tasks around a security responsibility. The initial four are Triage, Hunt, Detection, and Forensics.

Worker: A defined task implemented as a workflow in Elastic Workflows, using agents and skills to produce findings, evidence, and supported actions.

Proposed Actions: Recommended changes with supporting evidence and rationale, presented for approval where review is required.

Investigation: The shared record for a line of inquiry, bringing together findings, affected entities, evidence, and Proposed Actions.

Escalation: A conversation that a person creates to coordinate work around linked Investigations. Teammates can discuss evidence and ask agents questions; visibility can be public or private.

Autonomy setting: A per-Worker control over how much work can proceed without review. Its behavior depends on the task.

Consequential action: An operation that changes the environment, such as isolating a host or editing a rule.

Elastic Defend: Elastic's endpoint security capability, providing supported endpoint response actions.

Attack Discovery: A capability that connects related alerts into suspected attacks. The Triage Watch uses it to open an Investigation for each identified attack.

Elastic Agent Builder, Elastic Workflows: Extensible building blocks for Watches: Agent Builder provides agents, tools, and skills; Elastic Workflows coordinates execution.

Product & Roadmap.title: Introducing Wiz AI SAST: Application Security that Understands Your Code and Your Infrastructure
Product & Roadmap.context: We’re excited to announce that Wiz AI SAST is available as a Public Preview capability, bringing frontier-grade vulnerability discovery to all Wiz Code customers
Product & Roadmap.full_text:
We’re excited to announce that Wiz AI SAST is available as a Public Preview capability, bringing frontier-grade vulnerability discovery to all Wiz Code customers.

AI models have become highly adept at finding complex flaws in application code that traditional scanners often miss. Security teams historically addressed this gap with manual reviews and quarterly pentesting, but neither of those approaches scale in a world where code is written and exploited at machine speed.

Wiz AI SAST addresses this gap by analyzing how your application actually behaves to uncover a broader range of weaknesses (CWEs) that typically go undetected by rules-based scanners. It's powered by the Atlas harness we shared earlier this year, grounded in Wiz Research, and continuously refined by our investments in AI security.

Code findings are correlated with what is actually running in production on the Wiz Security Graph, so teams instantly understand which vulnerabilities matter most. Prioritized findings flow through the existing policy, ownership, and remediation workflows AppSec teams already use, making AI-powered vulnerability detection part of your existing program rather than another tool to manage.

As a core part of our AI Threat Readiness Framework, Wiz AI SAST complements a broader portfolio of solutions designed to help organizations stay ahead of cyberthreats in the AI era.

Frontier Grade Code Analysis without the Overhead

Running AI code scanning in production takes far more than a capable model. Teams have to build a harness that turns that model into a capable security researcher, evaluate new models as they ship, and manage the lifecycle of findings into security workflows. Done in-house, it requires a significant, ongoing investment from skilled security and engineering teams. Wiz AI SAST handles all of that out-of-the-box so organizations can operationalize AI code scanning quickly to improve their risk posture.

A Harness Backed by Research and Results

Wiz AI SAST shares the same underlying technology as Atlas, a research initiative we shared earlier this year. At the time, Atlas held the number one spot on CyberGym and uncovered more than 200 vulnerabilities in widely used open source software.

We continuously tune our harness with learnings from real-world vulnerability research, attacker techniques, and scanning across Wiz's cloud security footprint. Organizations benefit from our expertise without having to build and maintain the complex AI infrastructure required for security specific use cases.

Model Selection Driven by Continuous Benchmarking

Our work on the Cyber Model Arena shows that AI security performance isn't a property of the model alone. It depends on the model and harness together. That makes evaluation a moving target: every new model release means retesting every pairing against real-world security tasks.

As an AI vendor-agnostic platform, we continuously run these evaluations and swap the strongest—and most efficient—model into the AI SAST harness. This includes cutting edge cybermodels made available to us through our partnership with Google DeepMind.

For security teams, the value is simple: you don’t need to constantly track new model releases, benchmark them against security tasks, or decide which model to use. We handle that complexity behind the scenes, ensuring your code and applications are always scanned with the best model.

Turning Non-Deterministic AI into a Scalable Security Program

Delivering an enterprise-grade AI AppSec program requires managing the full lifecycle of vulnerability discovery, starting with deciding what to scan. AI code analysis is resource intensive and not every asset requires the investment of AI reasoning. Using Mika AI, security teams can prioritize the critical repositories that warrant AI code scanning by drawing on context such as cloud exposure, access to sensitive data, and business criticality.

Once those prioritized scans are running, Wiz addresses the next phase of the lifecycle: the outputs. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are inherently non-deterministic, they can generate different results from one run to the next. This creates a major operational challenge for security teams who need consistency in findings.

To solve this we supplement the AI scan engine with automated lifecycle management to maintain finding states across scans:

Retest: Before scanning for new risks, the engine re-examines existing findings to confirm they're still valid. If the code has been fixed, the finding is automatically marked resolved.

Deduplicate: Rather than matching on line numbers or file paths, the engine correlates new findings with existing ones using security context and code semantics. Even if the AI changes a bug's title or description, our AI SAST recognizes the underlying root cause and reconciles it into a single, stable finding.

Wiz handles this lifecycle between scans automatically, ensuring teams work with stable findings that can be assigned, tracked, remediated, and closed—not a new, disconnected set of AI outputs after every scan.

As a result customers get the deep detection benefits of AI without giving up the predictable workflows they expect from enterprise security tools. By eliminating the manual burden of managing non-determinism, this built-in continuity dramatically reduces the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) of AI-powered security.

Click through the feature tour

See how Wiz AI SAST works

Visibility into a New Class of CWEs

Wiz AI SAST extends detection coverage into the logic-based vulnerabilities that have always been hardest to catch, like broken access control, flawed input validation, and misapplied cryptography. Finding them requires a semantic understanding of what the code is supposed to do, which is something AI does exceptionally well.

A practical example can be found below. Wiz AI SAST detected an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) flaw in an E-commerce basket endpoint, where any authenticated user could read another user's cart by changing the ID in the URL. Rules based engines would miss this type of risk because the syntax of the code is fine but it's the missing ownership check that makes it exploitable.

The practical takeaway for AppSec teams is that AI analysis doesn’t replace rules based scanning completely, but rather it extends it. Deterministic scanning provides fast, cost-effective coverage for syntax based flaws, while AI SAST adds the deep reasoning needed to catch intent-dependent flaws like the IDOR above. Together, they give AppSec teams broader coverage of risk across the entire application attack surface.

Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Infrastructure Context

The best AI models in the world are ultimately limited by their access to relevant context. A model evaluating code in a vacuum is blind to how that application actually operates in the real world.

By grounding our AI SAST engine in the Wiz Security Graph, the model investigates your code with full awareness of your infrastructure, identity configurations, and runtime environment. This context serves two critical purposes:

Uncovering Hidden Risk: It allows the AI to discover complex vulnerabilities that only exist at the intersection of application logic and infrastructure flaws that standalone AI code scanners cannot detect.

Prioritizing True Attack Paths: It drastically reduces triage fatigue by correlating code weaknesses with additional context to surface critical attack paths that matter most for remediation.

That same deep context is what allows our Red Agent to validate exploitability from the outside in, testing these AI-discovered findings against your live environment exactly the way an attacker would.

Remediate at Machine Speed with the Green Agent

Detecting and validating risk at machine speed only pays off if remediation keeps up. The Wiz Green Agent investigates the underlying findings and builds a remediation plan grounded in the full context of your code, pipeline, infrastructure, and runtime, going beyond the generic guidance a standalone model produces.

It pinpoints the right owner, maps the steps to fix the root cause, and can even share context with an AI coding agent like Claude Code to carry out the fix in code. And with Wiz Workflows, teams can turn Green Agent’s intelligence into multi-step automated response chains tailored to their DevSecOps playbooks.

Get Started

In the AI era, the best form of defense is to use AI on ourselves before threat actors can. Wiz AI SAST gives defenders a scalable solution to apply that philosophy against application code. But, it’s just one component of our broader vision for Agentic Code Security where specialized AI agents work alongside security teams to autonomously investigate, prioritize, and remediate risk across the entire AI development lifecycle.

Wiz AI SAST is available now in Public Preview. If you’re an existing Wiz Code customer, get started by visiting our documentation. If you’re new to Wiz, request a demo to experience frontier-grade vulnerability discovery first hand.

General Security News.title: Smashing Security podcast #491: How AI agents are spooking the banks
General Security News.context: So it's generating virtual cards for transactions
General Security News.full_text: So it's generating virtual cards for transactions. And I imagine there's a bit of guardrails involved there, isn't there? There's an extra little bit of protection. It has this safety layer called Sentinel built into it. Now, if any listeners are fans of the X-Men, you'll know that the Sentinels were genocidal robots. And in The Matrix, Sentinels are those squid-like things which went around hunting the humans. So great choice by Facebook's marketing department to call their safety level Sentinel. I'm sure they've thought carefully about that. Anyway, the thing is, there are lots of AI agents out there. It's not just Muse, but there are browser-based agents, there's open-source automation tools, there's agentic wrappers, all kinds of software which promises to automate your digital life if you will just give it access to your accounts. And of course, that's where things can go terribly, terribly wrong. So people are typing their actual banking credentials into AI assistants. That's why Bank of America has warned about this. Not necessarily Muse specifically, 'cause that's using Stripe for payments, as I said, but there's this whole ecosystem of AI agents out there which are promising to handle your finances. You might think, well, isn't that great? I can say to it, hey, log into my bank, check my balance, move this amount of money into my savings account, pay my credit card bill. But other banks are worried about this as well. So JPMorgan Chase, another whoppingly large bank in America, they came out middle of October — they had their earnings call — and CEO Jamie Dimon said that they were blocking outside agents from accessing customer accounts. So they've warned, we don't want your rogue agents coming in. He made it clear that if you give an AI agent your password and that agent does something you don't like, that is not fraud. That's you giving your password to someone else. It is your problem, not theirs. So if your agent decides to go and spend $1,000 on novelty socks, that is gonna be your problem. A few days later, Charles Schwab's CEO said that they're also blocking outside agents that attempt to log in with credentials of clients. So it's no wonder that at the end of last month, Axios reported that most of the major US banks are taking action against unauthorised third-party AI agents operating inside their customer accounts, because they say they appear to be taking actions which are independent of user instructions. And that's really the worry, isn't it? We know that AIs can hallucinate. We know that AIs can be subverted or hijacked by hackers. They can make mistakes as well as being duped through social engineering, even to make bad decisions. And that's gonna be really risky for your finances. So I think one of the things we have to wonder is, if the AI is messing around in bank accounts, what would they possibly need money for? And I was thinking about this — what does everybody have these days that AI doesn't have so much? It's either they're gonna be buying Casper mattresses or they'll be wanting their own podcast maybe, 'cause everybody's got a podcast these days. Actually, there are AI-driven podcasts as well, aren't there? Renee, what do you think these AI agents, if they were going to pinch some money, what do you think they'd be doing with it?

General Security News.title: Ballots, bots, and backlash.
General Security News.context: Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces.
General Security News.full_text:
Election Day brings typical cyber threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. Hackers tamper with European refrigeration systems. OpenAI faces questions over years of security warnings. Nvidia reportedly restricts business with Chinese data center customers. Binance details a six-billion-dollar heist attributed to North Korea. Barracuda patches critical security flaws. Gartner predicts an engineering-heavy future for security operations. Canadians face charges for hacking U.S. universities. Our guest is Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

Today is Wednesday November 4th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Election Day 2026 brings a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation.

Election Day 2026 brought a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. But the biggest technology story emerging from the midterms may be voters' growing resistance to artificial intelligence.

According to Nextgov, election officials reported unsuccessful attempts to penetrate online services, including efforts to guess login credentials. One state election office experienced five spikes in traffic to its ballot drop-box locator, which subsided after officials implemented a CAPTCHA. As of Tuesday evening, election security analysts had received no reports of foreign influence operations.

Meanwhile, ballot scanner malfunctions in New York's Westchester County quickly became fodder for election conspiracy theories. Officials initially attributed rejected ballots to problems with their thickness. Voters were instructed to deposit affected ballots in secure emergency bags for later counting. Despite no evidence of deliberate interference, misleading claims spread rapidly on X, reaching as many as 100 posts per minute.

Beyond election security, voters delivered a significant political setback to the technology industry's ambitious AI expansion.

Axios reports that roughly two dozen ballot measures restricting data center development appeared headed for approval. In Texas, Democratic gubernatorial winner Gina Hinojosa campaigned on maintaining a construction moratorium until lawmakers address environmental and infrastructure concerns.

With Democrats also winning key races in Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona, analysts estimate nearly two-thirds of planned U.S. data center capacity for 2028 could face delays.

The emerging message from voters: They're increasingly concerned about AI's impact on electricity prices, water supplies, and their communities. Silicon Valley may have enormous ambitions, but it turns out the people living next door to those data centers get a vote, too.

Hackers target refrigeration systems across Europe.

Hackers are targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, remotely changing temperature settings and forcing supermarkets to throw away spoiled food.

Attacks reported in November affected stores in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Germany, along with food suppliers in the UK. In some cases, attackers switched refrigeration equipment into defrost mode or disabled temperature alarms. Retailers have responded by disconnecting vulnerable equipment from the internet.

The attacks have also raised concerns about medical supplies. In France, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration equipment supplied to the French Blood Establishment, changing freezer settings from minus 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees. An alert technician caught the problem before it disrupted operations, according to French health officials. There's no confirmed loss of blood plasma or harm to patients.

Authorities haven't identified the perpetrators or established whether the incidents are connected. French cybersecurity officials are urging organizations to secure remote access to refrigeration controllers, update firmware, and eliminate default passwords.

The incidents demonstrate how compromising ordinary industrial equipment can have very real physical consequences.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses that could expose sensitive AI research to competitors and foreign governments.

According to Reuters, concerns included broad employee access to internal code repositories, sensitive research documentation, and inadequate security reviews of internal tools. Some employees believed leadership prioritized development speed over security.

Those concerns gained urgency following several incidents, including the arrest of a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a listening device in an executive conference room, and researchers using a rival AI model to access employee accounts and internal systems.

OpenAI disputes suggestions that it neglected security, pointing to restricted repositories, increased investment, and regular reviews. The company reportedly reassigned a quarter of its production engineers to security improvements in August.

The larger challenge: protecting increasingly valuable AI technology without slowing the research that makes it valuable.

Nvidia sets limits on Chinese data center customers.

Nvidia is reportedly imposing new restrictions on data center customers that provide computing services to Chinese companies.

According to the Financial Times, Nvidia has told operators they must limit Chinese customers to no more than 49 percent of their overall business, with the remaining 51 percent coming from non-Chinese companies.

The policy would require data center operators to track how much business they conduct with Chinese firms, potentially complicating operations for providers serving customers in both China and elsewhere.

The Financial Times says Nvidia's sales representatives and regional teams have communicated the restrictions directly to customers, but the company apparently hasn't issued formal written documentation.

The reported move introduces a new limitation on how Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure can be used, adding another consideration for data center operators navigating business relationships with China.

Binance describes the $6 billion North Korean heist.

North Korea has launched several missiles toward the sea, hours after rejecting FBI accusations that its hackers stole more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Pyongyang denies responsibility and says the accusations undermine prospects for renewed diplomacy with Washington.

Meanwhile, Binance has revealed how the attack unfolded. Hackers spent months compromising three engineers' computers, using malicious software disguised as developer tools and a fake job interview featuring a rigged coding assignment.

Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. The company hasn't explained precisely how the AI tool was abused.

Binance says approximately $2.85 billion in stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted, and affected systems have been rebuilt.

Barracuda patches Email Security Gateway vulnerabilities.

Barracuda Networks is urging customers to patch two vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances that could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges.

One critical flaw enables unauthorized changes to global configurations, while the second allows users with administrator permissions to inject operating system commands.

Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces. Chaining the vulnerabilities could allow them to bypass authorization controls and gain root access.

The company has released patches and recommends updating firmware, applying security fixes, and restricting administrative access to trusted internal networks.

Gartner predicts SOCs will shift toward more engineers.

By 2028, security operations centers could employ 50 percent more engineers than analysts, according to a new Gartner report. The shift reflects AI's growing ability to handle routine security alerts, freeing human analysts to focus on investigating cases, making decisions, and coordinating responses.

Gartner predicts SOCs won't necessarily shrink. Instead, engineers will increasingly build, test, and refine AI workflows, while analysts expand into threat hunting and exposure management.

The transition creates challenges for entry-level analysts, who traditionally learned their craft by processing alerts. Organizations will need new approaches to training and developing expertise.

Gartner also recommends replacing traditional alert-volume metrics with measures of case accuracy and decision quality.

By 2030, the firm expects SOCs to become more proactive, continuously testing their own defenses rather than primarily responding to alerts.

Canadians are indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities.

Two Canadian men have been indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities to steal data and mine cryptocurrency.

Prosecutors say Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings targeted institutions in four states between 2016 and 2019, deploying malware, stealing credentials, and exploiting university supercomputers. They allegedly used servers registered under false identities and compromised systems to conceal their activities.

Roach has been extradited to the United States, while Stubbings awaits extradition. Both face up to ten years in prison and fines of $250,000 if convicted.

Stick with us after the break, we are joined by Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. And….

Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box,sat down with me to discuss Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. Here’s our conversation.

That was Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. If you enjoyed this conversation check out the full interview in the show notes.

AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

WIRED's Will Knight decided to see whether artificial intelligence could outperform him at fantasy soccer. He assembled a team of AI agents, handed them control of his lineup, and waited for the tactical brilliance to begin.

Their opening move? Bench Erling Haaland, one of the world's most prolific goal scorers. Not exactly an auspicious start.

The AI eventually reconsidered, but its subsequent decisions haven't been particularly impressive. After several weeks, Knight's AI-managed team still hasn't outperformed the average fantasy squad.

Meanwhile, researchers studying AI forecasting have found that leading models can sometimes outperform ordinary people at predicting events, although expert human forecasters generally remain formidable competition. Some experiments suggest AI is closing that gap.

Knight suspects AI could eventually become an unbeatable fantasy manager. But he's not particularly enthusiastic about that prospect. After all, fantasy sports are supposed to reward human judgment, even when that judgment is spectacularly wrong.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

General Security News.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
General Security News.context: Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their...
General Security News.full_text:
Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.

Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.”

In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.

Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.

Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.

Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks, a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI.

Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.

“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”

Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

General Security News.title: Who Holds the Keys to Your ChatGPT Workspace?
General Security News.context: Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal...
General Security News.full_text:
Picture a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace a year after rollout. The IT lead who bought the licenses is still an Owner. So are the two admins she added during a busy week, and the director who asked for access “just to check something.” A contractor who left in the spring still has an account, because he was added by hand instead of through the identity provider. And a service account someone set up to run Codex jobs has a credential that never expires.

None of this is unusual. It’s what happens when a tool goes from pilot to every department in a few months, and nobody’s job is to keep an eye on the admin console.

Most of the security conversation around ChatGPT is about what people paste into it, and that’s fair. OpenAI’s Compliance Platform lets DLP and data security tools read conversations. But a more basic question usually goes unanswered: who actually holds the keys to the workspace?

Why nobody owns this

ChatGPT Enterprise falls between teams, so each one assumes someone else is watching it:

Identity teams own the identity provider, but SCIM provisioning to ChatGPT is optional. Anyone added directly in the admin console never shows up in their access reviews.

Cloud security teams own AWS, Azure, and GCP. A ChatGPT workspace isn’t a cloud account, so their CNAPP never sees it.

The workspace owner is usually whoever bought the licenses. Owner access gets handed out to get things done, and it rarely gets taken back.

Rolling out an enterprise AI platform is still the right call. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal accounts. But someone still has to check how that tool is set up.

What Orca checks in ChatGPT Enterprise

You connect ChatGPT Enterprise to Orca with one read-only Admin API key. There’s nothing to install and no change to how anyone uses ChatGPT. Orca pulls in every user, group, service account, and service-account credential in the workspace, and flags issues like these out of the box:

Orca detects

Why it matters

A user with the workspace Owner role

Owners control every setting, member and key in the workspace. Each one is a high-value account

A workspace with more than three owners

Owner access tends to spread and rarely gets revoked. The same rule applies to Azure subscriptions and Supabase

A service-account credential with no expiration date

A token that never expires stays valid long after the job or person that needed it is gone

A service-account credential not rotated in 90 days

OpenAI suggests token lifetimes of 7 to 90 days. Older tokens have had more time to leak

A user not provisioned through the identity provider

Users added by hand skip your joiner-mover-leaver process, so offboarding may never reach them

A group managed by hand instead of synced from the identity provider

Manual groups drift from the access you approved in the IdP

A group with no members

Empty groups are leftovers that can quietly grant access to the next person added

Screenshot caption: A ChatGPT service-account credential with no expiration date, shown in Orca with its workspace, creation date and remediation steps.

ChatGPT belongs next to the rest of your risk

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security brings those parts into one platform. ChatGPT Enterprise sits next to Claude Enterprise at the model layer, alongside Vercel and your AWS, Azure, and GCP accounts.

That matters because OpenAI shows up in a lot more places than the ChatGPT admin console. At most companies, it looks something like this:

ChatGPT owners get reviewed in a spreadsheet once a quarter, if at all.

A DLP tool reads chats, a secrets scanner finds OpenAI API keys in repos, and the CNAPP covers Azure OpenAI.

Each tool sees its own piece, so nobody can say how exposed the company is to OpenAI overall. In Orca, ChatGPT users, groups, and credentials sit in the same inventory as OpenAI API keys found in code and container images, workloads calling OpenAI models (seen by the Orca Sensor), and Azure OpenAI resources. They land in the same queue as your Claude Enterprise and Vercel findings, too.

Screenshot caption: The Orca AI Security dashboard showing ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise workspaces side by side with cloud AI services.

The goal isn’t to slow anyone down. Your builders keep using ChatGPT the way they already do, and security finally gets a clear look at who holds the keys, without reading a single prompt.

Want to see your ChatGPT Enterprise workspace in Orca? Book a demo today.

About the Orca Platform

Orca Security delivers security for the companies that build. As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. Trusted by hundreds of organizations, including SAP, Autodesk, Gannett, Lemonade, and Digital Turbine, Orca is backed by leading investors including Temasek, CapitalG, ICONIQ Capital, and Redpoint Ventures.

General Security News.title: Rapid7 Achieves ISO/IEC 42001 Certification for its AI Management System
General Security News.context: Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)
General Security News.full_text:
Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider.

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle.

This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active.

Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important?

AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability.

It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point.

As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model. Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. Customers remain in control of how they use AI outputs within their own security operations.

Which AI systems are in scope?

The certification covers the AIMS supporting the following AI systems developed within Rapid7 products:

Agentic AI Workflow for MDR (Managed Detection and Response)

AI Dashboard Summary Card (Managed Detection and Response)

AI-Generated Risk Summaries (Exposure Command and Surface Command)

AI-Powered Log Search (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

AI-Powered Log Summary (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

Attack Surface Management (Surface Command)

ICS Runtime Event Story (InsightCloudSec / Cloud Runtime)

Most of these are capabilities customers use directly within the product. Agentic AI Workflow for MDR supports Rapid7's own SOC analysts as they investigate and respond on behalf of MDR customers.

What's next?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification joins Rapid7's existing security and compliance program, which includes ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, IRAP, ENS, BSI C5, as well as U.S. and international cybersecurity regulations. Each is independently assessed against its own defined scope, with details available in the Rapid7 Trust Center (reach out to your Account Executive for access).

As our AI capabilities grow, our AI governance program will grow with them. As such, we'll update this post if the scope of certification changes.

Customers can request a copy of the certificate through their Account Executive or Rapid7 representative. The certificate can also be independently verified in Schellman's public certificate directory.

General Security News.title: Researchers Uncover Prompt Adware Hidden in OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit
General Security News.context: " As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026
General Security News.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway.

The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research.

Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses.

"The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service."

Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails.

The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top."

Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering.

However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026.

It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants.

What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface.

"The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said.

While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks.

"As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

General Security News.title: Cloud Agent, now in a Container: Host Security for Nodes You Can’t Touch
General Security News.context: TotalCloud KCS also holds the Red Hat Vulnerability Scanner Certification, which extends its detection accuracy to Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, and CoreOS
General Security News.full_text:
A single container image that brings Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node, on immutable and mutable Linux alike, deployed the way your container workloads already are.

Key Takeaways

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image on Docker Hub, bringing host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node without touching the host’s package manager.

It runs as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so every node that joins the cluster automatically gets an agent. It can be deployed and upgraded through YAML manifests or a unified Helm chart that also deploys Qualys Container Security sensors, for full-stack coverage in a single install.

A single image covers container-optimized operating systems such as AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS, and Red Hat CoreOS, as well as RPM- and Debian-based Linux, including Azure Linux, on both Intel/x64 and ARM.

Policy Audit includes CIS-certified policies for AWS Bottlerocket and Google Container-Optimized OS, and all findings are prioritized with Qualys TruRisk alongside the rest of your estate.

Paired with Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS), it delivers full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane.

The AI Era Is a Container Era

The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now.

That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it.

Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads.

The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms

For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways.

Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container.

Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically.

The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload.

The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account. It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager.

Qualys Cloud Agent container images on Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher.

The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it.

Intel/x64 image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-x64

ARM image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-arm

How Qualys secures the container stack, from the host operating system to running containers and the Kubernetes control plane.

Once you’ve pulled the image, you can download the deployment YAMLs, and a Qualys Helm chart is published on Artifact Hub so the agent can be installed, versioned, and upgraded through the same Helm workflow as the rest of your cluster.

Why It Matters: The Benefits

Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection.

Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems

Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. If you can’t install anything, you can’t install a traditional agent, and many teams have run these nodes blind. The Containerized Cloud Agent closes that gap. It runs as a privileged container with the host mounts it needs to assess the underlying OS, so Bottlerocket, COS, and CoreOS nodes get the same vulnerability and compliance visibility as a conventional Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) server, with no changes to the host image and no compromise to the immutability that made you choose that OS in the first place.

Qualys has been building this coverage across the major cloud platforms for years:

Securing Red Hat CoreOS on OpenShift

Scanning AWS Bottlerocket in Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS

Scanning Container-Optimized OS in Google Kubernetes Engine

Qualys for Microsoft Azure Linux in AKS and Azure Container Instances

Your Choice of Agent on Mutable Linux, Too

The Containerized Cloud Agent isn’t limited to immutable operating systems. It also runs on the RPM- and Debian-based distributions that make up the bulk of self-managed and cloud Kubernetes nodes today. That’s a meaningful change. Previously, a RHEL or Ubuntu node meant installing the RPM or DEB package, full stop. Now you choose. Teams with a mix of virtual machines (VMs) and containers can keep the package on VMs and use the Containerized Cloud Agent on cluster nodes. Teams that are all-in on Kubernetes can standardize on the Containerized Cloud Agent everywhere and never manage a host package again. Either way, the data lands in the same place, with the same detections and the same TruRisk scoring.

Deployment That Fits How You Already Run Kubernetes

The Containerized Cloud Agent is a DaemonSet, which means the orchestrator guarantees one agent per node, on every node, for the life of the cluster. Autoscaling node pools, spot instances that get reclaimed, and cluster upgrades that replace every node are all handled without a ticket, a script, or a human. Coverage becomes a property of the cluster rather than a task someone has to remember.

Because it’s delivered as a Helm chart and YAML manifests, the agent lives in the same GitOps repository as your workloads. Upgrading is a tag change and a pull request. Rolling back is a revert. Node selectors and tolerations let you target specific pools, and the same manifest works across dev, staging, and production. Security stops being the exception to your deployment model.

One Image Across Every Operating System

You don’t need a Bottlerocket build, a CoreOS build, and an Ubuntu build. A single Containerized Cloud Agent image runs across all supported operating systems. That collapses your deployment matrix: one image to vet through your supply-chain controls, one image to pin and version, one DaemonSet manifest to maintain. When a new agent release ships, it’s one tag to update across the entire estate. Images that comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are available for environments that require them.

Complete Coverage Across Intel and ARM

Cluster node pools increasingly mix x86 and ARM instances, with Graviton, Cobalt, and Axion sitting alongside traditional Intel and AMD nodes. Images are published for both Intel/x64 and ARM, so a multi-architecture cluster gets consistent coverage without special-casing by pool.

Full-Stack Coverage at a Glance

The Containerized Cloud Agent runs the complete Qualys Cloud Agent on every node, assessing the host OS against the Qualys KnowledgeBase for vulnerabilities and against Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks through Qualys Policy Audit. Here’s how coverage splits across the stack:

Capability

Covered by

Vulnerability Management

Drift detection

Data plane: Qualys Policy Audit. Control plane: TotalCloud KCS (Kubernetes Security Posture Management, or KSPM)

Threat detection and response/runtime security

TotalCloud KCS, via eBPF runtime sensors

Findings from both Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit flow into the same Enterprise TruRisk Platform views, dashboards, and workflows your teams already use. A Kubernetes node is just another asset with a Qualys TruRisk score, sitting next to the VM, the laptop, and the cloud account, and prioritized the same way.

Getting Started

Pull the image from Docker Hub: Intel/x64 or ARM.

Download the deployment YAMLs or use the Qualys Helm chart.

Deploy as a DaemonSet to your cluster with your Agent Activation Key, following the Intel or ARM getting started guide.

Platform-specific guides are available for AWS Bottlerocket, Google COS, and Red Hat CoreOS.

Coming in Cloud Agent 2.9.0

Today, images are available on Docker Hub. With Cloud Agent release 2.9.0, you’ll be able to download the Containerized Cloud Agent package directly from the Qualys platform alongside every other Cloud Agent installer. The Common Container tiles will appear in the Download and Install Cloud Agent workflow, with your activation key, supported OS list, and installation steps right there.

Common Container installation instructions in the Qualys Cloud Platform (Cloud Agent 2.9.0).

The Host Is Half the Story: Securing the Whole Container Stack with TotalCloud

The Containerized Cloud Agent secures the layer beneath your workloads. It doesn’t look inside the containers running on top of it, and it isn’t meant to. That job belongs to Qualys TotalCloud, and the two are designed as complementary halves of a single answer to the question every platform team eventually has to answer: how exposed are our container workloads, end to end?

Container risk doesn’t live in one layer. It spans the cloud account the cluster runs in, the node operating systems, the Kubernetes control plane and its configuration, the images in your registries, the containers running in production, and the identities and network paths that connect all of it. Securing any one of those layers in isolation leaves you with a partial view and a false sense of coverage. TotalCloud is built to cover all of them on one platform, with one risk score.

Container Security: From Registry to Runtime

TotalCloud’s Container Security sensor picks up where the host agent leaves off. Deployed as a lightweight container alongside your workloads, it discovers and inventories every image, container, and cluster across your environment and assesses them at every stage of the lifecycle:

Build and registry: images are scanned for OS and application-layer vulnerabilities and embedded secrets as they land in registries or move through continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, so a critical Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry in a base layer is caught before it’s ever deployed, and admission policies can block it from being scheduled at all.

Running containers: containers in production are continuously assessed against the same KnowledgeBase, with drift detection that flags containers that no longer match the image they were launched from.

Kubernetes posture: clusters, namespaces, workloads, and role-based access control (RBAC) are assessed against CIS Kubernetes Benchmarks and best practices to surface over-privileged pods, exposed dashboards, missing network policies, and other control-plane misconfigurations.

Runtime defense: behavioral monitoring of running containers detects and blocks malicious activity such as unexpected process execution, file tampering, and anomalous network connections, so an exploit that slips past the earlier stages is caught in the act.

TotalCloud KCS also holds the Red Hat Vulnerability Scanner Certification, which extends its detection accuracy to Red Hat OpenShift, RHEL, and CoreOS.

Want to see how TotalCloud secures containers from registry to runtime?

Start Free Trial

Cloud Posture, Identity, and Infrastructure-as-Code

Clusters don’t run in vacuums. TotalCloud’s cloud security posture management (CSPM) continuously assesses the AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts your clusters live in, covering misconfigured storage, over-permissive identity and access management (IAM) roles, exposed services, and hundreds of other controls mapped to CIS and regulatory frameworks. Infrastructure-as-code scanning applies the same checks to Terraform, CloudFormation, and Kubernetes manifests in your repositories, so misconfigurations are fixed in the pull request rather than in production. Together, they close the loop around the cluster itself.

One Risk Picture, Scored with TruRisk

What makes this a platform rather than a collection of tools is that every finding, from the host agent, the container sensor, and the cloud posture assessment, is normalized, correlated, and scored with TruRisk in one place. That changes what you can see. A vulnerable kernel on a Bottlerocket node, a critical CVE in a base image, an over-privileged pod running on that node, and a public ingress in front of it are no longer four alerts in four consoles. They’re one attack path, with one risk score, and one clear answer to what to fix first. The same correlation lets you dismiss noise with confidence: a critical CVE in an image that never runs, on a node with no external exposure, is scored accordingly.

And because it’s all on the Enterprise TruRisk Platform, container risk sits alongside the rest of your attack surface. The Kubernetes node, the VM it replaced, the developer laptop that pushed the image, and the cloud account that owns all of them are managed, prioritized, and reported on the same way, by the same teams, with the same workflows.

Close the Gap from Host to Cloud

A clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload. Pull the Containerized Cloud Agent from Docker Hub today and bring your Kubernetes nodes into the same Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit coverage as the rest of your estate. Then talk to your Qualys representative about TotalCloud to extend that coverage from the host to every image, container, cluster, and cloud account your workloads depend on.
