General Security News.title: Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3
General Security News.context: On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be...
General Security News.full_text:
What happened?

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be derived from their public certificates. The derived private keys can be used to issue certificates for any domain, and software that trusts the eMudhra root will accept them.

Mozilla, Google, Apple, and Cloudflare have blocked the affected intermediates. Mozilla has removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from its trust store, and Chrome will remove it on October 27, 2026. eMudhra has revoked the intermediates.

Okta’s response

Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3 and the eight affected intermediates across our services.

Security Patching Services: The change has been deployed across Okta’s production environment. The change is continuing to roll out across Auth0 production.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

Only if Okta or Auth0 connects to a server you control and that server's certificate chain includes the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3. Inbound access to Okta and Auth0, including sign-in, is not affected.

The case to check is a non-browser connection or webhook that calls your own API, such as an Okta Inline Hook or Event Hook, or Auth0 Action, Custom Database connection, or Auth0 Federated Connection.

These connections may not have shown you any error before now. Run

openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <your-host>:443

and look for "emSign" in the chain. If you find it, replace the certificate with one from another trusted CA. Connections to that endpoint will fail once our change is applied to your tenant.

References

eMudhra Statement on distrust of select Global TLS Intermediate and one Root CA

Google - Protecting Chrome and Android Users from Compromised eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates

Mozilla - Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates

General Security News.title: What We Missed: Feds Lasso Texas Laptop Farms
General Security News.context: In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from busting up North Korea's stateside infrastructure in "Operation Lonestar...
General Security News.full_text:
The US government is striking back against the ever-persistent threat of fake IT worker schemes run by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

In this episode of "What We Missed," Dark Reading's Rob Wright and Alex Culafi discuss some of the recent news events and topics that didn't make it into the publication, starting with FBI raids across more than 40 Texas residences that were allegedly running "laptop farms."

The law-enforcement action, dubbed “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” seized 187 devices, charged 14 people, and arrested individuals accused of facilitating North Korean threat actors running fake IT worker schemes. The schemes disrupted by Operation Lonestar Roundup impacted more than 70 US companies, according to the FBI.

Fake IT worker schemes typically involve DPRK actors masquerading as IT professionals and developers, either using fake or stolen identities, to gain employment at US companies. The threat actors then use their positions to exfiltrate sensitive data, steal intellectual property, and gather intelligence.

Related:Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained After Planting Secret Recorder at HQ

Also discussed on this episode: Russian police arrested alleged members of a cybercriminal group known as the "DataSuckers," which has taken credit for several breaches against companies in Russia and Ukraine; and according to a report from 404 Media, a Chinese criminal operation breached Staples' internal customer support system and used it to issue thousands of gift cards, worth $5 million.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles.

What We Missed With Rob Wright & Alex Culafi: Full Transcript

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright with Dark Reading.

Dark Reading's Alex Culafi: And I'm Alex Culafi with Dark Reading.

DR's Rob Wright: And this is "What We Missed," a discussion about some of the recent headlines we did not get a chance to cover in the pages, pods, or videos of Dark Reading. Alex, this is an eventful one. We don't have any real AI news, so that's good. We get a break from AI news.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yep.

DR's Rob Wright: But we'll kick it off with an interesting one. So there was a big federal crackdown on North Korean IT worker schemes. There was a raid on a laptop farm in Texas. An interesting one. An interestingly titled operation. Busted a bunch of laptop farms. And yeah, it seems like the government is getting into the business of trying to take down these North Korean IT worker schemes. What'd you think of this?

Related:When AI Agents Commit Breaches, Humans May Not Be Held Liable

DR's Alex Culafi: I think this is an issue that will persist for a while, which isn't very specific. But I guess I'm thinking about … I was watching something about this on YouTube the other day, even, and it was about a woman who was an office worker — I think this was back in like 2024 — who had gotten hired for a job, and she was just like a normal, nice, well-intended Southern lady. And they were sending her laptops and she thought she was just doing her job, and then it turns out that she was hooking up dozens of laptops. And later on in the video I think it sort of went into maybe she knew more than she was letting on at first.

DR's Rob Wright: Right.

DR's Alex Culafi: But I do think, especially in times of economic hardship — which a lot of the US is in right now, and a lot of the world is experiencing right now — I think we're gonna continue to see these stories where normal people who don't see themselves as spies or as traitors to the United States, or as sympathetic to the North Korean regime or whatever, are gonna get in these situations. Now, this sounds like a farm, which is a little different.

DR's Rob Wright: A little different.

Related:Prominent Ransomware Negotiator Faces Extortion Charges

DR's Alex Culafi: But as we're on this topic, I think this story — whether it's a farm or it's a person who didn't realize what they were doing at first and then found themselves too deep in — I think we're going to see this for a while, no?

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, yeah. I think we're going to see more operations like this. So, first of all, I had a tough time intro-ing this one because the operation is called "Operation Lonestar Roundup." And every time I hear Lonestar I — and this is my cross to bear — but I think of Spaceballs and I just start cracking up.

DR's Alex Culafi: [laughs] OK.

DR's Rob Wright: That aside, no, the data here is interesting. One hundred and eighty-seven devices seized. I think there were 14 people who were charged. I think there were a few arrests. But to your point, I think this is like a gig economy thing. I mean, we've had laptop farms for other stuff — click fraud, malvertising, stuff like that — for a long time. And I think we're just gonna start to see more schemes like this take advantage of existing laptop farms and people that, to your point, may not totally know what they're doing or who's using them. So we'll see.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yep. And the thing I'll also add is thinking about where things were with this North Korean IT worker fraud back a couple of years ago. I know it extends further back than that. When it was still new and popping off, a lot of researchers we were talking to were like, 'No, this is real and this is a big problem.'

DR's Rob Wright: Yes. Yep.

DR's Alex Culafi: And I doubted them at the time because I thought it was just the new story to talk about to get press attention. And maybe it also was that. But no, totally. This is pervasive. Organizations at every level are dealing with North Korean operators trying to either get paychecks to send back to North Korea or to get data that they can use to exploit later, and it's — I don't know if it's getting uglier, but it remains very ugly a few years later.

DR's Rob Wright: Yes, indeed. What've got next here?

DR's Alex Culafi: We have an interesting story. Russian authorities arrested three suspected members of the hacking group Data Suckers, including a 19-year-old member. And this is following the breach of Russian pizza chain Dodo Pizza —

DR's Rob Wright: Of course.

DR's Alex Culafi: — which is a longstanding pizza chain in Russia, that reportedly exposed massive amounts of customer data. A lot of that would have been Russian customers, obviously. The group has also claimed attacks against Tez Tour, which is a Russian travel company, and Ukrainian grocery giant ATB, which is very unusual. Because by all accounts, expert accounts, they don't seem to be politically motivated in the same way that a lot of Russian operators are, either working on behalf of the Russian government or actively participating in the war on Ukraine.

But it's doubly interesting because for as long as I can remember, one of the golden rules among Russian hackers was not to hack Russians, for multiple reasons. One, because the government can sometimes provide cover for you, I've heard, for the activities you're doing externally. And two, Russian authorities, if they think you're messing with their civilians, they are very, very harsh, historically.

DR's Rob Wright: Yes.

DR's Alex Culafi: So this is really interesting that it's Russia arresting Russian hackers. What do you think of this?

DR's Rob Wright: I also thought it was interesting. I'm a little confused, I admit. When I read the story, one of the alleged DataSuckers hackers is a 19-year-old named Dennis Fridman. That does not sound like a Russian surname to me. So I don't know where he hails from, if he was just living there, or if he is a Russian citizen. The thing that, to your points, the thing that really stuck out to me beyond Russia making some arrests here was I immediately thought, we're failing the kids these days. We're failing them.

DR's Alex Culafi: Mm-hmm.

DR's Rob Wright: These guys, this is just another example of an organization, a hacking group with teenagers who are obviously skilled and can do stuff that's just out there. They're like, "Let's hack Dodo Pizza." I mean, I don't know. We gotta start recruiting these kids — the government, and preferably not the Russian government, but the US, Canada, Five Eyes, whatever. We need to get out there and start finding these guys on like game forums and whatnot. Because this is just getting out of control with the number of quote-unquote kids who are doing this stuff.

This came up in the documentary Midnight in the War Room. There's a segment all about this, about how hackers get into the cybercriminal lifestyle. And it's all younger kids, you know, preteens, teenagers, that are big gamers and then they get into this stuff. And now, the next thing you know, they're in a Russian gulag. Well, I don't know that this guy's going to a Russian gulag or any of them are, but you get the point.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yeah. No, and your point is also valid. Maybe Russia does hire these kids. They say, 'Hey, we'll let you go, but also we own your career now.'

DR's Rob Wright: I know, I know. Yeah.

DR's Alex Culafi: And then, you know, maybe that's an appealing deal for them. Maybe they treat them right, or maybe they do send them to a gulag. Who knows? But it is interesting. Russia-on-Russia hacking. Yep.

DR's Rob Wright: Indeed, indeed. All right. Last up, we have a story ... I think this just happened this week. It is from 404 Media. There was a big breach at Staples. Apparently, a cybercrime ring out of China hacked into Staples' support system and issued $5 million, churning out gift cards. Gift cards are just shooting out, and $5 million worth of these gift cards. And I guess the 404 Media reporters found this in court records. Raises a lot of questions for me about why this was not ... I guess this was not disclosed prior to this.

But gift cards, yeah. A big breach, a big breach of a customer support system. And we know from other attacks similar to this, when you get into a support system, you can do quite a bit of damage. You can obtain a lot of secrets. You can obtain a lot of sensitive data. This one really was a little surprising to me. So Alex, what'd you think of this?

DR's Alex Culafi: Stinks, obviously. I hope that —

DR's Rob Wright: [laughs]

DR's Alex Culafi: No, I mean, it's a tough one, right? Because you hope that they can track these gift card serial numbers and invalidate them.

DR's Rob Wright: Exactly, yeah.

DR's Alex Culafi: Or that insurance takes care of it. And this is a little off track, but I kind of have a soft spot for modern Staples as like one of these little companies that are a place where you can get passports, where you can get the international clearance to travel. They have great copy printing services and they seem like a company that should have shuttered a long time ago but is finding new ways to become relevant in the 21st century, the 2020s. So I hope they figure this out. Other than that, for the purposes of a cybersecurity audience, I don't know what else to say other than it stinks. I don't know.

DR's Rob Wright: I know, I know. I mean, there's a lot of details here that have not been cleared up about how the hackers got into — I think it was called Nexus — the internal sort of support system, how they were able to get into applications or processes or systems to issue these gift cards. But 15,000 gift cards?

And you know what they use them for — scams and whatnot. And they use it to launder money. And I just think it's one of these cases where I'm sure Staples ... their cybersecurity posture is probably pretty good, but this is one area that maybe they didn't shore up because they didn't think it was going to be targeted. And it's like, every part of your infrastructure and your network and your environment is going to be targeted these days if you're a big company. So, you know, it's a painful lesson.

DR's Alex Culafi: You know, that's true. And especially as these AI-orchestrated attacks get more powerful, the idea that having one blind spot will hurt you. But I don't know. This is tough, and it kind of stinks that maybe their posture is good elsewhere, but it just takes one weakness, one blind spot for something like this to happen.

DR's Rob Wright: Exactly.

DR's Alex Culafi: So I don't know if there's a lesson learned, but it is a bummer.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah. All right, well, that's it for this week, Alex. Thank you so much for joining me. I appreciate it.

DR's Alex Culafi: Thanks, Rob.

General Security News.title: Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour
General Security News.context: ICS/OT Security Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Cyber Risk Vulnerabilities & Threats Research Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around...
General Security News.full_text:
Read in English: Click Here

This translation is provided by our internal AI translation tool.

Des centaines de supermarchés français ont subi cette semaine des pertes s'élevant à plusieurs dizaines, voire plusieurs centaines de millions d'euros, à la suite de cyberattaques qui ont perturbé leurs systèmes de réfrigération.

Dans la nuit de lundi, des pirates informatiques ont piraté les contrôleurs des systèmes de réfrigération commerciaux de grandes chaînes de supermarchés françaises. Ils ont transformé les réfrigérateurs, les congélateurs et les chambres froides en appareils de chauffage, faisant grimper leur température jusqu’à 50 degrés Celsius (plus de 120 degrés Fahrenheit), ce qui a complètement abîmé tous les aliments qu’ils contenaient et aurait même provoqué quelques petits incendies. L’identité et les motivations de l’auteur de cette attaque restent inconnues.

Les contrôleurs de réfrigération permettent aux commerçants de régler et de surveiller à distance la température de leurs réfrigérateurs, 24 heures sur 24 et 7 jours sur 7. Il s’ensuit donc que les gérants de magasin auraient pu être alertés ou se rendre compte manuellement que quelque chose n’allait pas. Pour empêcher cela, des sources françaises indiquent que les attaquants ont prolongé les cycles de dégivrage des systèmes ciblés — processus au cours duquel les congélateurs font fondre intentionnellement le givre et la glace accumulés — afin que le réchauffement passe pour un entretien de routine.

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Selon les propres rapports des entreprises, les attaques ont touché un peu plus de 700 magasins d’alimentation et commerces de détail, tous au cours de la même nuit. Un analyste de la société française de cybersécurité Sekoia a déclaré à Reuters que l’Espagne, le Portugal, la Pologne, l’Allemagne et la Belgique avaient également été touchés, et qu’une grande chaîne de supermarchés aux Pays-Bas avait mis ses systèmes hors service par mesure de précaution, selon l’AP. Une seule chaîne française, Intermarché, a fait état de pertes s’élevant à plusieurs dizaines de millions d’euros.

Pire encore, les experts soulignent que ces attaques auraient très certainement pu être évitéesgrâce à des mesures élémentaires de cybersécurité.

Qu'est-ce qui a provoqué l'incendie des congélateurs ?

Les premiers rapports suggéraient que les attaques de lundi étaient liées aux contrôleurs de réfrigération du fabricant danois Danfoss. Danfoss occupe une place importante dans le domaine des solutions de contrôle pour les supermarchés et la grande distribution alimentaire, avec plus de 50 000 installations de sa technologie à travers le monde, selon son site web.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

Le 9 août, des chercheurs en cybersécurité de l’équipe Team82 de Claroty ont révélé trois vulnérabilités dans la plateforme AK-SM 800A de Danfoss. Ces failles — référencées sous les numéros CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451 et CVE-2025-41452 — permettaient aux attaquants de procéder à l’exécution de code à distance (RCE) ou à un déni de service (DoS) contre les parcs de réfrigération des entreprises. Danfoss a corrigé ces failles mais comptait sur ses clients pour mettre à jour eux-mêmes leurs systèmes.

Dans une déclaration à Reuters, Danfoss a rejeté la responsabilité sur les clients utilisant un micrologiciel obsolète, indiquant qu’elle « conseillait depuis longtemps à ses clients de maintenir les systèmes pris en charge à jour avec le dernier micrologiciel et de migrer les systèmes hérités vers des solutions de dernière génération ».Le fabricant d'équipement d'origine (OEM) a fourni davantage d'informations à une publication spécialisée dans la réfrigération, Cooling Post. Selon lui, la « majorité » des unités concernées fonctionnaient sous AK-SM 800 ou son prédécesseur, l'AK-SC355. Ces deux systèmes ont depuis longtemps atteint leur fin de vie : le premier en 2021, le second en 2016.

Related:AI-Driven Cyberattack on Mexico Couldn't Breach OT Systems

Mardi, le CERT national français (CERT-FR) avait identifié qu’une autre plateforme de contrôleurs de réfrigération — « XWEB », des fournisseurs Dixell et de sa société mère Copeland — avait également été impliquée dans les attaques. Il n’a pas précisé quelles vulnérabilités ou versions de micrologiciel pouvaient être en cause, bien que les indices circonstanciels indiquent désormais clairement que les auteurs de ces menaces s’appuient sur les recherches de Team82. Le jour même où ils ont révélé ces vulnérabilités affectant Danfoss, ces mêmes chercheurs ont divulgué 23 autres touchant XWEB Pro, dont 21 de gravité élevée.

Les commerçants ont été avertis de possibles attaques contre leurs réfrigérateurs

Le 26 août, une série étrange de rapports similaires a commencé à filtrer depuis des installations militaires américaines.Les groupes frigorifiques tombaient en panne. Dans chaque base où cela se produisait, les gens ont probablement pensé qu’il s’agissait d’un problème électrique inhabituel. Mais peu à peu, de plus en plus de sites ont signalé le même phénomène.

Après être tombée sur ces rapports étranges sur les réseaux sociaux, une journaliste indépendante a émis une hypothèse hasardeuse. « Je suis suffisamment lucide pour savoir que cela semble insensé, mais je vous demande de me suivre », a écrit M. Elizabeth sur Substack. « Je pense qu’il y a une probabilité non nulle que quelqu’un ait piraté les congélateurs des commissariats. »

À ce jour, l’armée américaine n’a pas confirmé qui ou quoi était à l’origine des pannes survenues dans les cantines réparties sur au moins 14 bases de l’armée de l’air, installations de la marine et postes de l’armée de terre distincts. Il se pourrait que ce soit une coïncidence que ces attaques aient eu lieu seulement deux semaines après la divulgation des vulnérabilités par Danfoss.

Ce serait d’autant plus une coïncidence que la Defense Commissary Agency (DeCA) — l’agence centrale du ministère de la Défense (DoD) chargée de superviser les magasins militaires — a explicitement mentionné avoir utilisé les technologies de Danfoss par le passé. Par exemple, dans un modèle de cahier des charges techniquedestiné aux prestataires des magasins militaires datant de juin 2022, la DeCA citait le Danfoss AK-SM 800A comme « base de conception » pour les différentes unités de contrôle.

Attention, commerçants du monde entier

Fort de son expérience, Bill Moore, PDG de Xona Systems, se souvient : « Dans bon nombre de ces magasins physiques — mais aussi dans les usines de fabrication, les centrales électriques, les sites pétroliers et gaziers, c’est le cas partout —, le plus gros problème est que les organisations parviennent plutôt bien à segmenter leurs propres réseaux. Mais en matière de technologies opérationnelles (OT), il y a tous ces équipementiers et tiers qui ont besoin d’un accès. Et les entreprises n’y ont pas vraiment prêté attention. »

En accordant à de nombreux fournisseurs et équipementiers l’accès à leurs systèmes, les entreprises finissent par s’exposer à des attaques à distance. « Et il n’y a littéralement aucune visibilité ni gouvernance sur bon nombre de ces connexions. Je dirais que c’est vrai dans un pourcentage élevé de cas — la moitié, peut-être plus, dans l’ensemble. Elles laissent en quelque sorte tous leurs équipementiers agir à leur guise, mais nous avons constaté que de nombreux pirates compromettent ces connexions tierces », déplore-t-il.

Dans un e-mail adressé à CNBC, Les Mousquetaires — société mère d’Intermarché et de Netto — a expliqué que l’attaque avait eu lieu via un prestataire de services chargé des systèmes de réfrigération dans certains de ses magasins.

« En résumé : déconnectez vos équipements d’Internet », déclare Andrew Ginter, vice-président chargé de la sécurité industrielle chez Waterfall Security Solutions. Les recherches effectuées cette semaine sur Shodan ont par exemple révélé des milliers de systèmes Danfoss exposés sur Internet, dont environ 1 500 rien qu’en France.

« Dans un monde idéal, les entreprises protégeraient leurs systèmes de contrôle derrière un accès à distance contrôlé par du matériel », explique M. Ginter, « mais même un simple pare-feu entre ces appareils et Internet serait déjà utile. »

Pour les pare-feu de base, il conseille aux entreprises :

De mettre en place une règle « tout refuser »

De n’autoriser les connexions qu’à partir d’adresses IP spécifiques

D’appliquer un mot de passe et une authentification à deux facteurs à ces connexion

De mettre à jour automatiquement le pare-feu, pour éviter de l’oublier

Utilisent des appareils de qualité commerciale ou industrielle, et non grand public ; de nombreux appareils grand public ne proposent pas de mises à jour, ou ne se mettent pas à jour rapidement

Enfin, ajoute-t-il, « Remplacez le pare-feu strictement tous les quatre ans. Pourquoi ? Parce que si nous avons des appareils exposés à Internet, neuf fois sur dix, nous n’avons pas d’équipe de sécurité, et nous ne remarquerons pas quand nos pare-feu ne seront plus pris en charge et que les mises à jour automatiques cesseront. »

« Les mesures de base ne suffisent pas pour les infrastructures critiques de grande envergure ou l’industrie lourde, mais elles contribueront grandement à empêcher les hacktivistes de s’introduire dans vos congélateurs », conclut Ginter. « Retirez vos équipements d’Internet. Faites-le de toute urgence. »

General Security News.title: How to contain shadow AI, as it takes on multiple forms and spreads throughout your environment
General Security News.context: That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data
General Security News.full_text:
Shadow AI used to be confined to a few simple scenarios, such as AI chatbots and AI browser extensions. Today, it spans a broad spectrum of complex vectors, making it harder to detect and control. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how employee security training, AI usage governance, and exposure management can help you tackle shadow AI successfully.

Key takeaways

Integrating shadow AI into security awareness training helps employees recognize its risks and learn how to safely adopt AI tools. Security teams should foster open communication with employees and try to understand why they use unsanctioned AI products.

Shadow AI now spans local models, AI coding assistants, autonomous agents, and many other asset types across your environment, making it a pervasive and complex problem.

You can reduce shadow AI incidence by enacting an AI acceptable use policy that provides clear guidelines and a list of approved AI tools, and by addressing shadow AI as part of your unified exposure management program.

It’s an ordinary workday at a typical mid-to-large enterprise, and the following is happening without the knowledge of the IT and security departments:

A marketing manager installs an unvetted, open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to secretly bridge his desktop AI assistant with the company’s internal customer database.

A sales executive downloads a free AI browser extension to summarize a web page, unknowingly granting a third party read-access to her confidential CRM dashboards.

An accounting supervisor creates custom AI chatbot skills to automate his reporting, feeding unredacted financial projections into a public generative AI tool.

An engineer bypasses software restrictions to download and run an unvetted, locally hosted AI model, creating a massive blind spot for endpoint security.

A business analyst hands over her broad administrative credentials to a consumer-grade AI agent so it can autonomously crawl the company’s private data warehouse.

A developer pastes proprietary, unreleased source code into a free, web-based AI assistant for quick debugging, inadvertently surrendering corporate IP to a public model’s training set.

Yes, we’ve come a long way from the days when instances of shadow AI consisted mostly of employees oversharing work information with their personal AI chatbot. With AI now permeating enterprises’ operations, shadow AI has spread and morphed accordingly across the attack surface. It has become riskier and harder to detect, especially as autonomous AI agents proliferate.

For example, security incidents involving organizations’ shadow AI assets have more than doubled to 43%, compared with 20% last year, according to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report.” Meanwhile, the average data breach cost of shadow AI-related incidents hit $5.39 million, about $400,000 above the global average.

IBM's report found a direct impact on data privacy, operations, and compliance:

Almost half of shadow AI security incidents resulted in data loss or data compromise

42% caused operational disruption

21% triggered regulatory fines

During a 30-day period earlier this year, the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform found 457 million security issues across 7,000 customer environments using 274 detection plugins built specifically for AI. That averaged out to about 62,000 AI-related exposures per customer.

“The enterprise AI landscape of 2026 bears little resemblance to the AI landscape of even three years ago,” the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) wrote in its April report, “The Invisible Enterprise: Shadow AI and the Ungoverned Frontier.”

Because AI adoption has “dramatically outpaced” organizations’ AI governance, many enterprises now have a dangerous “invisible layer of AI infrastructure” that hasn’t been inventoried, and thus isn’t subjected to policy enforcement, access controls, or audits, according to the CSA report.

In this third installment of Tenable’s weekly Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, we’ll unpack best practices organizations can adopt to tackle shadow AI in its multiple forms — AI code assistants, models, applications, APIs, embedded features, agents, MCP servers, training data, browser extensions, and more — and mitigate its risks, such as compliance failures, system breaches, and data leaks.

3 steps to help you mitigate the risk from shadow AI

1. Boost employee and leadership awareness and education

A logical place to start your campaign against shadow AI is by teaching employees and leaders how to recognize and prevent the issue.

Employees

Just last month, the U.K. government stressed how important it is for organizations to address the human factor in shadow AI, specifically the disconnect between employees’ fast adoption and organizations’ lag in approving AI tools and setting AI usage policies.

For example, 34% of employees polled in Thomson Reuters’ “Future of Professionals 2026” report admitted to knowingly and deliberately using AI wares their organization hasn’t approved.

Why? “They are frustrated by the quality of sanctioned tools or the lack of a clear AI strategy,” reads a Thomson Reuters article about the report, published in June.

The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends focusing on three key elements:

Understand why staffers use unapproved AI tools.

Establish a “positive cybersecurity culture” marked by open communication between employees and the security team.

Securely integrate AI systems into the workplace.

“By raising awareness of the risks of shadow AI use within your organization and understanding the needs of employees, you can help them get the benefits of new technologies while using them securely,” an NCSC cloud researcher wrote in the blog “The hidden risks of shadow AI.”

In other words, focus on employee education, not punishment, and include shadow AI in your security awareness program training.

Business unit leaders

Proactively reach out to business unit leaders to learn about the AI tools they’re using, their reasons for using them, and the benefits they yield. Engaging in this needs-assessment exercise can help you decide which AI tools to allow and which ones to prohibit.

2. Establish a clear AI governance policy

Avoid being seen as an enemy of AI adoption. Extremely restrictive approaches, such as “block by default” policies, tend to backfire because they drive employees and teams to push their AI usage further underground, especially if these tools boost their productivity.

Instead, you should adopt an AI acceptable use policy that outlines clear rules for who can use AI, which tools they can use, and what data they can input, in a way that doesn’t compromise security and compliance.

Your AI policy should also clarify levels of accountability by outlining the responsibilities of employees, managers, and the AI governance team. For example, it should stress that employees must verify the accuracy of AI-generated content, because each individual is ultimately responsible for the quality of their work.

The comprehensive policy should clearly outline AI usage guardrails, such as rules for data handling, detail the formal process and criteria that the security and IT teams will use for approving and adopting AI tools, and provide a curated list of authorized tools.

It should further help you assess whether you should outright block a discovered shadow AI tool, or whether you can allow it with the appropriate controls.

Some questions to ask:

Does the AI vendor claim ownership of what your users input into its tool?

Does the tool encrypt data in transit and at rest?

What are the vendor’s vulnerability and incident disclosure processes?

Does the product comply with regulations relevant to your organization, like HIPAA?

Does the vendor use your data to train public AI models?

In which geographic region does the vendor house your data?

Which types of industry compliance does the AI vendor adhere to?

Finally, the AI usage policy should be a living document your organization continually revises, as AI technology advances and the organization’s usage evolves.

“Leaders should focus on creating a governance framework that balances innovation with risk management, ensuring employees feel empowered to use GenAI responsibly,” reads Deloitte’s “GenAI Workforce Survey,” which was published in September. The report found that 31% of U.K. employees use AI tools without their organizations’ permission.

3. Address shadow AI as part of your broader exposure management program

With AI now pervasive across most enterprises, shadow AI is present throughout your IT environment in a wide variety of manifestations. This is precisely the type of complex and multidimensional security issue that a unified exposure management platform helps untangle.

At Tenable, we believe that trying to detect and control shadow AI as a standalone problem with isolated point tools is the wrong approach.

To successfully mitigate AI security risks, including shadow AI, you need to gather contextually rich AI security data, so you can correlate and analyze it alongside your other exposure data. That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data.

These are some key ways in which an exposure management platform can help you address shadow AI risk.

Obtain comprehensive visibility of your AI environment via a continuously updated inventory of your AI assets – what they are, who and what can access them, and which data they can access – wherever they are in your environment including in your:

Data centers

Endpoints

Web apps

Cloud workloads

Network traffic

Application development pipelines

Enterprise AI platforms

Operational technology (OT) systems

IoT infrastructure

Detect shadow AI assets’ security flaws, including vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, excessive permissions, insecure output handling, and exposed training data.

Contextually map and prioritize the security issues that require immediate attention across your entire attack surface based on factors like AI asset criticality and business impact.

Take action and automate remediation, including by leveraging agentic AI capabilities, to carry out the fixes needed to close your shadow AI exposures.

Reduce the risk of data getting shared improperly via AI prompts and uploads by:

Discovering and classifying sensitive data

Auditing AI assets’ permissions and enforcing least-privilege policies

Monitoring data flows in real time

Detecting and blocking sensitive intellectual property, proprietary source code, and customers’ personally identifiable information (PII) before exposure or compromise

Check back next week when we’ll finish our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series with a blog about the cybersecurity challenges of state and local governments. Read the first two blogs in the series:

How to mitigate the risk from AI-generated apps built by your '‘citizen coder’ employees

Critical infrastructure orgs face heightened cyber risk from nation-state groups, AI threats

To learn more about shadow AI and how Tenable can help you address this issue, check out the following resources:

What is shadow AI? (guide)

Introducing Tenable One AI Exposure: A new standard for securing AI usage at scale (blog)

Security for AI: A strategic framework for closing the AI exposure gap (blog)

Mastering AI security risks with unified exposure management (on-demand webinar)

Tenable Hexa AI: Automating exposure remediation with agentic routines (blog)

What is AI security posture management (AI-SPM)? (guide)

What is an AI acceptable use policy (AUP)? (guide)

General Security News.title: Cloud Security Maturity Lags Despite Widespread Adoption, SANS Warns
General Security News.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
General Security News.full_text:
Nearly all organizations now run production workloads in the cloud, yet only 40% consider their cloud security strategy advanced or optimized, highlighting a significant maturity gap, according to SANS.

This is according to the 2026 SANS Cloud Security Survey Insights report which surveyed 400 IT and security professionals.

SANS found that 51% of respondents were running enterprise-scale (2501 to 10,000 workloads, containers, or instances) or hyperscale (more than 10,000) environments and 73% already having a dedicated cloud security team or role.

The report also noted that 93% of organizations already run production workloads in the cloud and 65% run more than one provider.

SANS noted that because so many respondents have a dedicated team for cloud security, it indicates that a maturity gap persists despite organizations being well-resourced.

Overall, 45% of respondents described their cloud security strategy as “intermediated” with partial implementation of a defined strategy.

This partial implementation is an issue, according to the report, and leads to security incidents.

Misconfiguration Make Up Nearly Half of Critical Cloud Incidents

The report found that misconfiguration is the leading cause of critical cloud incidents (45%), close to double that of the next highest factor, credential theft, which made up 22% of incidents.

What’s more, misconfigurations often remain in place for significant periods, with around half of organizations (49%) found to need more than 24 hours to close a known critical gap.

"Misconfiguration is not an exotic attack class. It is a known gap sitting in an account somebody already owns," said Serge Borso, SANS Principal Instructor. "What makes it persist is not the attacker. It is the distance between finding the gap and fixing it, across too many consoles with nobody clearly owning the result. That is why consolidation and enforcement matter more right now than implementing yet another detection tool. The industry has finished deciding to move to the cloud and is now paying for how fast it did.”

Despite the security maturity gap, cloud security budgets were found to be increasing for most, with 28% of respondents reporting significant investment to modernize or adopt new technology such as AI or Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), and another 42% reporting incremental growth.

Overall, 70% of organizations are spending more on cloud security than a year ago. Only 7% reported budget cuts.

Just 21% of respondents said their organization runs a single consolidated CNAPP platform. Meanwhile, 31% still maintain separate point solutions across Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM). Of those surveyed, 23% are actively evaluating a move to consolidate.

The SANS data points towards three priorities for security teams in the year ahead:

Strengthen cloud security by enforcing automated policy checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines, preventing misconfigurations before deployment

Reduce security tool sprawl by consolidating posture management, workload protection and identity security tools into unified platforms

Extend zero trust beyond authentication by adopting continuous, context-based controls that limit what users and workloads can access after login

General Security News.title: Okta's Response to PHP2Shell
General Security News.context: Okta tested the publicly available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits against Okta Access Gateway in its default configuration, and none achieved code execution
General Security News.full_text:
On October 21, 2026, industry-wide third-party critical PHP pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were disclosed, both with CVSS scores of 9.2.

Okta tested the publicly available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits against Okta Access Gateway in its default configuration, and none achieved code execution.

Okta’s Response

Cloud services: Not affected. Okta and Auth0 cloud service platforms are not affected by these vulnerabilities.

On-premise software: Okta Access Gateway (OAG) requires a patch. Customers should upgrade to Okta Access Gateway version 2026.44.0.

Action for Okta Access Gateway (OAG) Customers

Customers running Okta Access Gateway appliance versions prior to 2026.44.0 should upgrade to version 2026.44.0. For complete vulnerability details and remediation guidance, refer to the Security Advisory:

PHP Runtime Vulnerabilities Affecting Okta Access Gateway CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619

Action for Auth0 and Okta SDKs users

For actions required and developer guidance, please refer to the appropriate KnowledgeBase article:

PHP Critical Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)

General Security News.title: No time to PHP around.
General Security News.context: Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.
General Security News.full_text:
Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Weak certificates from an Indian authority spark a global security scramble. Investigators probe a U.S. consulting executive’s alleged ties to ShinyHunters. SafePay ransomware hits at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations. Researchers find troubling security biases in Chinese AI-generated code. A $10 million initiative bolsters cybersecurity for small U.S. utilities. An American pleads guilty to stealing from thousands of servicemembers and veterans. Leo Scott, Managing Director of DataTribe, is talking about their upcoming Cyber Innovation Conference and the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

Today is Wednesday October 21st 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

PHP vulnerabilities put millions of web sites at risk.

PHP is a widely used, open-source programming language that powers the behind-the-scenes functionality of websites. It runs on web servers, handling tasks like processing forms, managing user accounts, interacting with databases, and generating web pages. Popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla rely on PHP. Because it’s so widely used, a serious PHP vulnerability can potentially affect millions of websites.

Now, PHP administrators are bracing for two potentially critical vulnerabilities that could put millions of websites at risk. PHP maintainers have announced plans to release patches for two flaws, each carrying a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.

The warning follows leaked, but unverified, details of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell, reportedly capable of executing code on servers running popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento.

Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.

One researcher estimates that 1.3 million internet-connected hosts may be affected.

Administrators are being urged to inventory their PHP applications, prepare backups, and arrange emergency maintenance windows. Patches are scheduled for release at 14:00 UTC, though maintainers warn they could arrive earlier if exploitation is detected.

Given PHP’s enormous footprint, the potential consequences extend across much of the web.

An Indian cert authority unlocks a global security headache.

Security teams worldwide are scrambling to contain a potentially massive Internet security problem after researchers discovered eight digital certificates with private keys so weak that attackers could use them to impersonate virtually any website.

The certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra. They’re intermediate certificates, meaning they can be used to issue other certificates that browsers and applications automatically trust.

Normally, cracking their encryption would be practically impossible. But these keys were astonishingly weak, containing as little as three to eight bits of entropy. One researcher described the situation as “bonkers.”

Major browsers and several applications have already blocked the certificates, and there’s currently no evidence they’ve been maliciously exploited. But cleaning up the broader Internet could take years.

Cryptography expert Filippo Valsorda compares the challenge to the 2014 Heartbleed vulnerability, warning that this recovery could be even more complicated. Linux systems, embedded devices, forgotten servers, and Internet of Things equipment may require individual updates.

The immediate concern involves attackers intercepting encrypted communications, particularly VPN connections. Exploitation requires positioning oneself between communicating parties, something that’s easier for attackers controlling local networks or possessing sophisticated surveillance capabilities.

Most modern browsers have implemented protections, although Microsoft’s Edge on Windows 10 reportedly remained vulnerable in some circumstances.

The incident exposes a fundamental weakness in Internet trust: even the strongest encryption depends on the security of the organizations issuing certificates.

And when one of those organizations gets the fundamentals spectacularly wrong, the cleanup becomes everybody’s problem.

Investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters.

Federal investigators examining the ShinyHunters hacking group are scrutinizing executives at two ransomware negotiation firms over their alleged relationships with the cybercriminals.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters’ extortion website, which pressured nearly 100 victims to pay ransoms.

Authorities have also arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky on extortion-related charges. Investigators reportedly uncovered communications linking him and other negotiators to ShinyHunters after Dutch police arrested a suspected group member and accessed his Signal messages.

The investigation raises troubling questions about conflicts of interest in the ransomware negotiation business. Some firms reportedly collect fees based on the size of ransom payments, creating financial incentives that may favor the criminals over their victims.

The allegations remain under investigation.

SafePay ransomware has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide.

The SafePay ransomware group has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since emerging in August 2024, according to a joint advisory from U.S., German, and British authorities.

SafePay has become one of 2026’s most active ransomware operations, targeting organizations across four continents.

The group gains access through stolen credentials, brute-force attacks, vulnerable VPNs, and exposed network devices. Once inside, attackers escalate privileges, move laterally using legitimate administrative tools, disable security software, and steal sensitive data before encrypting systems.

SafePay employs double extortion, demanding cryptocurrency payments in exchange for decryption tools and promises not to publish stolen information.

The group also reportedly calls victims directly to pressure them into paying.

Authorities are urging organizations to strengthen defenses against SafePay’s increasingly widespread operations.

New research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

The United States has banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, citing national security concerns. The Department of Homeland Security says DeepSeek’s China-based infrastructure could expose sensitive American data to Chinese authorities.

Beijing condemned the restrictions and warned of possible retaliation, adding another complication to already strained U.S.-China technology relations.

Meanwhile, new research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

Cybersecurity startup Hirundo tested Alibaba’s Qwen3-Coder and found it produced significantly more vulnerable applications for American defense contractors than Chinese ones. Seventy percent of applications generated for U.S. contractors were exploitable, compared with 59 percent for Chinese contractors.

Applications built for a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group were also more likely to leak secrets.

Hirundo says the discrepancies disappeared after researchers modified the model to remove what they characterize as Chinese Communist Party political alignment.

The findings suggest that AI coding assistants may introduce security risks influenced by their training and underlying model behavior.

A $10 million initiative looks to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute are launching a $10 million initiative to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

The new nonprofit Community Cyber Resilience Foundation will initially provide free cybersecurity technology, hardware, deployment assistance, and training to as many as 500 water, wastewater, electric, and natural gas utilities.

The announcement follows a surge in cyberattacks affecting more than 100 American water systems across over a dozen states.

Eligible utilities must have annual revenues below $100 million, a threshold covering more than 50,000 organizations nationwide.

Participants will receive access to Dragos security technology, Accenture implementation support, and SANS operational technology training.

The initiative aims to address a growing cybersecurity divide between large infrastructure operators and smaller utilities struggling with limited budgets, aging equipment, and staffing shortages.

An American pleads guilty to an identity theft scheme targeting U.S. service members.

A 45-year-old American has pleaded guilty to orchestrating an identity theft scheme that targeted thousands of U.S. servicemembers and veterans.

Robert Wayne Boling Jr. operated from the Philippines, using stolen personal information to access victims’ bank accounts and steal money and veterans’ benefits between 2014 and 2019.

Prosecutors say Boling obtained sensitive records from a former U.S. Army medical records contractor stationed in South Korea.

The operation relied on dozens of money mules in the United States who received stolen funds and transferred portions of the proceeds to the Philippines.

Boling was deported to the United States and arrested in May. Two accomplices have already been sentenced, while two others remain fugitives.

Boling faces up to 40 years in prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering.

Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

A Brazilian electronics distributor is looking for nearly half a million dollars’ worth of missing graphics cards, and it’s taking its search to Instagram.

Oderço says two pallets of high-end Nvidia RTX 5090 GPUs arrived at São Paulo’s Guarulhos International Airport, then apparently vanished.

After getting nowhere with official inquiries, the company turned to social media, saying nothing like this has happened in its 38-year history.

The missing shipment is valued at roughly $470,000, although the company hasn’t disclosed exactly how many cards disappeared, or when.

The timing is particularly unfortunate. RTX 5090s are already in short supply, with retail prices reaching thousands of dollars per card.

Whether the shipment was stolen, misplaced, or swallowed by some bureaucratic black hole remains unclear.

For now, Oderço is hoping the internet can help locate its missing hardware.

Which is perhaps fitting, considering how many people have already been searching the internet for an RTX 5090.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music and sound design by Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

General Security News.title: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI
General Security News.context: This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs
General Security News.full_text:
Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption.

In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation.

Note: As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments.

X.509 certificates for workload identity

If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes.

As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs. In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA). To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes.

Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services

Temporary access credentials

Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor.

To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session.

Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate

Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information.

Create a trust anchor.

Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload.

Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles.

Trust model

The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor. The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA.

Certificate attributes

Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation.

The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl.

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE MQswC ........... -----END CERTIFICATE---- Certificate: Data: Version: 3 (0x2) Serial Number: e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3 Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA Validity Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (384 bit) pub: 04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05: X509v3 extensions: X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical CA:FALSE X509v3 Key Usage: critical Digital Signature Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66:

IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation.

"aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA"

Note: An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere.

Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials

IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession. To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": [ "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID" ] } } } ] }

As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown in the preceding trust policy helps establish the trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and the CA in your PKI.

Plan for trust anchor placement

Depending on the CA platform, you can configure one or more intermediate certificates in your PKI certificate hierarchy, as shown in Figure 3. The certificate level the trust anchor is placed at affects which end-entity certificates IAM Roles Anywhere accepts, and therefore which workloads are authorized to assume a role. To create a trust anchor, export the certificate bundle for the issuing CA certificate from your external CA platform in PEM-encoded format and upload it to the trust anchor console.

Figure 3: Certificate hierarchy in an external PKI

See the Solution deployment section to onboard a sample solution and verify your certificate bundle.

Fine-grained access control is vital for security because it allows organizations to precisely define and restrict permissions, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. The effective permissions of the temporary security credentials are an intersection of resource-based, identity-based, and session policies as shown in Figure 4. By setting up the trust anchor and profile configuration in IAM Roles Anywhere with session policies, you can limit the permissions for each session.

Figure 4: Effective permissions of session credentials

Credential helper

To obtain temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere, use the credential helper tool. This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs. The credential helper manages the process of obtaining temporary security credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere and returns them in JSON format. The private key of the workload and its CA signed certificate are the two critical parameters provided to the credential helper tool. To use this tool, you need both an end-entity certificate and a trust anchor created in IAM Roles Anywhere. As of December 2024, the credential helper (version 1.4.0 and later) supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0.

The following is an example of how to obtain temporary security credentials:

$ ./aws_signing_helper credential-process \ --certificate /path/to/certificate \ --private-key /path/to/private-key \ --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \ --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path

When credential-process is used with AWS SDKs, the temporary credentials are stored in memory and refreshed automatically. However, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) invokes credential-process on every command. Each invocation creates a new IAM Roles Anywhere session, which adds latency to every CLI call. To avoid this delay when using the AWS CLI, we recommend using the update command, which writes refreshed credentials to a file that the CLI reads on each invocation without calling credential-process again.

When you use update, credentials are written to a credential file on disk and any user or process who can read the credential file might be able to read and use those AWS credentials, so it’s recommended to use serve unless your business has a specific use case that needs to read AWS credentials from a file. The serve command can be used to vend temporary credentials through an endpoint running on the local host using the same URIs and request headers as Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2). When using serve, no AWS configuration files are needed because the AWS SDKs can discover the server endpoint.

Just-in-time compared to short-lived certificates as workload identities

To help mitigate the risk around the exposure of your business-critical resources to compromised certificate user sessions, it’s recommended to use certificates with just-in-time credentials or short-lived access credentials. Just-in-time certificates are issued by a CA for immediate use for authentication on a system or application. The CA uses the roles and policies defined in IAM to determine when, and under what conditions, a workload can establish a session. With just-in-time access, admins don’t have to worry about revoking access if the users’ access roles change. Because the access credentials are recreated for each access request, any role changes can be applied in real time. Just-in-time access requires support from your CA, so verify compatibility with your CA before implementing it.

It’s recommended to tailor the validity periods for short-lived certificates to align with business requirements, workload lifecycle, and your organization’s risk tolerance. AWS Private CA offers a short-lived CA mode specifically designed for certificates with validity periods under 7 days. This mode is priced at $50 per month (compared to $400 per month for general-purpose CA mode), making it cost-effective for high-volume, ephemeral workload identities such as containers and serverless functions. For more information, see AWS Private Certificate Authority and How to use AWS Private CA short-lived certificate mode. See Zero trust on AWS for information about how short-lived credentials support a zero trust architecture.

Best practices for private key storage

Safeguarding private keys is of paramount importance in any environment. A private key is created by the certificate owner when requesting certificates with a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The CA providing your certificate doesn’t create or have your private key. In fact, it’s recommended that no one outside your administrators should ever be given access to this material. Guardrails should be implemented to make sure the keys aren’t stored in an online repository.

Using the credential helper with IAM Roles Anywhere, you can integrate with PKCS #11-compatible modules. For implementation details, see How to implement cryptographic modules to secure private keys used with IAM Roles Anywhere. With the credential helper (version 1.1.0 and later), IAM Roles Anywhere supports PKCS #11 integration, so you can use private keys stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-based secure stores and avoid storing them to disk. Additionally, as of December 2024, the credential helper supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, enabling private keys to be generated inside the TPM and marked as non-exportable. With TPM-backed keys, the private keys can’t be extracted even if the workload host is compromised. This is the strongest private key protection available for on-premises and hybrid workloads using IAM Roles Anywhere.

If your organization doesn’t implement PKCS #11–compatible modules, IAM Roles Anywhere supports credential helper version 1.0.5 for X.509 certificates and private keys stored in macOS and Windows certificate stores. This delegates the signing operations to keys stored within those OS-specific certificate stores. In Windows, both CryptoAPI and Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) are supported; in macOS, Keychain is supported. In these environments, the private key will never be directly readable, and the signing operation would be delegated to the secure store instead, which will improve security posture of your environment. If you have multiple certificates, then use the --cert-selector flag of the credential helper tool to search for a specific certificate (and associated private key) through the certificate subject, issuer, and serial number. The corresponding keys are x509Subject, x509Issuer, and x509Serial, respectively. These keys can be specified either through a JSON file format or through the command line. The following is an example of both approaches:

If you want to use a JSON file, it should be similar to this:

[ { "Key": "x509Subject", "Value": "CN=Subject" }, { "Key": "x509Issuer", "Value": "CN=Issuer" }, { "Key": "x509Serial", "Value": "15D19632234BF759A32802C0DA88F9E8AFC8702D" } ]

If the preceding example is placed in a file called selector.json, it can be specified with the --cert-selector flag through file://path/to/selector.json.

The same certificate selector argument can be specified through the command line as shown in the following:

--cert-selector Key=x509Subject, Value=CN=Subject Key=x509Issuer, Value=CN=Issuer Key=x509Serial, Value=15D19632

Monitoring trust anchor certificates

Monitoring certificate expiry in PKI is crucial for maintaining secure communication, because expired certificates can lead to authentication failures, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized access. Compliance and regulatory requirements often mandate timely renewal of certificates, making monitoring certificate expiry essential to avoid legal penalties and maintain organizational integrity.

Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can receive notifications for CA certificate expiry and end-entity certificate expiry. IAM Roles Anywhere can send metrics, events, and notifications through multiple notification channels as shown in the following table:

Event

Channel

Threshold

Enabled

CA certificate expiry

CloudWatch, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Health

45 days before expiry

TRUE

End-entity certificate expiry

EventBridge and AWS Health

45 days before expiry

TRUE

The preceding notifications thresholds are default settings, which you can customize using the steps in Customize notification settings in IAM Roles Anywhere.

Best practices for trust anchor certificate rotation

Consider rotating your certificates using blue/green deployments to seamlessly roll out new certificates without affecting service availability. Use automation to integrate certificate rotation testing in your blue/green deployment pipeline. See the sample AWS CloudFormation template in the Solution deployment section to build your automation pipeline.

As shown in Figure 5, two trust anchors have been created; one for each environment. Using this approach, you can test the certificate rotation process in a controlled staging environment before applying it to the production environment, thus reducing the risk of certificate-related outages.

Figure 5: Trust anchor certificate rotation in blue/green deployment

Solution deployment

The sample solution template is available in the IAM Roles Anywhere — External PKI Integration repository on GitHub. It contains the following main steps:

Creates a distinct IAM role with policies scoped to the resources that workload requires.

Assigns a trust relationship to a IAM Roles Anywhere principal.

Creates a trust anchor using a certificate bundle from an external CA.

Creates a profile with the required IAM Roles.

Parameters for this deployment are shown in the following table:

Parameter

Required

Default

Description

TrustAnchorCertificateBody

—

PEM-encoded X.509 certificate of your CA (includes BEGIN and END markers)

WorkloadSubjectCN

No

WorkloadA

Subject CN from the workload certificate, used in trust policy conditions

WorkloadIssuerCN

No

MyCompany CA

Issuer CN from the CA certificate, used in trust policy conditions

WorkloadSANCN

No

WorkloadA

SAN CN from the workload certificate, provides additional identity assertion

SessionDurationSeconds

NotificationEmail

(empty)

Email address for certificate expiry notifications. When provided, creates an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic and an EventBridge rule

Important: The SessionDurationSeconds value must not exceed the IAM role’s MaxSessionDuration setting, which defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you request a longer session than the role allows, the CreateSession API returns an error. The companion template keeps both values in sync by setting the role’s MaxSessionDuration to the same parameter value. If you configure the role separately, update its MaxSessionDuration to match your desired session length. For more information, see IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API.

If the workload’s subject CN (WorkloadSubjectCN) doesn’t match the x509Subject CN of the authenticating certificate, the CreateSession call is denied. The same conditional verification applies to WorkloadIssuerCN and WorkloadSANCN.

The template enforces three certificate attribute conditions in the IAM trust policy: issuer CN, subject CN, and SAN CN must all match the values configured as parameters. Additionally, the trust policy scopes role assumption to the specific trust anchor Amazon Resource Name (ARN), preventing other trust anchors in the same account from assuming that role.

Conclusion

In this post, we discussed how AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, empowered by X.509 certificates, introduces a dynamic and secure way to manage workload identities and issue temporary access credentials. By understanding the trust model, using certificate attributes, and implementing fine-grained authorization, organizations can gain granular control over the effective permissions of these credentials.

The choice between just-in-time and short-lived certificates as workload identities depends on your specific requirements.

Adhering to best practices for private key storage is essential to maintain the integrity of your security infrastructure. Regularly rotating trust anchor certificates helps ensure the long-term trustworthiness of your system.

As you embark on your journey to implement IAM Roles Anywhere and integrate it with your PKI, remember that a well-architected approach to certificate management is a cornerstone of robust and resilient cloud security.

For additional deployment guidance, see Planning for your IAM Roles Anywhere deployment, which covers end-to-end deployment planning including network architecture, monitoring, and operational considerations.

If you have questions, you can start a new thread on AWS re:Post or reach out to AWS Support.
