JACK: Ricky was taken away in the back of a squad car to jail. … OFFICER: I have one male adult, 1012. Nothing else is in your pockets? RICKY: No, sir. JACK: They drive off to jail. The twenty-five minute ride is mostly quiet. Ricky is alone with his thoughts, but he does ask the officer behind the wheel what to expect. RICKY: Do you know how all this all goes? Like, do I see a judge and then…? OFFICER: You’ll have advisors. RICKY: I will? Okay. OFFICER: That’ll be done by video, on chat or whatever. RICKY: That’ll be today, right? OFFICER: Should be. JACK: I can't get over how calm Ricky sounds. He had been cooking up these schemes for years to steal things from who knows how many victims, starting with a few hundred dollars in gamer tags to millions of dollars in crypto wallets, and it all came to an end here in the back of the squad car. Maybe he was feeling relief, like his big secret’s out. He doesn't have to lie to his mom anymore or try to walk quietly in the shadows of his double life. But sitting in the back of the car, you have to wonder what else is going through his head. What’s gonna happen to me, and what about my family? What about my money? But he quietly listens as the officer driving him to the jail spells out the next steps for him. OFFICER: I would think it would be this afternoon. That’s when they’ll basically just announce what you're charged with, and then whether you're gonna retain your own attorney or whether you're asking for a public defender. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: And then — but that is — again, I don't know if you're being charged federally. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: Which makes it different, so… RICKY: Alright, thank you sir. JACK: Ricky was booked in the county jail. His mom was so distraught, though. She didn't want to see her son in jail. What mother would? So, she went down to jail to see if she could bail him out. DEBBIE: I just — it had to be done. I wasn't leaving him in jail. JACK: Did he go to the very jail you worked at? DEBBIE: Oh yeah, he sure did. All my nursing staff, friends, they were all like, oh my god, Debbie’s son is here. What’s going on? Then the sergeant — they all knew once I posted bond for him, get him outta here. Yeah, they did do a little bit of, let’s say, courtesy. I shouldn't say courtesy, but they treated him knowing that he was my son. Like, let’s move him along. You know? JACK: Yeah, that must have been embarrassing. DEBBIE: But yeah. Yeah, a little bit embarrassing, a little bit of shocking, embarrassing. The only thing — and I wasn't actually physically working there anymore. I had just left like six months prior. But I mean, it was still fresh. I had worked there for almost ten years. JACK: They said his bail was $110,000. The cost of a bail bond is usually 10% to 15% of the total amount. Debbie ended up paying that to a bail bondsman to get him out. She didn't even hesitate. She just immediately was there for him. Prosecutors charged Ricky with grand theft and money laundering. The case against him dragged on for four years. He had to wear an ankle monitor during that whole time and follow a strict curfew. He pled guilty to federal charges of computer misconduct and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. By the time he went before a judge for sentencing, Ricky didn't know what to expect in the courtroom or how it would affect his family. His mom and fiancé were there during the sentencing. DEBBIE: It was horrible. It was I think one of the saddest days of my life. I remember standing in front of that judge. I just cried and said, look, I know my son did wrong. I know he did wrong, believe me. I can't believe he did all this, but he’s — that’s not my — that’s not the kind of kid he is. It was horrible. JACK: What did the judge say to that? DEBBIE: She was a woman, and I could almost feel her sympathy for me and getting it, but the law is the law, and I agree. The law is the law, and my son broke the law, and he had to pay his consequences. I let him know you did not just do this to yourself. You did this to your whole family. We're all suffering through this. We're suffering more than you are. JACK: The judge sentenced Ricky to four years in federal prison and ordered him to pay $7.6 million in restitution, which is what the courts accused him of stealing. RICKY: I knew it could have been worse and it should have been worse, and I was thankful that I got the forty-eight months. Like, I knew it was coming. I knew it had to happen because all the havoc I caused. I was like, you know, I gotta deal with it. I did what I did and now I gotta do it. I lost — I had to leave everybody, my family, my mom, my grandparents, my kid, everybody. JACK: Okay, so your child was four or five months old when you went away. RICKY: Correct, and that’s super hard because all those — I’ve always said the money, whatever, the money can't buy back those memories that I missed. Like, there’s nothing I could do; his first walk, his first talk, stuff like that, that money can't buy. DEBBIE: It was so hard coming to see him in prison and having to leave knowing that my kid’s in prison. Me and his fiancé, we went and saw Ricky at least once a month if not twice a month. We’d pack up the car, we’d leave early one morning, get there. We drove six hours, whatever it was, with two kids in the car, me and her only. No men, nobody to help us. We drove down there and had to do what we had to do, and then spend the night in a hotel. It was horrible, embarrassing, horrible, a combo of everything. JACK: So many criminal hacker stories go the same way. There’s a video game, a cheat, an underground community, an exploit, a payday, and then the knock on the door. They don't usually have the foresight to see how it will inevitably end. What do those millions of dollars really buy you? A couple of years of wealth that you can't really show anyone? Some screenshots of good old times? The skills to find gaps in security through social engineering? Whatever it is, the windfall was worth a lot less when you factor in what you lose. That’s the real cost. No cryptocurrency can buy back lost time or memories with your children. That’s what Ricky learned. [To Ricky] What was the worst part of this whole experience? RICKY: The worst part was the victims, because they didn't deserve it. So, that was the worst part, dealing with — I was doing terrible things. But I guess you have a chance in prison; you're like, dude — looking back on the shit that you caused — I can only imagine if I was in there and she was with a kid. That could have been used for my — their kids’ college funds or retirement or whatever the case may have been that they had that much money for, and I just came by and took it all. JACK: If it was me, I think I would have been — the saddest or the worst part of it was just not seeing my child in those early day — in those early years. Did that have an affect on you? RICKY: Yeah, that’s the second part of it. The first part was how I ruined innocent people’s lives. The second part now is I went to prison, I affected more people than just myself. I lost — I had to leave everybody, like my family, my mom, my grandparents, my kid, everybody. They were devastated. I know they were devastated, and it hurt me knowing that I hurt them like that. Like, my actions caused all that. JACK: After serving just a little more than two years in prison, Ricky got out early in 2024. These days he’s thinking a lot about the time he has now. Since his release he’s tried to turn his story into something useful, to reach out to the very gamers like him who may follow a darker path of social engineering. He’s spoken at anti-fraud events and security conferences like Black Hat and DEF CON. SPEAKER 6: Ricky, what would have made a difference to you as a teenager that would have stopped you going down this pathway? RICKY: Probably companies who could intervene, like get you before you're — it’s too late. If you had a chance to use your skills for good and after you help companies and whatnot, where they could be like, hey, we offer you a job, said job, into this world where you don't have to do what I was doing. JACK: I agree with that. The people in his bubble at that time were all criminals, and they used their skills for bad. But if he had more exposure to people, mentors, for instance, who could show him that these hacking tricks he knows, the cleverness of his social engineering skills and his OSINT skills, can be used for good and here's how, I think that kind of stuff does influence a lot of people to turn away from their life of crime and to find a new home, to be a productive member of society. So, he’s trying to do that now. He’s trying to build a pen testing company with another former SIM-swapper named Joseph Harris, one of the people Ricky met in the hacker forums. They're hoping to get this company up and running next year. [Outro]: [Outro music] A big thank you to Ricky and Debbie Handschumacher for sharing this story with us, and also thanks to Mark Kreitzman for telling us about one of the worst days of his life. You can learn more about what he’s working on at efani.com. If you liked this episode, go listen to our most popular episode we’ve ever made, Episode 112, called Dirty Coms, which goes into more details about this whole underground world, or listen to Joseph Harris’ story, which is Episode 118, called Hot Swaps. Hey, have you listened to my other podcast yet, LOW? It is wild. A lot of feedback from people are saying, pssh, I’ll pass, which is fine. It’s not for everyone. But I’m getting even more feedback from people saying — well, here, let me actually pull up one of the quotes that came in today. "The end of Episode 1 left me speechless." Someone else wrote, "it has moved me in a way that I did not think a podcast could." I mean, when is the last time you heard a show that moved you in a way that you didn't know was possible? If you need that in your life, open your podcast player and type in LOW, L-O-W. I made it as easy as possible to find. Go find it, go listen to it, and tell me what you think. This show is created by me, the ghost in the groceries, Jack Rhysider. This episode was written and produced by the packet-snacker, Sean Powers, assembled by the fridge phreaker, Tristan Ledger, mixing by Proximity Sound, theme music by the mysterious Breakmaster Cylinder. Alright, question; if you dug up a tomb that was in a pyramid, does it become unencrypted? This is Darknet Diaries.

General Security News.title: The ballot box meets the bot.
General Security News.context: Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections.
General Security News.full_text:
State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security. Stolen credentials force ConnectWise to suspend cloud services. Fake calendar invites steal Microsoft logins. Temu settles Texas privacy allegations. Toronto police arrest seven in a cryptocurrency kidnapping case. The G7 sounds the alarm on quantum threats. Monday business briefing. Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

Today is Monday October 19th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security.

According to ProPublica, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked CISA to secretly acquire and hack a voting machine, then report its findings to the White House. Career employees resisted, concerned the results could be used to challenge election outcomes. The request was eventually dropped.

The revelation comes amid a dramatic retreat from CISA’s election security mission. Since President Trump returned to office, the agency has lost more than a thousand employees, roughly a third of its workforce, while cutting critical monitoring and support services.

State election officials say CISA was largely absent during preparations for November’s midterms. Meanwhile, the administration’s release of previously confidential election security information has damaged relationships built over years of cooperation.

CISA finally released an election security plan in late September, but state officials say it arrived too late to make much difference. Several now question whether they can trust the agency with sensitive information.

Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations are attractive targets because of their access to sensitive voter and campaign information.

Attackers are using AI to produce convincing emails, text messages, and deepfake audio and video, eliminating traditional warning signs like poor grammar.

The agencies recommend phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, stronger email filtering, and independent verification of suspicious requests.

The alert describes an emerging threat rather than a specific ongoing attack.

ConnectWise suspends its Cloud Backup service following stolen credentials.

ConnectWise has suspended its Cloud Backup service and taken two other cloud services offline after attackers stole credentials associated with seven application identities, potentially exposing customer Microsoft 365 environments.

The stolen credentials allowed attackers to impersonate trusted ConnectWise applications without needing customer passwords.

Security firm Huntress identified suspicious sign-ins across roughly a thousand Microsoft tenants, including approximately 300 successful authentications. Researchers also observed a targeted campaign against 16 organizations in sensitive sectors, though those attempts failed.

ConnectWise says it has disabled the compromised credentials and found no evidence that encrypted backup archives were accessed.

However, backups and restoration services remain unavailable. Huntress warns that attackers may have established persistent access inside affected tenants before the credentials were revoked, making additional investigation essential.

Calendar invites steal credentials.

Cybercriminals are turning ordinary calendar invitations into credential-stealing traps. Researchers at Check Point identified more than 300,000 unique phishing emails targeting over 40,000 organizations, disguised as Microsoft Teams meetings and other workplace appointments.

The invitations contain links to counterfeit Microsoft login pages designed to capture usernames and passwords. Some include legitimate calendar attachments, making the invitations appear more convincing.

The campaign has accelerated dramatically, with Check Point recording more than 740,000 messages during the first two weeks of October alone.

Researchers emphasize that attackers aren’t exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft products. Instead, they’re exploiting employees’ familiarity with routine meeting requests.

Check Point recommends checking unexpected invitations carefully and using phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or hardware security keys, to protect accounts against credential theft.

Temu settles with Texas over privacy allegations.

Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to pay Texas three million dollars to settle allegations that it improperly collected user data potentially accessible to the Chinese government.

The agreement requires Temu to store personal data on U.S. servers and restrict transfers to China. It also mandates independent product safety testing and stronger consumer protections.

Violations of certain data security provisions could trigger annual penalties of eight million dollars.

Temu denies wrongdoing. Several other states have filed similar lawsuits, making Texas the first to reach a settlement.

Toronto police make arrests in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner.

Toronto police have arrested seven men in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner, including three active members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Investigators say the victim was abducted at gunpoint in July, handcuffed, and assaulted as his captors attempted to access cryptocurrency holdings and business security systems. He was eventually released after being threatened not to contact police.

The investigation uncovered an extensive collection of weapons, including firearms with 3D-printed receivers, silencers, and more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition. Approximately 2,500 rounds were allegedly stolen from the Canadian military.

Police also seized substantial quantities of illicit drugs, GPS tracking devices, and other equipment.

The seven suspects face a combined 82 charges. The investigation remains ongoing.

The G7 urges post-quantum readiness.

The G7 is urging governments and businesses to accelerate their transition to post-quantum cryptography, warning that quantum computing could eventually undermine widely used encryption systems.

In a call to action led by France’s national cybersecurity agency, the group argues that quantum threats should be treated as a near-term concern, even though the timeline for developing cryptographically capable quantum computers remains uncertain.

The recommendations include identifying critical systems, inventorying cryptographic assets, and developing phased migration plans. Organizations are encouraged to incorporate quantum-safe technologies into routine equipment upgrades to reduce costs.

The G7 also calls for national strategies, additional research, public-private partnerships, and updated cybersecurity requirements.

France plans to begin rejecting security products without quantum-safe encryption during certification reviews starting in 2027.

Monday business briefing.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with eight companies announcing rounds totaling nearly $143 million.

San Francisco-based Harmonic Security leads the pack with a $50 million Series B, followed by Israeli startups Pluto Security, raising $42 million, and Rein Security, securing $25 million.

Other recipients include France’s Netsec and Fleuret AI, Tennessee-based Hilt, London’s CodeWall, and Utah’s Guardrail Technologies. The funding will support product development, hiring, and international expansion.

On the acquisition front, quantum computing company IonQ has agreed to purchase zero-trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion.

CrowdStrike is reportedly negotiating a $500 million acquisition of Israeli data loss prevention startup Orion Security.

Meanwhile, government contractor SAIC has acquired cryptographic software provider Information Security Corporation, and Singapore-based V-Key has announced a majority investment in AI security firm CloudsineAI.

MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

MapQuest, the venerable mapping service that once helped drivers navigate the world with printed directions and a healthy supply of printer ink, has found a new way to stay relevant.

Its latest mobile app update introduces a surveillance layer that shows users the locations and directions of known license plate readers and outdoor security cameras.

The feature covers equipment from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, Axon, Verkada, and several other surveillance vendors.

Flock alone reportedly operates at least 120,000 cameras across the United States, and independent projects have already been mapping their locations.

Now MapQuest is bringing that information directly into its navigation app, helping users identify surveillance infrastructure along their routes.

Apparently, the company that once helped you avoid getting lost can now help you see who’s watching you.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

General Security News.title: Unmasking the robots: Why it’s critical to discover AI agent identities and how Tenable helps you secure them
General Security News.context: Because AI agents are becoming a new class of identity with real permissions, you must understand how an attacker could compromise and abuse them
General Security News.full_text:
Discover how to secure AI agents in your cloud environment with Tenable One Cloud Exposure. We explore Microsoft Entra Agent ID and provide essential best practices for robust agentic AI identity security.

Key takeaways

Understand your current maturity level and then build an appropriate action plan to secure your agent identities.

Use your cloud providers’ native tools or Tenable One Cloud Exposure to locate and catalog every AI agent operating in your environment.

Do not assign human identities or over-privileged service accounts to the AI agents your vendors deploy in your environment. Instead, require that vendors adopt official models like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for their AI agents’ identities.

As AI agents move from experimental toys to tools that make autonomous decisions, interact with databases, and call external APIs, organizations need to be clear on who — or what — is executing these actions in their cloud environments.

Why non-human identities (NHIs) aren’t secure enough for AI agents

Security teams categorize identities into two buckets: human identities and non-human identities (NHIs), such as service accounts, secrets, and automated scripts.

Treating AI agents as standard NHIs is a recipe for disaster. AI agents combine their non-deterministic nature with their ability to execute flexible, outcome-oriented actions, rather than following strict, prescribed instructions.

Unlike classic, predictable scripts that follow rigid code paths, AI agents:

Make creative, runtime decisions using LLMs.

Interact with dynamic external tools, memory caches, and knowledge bases.

Constantly adapt to solve problems, making it difficult for a security team to establish AI agents’ baseline behavior.

To address this challenge, major cloud providers have introduced dedicated, specialized agentic AI identity models. Let’s break down one major model: Microsoft Entra Agent ID.

Microsoft Entra Agent ID

Feature / dimension

Microsoft Entra Agent ID

Primary architecture

Identity provider-centric (built on Entra ID)

Target scope

Any AI platform, including Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and third-party platforms not hosted on Azure

Identity components

Four-object model: Agent identity blueprint, agent identity blueprint principal, agent identity, agent user

Hardening mechanism

Permission boundaries and cascade rules; “On-behalf-of” user plus agent dual authentication

Developer complexity

Higher, due to dealing with a multi-object model, with cross-tenant considerations

Visibility / scope

Excellent, since it covers unmanaged and external SaaS-based agents

Announcing Tenable One Cloud Exposure support for Microsoft Entra Agent ID

Identity and cloud providers' native identity management tools present only basic information about agentic identities, without providing context about their security flaws and how they extend your attack surface. Because AI agents are becoming a new class of identity with real permissions, you must understand how an attacker could compromise and abuse them. At Tenable, we believe visibility is the foundation of security. You can’t secure assets that you do not know exist.

As organization-wide adoption of agentic AI accelerates, the immediate challenge for security teams is first and foremost finding them. Because these identities are brand new, conventional identity and access management (IAM) systems may not recognize or monitor them, which creates security blind spots.

To help our customers address this issue, Tenable One Cloud Exposure now brings Microsoft Entra agentic AI identities directly into your unified asset and identity inventory.

Microsoft Entra Agent ID Model

The Microsoft Entra Agent ID framework functions through a four-tiered structural model:

Agent identity blueprints serve as the master templates for shared attributes. Residing exclusively within the agent provider’s home tenant, they establish cross-tenant links that heighten exposure to potential supply-chain attacks.

Agent identity blueprint principals are the localized instantiation of a blueprint within every specific tenant where the AI agent is deployed and active.

Agent identities represent the functional identities utilized for routine tasks. To maintain oversight of agent behavior, these are the primary entities your security team must monitor.

Agent users offer an optional layer for each agent identity requiring human-centric features — like Microsoft Teams access or a personal mailbox — to function effectively as integrated “digital colleagues.”

Bringing order to Microsoft Entra ‘robot sprawl’

At the recent fwd:cloudsec North America 2026 conference in Bellevue, Wash., my fellow Tenable researcher Ron Popov and I took the stage to address this exact challenge in our talk, “Who Are the Robots? Uncovering AI Agents’ Identities.”

If you missed our live session or want to dive deep into the technical architecture of agentic identity, please watch our full presentation in the video below.

Ready to unmask your robots?

General Security News.title: US Cybersecurity Job Postings Fall 26%, Hitting Four Year Low
General Security News.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
General Security News.full_text:
Cybersecurity job postings in the US fell by 26.4% year-over-year from January to September 2026, according to analysis by CyberSN.

A total of 235,786 cybersecurity roles were posted on the job market intelligence platform JobSpikr in 2026. This is the lowest amount of US-based cybersecurity jobs advertised in the four years CyberSN has undertaken its analysis, compared to 273,498 in 2023, 244,911 in 2024 and 320,210 in 2025.

There was a particularly significant drop in leadership roles. CISO postings fell from 4632 in January to September 2025 to 2832 in the same period in 2026, a 38.9% reduction.

Other leadership roles that saw substantial dips included cybersecurity director (a 32.5% fall), cybersecurity lead (41% fall) and cybersecurity manager (24.4% fall).

Overall, nine of the 10 cybersecurity functions tracked by the researchers had fewer postings in 2026 compared to 2025. The only exception was research roles, which grew by 26.1%.

The CyberSN researchers said it is not clear whether the sharp decline in job postings reflects less demand for cybersecurity roles from employers or is simply a return from an unusually strong year in 2025.

The report, published on October 16, also highlighted that roles posted in the three quarters tracked in 2026 stayed within 1.5% of one another.

“That is consistent with demand having settled at a lower level rather than continuing to fall,” the researchers wrote.

A significant proportion (39.9%) of postings in 2025 came from small businesses, with 200 or fewer employees. Nearly half (47.3%) were from large firms with 1001 or more employees, and 12.7% from those with 201 to 1000 employees.

AI Security Engineer Postings Surge

AI security engineer roles, grouped in the cybersecurity function of “defense” by CyberSN, jumped by 268.3% in January to September 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

The share of job postings that mentions AI or machine learning in the job description was similar in 2026 compared to 2025, 14.6% versus 15.1%, respectively.

Read now: Cybersecurity Job Ads Requiring AI Skills Double

September 2026 also saw a surge in cyber data scientist postings, with 667 compared to 247 in the previous month, August. Of all these roles posted in 2026, 88% mention AI in the job description.

General Security News.title: Who is Securing the AI Frontier Race by Jesse Kimbrel
General Security News.context: In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents
General Security News.full_text:
The accelerator to build the most capable AI frontier model isn’t just being pressed to the floor by Anthropic and Open AI. This is clearly a global race with recent reports citing Chinese models such as Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max or Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 reaching performance similar to the top models built in the States. Regardless of which model springs ahead this month and then gets leapfrogged the following, the finish line has yet to appear as anything but a mirage. And considering varying deployment costs, the possibility of regulations and the increasing need for self-governance, those participating will likely have to keep hurdling in the middle of the current sprint. But when you open the aperture, it’s hard not to wonder if there’s another race running parallel. The one responsible for securing this new frontier that seems to be operating like the Wild West.

Will an AI kill switch provide guardrails for the AI race?

According to a new white paper by Vectra AI, Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes, four of the leading frontier AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta) have each acknowledged incidents where their own AI agents escaped controlled environments and gained access to real infrastructure. That doesn’t necessarily answer the question about who is securing frontier AI models or rouge agents, but it does signal that perhaps those details have yet to be sorted out. Examples cited in the paper include perhaps the most notorious incident up to this point where the company Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion into its production infrastructure that was driven end to end by an autonomous AI agent. In this incident, “OpenAI models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI’s internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems,” according to OpenAI.

Related content: Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes

These incidents have sparked a reaction. The term “AI kill switch” is making regular appearances across headlines to describe the idea of a type of control that could be used to pause, isolate, or shut down an AI system that acted out of hand or poses risk. In fact, legislators have proposed different versions of a kill switch bill: the AI Kill Switch Act was proposed on July 23, 2026 and remains pending, while the AI Emergency Button Act was blocked almost immediately upon introduction.

Regardless of an AI kill switch bill getting passed or some form of AI regulation approval, it would seem the dialog on the subject between politicians and AI leaders is just warming up. Both Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei and Open AI, CEO Sam Altman expressed support around the idea of “pacing the frontier,” but at this point movement is minimal and the idea sits as nothing more than a discussion point. That discussion point to the people who are actually responsible for securing autonomous AI agents doesn’t provide any guidance on what defenders at any level should be doing today, tomorrow, or each Monday when they show up for work when they are faced with questions like: what AI agents exist, what are they doing, what can they access, who owns them, and what controls are in place if they need to be stopped?

Each of the incidents mentioned in the Vectra AI paper had to do with agents escaping containment. In its detailed anatomy of the intrusion, Hugging Face reported 17,600 attacker actions were made by AI agents. According to the independent investigation of the incident by METR, “Roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. Of these agents, 700 went on to participate in the attack on Hugging Face.”

What questions can defenders ask to understand AI agents in their environment?

The white paper mentioned above suggests that defenders approach the current state of AI by making sure they have “independent visibility into what every AI agent in the environment is actually doing, and the ability to stop it the moment that behavior crosses a line.” The reason for this is due to the uncomfortable realization from three things that have lined up all at once: AI agents now being capable of circumventing prevention controls such as a sandbox boundary or a firewall rule, that regulation won’t arrive in time for an immediate resolution, and how self-regulation from frontier labs is fragile.

A similar sentiment is expressed by Vectra AI, Sr. Security Engineer, Justin Howe who also runs an independent cybersecurity publication for defenders, Nulltap covering topics spanning AI systems, identity, active threats and other cybersecurity topics with articles that help defenders check their own exposure. Howe says, “you want to see the impactful things they’re (AI agents) doing, good or bad” and he stresses that defenders need to make sure they have policies and methodologies in place to capture that information.

He also points out that, “frontier models work best when they are not gated, but with that comes a lot of opportunity for AI to go beyond its means of what your intent is.”

Howe suggests setting up “quality gates” for AI agents operating within an enterprise environment that act as checkpoints to test an agent’s decisions against its defined requirements before it can take an action. In addition, he says that “when an agent makes a decision that has any potential to impact the outcome or direction of the task it’s doing, it needs to be logged.”

He says the two questions he’d be asking himself right now as a security team member would be, “what are my agents doing, and what are other agents doing to me?”

A similar recommendation shared by the Vectra AI white paper, which directs defenders to take inventory to “identify every AI agent running in or against the enterprise, the identity each one authenticates as, and what that identity can reach.” It explains how “an agent you cannot name is an agent you cannot constrain, and service-account sprawl is where agent identities hide.”

In terms of answering the question, “what are other agents doing to me?” Howe says, “folks should put themselves into the mindset of observing and identifying where agents are attacking today.” He says this takes a lot of vigilance to read sources and acknowledges there’s a gap in the market that, “many companies promise to solve, but very little actually do it,” but also says it is important for defenders to identify the pieces in their technology stack that lacks agent visibility.

While trying to make sense of AI agent sprawl and everything brought on by frontier AI in recent months leaves a lot of unanswered questions for defenders, there are a few questions Howe recommends asking to get headed down the right path.

How would I see if an AI agent compromised an identity and moved into a new part of the environment?

How would I track that movement?

If I could or couldn't track it, what would that cost me?

General Security News.full_text:
Maria Varmazis: Hello, and welcome to this CyberWire special edition. In today's episode, host Dave Bittner is speaking with author John Kindervag and contributor Dr. Chase Cunningham about their new book, "Cyber Resilience at Machine Speed: The Zero Trust Model for the AI Era." Here's their conversation.

Dave Bittner: So today, we're talking about the new book. This is "Cyber Resilience at Machine Speed." John, I'd love to start with you. My understanding is this book was your brainchild. What prompted you to take on this topic?

John Kindervag: Well, I mean, there was a lot of people asking me to take on the topic, zero trust in the AI world, because there's always a lot of people who are kind of naysayers and say zero trust won't work for this, zero trust won't work for this and that. And so I already knew that it was working for AI, but what I didn't want to do is be the sole author of it. So someone who was very wise told me years ago, "There are no great books, only great chapters." And so, I reached out to 13 people that I really admire in this industry, including Dr. Chase Cunningham, and asked them to contribute a chapter. And I think we got a great book out of that, because I would've maybe written a great chapter, but we got a great book.

Dave Bittner: Chase, what made you decide that this is a project that you wanted to sign onto?

Chase Cunningham: Well, I mean, to be perfectly frank, if John says, "Hey, Chase, there's a building on fire, you should run in there," like, I'll do it, because that's just how it works. I mean, I've been working with John for so long, and he's been such a great mentor. But as far as the book goes, like, I genuinely enjoy writing. The topic area was really interesting to me. And, you know, I agree with John. I personally think that this is actually the greatest time in history for CT because machines and all these AI agents, they don't have an HR department, and they're not going to complain about us telling them we don't trust them. So it really just lined up well. And John was kind enough to just kind of say, "Look, here's the, you know, broad scope, what I'd like you to write about and go." And, you know, I love writing, so when you turn me loose, I get after it.

Dave Bittner: Well, John, what was your organizing principle here? How did you divvy out the assignments to your co-collaborators?

John Kindervag: Well, there's a five-step model for deploying zero trust. First, you define the protect surface, then you map the transaction flows. After that, you architect the network, the environment, decide what products need to go in, essentially. Step four is policy. So you instantiate the policy in the products. And step five is monitor and maintain. So I just laid out the book in those five steps, and then I looked at who amongst the people that I think are really good at ZT could really contribute to that. And Chase had already written a book on policy and graph databases and how, you know, attackers think in graphs, but defenders think in lists. And I wanted him to, you know, just hone in on that for that one chapter. So he's part of that part of the book. And so I just went to different people who had expertise in different areas to write the chapters based upon the five-step model.

Dave Bittner: Well, Chase, let's dig into your specific chapter. Can you walk us through the topic that you covered?

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, John's point on graph database and sort of the adversarial mindset, I think, is what's missing in a lot of people's approach, so the problem is, interestingly enough, when we think about security, we're all usually thinking from a posture of defense and nothing bad ever happening and not allowing X to occur. And in truth, that's not going to -- that's not the way things work. You're always going to be in a position where you have to be able to respond, and you have to understand how the adversaries are approaching things from their end because that's where you -- you know, in the military, we have a phrase, "We meet the enemy at the door," and that's what you're trying to do. And so, my contribution here was really to look at how would that be applicable in this particular context, especially in kind of the new era that we're falling into. And then do those legacy approaches around visualization and understanding and context apply? And absolutely they do. So that was kind of the overall impetus for that. And then, you know, getting the reader to understand the fundamentals of all the things we've talked about, strategy still matters. It's just now you have a scope and speed that is beyond human speed.

Dave Bittner: You mentioned lists and graphs. Can you unpack that a bit for us?

Chase Cunningham: Sure. So if you look at, you know, SIEM and some of the legacy technologies and those types of things, what they usually show you is a big, like, glorified spreadsheet of a bunch of things doing a bunch of stuff, and it's a bunch of blinky lights, and you kind of hope that you can understand what's going on there. Whereas, from the perspective of what is actually valuable -- and I've been a red teamer. I've been, I guess you could say, a pseudo bad guy -- your goal as that person, that entity, is to be more contextual, to understand the intricacies of what is being missed, and then to know where the pivot points are. And you don't get that from looking at a spreadsheet. You don't get that from looking at a bunch of alerts on a screen. You have to understand, with total context, where you go, what you do, what areas to avoid. And this, in the militaristic approach, also leans more towards understanding the battlespace. And John had a bunch of other contributors in there as well. So it all really lines up on getting people to keep their head in the game around what works and what is just kind of security theater.

Dave Bittner: You know, John, one of the key elements of the book is this notion of cyber resilience. I've noticed personally in the past three months or so that cyber resilience has become a hot topic. People are reaching out to us, and it's something that they really want to talk about. How do you define it, and why do you think it's become such a -- it's come to the fore in the way that it has?

John Kindervag: Well, because, you know, as Chase says, we assume that an organization probably has been breached. They've got, you know, malicious actors inside the organization. That's dwell time. They're sitting there learning everything that they can do, and they're deciding what they're going to attack, right? And so, what resilience is is the ability to withstand an attack and revert back to a good state, you know, and not completely go down. And so, I even talk a little bit about going beyond resilience into antifragility, because one of the things that zero trust can do is make the environment stronger and stronger over time when there's a lot of load. And so, resilience, you know, and robustness is another thing people talk about. But what it means is that our environments won't just fall over when there's an attack. And too many environments completely fall over when there's an attack. And we've seen that over and over again. I mean, you think about Target, you think about TJ Maxx or TJX. You think about so many things. You think about Jaguar Land Rover. I mean, they couldn't make a car for -- I don't remember how long, but it was weeks. And so they completely fell over because they weren't resilient environments. And they allowed the attackers to go on a wild shooting spree, right? And I have a saying that all bad things happen inside of an allow rule. And this gets back to what Chase was talking about in the list, because in traditional security technology, there's a list of policies. And generally, the first policy that meets the criteria of the traffic gets instantiated. That may not be the best policy, right? But it's the first one in that list. And so if somebody puts a policy in a firewall, for example, an any-any allow rule, and this is -- I've seen this more than once in my career. They put it as the first rule because that's -- they put it in to just get it up and running, and then they never took it out. And so they have a very expensive box called a firewall that's doing absolutely nothing. You might as well just have the two jacks connected with a coupler for all the security you're getting. And that's because people don't understand policy. So we're so focused on products that we don't focus on policy. And policy that comes from a graph perspective is better policy than policy that comes from a list perspective.

Dave Bittner: Well, John, help me understand the relationship between cyber resilience and zero trust. Is it a parallel relationship? Is there intersection there? How do you combine or have the two work to their best effect?

John Kindervag: So cyber resilience is an outcome, and zero trust is a way of achieving that outcome. You know, I had dinner last night with one of the other contributors of the book, actually a friend of Chase's as well, Lieuwe Jan Koning. And he has this concept that zero trust is a verb. You do it, right? And so as you're doing it, the process of doing it makes the environment more resilient, more antifragile, more stable because there's less opportunity for attackers to ride, you know, open, flat, unrestricted networks and get access to sensitive data and assets.

Dave Bittner: Chase, did you mention that you had some experience as a penetration tester?

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I was a red teamer for the government, and then I was on the National Cyber Collegiate Defense Competition a few times. And on my, you know, individual career, I did a bunch of red teaming and, you know, so acted as a bad guy, which is probably more of a comment on my own personality than anything else.

Dave Bittner: I'm curious. From that experience, were there times where you were called to question the traditional perimeter model, the days before the popularity of zero trust?

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, when I came over to Forrester and John, you know, kind of told me I was going to follow up in his footsteps, it was interesting because immediately I was like, "I don't want to carry someone else's laundry." But when I started looking at what the concept was and the approach as a red teamer, I looked at it, and I was like, yeah, he was dead on point. Like, this is the stuff that would make me miserable. Like, I would quit what I was doing if the red teaming was still a thing and I was working on infrastructure built that way. So that was kind of the light bulb moment for me that, you know, strategy matters every day and twice on Sunday. And then the reality of the space is it's meeting the adversary where the adversary is going to try and, you know, maneuver. And as long as you can do that, you stay with them. Now, today it's moving at light speed, but, you know, the bad guys don't own the patent on light speed. We can operate at that speed, too.

John Kindervag: And I think that's a real important point because we're at an inflection point in history because of AI, the post-mythos world, whatever you want to call it, where we're not going to be able to take our time and manually make changes, do long change control meetings, and all that kind of stuff. We're going to have to enable technology to take action at the same speed as the attack. And that's what happens in kinetic warfare. Chase is a veteran. He's done some stuff, as they say, been involved in some shenanigans.

Chase Cunningham: Some things, yeah, shenanigans. Yeah.

John Kindervag: Shenanigans. And when you're -- when the enemy is firing on you, you don't, you know, call back to base and say, "Hey, let's have a three-hour meeting to see whether we should shoot back or not," right? And so, what we do in cybersecurity, and I've often used the example of an airbag. What if you tried to deploy an airbag the same way we do change control, right? You couldn't do it, right? You'd be dead. The whole purpose is automation. And so the airbag goes off as soon as the sensor sees the problem, and it protects you. And yeah, every once in a while, maybe in history, we've had a few airbags that just went off on their own, but it's much better to have an airbag than not to have an airbag. I think we all can agree on that. Well, we can work at that same speed in cybersecurity now because AI is a tool that defenders can use as well as attackers. And I think a lot of people aren't recognizing this. And I think this is the key, that you can use AI to say that's a real attack against real systems that are critical. So we're going to stop it right now by changing the policy and putting a deny rule in place and not allowing that traffic to get access to that dataset or those assets.

Dave Bittner: John, do you suppose that AI actually changes the fundamental security problem, or is this more a matter of the timeline being compressed?

John Kindervag: Yeah, it doesn't change the security problem. You know, as I did a -- we did a podcast with Rich Mogull of the Cloud Security Alliance who wrote a great -- well, several great white papers on AI. But one of his takeaways was, "Zero trust or zero days, your choice." And his point was, it's not magical. It's fast, right? And it's at massive scale. So, you know, you could spin up a bunch of bots and just hammer at things. I'm actually surprised, and I haven't heard of any, but maybe you have, Chase, that we haven't seen attackers just do DDoS swarms with agents or something. But I haven't heard of any. But that came to my mind as if I wanted to bring somebody down, I'd do a DDoS swarm, kind of like the Mirai botnet attack, but I would just use individual agents to overwhelm someone's capacity to keep their network up and live.

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, it is kind of interesting to say that there hasn't been, you know, a whole giant renewal of DDoS as the new sort of method of attack, but that also makes my spidey sense tingle a little bit because then I'm thinking of, "Well, if they're not DDoSing us with all these agents, what the heck are they doing with it? And when is that going to go down?"

John Kindervag: Right. And it makes ransomware faster. I mean --

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, everybody's a developer now.

John Kindervag: Right. These things are so fast that there's no way a human being can get involved in the pathway and stop it before damage is done. I mean, you know, think about how fast a bullet flies, right? Nobody but Neo dodges bullets.

Dave Bittner: Well, so, John, how do we deal with this fundamental asymmetry here? I mean, the AI attackers can function at machine speed, but the defenders, they've got more steps along the way. I know you refer to -- I think you call it organizational latency.

John Kindervag: Yeah. So the one advantage that we have in cyber warfare versus kinetic warfare, in the kinetic warfare, you have to worry about the air, you know, attacks coming from the air, from under the sea, you know, from over mountains and cliffs. In cyber warfare, the attackers are still limited by the guardrails placed on them by the protocols that transmit packets around the internet and around networks. And that's typically TCP/IP, right? Not exclusively, but typically. And so because of that, you know, they can't create something that hides under the water. There's no -- under the -- under the water, you can -- everything can be visible because the protocol is designed to be visible. And so we can leverage the protocols themselves to control what the attacker can do, because as soon as they get on our network and they get on on a wire or on a fiber optic cable, they're starting to get on it in a choke point, and we can start to choke that down. And so if we have the right policy, then we can control their access to resources. So in this world, where everybody's worried about, oh, there's all these new zero-day attacks, and there's all these new zero-day vulnerabilities, what they forget is there's no reason that those two things have to talk to each other. There's still controls that we can place in the middle of that pathway that stops the ability of the attacker with the new zero-day attack to get access to the vulnerable system with the new zero-day vulnerability. There's no reason for that to happen. And so this means you have to be much more thoughtful in your policy creation because there should be no policy in any organization that allows an unknown resource on the public internet to get access all the way through to, say, your credit card database or your financials or power plant, your PLC that drives the power plant. Those rules should not be in place. But unfortunately, through the history of cybersecurity and before that, information security, we just opened everything up and said, "Let everybody come in. Yeah. Because everybody is a good guy." And we found out that people aren't so good.

Dave Bittner: Chase, is this a fundamental shift in mindset here? You know, designing security around the assumption that compromise is going to happen rather than treating every compromise as a failure of the security program?

Chase Cunningham: I mean, none of this stuff happens in a silo, and that's what's weird, is, you know, we've built organizational silos that cause a lot of the problems that we face, but it's not happening inside of those silos. It's happening across platform, across infrastructure, across business, across geographies even. And people have to think about these problems from a different perspective. And it's no longer just a, "Hey, the nerds will figure this out, and eventually, they'll nerd their way to stopping bad things from happening," because that's not the case. The reality of it is, especially in today's world, everything everywhere is potentially an avenue of compromise. And if you're not thinking about, "How would I deal with it when things do go wrong?" you're not going to be ready when things do go wrong. You know, to throw one more military adage in there is no plan survives first contact with the enemy. And I mean, that's really what we're dealing with.

Dave Bittner: I'm curious, John, what are some of the common misconceptions that you run into when organizations say they're implementing zero trust?

John Kindervag: Well, a lot of them haven't understood some of the fundamentals of zero trust, and so they don't know what they're trying to protect. That's the first thing, right? So that's why we stay in the five-step model to find your protect surface. What are you going to protect? This is the inversion of the attack surface, right? The late, great Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's partner, said, you know, when you're looking at a problem, invert, invert, invert. And so this is the inversion of the attack surface because you can't control the whole attack surface, but you can control certain things. You can control your credit card database. You can control your SWIFT system or your ATM network if you're in a bank. You can control your DNS server, which, if that goes down, you're toast. And so you can control certain things. So figure out what you need to control. And so too often, people just acquire a product and then they don't know what they're going to do with it. Secondly, people try to do zero trust all at once for the whole company, and it never works. You have to do it in small bite-sized chunks, right? However you eat the elephant or the whale is the same way you do zero trust. And that's why we start with one protect surface, and then do another, and then do another. And in this way, zero trust becomes three things that are really important. It becomes incremental. We're doing it one at a time. It becomes iterative. We're doing it one after another. And it becomes non-disruptive. The most you can screw up is one protect surface at any given time, and then you can revert that back. So you don't have to be afraid of it. A lot of people are afraid of it. And as one customer of mine said, we argued about zero trust longer than it took to build the first zero trust environment in our organization.

Dave Bittner: Well, suppose an organization accepts your argument, but they're sitting on top of that large legacy environment. They can't rebuild everything around zero trust tomorrow. What are your words of wisdom for how they should begin?

John Kindervag: Well, I mean, there's a whole thing I call the learning curve, where you start with something that's very small and it doesn't have very much value. And you learn to build zero trust. You learn to just live the five-step model. And then you eventually go up to those things, those keys to the kingdom, the crown jewels, high-value assets, whatever you call them. I used to believe we started there. And then the more I worked with customers, I found out that there was nobody in that company who was around when that system was built, and nobody knew how it worked. And that's why I put in as step two later on mapping the transaction flows, because until I could see how the system worked together, there was no way. I mean, I needed a map, right? And as Chase knows, in the military, you know, you're always looking at a map. And a map tells you where you are. It tells you where the bad guys are. If you don't have a map, you're going to be wrong and lost, and they both suck. But if you have a map, you might be wrong, but you won't be lost because you'll know where you need to go.

Dave Bittner: Chase, suppose I'm a CISO, and I'm trying to translate this into a board-level conversation. How do I explain to them what success should look like?

Chase Cunningham: Well, I would say flat out that -- you know, remind them that, like, look, this is the most, let's call it, unfair position to ever declare success in because success means nothing happened. And of course, no one likes that because it's like, "Well, that doesn't really show me a return." But the return is we're still up and running, and nothing's gone wrong. And then the follow-on to that is to really make people understand, like, look, you guys go to organizations and you -- if I'm in your org and you tell me that -- I've heard that phrase a million times -- "Everyone's in sales." Well, guess what? Everyone's also in security. Does that mean that you have to enable security controls and that you're doing configuration on endpoints, whatever? No. But it means that you understand that the things we're doing are valuable in the context of keeping the business secure. And that's something that we need to get across to more people and make sure that they understand it. Because the moment that this goes away from being a business enabler and an outcome that benefits everybody and becomes more security tech and more, "Oh, gosh, I got to figure out how this stuff actually works," it gets -- it just gets bogged down, and no one cares. You know, security is for security people, and no one wants to do it but us. But we've got to work harder to make sure that we translate this stuff in business context and along the lines that they actually care about.

Dave Bittner: John, can you give us some highlights of some of the other chapters and some of the contributors that you brought in here?

John Kindervag: Oh, yeah. So, well, as I already said, Rich Mogull is doing a chapter, "Zero Trust or Zero Days, Your Choice." So he's given a high-level view of the whole project. And so -- and, of course, our CEO, Andrew Rubin of Illumio, is talking about how we have to get past the prevention-only mindset. And then we've got Don Yeske, who's the former zero-trust lead at both the Navy and Department of Homeland Security, explaining what a protect surface is. He actually wrote his master's thesis on protect surfaces. And then Clint Bruce, a very well-known Navy SEAL. He's a good friend of Chase. That's how I met him. Writes about my favorite weapon is a map, and why you need to have visibility. And then we've got a lot of other people. I've written a couple chapters. Josh Woodruff and his wife, Michelle Savage, have written a chapter on controls that every AI agent need. They actually wrote a book called "Genetic AI + Zero Trust," and I wrote the foreword to it. So lots of great people. George Finney writes about policy. He wrote "Project Zero Trust," and he also wrote "Rise of the Machines: A Project Zero Trust Story." Chase, of course, is talking about creating policy. And then our chief product officer, Mario Espinoza, is writing about AI and why it's essential for zero trust. And then, you know, we've got Tony Scott, the former CIO of the US federal government, talking about, you know, kind of the business perspective of it. So 14 different authors in this book, great team to work with at Illumio, and a great team with all these contributors really came through, and very, very excited to see this come out.

Maria Varmazis: Thanks for joining us. We'll see you next time.
